inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged vertigo without hearing loss, distinguishing it from labyrinthitis.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Which of the following is a common complication of ototoxicity?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Ototoxicity typically leads to high-frequency hearing loss, affecting outer hair cells first.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: How does labyrinthitis differ from vestibular neuritis in terms of clinical presentation?

options.text: Labyrinthitis involves hearing loss, vestibular neuritis does not
Labyrinthitis is bilateral, vestibular neuritis is unilateral
Labyrinthitis has a longer duration of vertigo
Labyrinthitis is caused by ototoxic drugs

inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Labyrinthitis presents with both vertigo and hearing loss, while vestibular neuritis spares hearing.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: How does the mechanism of hearing loss in Ménière disease relate to inner ear disorders?

options.text: It results from cochlear nerve damage
It is due to endolymphatic hydrops affecting hair cells
It is caused by ototoxic medications
It is related to temporal bone fractures

inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Ménière disease involves endolymphatic hydrops leading to hair cell damage and fluctuating hearing loss.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Which condition shares a similar pathophysiological mechanism with vestibular neuritis?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Post-viral vestibular dysfunction is similar to vestibular neuritis as both can follow viral infections and present with vertigo.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Regarding vertigo ± hearing loss — which is correct?

options.text: Acute vertigo lasting days with hearing loss is vestibular neuritis
Vestibular neuritis spares hearing; vertigo WITH hearing loss is labyrinthitis (or a central cause)

inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Vestibular neuritis affects only the vestibular nerve (no cochlear symptoms), whereas labyrinthitis involves the whole labyrinth and adds SNHL — the presence of hearing loss separates them.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brief positional vertigo + fatigable nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Brief positional vertigo + fatigable nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike → Posterior-canal BPPV.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness → Ménière (endolymphatic hydrops).

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Inner Ear Disorders & Temporal Bone”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the parotid and temporal regions aids in grasping ear disorders.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: A patient with a pituitary macroadenoma is most likely to show which visual field defect?

options.text: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: A pituitary tumor compresses the optic chiasm, damaging the crossing nasal fibers and producing a bitemporal (heteronymous) hemianopia.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: What type of visual field defect is most commonly associated with a pituitary tumor?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia occurs due to compression of the optic chiasm, which is often caused by pituitary tumors.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Which visual field defect is characterized by a 'pie in the sky' appearance?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Superior quadrantanopia, or 'pie in the sky', results from lesions affecting the temporal lobe's optic radiation (Meyer’s loop).

visual-pathway-fields.stem: A patient presents with a right homonymous hemianopia. Where is the likely location of the lesion?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: A right homonymous hemianopia indicates a lesion in the left occipital lobe, affecting the visual field from the right side.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Which mechanism explains the presence of macular sparing in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia?

options.text: Dual blood supply to the occipital pole

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Macular sparing occurs due to the dual blood supply from the MCA and PCA to the occipital pole.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: A patient has a bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: It is caused by a lesion in the optic nerve.
It localizes to the optic chiasm.
It is always associated with macular sparing.

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia specifically indicates a lesion at the optic chiasm, affecting the crossing nasal fibers.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: In the context of diabetic retinopathy, which visual pathway defect might be observed?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy can lead to monocular field loss due to optic nerve damage or retinal issues.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: How might optic nerve disorders affect visual field defects in a patient with a history of optic neuritis?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Optic neuritis typically results in monocular field loss, often accompanied by a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Regarding bitemporal vs homonymous — which is correct?

options.text: Any hemianopia points to an occipital stroke
Bitemporal (heteronymous) hemianopia localizes to the optic chiasm; a homonymous hemianopia is retrochiasmal

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Only a chiasmal lesion splits the two temporal (crossing nasal) fibers to give a bitemporal pattern; any lesion behind the chiasm produces a same-sided (homonymous) defect in both eyes.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bitemporal hemianopia”?
What best explains the finding: “Congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing”?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing → Occipital (PCA) lesion.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Which should you review before “Visual Pathway & Field Defects”?

options.text: Outbreak Investigation: Steps, Epidemic Curve & the Box Jellyfish Case

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Basic understanding of investigation steps may aid in clinical context.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: A 68-year-old with hypertension has sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in one eye. Fundus shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot. The diagnosis is:
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Sudden painless monocular loss with a pale retina and cherry-red spot is central retinal artery occlusion — a retinal stroke requiring urgent management and vascular workup.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What is the most characteristic fundoscopic finding in central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)?

options.text: Pale retina with a cherry-red spot

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRAO is characterized by a pale retina with a cherry-red spot due to the intact choroidal circulation.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Which of the following is a common risk factor for central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Hyperlipidemia is a recognized risk factor for CRVO, along with hypertension and diabetes.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What is the primary mechanism leading to visual loss in CRAO?

options.text: Retinal ischemia due to arterial occlusion

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRAO causes retinal ischemia due to occlusion of the central retinal artery.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: A patient presents with sudden painless monocular vision loss and a cherry-red spot on fundoscopic examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: The presentation is classic for CRAO, characterized by sudden painless vision loss and a cherry-red spot.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates CRAO from optic neuritis?

options.text: Both conditions present with painful vision loss.
CRAO is associated with a cherry-red spot, while optic neuritis is not.
CRAO typically occurs in younger patients than optic neuritis.
Optic neuritis is caused by emboli.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRAO is characterized by a cherry-red spot, while optic neuritis presents with pain and is often seen in younger patients.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: How does central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) typically appear on fundoscopic examination?

options.text: Diffuse retinal hemorrhages and dilated veins

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRVO is characterized by a 'blood-and-thunder' appearance with diffuse retinal hemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: In patients with diabetic retinopathy, what is a potential complication that can also occur in CRVO?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Neovascularization can occur in both diabetic retinopathy and CRVO due to retinal ischemia.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Which condition shares similar risk factors with CRAO and is also relevant when assessing visual loss?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRVO shares similar risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes with CRAO, making it relevant in the assessment of visual loss.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Regarding painless vs painful acute visual loss — which is correct?

options.text: Sudden monocular visual loss needs urgent steroids for optic neuritis
Painless sudden loss with a cherry-red spot is CRAO (a retinal stroke); optic neuritis is painful and occurs in young women

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRAO/CRVO are painless vascular events; optic neuritis and acute angle-closure glaucoma are painful — the pain history and fundus findings separate vascular from inflammatory causes.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale retina with a cherry-red spot + RAPD”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Pale retina with a cherry-red spot + RAPD → CRAO (inner-retinal infarction).

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diffuse retinal hemorrhages + dilated tortuous veins”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Diffuse retinal hemorrhages + dilated tortuous veins → CRVO (“blood-and-thunder” fundus).

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Which should you review before “Retinal Vascular Occlusions”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Understanding ocular anatomy is essential for grasping retinal vascular occlusions.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: A long-standing diabetic develops new vessels on the optic disc and a vitreous hemorrhage. Beyond glycemic control, the key retinal treatment is:
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Neovascularization defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy; panretinal photocoagulation (with anti-VEGF) ablates ischemic retina and reduces the VEGF drive, treating the new vessels and their complications.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What is the primary cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Macular edema is the leading cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy, as it directly affects central vision.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Microaneurysms are a hallmark of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What is the mechanism by which ischemia leads to neovascularization in diabetic retinopathy?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Ischemia leads to increased VEGF production, which drives neovascularization.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: Which treatment is most appropriate for a patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Intravitreal anti-VEGF is a key treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: In age-related macular degeneration, which of the following is a common symptom associated with wet AMD?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Central scotoma is a common symptom in wet AMD due to choroidal neovascularization.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: How does diabetic retinopathy relate to retinal vascular occlusions?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy and retinal vascular occlusions both involve microvascular damage.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What is a common clinical finding in both diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve disorders?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Central scotoma can be a finding in both diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve disorders due to macular involvement.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: Regarding cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy — which is correct?

options.text: Vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is mainly from the new vessels themselves
Diabetic macular edema is the leading cause of vision loss; neovascularization causes loss via hemorrhage, traction, and neovascular glaucoma

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Macular edema directly blurs central vision, while PDR threatens sight through its complications — both are treated, but the mechanisms of vision loss differ.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central scotoma + metamorphopsia (Amsler grid)”?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Central scotoma + metamorphopsia (Amsler grid) → Macular (AMD) involvement.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates”?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates → NPDR microvascular damage.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: A 2-year-old is brought in because a photograph showed a white reflex in one eye instead of red. The most important diagnosis to exclude is:
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child must prompt urgent evaluation to exclude retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood (RB1, 13q14).

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children, typically presenting before the age of 5.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with hereditary retinoblastoma?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: The RB1 gene mutation is associated with hereditary retinoblastoma, located on chromosome 13q14.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: A premature infant develops abnormal retinal neovascularization. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity occurs in premature infants and is characterized by abnormal retinal neovascularization.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What is the primary treatment for advanced retinoblastoma?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Enucleation is indicated for advanced retinoblastoma when the tumor is not amenable to other treatments.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: A child presents with leukocoria and strabismus. What is the most critical next step?

options.text: Schedule an eye exam in 6 months
Order a CT scan of the head

pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: A fundus examination is critical to rule out retinoblastoma, which is a life-threatening condition.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What is the most likely cause of painful red eye and hypopyon after ocular surgery?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Endophthalmitis is characterized by painful red eye and hypopyon, especially following surgery.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: How does retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) primarily develop?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: ROP primarily develops due to abnormal retinal neovascularization related to oxygen exposure in premature infants.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: A child with leukocoria is suspected to have retinoblastoma. Which of the following conditions must be urgently ruled out?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Leukocoria can be caused by several conditions, but retinoblastoma is life-threatening and must be ruled out urgently.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: How is diabetic retinopathy related to retinopathy of prematurity?

options.text: Both are caused by genetic mutations

pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Both diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity involve abnormal retinal neovascularization, though their causes differ.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: Regarding leukocoria in a young child — which is correct?

options.text: A white pupil in a child is usually a congenital cataract to be scheduled electively
Leukocoria must be worked up urgently — retinoblastoma (a life-threatening malignancy) is the key diagnosis to exclude

pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Although cataract, ROP and others cause leukocoria, retinoblastoma is a childhood cancer that can be fatal if missed — any white pupil warrants prompt fundus examination.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What best explains the finding: “Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child”?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child → Retinoblastoma / ROP / other.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful red eye + hypopyon after surgery/trauma”?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Painful red eye + hypopyon after surgery/trauma → Endophthalmitis.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: A 30-year-old woman has subacute loss of vision in one eye with pain on eye movement, an RAPD, and reduced color vision. The most likely diagnosis is:
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Painful (worse on eye movement) subacute monocular loss with an RAPD and color desaturation in a young woman is optic neuritis, strongly associated with demyelination/MS.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What is the most common cause of bilateral disc swelling in a young obese woman?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Papilledema is commonly seen in young obese women due to idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH).

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Which clinical finding is characteristic of optic neuritis?

options.text: RAPD and pain on eye movement

optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Optic neuritis typically presents with relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) and pain on eye movement.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What is the immediate treatment for arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Intravenous steroids are required urgently to prevent vision loss in arteritic AION due to giant cell arteritis.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Which of the following is a classic symptom of acute angle-closure glaucoma?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with a mid-dilated fixed pupil and is associated with severe pain.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: In a patient with sudden painless visual loss and a swollen disc, what should be prioritized?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Checking ESR/CRP is crucial to rule out arteritic AION, which requires immediate treatment.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: How does increased intracranial pressure lead to papilledema?

options.text: Increased blood flow to the optic nerve
Increased fluid in the optic nerve sheath

optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Increased intracranial pressure causes fluid accumulation in the optic nerve sheath, leading to disc swelling.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Which condition is characterized by both retinal vascular occlusion and disc edema?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy can lead to retinal vascular occlusions and is associated with disc edema.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What common mechanism links papilledema and retinal vascular occlusions?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Both conditions can arise from increased intracranial pressure affecting the optic nerve and retinal vasculature.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Regarding painful visual loss with a swollen disc — which is correct?

options.text: An older patient with sudden painless visual loss and a swollen disc just needs blood-pressure control
Check ESR/CRP — arteritic AION from giant cell arteritis needs immediate steroids to protect the fellow eye

optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Non-arteritic AION relates to vascular risk factors, but arteritic AION (GCA) can rapidly blind the other eye; the inflammatory markers (and jaw claudication, scalp tenderness) mandate urgent steroids.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What best explains the finding: “RAPD + pain on eye movement + red desaturation”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: RAPD + pain on eye movement + red desaturation → Optic neuritis.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bilateral disc swelling + headache + CN VI palsy”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Bilateral disc swelling + headache + CN VI palsy → Raised ICP → papilledema.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Which should you review before “Optic Nerve Disorders & Disc Edema”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Understanding edema mechanisms is crucial for optic nerve disc edema.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Twelve hours after a cardiac arrest, cortical neurons show shrinkage, nuclear pyknosis, and bright cytoplasmic eosinophilia. These “red neurons” indicate:
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Red neurons — eosinophilic, shrunken, pyknotic cells appearing 6–12 h after irreversible injury — are the earliest morphologic marker of acute hypoxic-ischemic neuronal necrosis.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What is the earliest histological marker of neuronal necrosis following acute hypoxia?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Red neurons appear 6–12 hours after irreversible injury and indicate acute hypoxic-ischemic necrosis.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Which process describes the degeneration of an axon distal to the site of injury?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Wallerian degeneration is the term for the degeneration of the axon distal to the injury site.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What histological change is characterized by hypertrophic astrocytes expressing GFAP?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Gliosis, marked by GFAP-positive hypertrophic astrocytes, is a non-specific marker of CNS injury.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What is the mechanism behind the formation of Rosenthal fibers?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Rosenthal fibers are associated with chronic gliosis and pilocytic astrocytoma.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Which of the following is a common misconception regarding CNS injury healing?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: The CNS heals by gliosis, not by fibroblastic scarring, which is a feature of peripheral tissue healing.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: In the context of traumatic brain injury, which cell type is primarily responsible for the inflammatory response?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS and play a key role in the inflammatory response to injury.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: How does gliosis differ from healing in peripheral tissues after injury?

options.text: It leads to scar tissue formation

cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Gliosis involves astrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, unlike the fibroblastic scarring seen in peripheral tissues.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Regarding marker of cns injury — which is correct?

options.text: A fibroblastic/collagen scar forms after CNS injury as in other tissues
The CNS heals by gliosis (reactive astrocytosis), not by fibroblastic scarring

cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Astrocytes, expressing GFAP, hypertrophy and proliferate to form the glial scar — gliosis is the universal histologic footprint of CNS injury, unlike the collagenous scars of peripheral tissues.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Eosinophilic shrunken neurons (“red neurons”)”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Eosinophilic shrunken neurons (“red neurons”) → Acute hypoxic-ischemic necrosis.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFAP-positive hypertrophic astrocytes (gliosis)”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: GFAP-positive hypertrophic astrocytes (gliosis) → Non-specific marker of CNS injury.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Cellular Reactions to Injury”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Understanding neuronal and glial structures is essential for grasping CNS cellular reactions.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: A person falls backward and strikes the occiput. Besides bruising at the impact site, injury is found in the frontal and temporal poles. This anterior damage is called:
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Damage opposite the impact site, as the brain rebounds against the skull, is a contrecoup contusion — classically at the frontal/temporal poles after an occipital blow.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What is the primary mechanism of injury in a concussion?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: A concussion is primarily caused by force that leads to a transient, reversible alteration in neurological function without structural damage.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of a coup contusion?

options.text: Focal deficit opposite the impact site
Focal deficit matching a contused gyral crest

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: A coup contusion occurs at the site of impact, leading to focal deficits that correspond to the contused area of the brain.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates concussion from contusion?

options.text: Contusion is always associated with loss of consciousness

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Concussion is characterized by transient neurological dysfunction without structural lesions, while contusions involve visible parenchymal damage.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What is the most likely neurological finding in a patient with a spinal cord injury at the cervical level?

options.text: Bilateral upper and lower limb weakness
Focal sensory loss in one limb

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Injuries at the cervical level can lead to quadriplegia, affecting both upper and lower limbs.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What is the hallmark pathology of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: CTE is characterized by the presence of tau tangles and brain atrophy, particularly in the frontal and temporal lobes.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: How does the brain's energy metabolism relate to traumatic brain injury?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Traumatic brain injury can lead to altered mitochondrial function, affecting energy metabolism and recovery processes.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Which psychological response is commonly observed following traumatic brain injury?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Acute stress disorder is a common psychological response following trauma, including traumatic brain injuries.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Regarding concussion vs contusion — which is correct?

options.text: Any post-traumatic loss of consciousness means structural brain damage
Concussion is a transient, reversible functional disturbance with no structural lesion; a contusion is a visible parenchymal bruise

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Concussion produces temporary neurologic dysfunction that recovers fully, whereas a contusion is direct tissue injury (coup/contrecoup) seen on imaging/pathology.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transient loss of consciousness with full recovery”?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Transient loss of consciousness with full recovery → Concussion.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sensorimotor level on the trunk after spinal trauma”?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Sensorimotor level on the trunk after spinal trauma → Cord injury at that segment.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Which should you review before “Traumatic Brain & Spinal Injury”?

options.text: Trauma, Acute Stress, PTSD & Psychological First Aid

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Psychological effects of trauma are closely related to brain injury outcomes.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: A patient with a large hemispheric mass develops a fixed, dilated right pupil and left-sided weakness with declining consciousness. This indicates:
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: An ipsilateral blown pupil (CN III compression) with contralateral hemiparesis and depressed consciousness is classic uncal (transtentorial) herniation — a neurosurgical emergency.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What is the primary consequence of added volume in the rigid skull?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Added volume in the skull leads to increased intracranial pressure, which can result in various neurological symptoms.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Which type of cerebral edema is characterized by breakdown of the blood-brain barrier?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Vasogenic edema occurs due to blood-brain barrier breakdown, leading to extracellular fluid accumulation.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What clinical finding is associated with uncal herniation?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Uncal herniation typically presents with ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis due to compression of CN III and the cerebral peduncle.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What is the Cushing response indicative of in a patient with raised ICP?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: The Cushing response is characterized by hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration as a compensatory mechanism to maintain cerebral perfusion.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Which of the following statements about cerebral edema is true?

options.text: All cerebral edema is due to blood-brain barrier leakage

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Vasogenic edema is characterized by extracellular fluid accumulation due to blood-brain barrier breakdown, while cytotoxic edema is intracellular.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: In a patient with tonsillar herniation, which vital center is most likely compromised?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Tonsillar herniation compresses the brainstem, particularly affecting the respiratory center, which can lead to respiratory failure.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: How does vasogenic edema differ from cytotoxic edema in terms of treatment response?

options.text: Only cytotoxic edema responds to steroids
Only vasogenic edema responds to steroids

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Vasogenic edema responds to steroids due to its nature of extracellular fluid accumulation, while cytotoxic edema does not respond to steroids.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Which type of herniation is most likely to cause ipsilateral CN III palsy?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Uncal herniation compresses the oculomotor nerve (CN III), leading to ipsilateral pupil dilation and other neurological deficits.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Regarding vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema — which is correct?

options.text: All cerebral edema comes from blood-brain-barrier leakage
Vasogenic edema is extracellular (BBB breakdown, tumor/inflammation); cytotoxic edema is intracellular (cell-membrane failure in ischemia)
Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: The two mechanisms differ in compartment and cause — vasogenic responds to steroids (tumor edema), whereas cytotoxic (ischemic) edema does not.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + contralateral hemiparesis”?

options.text: Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + contralateral hemiparesis → Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle).

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing”?

options.text: Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing → Cushing response to raised ICP.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Which should you review before “Raised ICP, Edema & Herniation”?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Understanding edema types is crucial for grasping raised ICP.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: A young man is struck in the temple, briefly loses consciousness, wakes and talks, then rapidly deteriorates. CT shows a biconvex hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines. The diagnosis is:
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: A lucid interval after temporal trauma with a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection that respects suture lines is an epidural hematoma from middle meningeal artery rupture — a neurosurgical emergency.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: What is the most common vessel involved in an epidural hematoma?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: The middle meningeal artery is the vessel most commonly ruptured in epidural hematomas, typically due to temporal bone fractures.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Which CT finding is characteristic of a subdural hematoma?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: A subdural hematoma appears as a crescent-shaped collection on CT, crossing suture lines but not the midline.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: A patient presents with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurological decline after a head injury. What is the likely diagnosis?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: The classic presentation of an epidural hematoma includes a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: In which scenario is a subdural hematoma most likely to occur?

options.text: In a young athlete after a concussion
In an elderly patient with brain atrophy
After a skull fracture in a child

epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Subdural hematomas are more common in the elderly due to brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes between epidural and subdural hematomas?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Subdural hematomas are crescent-shaped and can cross suture lines, while epidural hematomas are biconvex and do not cross sutures.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: How does an epidural hematoma typically present on CT imaging?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: An epidural hematoma appears as a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection on CT, which does not cross suture lines.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: How might an epidural hematoma lead to herniation?

options.text: By creating mass effect and raising ICP

epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Epidural hematomas create mass effect, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and potential herniation.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: In a patient with a subdural hematoma, which other condition should be considered due to its potential overlap?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Epidural hematomas can present similarly to subdural hematomas, especially in cases of head trauma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Which complication of a subdural hematoma may relate to the management of raised ICP?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Herniation is a serious complication of raised ICP, which can occur due to mass effect from a subdural hematoma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Regarding distinguishing extra-axial bleeds — which is correct?

options.text: A crescent-shaped bleed that crosses a suture line is an epidural hematoma
A crescent collection crossing suture lines (but not the midline) is a SUBDURAL; epidurals are biconvex and stop at sutures

epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: The epidural is bound by dural attachments at sutures (biconvex), while the subdural spreads in the subdural space across sutures but is halted by midline dural reflections (crescent).

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lucid interval then rapid decline after temporal trauma”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Lucid interval then rapid decline after temporal trauma → Arterial epidural hematoma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gradual confusion/headache in an elderly or alcoholic patient”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Gradual confusion/headache in an elderly or alcoholic patient → Chronic subdural (bridging-vein) hematoma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Which should you review before “Epidural & Subdural Hematoma”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the meninges is crucial for grasping hematoma formation.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: A 50-year-old suddenly collapses with the “worst headache of my life” and neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. The most likely cause is:
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: A thunderclap “worst headache of life” with subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns is a subarachnoid hemorrhage, most often from a ruptured berry aneurysm at the Circle of Willis.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysms are the most common cause of SAH, particularly at the Circle of Willis.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with berry aneurysms?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, particularly type IV, is associated with the development of berry aneurysms due to connective tissue abnormalities.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden onset of a severe headache and confusion. A CT scan shows a lobar hemorrhage. What is the most likely underlying cause?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Lobar hemorrhages in elderly patients are typically due to cerebral amyloid angiopathy, rather than hypertensive bleeds which are deep.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What mechanism primarily leads to intraparenchymal hemorrhage in hypertensive patients?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage is often due to the rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms affecting small penetrating arteries.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with seizures and a 'tangle of wormlike vessels' on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: The description of 'tangle of wormlike vessels' is characteristic of an arteriovenous malformation (AVM).

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: In a patient with a history of chronic hypertension, which location is most likely for an intraparenchymal hemorrhage?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Hypertensive hemorrhages typically occur in deep structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: How does cerebral amyloid angiopathy differ from hypertensive hemorrhage in terms of bleeding location?

options.text: Hypertensive causes deep, amyloid causes lobar
Amyloid causes deep, hypertensive causes lobar

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Hypertensive bleeds are typically deep, while lobar hemorrhages in the elderly suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: Which of the following findings would most likely indicate a subdural hematoma rather than a subarachnoid hemorrhage?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: A crescent-shaped mass on CT is characteristic of a subdural hematoma, while SAH typically presents with a thunderclap headache and meningeal signs.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: Regarding location of hypertensive hemorrhage — which is correct?

options.text: A lobar hemorrhage in an elderly patient is from chronic hypertension
Hypertensive bleeds are typically DEEP (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum); lobar hemorrhages in the elderly suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Hypertension damages small penetrating vessels deep in the brain (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms), whereas amyloid deposition in cortical vessels causes superficial lobar bleeds — location points to the cause.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden “worst headache of life” + meningismus”?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Sudden “worst headache of life” + meningismus → Aneurysmal SAH.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What best explains the finding: “Deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) hemorrhage in a hypertensive”?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) hemorrhage in a hypertensive → Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm rupture.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: A comatose patient has symmetric pupils, intact brainstem reflexes, no focal weakness, and no meningismus. The most likely category of cause is:
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: A non-focal, symmetric exam with preserved brainstem reflexes and no meningismus points to a diffuse metabolic or toxic encephalopathy — the third and most common category of altered mental status.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What is the primary function of the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS)?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: The ARAS is crucial for maintaining wakefulness and alertness.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: Which clinical finding is most indicative of metabolic/toxic encephalopathy?

options.text: Symmetric exam with preserved brainstem reflexes

altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: A symmetric exam with preserved brainstem reflexes and no focal signs suggests a metabolic or toxic cause.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: In a patient with altered mental status, which initial step should be taken?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Checking glucose levels is a critical first step to rule out hypoglycemia as a cause of altered mental status.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: Which of the following is a common cause of coma that does not present with focal neurological signs?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Metabolic derangements are a common cause of coma without focal neurological signs.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What finding would most likely indicate meningitis in a patient with altered mental status?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Neck stiffness accompanied by fever is a classic sign of meningitis.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: In which condition would you expect to see elevated ammonia levels leading to altered mental status?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is characterized by elevated ammonia levels due to liver dysfunction.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: A patient presents with altered mental status and a history of alcohol use. Which condition should be considered?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Wernicke's encephalopathy is associated with thiamine deficiency, often seen in chronic alcohol users.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: Regarding coma from a single lesion — which is correct?

options.text: A single unilateral hemispheric stroke explains the coma
Coma requires bilateral hemispheric dysfunction or a brainstem (ARAS) lesion — a unilateral hemisphere lesion alone does not cause coma unless it raises ICP and compresses the brainstem

altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Wakefulness depends on the brainstem ARAS projecting to both hemispheres; one hemisphere can be lost without coma unless mass effect secondarily compresses the brainstem.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric exam, preserved brainstem reflexes, no focal signs”?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Symmetric exam, preserved brainstem reflexes, no focal signs → Metabolic/toxic encephalopathy.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Focal weakness, gaze deviation, or cranial-nerve signs”?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Focal weakness, gaze deviation, or cranial-nerve signs → Structural (stroke/mass) cause.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use is confused, with nystagmus and an unsteady gait. The immediate treatment priority is:
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: This is Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia). Give IV thiamine before any glucose, because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen the encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What is the primary cause of Wernicke encephalopathy?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is primarily caused by thiamine (B1) deficiency, often due to chronic alcohol use.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Which of the following is part of the classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy includes confusion, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What is the mechanism by which thiamine deficiency leads to Wernicke encephalopathy?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Thiamine deficiency leads to midline necrosis of the brain structures, resulting in the symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: A patient presents with confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and ataxic gait. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: The most appropriate initial treatment is IV thiamine to prevent worsening of Wernicke encephalopathy before administering glucose.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of Korsakoff syndrome?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is characterized by anterograde amnesia and confabulation due to damage to the mammillary bodies.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: In a patient with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, which history is most relevant?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: A history of chronic alcohol use is highly relevant as it is a common cause of thiamine deficiency leading to Wernicke encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: How does thiamine administration impact recovery from Wernicke encephalopathy?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Thiamine administration prevents further brain damage by addressing the deficiency that causes Wernicke encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Which of the following conditions shares a common risk factor with Wernicke encephalopathy?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy shares a common risk factor of malnutrition and alcohol use, similar to Wernicke encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Regarding order of thiamine vs glucose — which is correct?

options.text: Give IV dextrose first to a confused, malnourished alcoholic patient
Give thiamine before (or with) glucose — a glucose load in thiamine deficiency can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy

wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine; loading glucose into a depleted patient can trigger or worsen Wernicke, so thiamine must come first.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Confusion + horizontal nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia + ataxic gait”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Confusion + horizontal nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia + ataxic gait → Wernicke (midline diencephalic/brainstem necrosis).

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation → Korsakoff (mammillary/Papez damage).

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Which should you review before “Wernicke Encephalopathy & Korsakoff”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Directly addresses thiamine deficiency and its role in Wernicke's.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: A cirrhotic patient becomes drowsy and confused with a flapping tremor after a gastrointestinal bleed. The best initial management is:

options.text: Lactulose plus treatment of the GI bleed (the precipitant)

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Confusion with asterixis in a cirrhotic after a GI bleed is hepatic encephalopathy. Lower ammonia with lactulose (± rifaximin) and treat the precipitant (the GI hemorrhage).

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What is the most characteristic clinical finding in hepatic encephalopathy?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Asterixis, or flapping tremor, is a hallmark sign of hepatic encephalopathy due to liver failure.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Which of the following is a common precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Hypokalemia is a known precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy, often exacerbating the condition.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What is the primary mechanism leading to uremic encephalopathy?

options.text: Accumulation of urea and other toxins

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Uremic encephalopathy is primarily caused by the accumulation of urea and other toxins due to renal failure.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What EEG finding is commonly associated with hepatic encephalopathy?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: EEG in hepatic encephalopathy typically shows triphasic waves, indicative of metabolic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: In managing hepatic encephalopathy, what is the most important step besides lowering ammonia levels?

options.text: Searching for and treating precipitating factors

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: It is crucial to identify and treat precipitating factors in addition to managing ammonia levels in hepatic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What is the primary treatment for uremic encephalopathy?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Dialysis is the primary treatment for uremic encephalopathy, as it removes accumulated toxins.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: How does hepatic encephalopathy relate to alcohol metabolism disorders?

options.text: It is caused by alcohol-induced liver failure.
It is unrelated to alcohol metabolism.
It is a direct result of ALDH2 deficiency.
It is a complication of acute alcohol intoxication.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy can occur due to liver failure from chronic alcohol abuse, linking it to alcohol metabolism disorders.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Which condition shares similar clinical features with hepatic encephalopathy, particularly in altered mental status?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Uremic encephalopathy presents with altered mental status and can be confused with hepatic encephalopathy due to similar symptoms.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Regarding managing hepatic encephalopathy — which is correct?

options.text: Treat hepatic encephalopathy by restricting protein and lowering ammonia only
Always search for and treat the precipitant (GI bleed, infection, hypokalemia, constipation, sedatives) alongside lactulose/rifaximin

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Most episodes of HE are triggered by an identifiable precipitant; correcting it is as important as lowering ammonia, and prolonged protein restriction worsens malnutrition.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Asterixis (flapping tremor) + confusion in a cirrhotic”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Asterixis (flapping tremor) + confusion in a cirrhotic → Hepatic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multifocal myoclonus ± seizures in renal failure”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Multifocal myoclonus ± seizures in renal failure → Uremic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Which should you review before “Hepatic & Uremic Encephalopathy”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Understanding liver function and cirrhosis is essential for hepatic encephalopathy.

periodic-paralysis.stem: A 25-year-old man has recurrent attacks of limb weakness after heavy dessert meals or stress; eye, bulbar, and breathing muscles are spared, and his father is similarly affected. The most likely diagnosis is:
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Episodic flaccid weakness triggered by carbohydrate load/stress, sparing ocular/bulbar/respiratory muscles, with autosomal-dominant inheritance is hypokalemic periodic paralysis — check potassium during an attack.

periodic-paralysis.stem: What is the primary characteristic of periodic paralysis?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Periodic paralysis is defined by episodes of flaccid weakness with normal strength between attacks.

periodic-paralysis.stem: Which of the following triggers hypokalemic periodic paralysis?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis attacks are often triggered by heavy carbohydrate meals.

periodic-paralysis.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with episodic flaccid weakness after heavy meals. His potassium level during an attack is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: The patient's symptoms and low potassium level during an attack are characteristic of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

periodic-paralysis.stem: Which finding is characteristic of hyperkalemic periodic paralysis?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Myotonia is a common feature associated with hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.

periodic-paralysis.stem: A patient presents with episodic weakness and a family history of similar symptoms. What should be prioritized in the workup?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Thyroid function tests are crucial to rule out thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, a treatable condition.

periodic-paralysis.stem: In a patient with periodic paralysis, which electrolyte disturbance is most likely during an attack of hypokalemic periodic paralysis?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Hypokalemia is the hallmark electrolyte disturbance observed during an attack of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

periodic-paralysis.stem: How can periodic paralysis be differentiated from other causes of episodic weakness?

options.text: By the pattern of weakness and potassium levels
By the presence of sensory symptoms

periodic-paralysis.explanation: Periodic paralysis is characterized by episodic weakness with specific potassium level changes, distinguishing it from other conditions.

periodic-paralysis.stem: A patient with periodic paralysis experiences confusion and altered mental status during an episode. Which linked condition should be considered?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Altered mental status can occur in hepatic encephalopathy, which may be linked to electrolyte imbalances in periodic paralysis.

periodic-paralysis.stem: In a case of periodic paralysis, which condition could lead to a similar presentation of weakness and altered mental status?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis can cause weakness and altered mental status, similar to periodic paralysis, especially in thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

periodic-paralysis.stem: Regarding episodic weakness workup — which is correct?

options.text: Recurrent limb weakness in a young man is a psychiatric or non-organic problem
Episodic flaccid weakness with a potassium shift (and often thyrotoxicosis or family history) is periodic paralysis — check K⁺ during the attack and thyroid function

periodic-paralysis.explanation: PP is a real channelopathy/electrolyte disorder; measuring potassium during an attack and screening for thyrotoxicosis identifies a treatable cause and prevents dangerous arrhythmia (Andersen-Tawil).

periodic-paralysis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Episodic flaccid limb weakness sparing eyes/bulbar/respiration”?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Episodic flaccid limb weakness sparing eyes/bulbar/respiration → Periodic paralysis (channelopathy).

periodic-paralysis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Attacks after heavy carbohydrate meals + family history”?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Attacks after heavy carbohydrate meals + family history → Hypokalemic PP.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: A neurotransmitter binds a receptor that directly opens a chloride channel within milliseconds, hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. This is:
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Direct, millisecond-scale opening of a Cl⁻ channel producing hyperpolarization (IPSP) is an ionotropic inhibitory receptor such as GABA_A — the target of benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Which type of receptor is responsible for the rapid inhibitory response in the CNS?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Ionotropic receptors, such as GABA_A, mediate fast inhibitory responses by opening Cl⁻ channels.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Why is L-DOPA preferred over dopamine for treating Parkinson's disease?

options.text: Dopamine is more effective than L-DOPA
Dopamine can cross the blood-brain barrier
L-DOPA can be converted to dopamine in the brain
L-DOPA has fewer side effects than dopamine

cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: L-DOPA can cross the blood-brain barrier via an amino-acid transporter and is converted to dopamine in the brain.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action for amphetamines in the CNS?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Amphetamines primarily promote the release of neurotransmitters, increasing their availability in the synaptic cleft.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What clinical finding would indicate a drug's poor CNS penetration?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: A delayed therapeutic effect suggests poor CNS penetration, often due to the drug's hydrophilicity and inability to cross the blood-brain barrier.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Which neurotransmitter's action is primarily mediated by metabotropic receptors?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Dopamine primarily acts through metabotropic GPCRs, leading to slower, modulatory effects.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: How does the blood-brain barrier affect drug design for CNS conditions?

options.text: Allows all drugs to enter freely

cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: The blood-brain barrier restricts entry, necessitating the design of lipophilic drugs or those that can utilize transporters.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: How do EPSPs and IPSPs contribute to neuronal firing?

options.text: EPSPs inhibit action potentials, while IPSPs excite them
EPSPs and IPSPs both depolarize neurons
EPSPs depolarize and IPSPs hyperpolarize, summing to determine firing

cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: EPSPs cause depolarization and IPSPs cause hyperpolarization; their summation determines whether the neuron reaches the firing threshold.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Which mechanism explains the effect of ketamine as an NMDA antagonist?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors, inhibiting excitatory synaptic transmission and leading to its anesthetic effects.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Regarding why give l-dopa instead of dopamine — which is correct?

options.text: Just give dopamine to replace the deficient neurotransmitter in Parkinson disease
Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; its precursor L-DOPA uses the amino-acid transporter to enter the brain

cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: The BBB excludes the polar dopamine molecule, so the lipophilic/transportable precursor L-DOPA is given and then decarboxylated to dopamine centrally.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rapid (ms) inhibitory response = GABA_A opening Cl⁻ channels”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Rapid (ms) inhibitory response = GABA_A opening Cl⁻ channels → Ionotropic receptor (fast IPSP).

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slow, lasting modulation (seconds) via second messengers”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Slow, lasting modulation (seconds) via second messengers → Metabotropic GPCR (cAMP/IP₃/DAG).

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Pharmacology Foundations”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Understanding EPSPs/IPSPs is essential for grasping CNS drug mechanisms.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: A patient on a typical antipsychotic develops a resting tremor and rigidity plus galactorrhea. These effects are explained by dopamine blockade in which pathways?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade produces extrapyramidal (parkinsonian) symptoms, and tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade removes dopamine’s inhibition of prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea).

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for excitatory signaling in the central nervous system?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, while GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Benzodiazepines enhance the activity of GABA_A receptors, leading to increased inhibitory signaling.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: A patient on antipsychotic medication develops galactorrhea. Which pathway is likely affected?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Galactorrhea is associated with tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade, leading to hyperprolactinemia.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of D2 antagonism in antipsychotic treatment?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: D2 antagonism can lead to extrapyramidal symptoms due to effects on the nigrostriatal pathway.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: Which drug class is used to treat depression by increasing serotonin levels?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) increase serotonin levels in the synaptic cleft to alleviate depression.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: How do triptans alleviate migraine symptoms?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that help constrict blood vessels and reduce inflammation in migraines.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: How does the mechanism of action of stimulants relate to neurotransmitter balance?

options.text: They enhance dopamine and norepinephrine release

cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Stimulants enhance the release of dopamine and norepinephrine, correcting the imbalance in neurotransmitter signaling.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What is the primary effect of GABA_A receptor activation?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Activation of GABA_A receptors leads to increased chloride ion influx, resulting in hyperpolarization and decreased neuronal excitability.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: Regarding antipsychotic side effects by pathway — which is correct?

options.text: A D2 blocker only affects the reward (mesolimbic) pathway targeted for psychosis
D2 blockade also hits the nigrostriatal pathway (→ extrapyramidal symptoms) and tuberoinfundibular pathway (→ hyperprolactinemia)

cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Non-selective D2 antagonism affects all dopaminergic pathways, so blocking mesolimbic dopamine for psychosis unavoidably risks EPS and raised prolactin.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Extrapyramidal symptoms on an antipsychotic”?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Extrapyramidal symptoms on an antipsychotic → Nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Galactorrhea/amenorrhea on a D2 antagonist”?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Galactorrhea/amenorrhea on a D2 antagonist → Tuberoinfundibular D2 block → hyperprolactinemia.

cns-stimulants.stem: A stimulant increases synaptic dopamine primarily by reversing the dopamine transporter and inhibiting vesicular storage and MAO. This describes:
cns-stimulants.explanation: Amphetamine raises dopamine by reversing DAT/NET, blocking VMAT storage, and inhibiting MAO — actively releasing catecholamines, unlike cocaine which blocks reuptake.

cns-stimulants.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of amphetamines?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Amphetamines primarily reverse the dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, leading to increased release of these neurotransmitters.

cns-stimulants.stem: Which of the following is a common clinical finding in cocaine toxicity?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Cocaine use, especially via nasal administration, can lead to nasal septal perforation due to its vasoconstrictive properties.

cns-stimulants.stem: What is the drug of choice for ADHD?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Methylphenidate is considered the first-line treatment for ADHD due to its efficacy and safety profile.

cns-stimulants.stem: Which of the following symptoms is most characteristic of chronic amphetamine use?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Chronic use of amphetamines can lead to formication, a sensation of insects crawling on or under the skin.

cns-stimulants.stem: What distinguishes the mechanism of action of cocaine from that of amphetamines?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Cocaine primarily blocks the reuptake of dopamine, while amphetamines actively promote the release of dopamine.

cns-stimulants.stem: How does nicotine primarily exert its effects on the CNS?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Nicotine activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, leading to increased dopamine release in the brain.

cns-stimulants.stem: Which neurotransmitter system is primarily affected by both amphetamines and cocaine?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Both amphetamines and cocaine primarily affect the dopamine system, leading to increased dopamine levels in the synaptic cleft.

cns-stimulants.stem: Which of the following CNS stimulants is most likely to cause nasal septal perforation when used intranasally?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Cocaine's vasoconstrictive effects can lead to nasal septal perforation when snorted.

cns-stimulants.stem: Regarding amphetamine vs cocaine mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: Amphetamine works mainly by blocking dopamine reuptake like cocaine
Amphetamine actively RELEASES catecholamines (reverses transporters, blocks VMAT/MAO); cocaine BLOCKS reuptake (DAT > NET)

cns-stimulants.explanation: Both raise synaptic dopamine, but amphetamine drives release from the terminal while cocaine simply prevents reuptake — a classic mechanism distinction.

cns-stimulants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Euphoria, hyperactivity, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia”?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Euphoria, hyperactivity, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia → Central + peripheral catecholamine excess.

cns-stimulants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nasal septal perforation”?

aeds-principles-targets.stem: A patient in status epilepticus is brought to the ED. The correct first-line pharmacologic treatment is:
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Status epilepticus is first treated with a benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam, or midazolam) to abort the seizure, followed by a longer-acting agent (phenytoin, valproate, or levetiracetam).

aeds-principles-targets.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) reduce neuronal excitability?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: AEDs primarily reduce neuronal excitability by blocking voltage-gated ion channels, thereby preventing excessive neuronal firing.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which of the following is the first-line treatment for status epilepticus?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Lorazepam is the first-line treatment for status epilepticus, providing rapid control of seizures.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: A patient presents with brief staring spells and 3-Hz spike-wave discharges on EEG. What type of seizure is this?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: The described EEG pattern is characteristic of absence seizures, which are typically brief and involve staring spells.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which of the following medications is contraindicated in a patient with absence seizures?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence seizures as it can worsen the condition; ethosuximide and valproate are preferred.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: How do GABAergic agents primarily exert their effect in the treatment of epilepsy?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: GABAergic agents enhance inhibitory neurotransmission by increasing GABA receptor activity, thereby reducing neuronal excitability.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which antiepileptic drug is specifically indicated for absence seizures?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Ethosuximide is specifically indicated for absence seizures and is effective in reducing their frequency.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: How might thiamine deficiency relate to seizure management in alcohol withdrawal?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Thiamine deficiency can precipitate seizures, particularly in alcohol withdrawal, necessitating its management alongside seizure treatment.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which of the following AEDs would be inappropriate for a patient with both absence seizures and a history of focal seizures?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Carbamazepine is inappropriate for absence seizures as it can worsen them, despite being effective for focal seizures.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Regarding drug choice in absence epilepsy — which is correct?

options.text: Carbamazepine is a good broad first choice for any seizure, including absence
Carbamazepine (and phenytoin, gabapentin, etc.) WORSEN absence seizures — use ethosuximide or valproate

aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Sodium-channel/GABAergic agents like carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures; ethosuximide (T-type Ca²⁺) and valproate are the appropriate choices.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brief staring spells with 3-Hz spike-wave”?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Brief staring spells with 3-Hz spike-wave → Absence seizure (T-type Ca²⁺, thalamocortical).

aeds-principles-targets.stem: What best explains the finding: “Generalized convulsion >5 min or recurrent without recovery”?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Generalized convulsion >5 min or recurrent without recovery → Status epilepticus.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which should you review before “Antiepileptic Drugs — Principles & Targets”?

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Before starting carbamazepine in a Thai patient, which test best reduces the risk of a life-threatening cutaneous reaction?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: HLA-B*1502 (common in Southeast Asians) strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN, so screening is recommended before starting the drug.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs primarily enhances Na⁺-channel inactivation?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker that enhances Na⁺-channel inactivation, making it effective for focal and tonic-clonic seizures.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which sodium channel blockers suppress seizure activity?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Sodium channel blockers stabilize inactivated Na⁺ channels, which suppresses rapid neuronal firing associated with seizures.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: A patient on phenytoin presents with gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism. What is the most likely cause?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are well-known chronic effects of phenytoin therapy.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Which of the following statements about phenytoin dosing is correct?

options.text: Doubling the dose will double the serum level
It has first-order kinetics at all doses
Small dose increases can lead to large increases in serum level
It is completely eliminated at therapeutic doses

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Phenytoin exhibits zero-order kinetics, meaning small increases in dose can lead to disproportionately large increases in serum levels.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: A patient with a history of carbamazepine use presents with hyponatremia and a rash. What genetic screening is recommended?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Patients of Asian descent should be screened for HLA-B*1502 due to the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome associated with carbamazepine.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: How does the mechanism of action of lamotrigine differ from that of phenytoin?

options.text: It blocks Na⁺ channels and decreases glutamate release
It has no effect on Na⁺ channels

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Lamotrigine blocks Na⁺ channels and decreases glutamate release, differing from phenytoin's primary action of stabilizing inactivated Na⁺ channels.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Which electrolyte imbalance is most commonly associated with carbamazepine therapy?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Carbamazepine can cause hyponatremia due to its effect on antidiuretic hormone, leading to SIADH.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Regarding phenytoin dosing kinetics — which is correct?

options.text: Doubling the phenytoin dose will roughly double the serum level
Phenytoin shows zero-order (saturable) kinetics at therapeutic doses — small dose increases can cause disproportionately large level rises and toxicity

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Once the metabolizing enzymes saturate, phenytoin clearance becomes constant, so level rises nonlinearly — a classic cause of unexpected toxicity.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gingival hyperplasia + hirsutism”?
What best explains the finding: “Hyponatremia + rash in an Asian patient on carbamazepine”?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Hyponatremia + rash in an Asian patient on carbamazepine → SIADH; HLA-B*1502 SJS risk.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Which should you review before “AEDs — Sodium Channel Blockers”?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Understanding sodium balance is crucial for grasping sodium channel blockers' effects.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: A child with pure absence epilepsy is best treated first-line with a drug that blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels, namely:
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and is the classic drug for absence seizures; carbamazepine, phenytoin, and vigabatrin can worsen absence.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of ethosuximide in treating absence seizures?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Ethosuximide primarily blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic neurons, which is crucial for controlling absence seizures.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Which AED is known to cause peripheral visual field constriction as a side effect?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Vigabatrin is associated with peripheral visual field constriction due to its irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What is a significant side effect of long-term use of benzodiazepines in seizure management?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA_A receptors, leading to sedation, which is a common side effect.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Which of the following AEDs is contraindicated in absence seizures?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Tiagabine is contraindicated in absence seizures as it can worsen the condition.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Gabapentin and pregabalin primarily act on which subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Gabapentin and pregabalin act at the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, not on GABA receptors.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Which AED is first-line for status epilepticus?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Phenobarbital is a first-line treatment for status epilepticus due to its GABA_A enhancing effects.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: How do ethosuximide and gabapentin differ in their mechanisms of action?

options.text: Ethosuximide blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels while gabapentin acts on α2δ subunit
Gabapentin enhances GABA_A receptors while ethosuximide does not

aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels, while gabapentin acts on the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Which AED is effective for both absence seizures and myoclonic seizures?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Clonazepam is effective for myoclonic seizures and can also be used for absence seizures.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Regarding gabapentin mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: Gabapentin, being a GABA analog, works by activating GABA receptors
Gabapentin/pregabalin act on the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, NOT on GABA receptors

aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Despite the name and structure, they do not bind GABA receptors — their anticonvulsant and analgesic effects come from reducing Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release via α2δ.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absence controlled by ethosuximide”?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Absence controlled by ethosuximide → T-type Ca²⁺ channel block.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral visual field constriction on an AED”?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Peripheral visual field constriction on an AED → Vigabatrin.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which antiepileptic drug is broad-spectrum (effective across absence, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures) but is strongly teratogenic and hepatotoxic?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Valproate acts at multiple targets and covers all major seizure types (plus bipolar disorder and migraine), but carries hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity (neural tube defects), so it is avoided in pregnancy.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of valproate?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Alopecia is a known side effect of valproate, while weight loss and kidney stones are associated with topiramate.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of topiramate?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Topiramate primarily acts by blocking sodium channels, in addition to enhancing GABA and inhibiting glutamate.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: A patient on levetiracetam presents with increased irritability. What is the most likely cause?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Levetiracetam can cause mood and behavioral changes, which is a known side effect of this medication.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which of the following AEDs is contraindicated in women of childbearing age due to teratogenic effects?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Valproate is highly teratogenic and should be avoided in women who may become pregnant.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: What is the mechanism of action of perampanel?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Perampanel acts as an AMPA receptor antagonist, which can lead to behavioral and psychiatric effects.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which AED is most likely to cause kidney stones and cognitive slowing?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Topiramate is associated with kidney stones and cognitive slowing due to its carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: How does the mechanism of action of valproate contribute to its broad-spectrum efficacy?

options.text: Multiple targets including sodium and calcium channels
