numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: A patient presents with a karyotype of 45,X. What condition is this indicative of?
numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: A karyotype of 45,X indicates Turner syndrome, which is characterized by monosomy X.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Which of the following describes the outcome of meiosis II nondisjunction?

options.text: Two disomic and two nullisomic gametes
Two normal and one disomic and one nullisomic gamete

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Meiosis II nondisjunction results in two normal gametes, one disomic, and one nullisomic.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates meiosis I from meiosis II nondisjunction?

options.text: Both errors produce the same four gametes
Meiosis I affects homologs, while meiosis II affects sister chromatids
Only meiosis I can lead to trisomy
Meiosis II always results in normal gametes

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Meiosis I nondisjunction affects homolog segregation, while meiosis II affects only one pair of sister chromatids.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: What is the chromosomal composition of a triploid individual?
numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Triploidy is characterized by having three complete sets of chromosomes, totaling 69 chromosomes.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: How does mosaicism relate to aneuploidy?

options.text: It is a form of polyploidy
It results from postzygotic mitotic errors
It is always associated with Turner syndrome

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Mosaicism arises from postzygotic mitotic errors, leading to a mixture of normal and aneuploid cells.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Which condition is most likely to be associated with a partial molar placenta?
numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Triploidy, often resulting from dispermy, is associated with the presence of a partial molar placenta.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Regarding meiosis-i versus meiosis-ii nondisjunction — which is correct?

options.text: Both errors produce the same four gametes
Meiosis I produces two disomic and two nullisomic gametes; meiosis II produces two normal, one disomic, and one nullisomic

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: The first error affects homolog segregation; the second affects only one pair of sister chromatids.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: A chromosome consists of two copies of its long arm and no short arm. This is:
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: An isochromosome contains mirror-image copies of one arm with loss of the other.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What is the primary consequence of a deletion in a chromosome?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: A deletion results in the loss of genetic material, which can lead to partial monosomy.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: Which of the following describes an isochromosome?

options.text: A chromosome that has lost one arm and duplicated the other
A circular chromosome with terminal deletions

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: An isochromosome is formed when one arm is lost and the other is duplicated, leading to partial trisomy and monosomy.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: Which clinical finding is associated with a deletion on chromosome 5p?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Terminal loss from 5p is characteristic of cri-du-chat syndrome, which results from a deletion.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What is a key characteristic of a dicentric chromosome?

options.text: It is a type of isochromosome

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: A dicentric chromosome contains two centromeres and is mechanically unstable, often leading to problems during cell division.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: How does a ring chromosome typically form?

options.text: By fusion of broken ends after terminal deletions

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: A ring chromosome forms when both ends of a chromosome break and the remaining ends fuse, often after terminal deletions.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: In patients with gastric carcinoma, which chromosomal abnormality might be observed?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Gastric carcinoma can be associated with various chromosomal abnormalities, including aneuploidy, isochromosomes, and ring chromosomes.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: Which chromosomal abnormality is likely to affect gene dosage in gastric MALT lymphoma?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: All these abnormalities can alter gene dosage, which is relevant in the context of gastric MALT lymphoma.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: Regarding isochromosome dosage — which is correct?

options.text: An isochromosome is balanced because it still has two arms
It duplicates one arm and deletes the other, causing partial trisomy plus partial monosomy

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Arm count is preserved, but genetic content is not.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Terminal loss from 5p”?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Terminal loss from 5p → Deletion causing partial monosomy (cri-du-chat pattern).

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mirror-image chromosome arms”?
Which is a clinical application of “Deletion, Duplication, Ring & Isochromosome”?

translocations-inversions.stem: Which segregation pattern in a reciprocal-translocation carrier can produce normal or balanced gametes?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Alternate segregation sends the two normal chromosomes together and the two translocation derivatives together, preserving balance.

translocations-inversions.stem: What is the primary risk associated with a balanced reciprocal translocation during meiosis?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Balanced reciprocal translocation carriers can produce unbalanced gametes due to improper segregation during meiosis.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a balanced Robertsonian translocation?

options.text: Loss of short arms of acrocentric chromosomes
Increased risk of Down syndrome in all offspring

translocations-inversions.explanation: A balanced Robertsonian translocation typically results in a carrier having 45 chromosomes with the loss of short arms but maintaining essential genetic material.

translocations-inversions.stem: A patient presents with recurrent miscarriages. Which genetic abnormality should be suspected?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Recurrent miscarriages can be indicative of a balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes.

translocations-inversions.stem: In a pericentric inversion, which of the following statements is true?
translocations-inversions.explanation: A pericentric inversion includes the centromere, which can lead to unbalanced gametes if crossover occurs within the inversion loop.

translocations-inversions.stem: What is the expected chromosome count in a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation?
translocations-inversions.explanation: A balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation typically has 45 chromosomes due to the fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes.

translocations-inversions.stem: How does a balanced Robertsonian translocation relate to aneuploidy?

options.text: It increases the risk of aneuploidy in all offspring
It is a form of aneuploidy
It can produce unbalanced gametes leading to aneuploidy

translocations-inversions.explanation: Balanced Robertsonian translocations can lead to unbalanced gametes, increasing the risk of aneuploidy in offspring.

translocations-inversions.stem: What is a common clinical finding in patients with a pericentric inversion?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Patients with a pericentric inversion may experience recurrent miscarriages due to the risk of producing unbalanced gametes.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which of the following statements is a trap regarding balanced Robertsonian translocation carriers?

options.text: They can have a normal phenotype
They are at high risk for severe phenotypes

translocations-inversions.explanation: Balanced Robertsonian translocation carriers can be phenotypically normal despite having 45 chromosomes.

translocations-inversions.stem: Regarding balanced robertsonian carrier — which is correct?

options.text: A person with 45 chromosomes must have monosomy and a severe phenotype
A balanced Robertsonian carrier can be healthy because the fused long arms preserve essential unique material
Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: Chromosome count and genetic dosage are related but not identical.

translocations-inversions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Phenotypically normal adult with recurrent miscarriage”?

options.text: Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: Phenotypically normal adult with recurrent miscarriage → Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes.

translocations-inversions.stem: What best explains the finding: “45 chromosomes with fused 14q and 21q”?

options.text: Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: 45 chromosomes with fused 14q and 21q → Balanced Robertsonian translocation.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Translocations, Insertions & Inversions”?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Basic science concepts may relate to clinical reflexes but are not directly linked.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which should you review before “Translocations, Insertions & Inversions”?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Aneuploidy is a key concept related to chromosome aberrations.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Two genetically distinct cell lines arise after mitotic nondisjunction in a single early embryo. This is:
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Both cell lines descend from one zygote, so the condition is mosaicism.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: What is the primary distinction between mosaicism and chimerism?

options.text: Mosaicism arises from one fertilization event, while chimerism involves multiple events.
Mosaicism is always associated with Turner syndrome, while chimerism is not.
Mosaicism results in a single phenotype, while chimerism results in multiple phenotypes.
Mosaicism only affects somatic cells, while chimerism affects germ cells.

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Mosaicism involves genetically different cell lines from a single zygote, whereas chimerism involves lines from multiple zygotes.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: In a patient presenting with 45,X/46,XX cell lines, what is the most likely underlying mechanism?
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: The presence of two different cell lines in one individual suggests a postzygotic error leading to mosaicism.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which of the following findings would suggest confined placental mosaicism?

options.text: Abnormal chorionic villus sampling but normal amniocytes
Mosaic Turner pattern in blood cells
Normal karyotype in both placenta and fetus

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Confined placental mosaicism results in discrepancies between placental and fetal cell lines.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: A patient has two genetically distinct cell lines, one from a fertilization event and another from a different embryo. This condition is best described as:
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Chimerism involves genetically distinct lines from separate fertilization events.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which of the following statements about mosaicism is FALSE?

options.text: It can arise from anaphase lag.
It can involve multiple tissues if the error occurs early.
It always results in a phenotypically normal individual.
It can be detected by specific karyotyping techniques.

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Mosaicism can lead to phenotypic abnormalities depending on the affected tissues.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: How does mosaicism relate to aneuploidy in terms of genetic origin?

options.text: Both arise from multiple fertilization events.
Mosaicism can result from aneuploidy occurring postzygotically.
Aneuploidy is always a result of mosaicism.
Mosaicism does not involve chromosomal abnormalities.

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Mosaicism can arise from postzygotic errors leading to aneuploid cell lines.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: A patient with chimerism presents with two distinct karyotypes. How is this condition related to chromosomal structure abnormalities?

options.text: Chimerism is a type of chromosomal deletion.
Chimerism can involve structural abnormalities from each zygote.
Chimerism is unrelated to chromosomal abnormalities.

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Chimerism can involve different chromosomal structures from each zygote, leading to distinct karyotypes.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Regarding mosaicism versus chimerism — which is correct?

options.text: Any person with two genotypes is a mosaic
Mosaicism arises from one zygote; chimerism combines cell lines from more than one zygote
Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: The number of cell lines is shared; their developmental origin distinguishes the terms.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “45,X/46,XX cell lines in one person”?

options.text: Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: 45,X/46,XX cell lines in one person → Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “46,XX/46,XY tissues after fusion of two embryos”?

options.text: Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: 46,XX/46,XY tissues after fusion of two embryos → Tetragametic chimerism.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mosaicism & Chimerism”?
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Some AEDs may have effects related to chromosomal abnormalities.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which should you review before “Mosaicism & Chimerism”?
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Understanding aneuploidy is essential for grasping mosaicism and chimerism.

options.text: A male with a deletion of 21

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: 47 chromosomes, XY (male), +21 (an extra chromosome 21) = a male with trisomy 21, i.e. Down syndrome. The + precedes the gained chromosome.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: What is the correct karyotype notation for a male with Down syndrome?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: The correct notation for a male with trisomy 21 is 47,XY,+21, where the + sign precedes the chromosome number.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the structure of a karyotype?

options.text: Numerical changes are written after structural changes.
The total chromosome number is written first.
Abnormalities are listed before sex chromosomes.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: In a karyotype, the total chromosome number is always written first, followed by sex chromosomes and then abnormalities.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: A karyotype shows 45,X. What condition does this indicate?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: The karyotype 45,X indicates Turner syndrome, characterized by monosomy X.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: In karyotype notation, what does the notation '47,XXY' represent?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: '47,XXY' indicates Klinefelter syndrome, which is characterized by an extra X chromosome in males.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Which of the following is a common trap in writing karyotypes?

options.text: Placing the + sign after the chromosome number.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: A common mistake is placing the + sign after the chromosome number; it should precede the number for whole-chromosome changes.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: How would you denote a mosaic karyotype with 10 cells showing trisomy 21 and 5 normal cells?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: The correct notation for a mosaic karyotype is 47,XX,+21[10]/46,XX[5], indicating the proportion of each cell type.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: How does the ISCN karyotype notation relate to blood gas interpretation?

options.text: Both use numerical values to indicate abnormalities.
Karyotype notation does not relate to blood gas interpretation.
Both require understanding of cellular structures.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: Both karyotype notation and blood gas interpretation involve numerical values that indicate specific abnormalities in the body.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Which of the following karyotype notations would be relevant when discussing structural rearrangements?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: The notation 47,XY,inv(7)(p14q34) indicates a structural rearrangement involving chromosome 7.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Regarding where the + or − sign goes — which is correct?

options.text: The sign precedes the chromosome for whole-chromosome changes: 47,XY,+21 (a trailing sign after a band would instead refer to arm gain/loss in older shorthand, which ISCN discourages)

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: ISCN puts +/− before the chromosome number for aneuploidy; "21q+" style shorthand is not used in a formal karyotype.

options.text: Mosaic: trisomy 21 in 10 cells, normal in 5
Mosaic: trisomy 21 in 10 cells, normal in 5

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ISCN Nomenclature: Symbols & Numerical Karyotypes”?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: Understanding karyotypes can aid in interpreting genetic conditions that may affect blood gas levels.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: A phenotypically normal woman has the karyotype 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10). What is she?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: A Robertsonian fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21 gives 45 total chromosomes with balanced material — a phenotypically normal carrier who has an increased risk of a child with translocation Down syndrome.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: What is the correct notation for a deletion on chromosome 4 at the short arm?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: The notation 46,XY,del(4)(p14) specifies a deletion at the short arm of chromosome 4 at the 14 position.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Which of the following describes a balanced Robertsonian translocation?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: A balanced Robertsonian translocation results in a chromosome count of 45 due to the fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: What is the karyotype for a patient with an isochromosome of the X chromosome?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: The karyotype 46,X,i(X)(q10) indicates one normal X chromosome and an isochromosome of the long arm of X.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: In mosaic Turner syndrome, what is the karyotype representation?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Mosaic Turner syndrome is represented as mos 45,X[12]/46,XX[8], indicating two cell lines with different chromosome counts.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Which of the following is a common misconception about balanced Robertsonian translocation carriers?

options.text: They have a higher risk of Down syndrome

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: A balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier has 45 chromosomes due to the fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes, despite being phenotypically normal.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: How does a deletion on chromosome 13 manifest in a karyotype?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: The notation 46,XY,del(13)(q12q14) indicates an interstitial deletion on chromosome 13 between the specified breakpoints.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: How does the structural rearrangement of chromosomes relate to metabolic disorders?

options.text: They can lead to insulin resistance

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Structural rearrangements can disrupt genes involved in metabolic pathways, potentially leading to insulin resistance.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: What is the significance of understanding structural rearrangements in the context of clinical genetics?

options.text: They are irrelevant to patient care
They are only important in prenatal diagnosis

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Understanding structural rearrangements can help predict treatment responses and guide management in various genetic conditions.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Regarding chromosome count of a balanced robertsonian carrier — which is correct?

options.text: A translocation carrier must have 46 chromosomes
A balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes — two acrocentrics fuse into one derivative, so the count drops by one while the genetic material is balanced

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Robertsonian fusion physically merges two chromosomes into one, lowering the total count even though the carrier is phenotypically normal.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ISCN Nomenclature: Structural Rearrangements & Mosaicism”?
Which should you review before “ISCN Nomenclature: Structural Rearrangements & Mosaicism”?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Understanding basic symbols and karyotypes is essential for grasping structural rearrangements.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: A newborn has hypotonia, a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, Brushfield spots, and a single palmar crease. Karyotype shows 46,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21. What counseling point is most important?

options.text: This is translocation Down syndrome — test parents, as recurrence risk may be high

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: The karyotype shows Down syndrome from a Robertsonian (14;21) translocation. Unlike free trisomy 21 (~1% recurrence), a translocation may be inherited from a balanced-carrier parent with substantial recurrence risk, so parental karyotyping is essential.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What is the most common autosomal trisomy that survives to birth?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Trisomy 21, or Down syndrome, is the most common autosomal trisomy that survives to birth, occurring in approximately 1 in 850 live births.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Clenched fists with overlapping fingers is a classic finding in Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What is the mechanism leading to Down syndrome (trisomy 21)?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Down syndrome is primarily caused by nondisjunction during meiosis, leading to an extra chromosome 21.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which statement about recurrence risk in Down syndrome is correct?

options.text: Every Down syndrome pregnancy carries a high recurrence risk
Only translocation Down syndrome has a high recurrence risk
Free trisomy 21 has a recurrence risk of 50%
All Down syndrome cases are inherited

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Only translocation Down syndrome has a high recurrence risk; free trisomy 21 recurs at approximately 1%.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which of the following is a common complication of Down syndrome?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Congenital heart disease is a common complication in individuals with Down syndrome, affecting 40-45% of cases.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which feature is associated with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Polydactyly is a characteristic feature of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: How does the mechanism of Down syndrome differ from that of autosomal deletion syndromes?

options.text: Down syndrome is caused by deletion
Down syndrome involves an extra chromosome

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Down syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome (trisomy), while deletion syndromes involve the loss of genetic material.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What is the relationship between maternal age and the risk of Down syndrome?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: The risk of Down syndrome increases with maternal age due to meiotic nondisjunction, particularly in maternal meiosis I.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Regarding recurrence risk in down syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: Every Down syndrome pregnancy carries a high recurrence risk
Only translocation Down syndrome (e.g. a carrier parent with rob(14;21)) has a high recurrence risk; free trisomy 21 (95%) recurs at only ≈1%

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Recurrence counseling hinges on the karyotype — a Robertsonian carrier parent changes the risk dramatically, so parental testing is essential.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypotonia + flat facies + single palmar crease + Brushfield spots”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Hypotonia + flat facies + single palmar crease + Brushfield spots → Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clenched fists with overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + micrognathia”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Clenched fists with overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + micrognathia → Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which should you review before “Autosomal Trisomies: Down, Edwards, Patau”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Understanding aneuploidy is essential for grasping trisomy mechanisms.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: An infant has a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, and severe developmental delay. Which chromosomal abnormality is responsible?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: The mewing cat-like cry with microcephaly and hypertelorism is cri-du-chat syndrome, a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−), critical region 5p15.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What is the chromosomal deletion associated with Cri-du-chat syndrome?

options.text: Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4
Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 4

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−).

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Which of the following features is characteristic of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome is characterized by the "Greek warrior helmet" facies and other features like microcephaly and growth retardation.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What is the mechanism behind the symptoms of Cri-du-chat syndrome?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: The symptoms of Cri-du-chat syndrome arise from the loss of a short-arm segment of chromosome 5, leading to a contiguous-gene syndrome.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: A child presents with a high-pitched cry, microcephaly, and hypertelorism. Which condition is most likely?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: These features are classic for Cri-du-chat syndrome, which includes a high-pitched cry and distinct facial features.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: In a family with a history of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, what genetic factor should be considered for recurrence risk?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Approximately 45-50% of Wolf-Hirschhorn cases arise from an unbalanced translocation, so parental karyotyping is important for counseling.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: How does Cri-du-chat syndrome relate to gas exchange abnormalities in infants?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange due to heart defects

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Infants with Cri-du-chat syndrome may have heart defects that can impair gas exchange, leading to respiratory issues.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Which of the following syndromes can be compared to Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome in terms of genetic deletion?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Cri-du-chat syndrome and Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome are both characterized by chromosomal deletions and share similar clinical features.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Regarding chromosome arm in cri-du-chat — which is correct?

options.text: Cri-du-chat is a deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5
It is a deletion of the SHORT arm of chromosome 5 (5p−), critical region 5p15

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Both classic deletion syndromes here (cri-du-chat 5p, Wolf-Hirschhorn 4p) involve the short (p) arm — a common point tested.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “High-pitched cat-like cry + microcephaly + hypertelorism”?

options.text: Consider a balanced translocation carrier parent

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: High-pitched cat-like cry + microcephaly + hypertelorism → Cri-du-chat (5p−).

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “"Greek warrior helmet" facies + seizures + growth failure”?

options.text: Consider a balanced translocation carrier parent

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: "Greek warrior helmet" facies + seizures + growth failure → Wolf-Hirschhorn (4p−).

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Autosomal Deletion Syndromes: Cri-du-chat & Wolf-Hirschhorn”?

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: A child with severe intellectual disability, an ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, and frequent inappropriate laughter has a 15q11-q13 abnormality. What is the parent-of-origin mechanism?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternally expressed 15q11-q13 (deletion, paternal UPD, imprinting defect, or UBE3A mutation), giving the ataxic "happy puppet" phenotype. Loss of the paternal copy causes Prader-Willi.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What is the primary mechanism leading to the different phenotypes of Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Both syndromes arise from deletions at the same locus, but the parent of origin (maternal vs paternal) determines the phenotype due to genomic imprinting.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Which clinical finding is characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome is characterized by neonatal hypotonia, which later progresses to hyperphagia and obesity.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Angelman syndrome?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Hyperphagia is characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome, not Angelman syndrome.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What is the genetic basis of Williams syndrome?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Williams syndrome is caused by a deletion at 7q11.23, which includes the elastin gene.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: In Prader-Willi syndrome, which genetic alteration is most commonly observed?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: The majority of cases of Prader-Willi syndrome are due to a paternal deletion of the 15q11-q13 region.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: How does Prader-Willi syndrome relate to the sex steroid synthesis module?

options.text: It involves hypogonadism affecting steroid synthesis
It is caused by a mutation in a steroid receptor
It leads to increased estrogen production
It is unrelated to steroid synthesis

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome includes hypogonadism, which can affect sex steroid synthesis and lead to various endocrine abnormalities.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Which feature of DiGeorge syndrome is also relevant to the understanding of microdeletion syndromes?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Thymic hypoplasia is a key feature of DiGeorge syndrome, which is also a microdeletion syndrome, highlighting the impact of chromosomal deletions on development.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Regarding prader-willi vs angelman — which is correct?

options.text: Prader-Willi and Angelman come from deletions on different chromosomes
Both involve the SAME 15q11-q13 region — Prader-Willi is loss of the PATERNAL copy, Angelman is loss of the MATERNAL copy (genomic imprinting)

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: The parent of origin, not the location, decides the phenotype — the classic teaching example of imprinting.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neonatal hypotonia → childhood hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism”?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Neonatal hypotonia → childhood hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism → Prader-Willi (paternal 15q loss).

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, inappropriate laughter”?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, inappropriate laughter → Angelman (maternal 15q loss).

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Microdeletion & Imprinting Syndromes”?

options.text: Sex Steroid Synthesis, Transport & Receptor Action

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Both modules involve genetic mechanisms but in different contexts.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: How many Barr bodies are present in a somatic cell with a 47,XXX karyotype?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one. With three X chromosomes, two are inactivated → 2 Barr bodies.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What is the expected number of Barr bodies in a 47,XXX individual?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The number of Barr bodies is calculated as (number of X chromosomes - 1), so 47,XXX has 2 Barr bodies.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: Which gene is responsible for initiating X-inactivation?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The XIST gene at the X-inactivation center is responsible for initiating X-inactivation.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: A 45,X individual presents with short stature. What is the underlying mechanism?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: Short stature in Turner syndrome (45,X) is due to haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: A 47,XXY male is found to have one Barr body. What is the reason for this?

options.text: He has an extra Y chromosome
Barr bodies depend on X count, not sex
He has a deletion on the Y chromosome
He is a mosaic with 46,XY cells

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: Barr bodies are determined by the number of X chromosomes; 47,XXY has two X chromosomes, resulting in one Barr body.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What is the role of the SRY gene in sex determination?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The SRY gene encodes Testis-Determining Factor (TDF), which is crucial for male sex determination.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: How does the presence of the SRY gene affect gonadal development?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The SRY gene initiates the formation of testes, leading to male development.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: In a patient with Turner syndrome (45,X), which of the following would be a relevant consideration when evaluating for acid-base disorders?

options.text: Potential respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation
Risk of metabolic alkalosis from excessive vomiting
Possible renal tubular acidosis due to kidney malformations
Increased risk of respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: Patients with Turner syndrome may have renal anomalies, which can lead to renal tubular acidosis.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: How might the SHOX gene's function relate to acid-base balance in a patient with sex chromosome aneuploidy?

options.text: SHOX is involved in respiratory drive
SHOX influences renal function and growth

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The SHOX gene influences skeletal growth and may indirectly affect renal function, which can relate to acid-base balance.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: Regarding barr body count — which is correct?

options.text: A 47,XXY (Klinefelter) male has no Barr body because he is male
Barr bodies depend on X count, not sex: 47,XXY has two X chromosomes → ONE Barr body
SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: One X stays active and the rest are inactivated regardless of sex, so the count is (X − 1).

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What best explains the finding: “47,XXY has one Barr body”?

options.text: SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: 47,XXY has one Barr body → Barr bodies = X − 1.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What best explains the finding: “SRY translocated to an X → 46,XX male”?

options.text: SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: SRY translocated to an X → 46,XX male → SRY is sufficient for testis determination.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: Which is a clinical application of “X-Inactivation, Barr Bodies & Sex Determination”?

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: A short 15-year-old girl has not started menstruating; exam shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and a history of coarctation repair. FSH and LH are elevated. What is the karyotype?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X): short stature, webbed neck, coarctation of the aorta, and ovarian dysgenesis causing primary amenorrhea with elevated (hypergonadotropic) FSH/LH.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What is the most common cause of male hypogonadism?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is the most common cause of male hypogonadism, characterized by tall stature and small firm testes.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in Turner syndrome?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Webbed neck is a classic physical finding in Turner syndrome, while the other options are associated with different conditions.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What is the mechanism leading to sex chromosome aneuploidies?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Nondisjunction during meiosis leads to sex chromosome aneuploidies such as Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: In Klinefelter syndrome, what is the expected laboratory finding for FSH and LH?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome results in primary hypogonadism, leading to elevated FSH and LH levels due to gonadal failure.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with short stature and primary amenorrhea. Which condition is most likely?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Short stature and primary amenorrhea are classic features of Turner syndrome (45,X).

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: How does Turner syndrome relate to disorders of sex development?

options.text: Both are caused by maternal age
Both are due to Y chromosome abnormalities

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Turner syndrome and disorders of sex development both involve mechanisms related to X-inactivation and sex chromosome abnormalities.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: Which of the following findings can indicate Klinefelter syndrome in a patient with suspected disorders of sex development?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: The presence of Barr bodies is indicative of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) and is a key finding in the evaluation of sex chromosome aneuploidies.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: Regarding gonadotropin levels in turner/klinefelter — which is correct?

options.text: Hypogonadism in these syndromes means low FSH/LH
Both are PRIMARY (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism — the gonad fails, so FSH/LH are HIGH with low sex steroids

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: The defect is at the gonad, not the pituitary, so feedback drives gonadotropins up (unlike central/secondary hypogonadism).

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Short female, webbed neck, coarctation, primary amenorrhea”?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Short female, webbed neck, coarctation, primary amenorrhea → Turner syndrome (45,X).

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia, ↑FSH/LH”?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia, ↑FSH/LH → Klinefelter (47,XXY).

dsd-fragile-x.stem: A phenotypic 17-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea. She has normal breasts, scant pubic hair, a short blind-ending vagina, no uterus, and 46,XY karyotype with intra-abdominal testes. What is the defect?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Complete androgen insensitivity: a 46,XY individual with an X-linked androgen-receptor mutation. Testes make testosterone and AMH, so the uterus is absent, but androgen resistance yields female external genitalia and scant sexual hair.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What is the primary genetic cause of Fragile X syndrome?

options.text: Expansion of CGG repeats in FMR1
Translocation of SRY to the X chromosome

dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is caused by an expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene, leading to gene silencing.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: A 46,XY individual presents with primary amenorrhea and absent uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: This presentation is characteristic of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, where the individual has male testes but female external genitalia and no uterus.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: In which condition would you expect to find a 46,XX male with small testes and gynecomastia?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: 46,XX testicular DSD occurs when SRY is translocated to the X chromosome, leading to male phenotype with testicular development.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What is the mechanism by which complete androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to female external genitalia?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: In CAIS, the androgen receptor mutation prevents the body from responding to testosterone, resulting in female external genitalia despite the presence of testes.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: A 10-year-old boy with macro-orchidism and intellectual disability is evaluated. Which genetic test would confirm the diagnosis of Fragile X syndrome?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: FMR1 CGG repeat analysis is the definitive test for diagnosing Fragile X syndrome due to the characteristic repeat expansion.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: How does the presence of AMH affect the development of Müllerian structures in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: AMH causes regression of Müllerian ducts, leading to the absence of uterine structures in CAIS despite the presence of testes.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: A 46,XY individual with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome is evaluated. What finding would you NOT expect?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: In CAIS, the uterus is absent due to AMH action, and Müllerian structures do not develop.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: How does the mechanism of X-inactivation relate to the expression of Fragile X syndrome?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: X-inactivation can silence the FMR1 gene, which is crucial in understanding the expression of Fragile X syndrome in females.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: Which condition's clinical features can be linked to sex chromosome aneuploidies?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is a type of sex chromosome aneuploidy characterized by the presence of an extra X chromosome in males.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: Regarding uterus in complete androgen insensitivity — which is correct?

options.text: A 46,XY person raised female should have a uterus
In CAIS the uterus is ABSENT — the testes secrete AMH, which regresses the Müllerian ducts, while androgen resistance produces female external genitalia

dsd-fragile-x.explanation: AMH still works even though the androgen receptor does not, so Müllerian structures involute despite the female phenotype.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What best explains the finding: “46,XY girl, primary amenorrhea, no uterus, testes in inguinal canal”?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: 46,XY girl, primary amenorrhea, no uterus, testes in inguinal canal → Complete androgen insensitivity (AR mutation).

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What best explains the finding: “Boy with intellectual disability, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism”?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Boy with intellectual disability, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism → Fragile X (FMR1 CGG expansion).

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: A pedigree shows affected males in several generations, all connected through unaffected females, with no instance of an affected father having an affected son. What is the inheritance pattern?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Affected males transmitted through carrier females with no male-to-male transmission is classic X-linked recessive inheritance (e.g. hemophilia, G6PD deficiency).

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: What is the recurrence risk of an autosomal recessive disorder if both parents are carriers?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: If both parents are carriers, there is a 25% chance that their child will inherit both mutant alleles and express the disorder.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Which of the following is a hallmark of X-linked recessive inheritance?

options.text: Affected males can transmit the disorder to their sons.
Carrier females do not express the disease.
Affected females transmit the disorder to all their sons.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: In X-linked recessive inheritance, carrier females typically do not express the disease, while affected males transmit the disorder to all their daughters but not to their sons.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: A family presents with a genetic disorder affecting males predominantly, but affected males have unaffected fathers. What is the most likely inheritance pattern?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: The absence of affected fathers in a family with predominantly affected males suggests X-linked recessive inheritance.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Which of the following patterns of inheritance is characterized by the presence of affected individuals in every generation?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders are typically seen in every generation due to the presence of at least one affected allele.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: A mother with a mitochondrial disorder has two children. What is the likelihood that both children will inherit the disorder?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: All children of an affected mother will inherit the mitochondrial disorder, as it is passed maternally.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: In a pedigree showing a genetic disorder with male-to-male transmission, which inheritance pattern can be excluded?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked recessive inheritance, as affected males cannot pass the X chromosome to their sons.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: A patient with Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) has a family history of similar congenital heart defects. Considering Mendelian patterns, what is the most likely inheritance pattern observed?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Congenital heart defects like TOF often follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, especially with a family history.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: In a family with a history of cystic fibrosis, which inheritance pattern is most likely responsible for the disease's transmission?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, requiring both parents to be carriers for a child to be affected.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Regarding distinguishing x-linked from autosomal dominant — which is correct?

options.text: A disease affecting mostly males in a family must be X-linked
Look for male-to-male (father→son) transmission — its PRESENCE excludes X-linked inheritance (a father gives his son a Y, not his X)

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Sex bias alone is not enough; father-to-son transmission is the decisive feature that rules out X-linkage.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Disease in every generation, both sexes, father→son transmission”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Disease in every generation, both sexes, father→son transmission → Autosomal dominant.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Affected males linked through unaffected carrier females; no father→son”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Affected males linked through unaffected carrier females; no father→son → X-linked recessive.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mendelian Inheritance Patterns”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot has genetic components that may involve Mendelian inheritance patterns.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: In a family with an autosomal dominant disease, one man clearly transmitted the mutant allele from his affected father to his affected son but shows no symptoms himself. This best illustrates:
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: An obligate carrier who is phenotypically normal demonstrates incomplete (reduced) penetrance — the disease genotype is present but the phenotype is not expressed.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: What is the definition of incomplete penetrance?

options.text: All individuals with the genotype express the phenotype.
Some individuals with the genotype do not express the phenotype.
The severity of the phenotype varies among individuals with the same genotype.
The phenotype appears later in life for some individuals.

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Incomplete penetrance occurs when not all individuals with a disease genotype show the expected phenotype.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which condition is an example of pleiotropy?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Marfan syndrome is characterized by a single mutation affecting multiple organ systems, including the eyes, skeleton, and cardiovascular system.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: A family has a history of Huntington disease. The affected individuals show earlier onset and more severe symptoms in each generation. This phenomenon is known as:
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Anticipation refers to the worsening of symptoms and earlier onset of disease in successive generations, commonly seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: An unaffected individual is found to be an obligate carrier of a genetic disorder. This scenario exemplifies which concept?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: This scenario illustrates incomplete penetrance, where the carrier genotype does not result in the expected phenotype.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates penetrance from expressivity?

options.text: Penetrance is about severity; expressivity is all-or-none.
Penetrance is whether a phenotype appears; expressivity is the severity of the phenotype.
Penetrance only applies to dominant disorders.

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Penetrance refers to whether the phenotype appears at all, while expressivity refers to the severity of the phenotype when it does appear.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: How does genomic imprinting affect inheritance patterns?

options.text: It causes all alleles to be expressed equally.
It leads to parent-of-origin specific expression of alleles.
It results in all offspring being affected.
It eliminates the effects of environmental factors.

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Genomic imprinting results in the expression of genes depending on whether they are inherited from the mother or the father.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: A patient presents with symptoms of Marfan syndrome. Which of the following findings would best illustrate the concept of pleiotropy?

options.text: A family history of the same mutation causing different diseases.
Multiple organ systems affected by a single mutation.
A mutation that only affects the cardiovascular system.
Variable severity of symptoms among family members.

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Pleiotropy is demonstrated when a single mutation leads to effects in multiple organ systems, as seen in Marfan syndrome.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which of the following best connects the concepts of incomplete penetrance and multifactorial inheritance?

options.text: Both can affect the same phenotype.
Incomplete penetrance can complicate the assessment of multifactorial traits.
Both are examples of Mendelian inheritance.

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Incomplete penetrance can complicate the assessment of traits that are influenced by multiple genetic and environmental factors in multifactorial inheritance.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Regarding penetrance vs expressivity — which is correct?

options.text: Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are the same thing
Penetrance is whether the phenotype appears at all (all-or-none); expressivity is how severe it is when it does appear

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: They are separate modifiers — a mutation can be fully penetrant yet variably expressed, or incompletely penetrant.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unaffected obligate carrier between two affected relatives”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Unaffected obligate carrier between two affected relatives → Incomplete penetrance (nonpenetrance).

inheritance-modifiers.stem: What best explains the finding: “One mutation → lens, skeleton, and aortic disease”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: One mutation → lens, skeleton, and aortic disease → Pleiotropy (Marfan).

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complications of Single-Gene Inheritance”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Single-gene inheritance concepts may relate to congenital heart defects.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which should you review before “Complications of Single-Gene Inheritance”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Understanding Mendelian patterns is essential for grasping inheritance modifiers.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: An autosomal recessive disease has an incidence of 1 in 10,000. Approximately what is the carrier frequency in this population?
What is the recurrence risk for first-degree relatives of a proband with a multifactorial condition like cleft lip?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: The recurrence risk for first-degree relatives of a proband with a multifactorial condition is typically 2–4%.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: In the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, if the incidence of a recessive disease is 1/2500, what is the carrier frequency?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: For a disease incidence of 1/2500, the carrier frequency can be calculated as approximately 1/25.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: Which of the following best describes the liability-threshold model?

options.text: Disease is caused by a single gene mutation.
Environmental factors have no role in disease development.
A threshold of liability must be crossed for disease to manifest.
All individuals have the same risk of developing the disease.

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: The liability-threshold model states that many genes and environmental factors contribute to a continuous liability, and disease appears once a threshold is crossed.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: What is the correct interpretation of q² in the context of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

options.text: q² represents the incidence of homozygous recessive individuals.
q² is the total population frequency of the recessive allele.
q² is the frequency of carriers in the population.

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, q² represents the incidence of homozygous recessive individuals, while the carrier frequency is approximately 2q.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: Which of the following conditions demonstrates a high carrier frequency due to heterozygote advantage?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Sickle cell disease shows a high carrier frequency in malaria-endemic areas due to the heterozygote advantage.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: How does the heritability estimate for a trait like height relate to twin studies?

options.text: It is derived from the difference in height between identical twins.
It is calculated from the concordance rates of monozygotic and dizygotic twins.
It indicates that height is solely determined by genetics.
It shows that environmental factors have no impact on height.

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Heritability estimates are derived from twin concordance rates, comparing monozygotic and dizygotic twins.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: A patient with a family history of diabetes presents with symptoms. What is the expected recurrence risk for their first-degree relatives?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: The recurrence risk for first-degree relatives of a proband with a multifactorial condition like diabetes is typically 2–4%.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: In a population with a known incidence of a recessive genetic disorder, how can the carrier frequency be estimated?

options.text: By using the formula q² = incidence to find q.
By calculating the average age of onset.
By assessing the phenotypic expression in the population.
By determining the environmental factors affecting the population.

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: The carrier frequency can be estimated using the formula q² = incidence to find q, then applying it to calculate 2pq.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: Regarding meaning of q² in hardy-weinberg — which is correct?

options.text: The carrier frequency equals the disease incidence
q² is the disease (homozygote) incidence; the CARRIER frequency is 2pq ≈ 2q ≈ 2√incidence — much larger than the disease rate

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Carriers (2pq) vastly outnumber affected homozygotes (q²) for rare recessive diseases, which is why carrier screening matters.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrence ~2–4% in first-degree relatives of a cleft-lip/NTD proband”?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Recurrence ~2–4% in first-degree relatives of a cleft-lip/NTD proband → Multifactorial inheritance.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “CF incidence 1/2500 → carrier frequency 1/25”?
Which is a clinical application of “Multifactorial Inheritance & Population Genetics”?

options.text: Drugs for Urinary Frequency, Incontinence & Enuresis

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: Which should you review before “Multifactorial Inheritance & Population Genetics”?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Understanding Mendelian patterns is essential for grasping multifactorial inheritance.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks has a positive cell-free DNA (NIPT) result for trisomy 21. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to a decision based on the NIPT
Confirm with a diagnostic test such as CVS or amniocentesis

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: NIPT is a highly sensitive screen but not diagnostic; a positive result should be confirmed with an invasive diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis) that provides a fetal karyotype.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What is the primary purpose of serum screening tests in prenatal care?

options.text: To estimate risk of fetal abnormalities

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Serum screening tests are designed to estimate the risk of fetal abnormalities, not to provide definitive diagnoses.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Which of the following patterns on a quad screen is most indicative of Down syndrome?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: The classic quad screen pattern for Down syndrome includes ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, and ↑inhibin A.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What is the risk associated with chorionic villus sampling (CVS) when performed very early?

options.text: Increased risk of neural tube defects

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: CVS performed very early carries a slightly higher risk of miscarriage compared to later procedures.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Which test is recommended for confirming a positive non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT) result?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: A positive NIPT result must be confirmed with amniocentesis or CVS to obtain a definitive karyotype.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: In the context of prenatal screening, what does a positive quad screen indicate?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: A positive quad screen indicates an increased risk of fetal abnormalities, but does not confirm any condition.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: How does advanced maternal age influence prenatal screening recommendations?

options.text: It eliminates the need for screening tests
It is a risk factor for aneuploidy
It guarantees a positive NIPT result

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Advanced maternal age is a known risk factor for aneuploidy, prompting recommendations for screening.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Which prenatal screening test is most sensitive for detecting trisomy 21?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: NIPT is the most sensitive screening test for detecting trisomy 21, but positive results require confirmation.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What is the relationship between thalassemia carrier screening and prenatal care?

options.text: It is unrelated to prenatal screening
It is performed only after positive NIPT
It helps identify couples at risk for affected offspring
It is a diagnostic test for fetal conditions

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Thalassemia carrier screening helps identify couples at risk for having affected children, which is relevant in prenatal care.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Regarding acting on a screening result — which is correct?

options.text: A positive NIPT or quad screen confirms fetal Down syndrome
These are SCREENS — a positive result raises risk and must be confirmed by a diagnostic test (amniocentesis or CVS karyotype) before any irreversible decision

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Screening tests have false positives; a definitive karyotype is required to diagnose aneuploidy.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Quad screen: ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, ↑inhibin A”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Quad screen: ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, ↑inhibin A → Down syndrome risk pattern.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Elevated maternal serum AFP”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Elevated maternal serum AFP → Neural tube / abdominal wall defect.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Prenatal Screening & Diagnosis”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Gestational diabetes is a key aspect of prenatal diagnosis and care.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: A couple is screened before pregnancy. Both have low MCV; PCR confirms both carry α-thalassemia-1 (SEA deletion). What severe fetal condition is this pregnancy at risk for?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Two α-thalassemia-1 carriers risk a fetus with all four α-globin genes deleted (--/--), causing Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, which is lethal in utero — the couple should be offered prenatal diagnosis.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What is the primary goal of Thailand's national thalassemia-prevention program?

options.text: To increase public awareness of thalassemia

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: The program aims to identify at-risk carrier couples and offer prenatal diagnosis to prevent severe thalassemia phenotypes.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which laboratory finding is indicative of β-thalassemia trait?

options.text: Low MCV with normal iron studies
Low MCV with high iron studies

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: An HbA₂ level greater than 4% is a hallmark of β-thalassemia trait.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: In thalassemia screening, what does a low MCV indicate?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: A low MCV flags a possible thalassemia trait, necessitating further confirmatory testing.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which of the following tests is used to confirm α-thalassemia-1 trait?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: PCR for α-thal-1 is the confirmatory test when a low MCV is detected.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: If both partners are carriers of compatible thalassemia traits, what is the next step?

options.text: Reassure them and schedule a follow-up

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: When both partners are carriers, prenatal diagnosis is offered to detect an affected fetus.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: How does thalassemia screening relate to prenatal care risk screening?

options.text: Both focus on maternal health only

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Thalassemia screening and prenatal care risk screening both involve genetic testing to identify risks to the fetus.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What is a common clinical finding in a patient with Hb E trait?

options.text: Low MCV with normal iron studies
Positive DCIP with an Hb E band

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: A positive DCIP test with an Hb E band indicates the presence of Hb E trait.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which of the following is NOT a severe phenotype targeted by thalassemia prevention programs?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Sickle cell disease is not one of the severe phenotypes targeted by thalassemia prevention programs in Thailand.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What is the relationship between thalassemia screening and prenatal screening & diagnosis?

options.text: Both aim to prevent genetic disorders

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Both thalassemia screening and prenatal screening & diagnosis aim to prevent genetic disorders in offspring.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Regarding interpreting a low mcv in screening — which is correct?

options.text: A low MCV in a prospective parent just means iron deficiency
In thalassemia screening a low MCV flags a possible thalassemia trait and triggers confirmatory testing (α-thal-1 PCR, HbA₂/Hb typing) — iron deficiency must be excluded but not assumed
α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Microcytosis is the entry point of the screening algorithm; missing a thalassemia trait risks an affected fetus if the partner is also a carrier.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low MCV with normal iron studies + positive α-thal-1 PCR”?

options.text: α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Low MCV with normal iron studies + positive α-thal-1 PCR → α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops).

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What best explains the finding: “HbA₂ > 4% on Hb typing”?

options.text: α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: HbA₂ > 4% on Hb typing → β-thalassemia trait.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Thalassemia Carrier Screening & Prevention”?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Both involve screening during pregnancy, but focus on different conditions.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which should you review before “Thalassemia Carrier Screening & Prevention”?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Foundational knowledge on prenatal screening is essential for understanding thalassemia screening.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Which macronutrient provides the greatest energy per gram?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Triacylglycerol yields about 9 kcal/g, compared with about 4 kcal/g from carbohydrate or protein.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Which macronutrient yields the highest energy per gram?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Fat yields 9 kcal/g, making it the most energy-dense macronutrient.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: What is the primary role of dietary protein in the body?

options.text: Amino acid supply for synthesis and repair

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Dietary protein primarily supplies amino acids necessary for synthesis and repair.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: What occurs during a negative nitrogen balance?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: A negative nitrogen balance indicates that protein breakdown exceeds protein synthesis.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Which statement about energy density is correct?

options.text: Protein gives more energy per gram than fat
Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient
Carbohydrates yield more energy than protein
Alcohol is the least energy-dense macronutrient

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient, yielding 9 kcal/g.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: How does the body achieve energy balance?

options.text: By matching energy intake with expenditure

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Energy balance is achieved when energy intake equals energy expenditure.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Which monosaccharide is primarily absorbed in the intestine?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: All of the listed monosaccharides are absorbed in the intestine.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: What is the primary function of chylomicrons in lipid digestion?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Chylomicrons primarily transport dietary fatty acids from the intestine to other tissues.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Regarding energy density — which is correct?

options.text: Protein gives more energy per gram because it is structurally complex
Protein and carbohydrate each yield about 4 kcal/g; fat yields about 9 kcal/g
Highly reduced carbon and anhydrous storage

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Energy yield depends on chemical reduction and storage hydration, not structural complexity.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which transporter mediates apical fructose uptake into an enterocyte?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Fructose enters through apical GLUT5; glucose and galactose use SGLT1, then all exit through GLUT2.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which enzyme is primarily responsible for the initial digestion of starch in the mouth?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Salivary amylase initiates starch digestion by cleaving α-1,4 bonds.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: What is the role of SGLT1 in monosaccharide absorption?

options.text: Exports fructose out of the cell

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: SGLT1 cotransports glucose and galactose with sodium ions across the intestinal apical membrane.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: A patient presents with watery diarrhea and bloating after consuming dairy products. What is the most likely underlying cause?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Lactase deficiency leads to unabsorbed lactose in the lumen, causing osmotic diarrhea and fermentation.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which of the following statements about monosaccharide transport is true?

options.text: Glucose and galactose exit the cell via GLUT5
All monosaccharides are absorbed via GLUT2

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Fructose is specifically absorbed via the apical transporter GLUT5, while glucose and galactose use SGLT1.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: After consuming a glucose-galactose solution, a patient shows improvement in dehydration. What mechanism explains this?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: The intact Na⁺-glucose cotransport via SGLT1 drives water absorption, improving dehydration.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: How does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase contribute to carbohydrate absorption?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the sodium gradient essential for SGLT1 function.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: A patient with malabsorption presents with symptoms after carbohydrate intake. Which linked module could provide insights into their condition?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: The Clinical Patterns of Maldigestion & Malabsorption module would help understand the malabsorption symptoms.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which process is directly affected by lactase deficiency in carbohydrate metabolism?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Lactase deficiency results in unabsorbed lactose that is fermented by bacteria, leading to gas and diarrhea.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Regarding apical intestinal transport — which is correct?

options.text: Glucose/galactose use apical SGLT1, fructose uses apical GLUT5, and basolateral GLUT2 exports all three
Unabsorbed lactose retains water and is fermented
Intact Na⁺-glucose cotransport drives water absorption

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: The apical transporter depends on the identity of the monosaccharide.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Carbohydrate Digestion & Monosaccharide Absorption”?

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Loss of brush-border enteropeptidase most directly prevents activation of which enzyme?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic protease zymogens.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: What is the primary function of gastric acid in protein digestion?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Gastric acid denatures proteins, making them more accessible to enzymatic digestion.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Which enzyme is activated by enteropeptidase in the small intestine?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen to trypsin, initiating the activation cascade of pancreatic zymogens.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: A patient presents with protein maldigestion due to pancreatic insufficiency. What is the underlying mechanism?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Pancreatic insufficiency leads to reduced delivery of proteases and other digestive enzymes necessary for protein digestion.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Which transporter is primarily responsible for the absorption of di- and tripeptides in the intestine?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Di- and tripeptides are absorbed through the H⁺-dependent PepT1 transporter in the brush border of enterocytes.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: A patient with Hartnup disorder presents with neutral aminoaciduria. What is the underlying defect?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Hartnup disorder is caused by a defect in the neutral amino acid transporter, leading to aminoaciduria.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: In a patient with protein maldigestion, which finding would most likely be observed on urinalysis?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Neutral aminoaciduria occurs due to defects in amino acid transport, as seen in conditions like Hartnup disorder.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: How does the mechanism of protein absorption differ from that of carbohydrates?

options.text: Proteins are absorbed as whole molecules
Proteins require bile salts for absorption

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Carbohydrates are absorbed as monosaccharides, while proteins are absorbed as free amino acids or small peptides.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: What is a common clinical finding in patients with lipid malabsorption compared to protein malabsorption?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Fatty stools (steatorrhea) are characteristic of lipid malabsorption, whereas protein malabsorption may lead to different findings.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Regarding protease activation — which is correct?

options.text: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen; trypsin then activates the other pancreatic zymogens
Reduced delivery of proteases and other digestive enzymes

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: The key small-intestinal activation cascade begins at the brush border.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: Which apolipoprotein is required for intestinal chylomicron assembly?
lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: ApoB-48 is the structural apolipoprotein assembled with dietary lipid in enterocytes.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: What is the primary function of bile salts in lipid digestion?
lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat, increasing the surface area for pancreatic lipase action.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: Which component is primarily responsible for the hydrolysis of triglycerides in the intestine?
lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: Pancreatic lipase, aided by colipase, hydrolyzes triglycerides to free fatty acids and monoacylglycerol.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: What clinical finding is indicative of fat malabsorption?
lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: Bulky, greasy stools are characteristic of steatorrhea due to excess fecal fat.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: In the enterocyte, which of the following correctly describes the fate of lipid products?

options.text: They are absorbed whole from micelles
They are directly released into the bloodstream
They remain in the lumen for recycling

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: Lipid products leave the micelle and enter the enterocyte, where they are re-esterified into triglycerides.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: What is the consequence of a deficiency in bile salts?
