Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Airway compromise, seizure, and arrhythmia make tetany an intravenous-calcium emergency.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trousseau sign”?

options.text: Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Trousseau sign → Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Laryngospasm, stridor, or seizure”?

options.text: Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Laryngospasm, stridor, or seizure → Severe hypocalcemic tetany.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: Which should you review before “Hypoparathyroidism: Recognition & Treatment”?
hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Understanding hypoparathyroidism is essential for recognizing its treatment.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: An asymptomatic adult has a fasting plasma glucose of 120 mg/dL. How should this be classified?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: FPG 100-125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose/prediabetes; diabetes begins at 126 mg/dL and generally requires confirmation if asymptomatic.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What is the fasting plasma glucose level that confirms a diagnosis of diabetes?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: A fasting plasma glucose level of 126 mg/dL or higher is diagnostic for diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: Which of the following is a classic symptom of diabetes?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: Polyuria is one of the classic symptoms associated with diabetes due to osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: In an asymptomatic patient, when should an abnormal glucose result be confirmed?

options.text: Diagnose diabetes based on one test

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: An abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient should be confirmed with repeat testing unless there is unequivocal hyperglycemia.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What is the threshold for diagnosing GDM using the one-step approach?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: In the one-step approach for GDM, a fasting glucose level of 92 mg/dL or higher is diagnostic.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What is the primary mechanism for screening and diagnosing diabetes?

options.text: Screen risk -> confirm dysglycemia -> classify context

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: The mechanism involves screening for risk factors, confirming dysglycemia, and classifying the context of diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: A 25-week pregnant woman has a fasting glucose of 94 mg/dL during a 75-g OGTT. What does this indicate?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: A fasting glucose of 94 mg/dL is above the threshold for GDM diagnosis in the one-step approach.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: How does the diagnosis of GDM differ from nonpregnant diabetes?

options.text: GDM requires a higher fasting glucose
GDM is diagnosed only with symptoms

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: GDM uses specific glucose thresholds for diagnosis that differ from those used for nonpregnant diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What is the significance of a HbA1c level of 6.0% in a pregnant woman?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: An HbA1c level of 6.0% indicates prediabetes, which requires monitoring but not immediate treatment.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: Regarding confirming diabetes — which is correct?

options.text: Any single abnormal screening value permanently establishes diabetes
Confirm an abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient unless hyperglycemia is unequivocal; symptomatic random glucose >=200 or crisis is diagnostic
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes
Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: Biologic and preanalytic variation matter when the clinical picture is not definitive.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss with random glucose 220 mg/dL”?

options.text: Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes
One abnormal one-step threshold is enough for GDM
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss with random glucose 220 mg/dL → Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What best explains the finding: “FPG 120 mg/dL without symptoms”?

options.text: Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes
One abnormal one-step threshold is enough for GDM

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: FPG 120 mg/dL without symptoms → Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: Which should you review before “Diabetes Diagnosis, Screening & GDM”?

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Why can glucose be falsely low when whole blood remains at room temperature before plasma separation?

options.text: Blood cells continue consuming glucose by glycolysis
The kidney clears glucose from the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: RBCs and WBCs remain metabolically active in vitro and consume glucose; prompt separation or an antiglycolytic tube limits the fall.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What is the primary reason for measuring fasting plasma glucose after an 8-12 hour fast?

options.text: To ensure accurate measurement of glucose levels
To prevent interference from dietary carbohydrates

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: An 8-12 hour fast minimizes the influence of recent food intake, allowing for a more accurate measurement of baseline glucose levels.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Which method is considered the reference enzymatic method for glucose measurement?
glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: The hexokinase method is the reference standard for measuring plasma glucose due to its accuracy and reliability.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What is the expected effect of delayed separation of blood specimens on glucose measurement?
glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Delayed separation leads to ongoing glycolysis, which decreases the measured glucose levels by about 5-10 mg/dL per hour.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: A patient presents with hypoglycemic symptoms but has a normal reading on their continuous glucose monitor (CGM). What is the most likely explanation?
glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: The interstitial glucose measured by CGM lags behind blood glucose levels, especially during rapid changes.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Why is a home glucose meter not suitable for diagnosing diabetes?

options.text: It can only measure serum glucose
Point-of-care meter error is too variable
It is not calibrated for accuracy

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Home glucose meters are designed for monitoring and have variable accuracy, making them unsuitable for formal diagnosis.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: How does glucose transport relate to glycolysis in the context of glucose monitoring?

options.text: Glycolysis occurs independently of glucose transport
Glucose transport is inhibited during glycolysis

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Effective glucose transport into cells is essential for glycolysis to occur, as glucose must enter the cell to be metabolized.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What is the relationship between HbA1c testing and glucose monitoring?

options.text: HbA1c is a direct measure of current glucose
HbA1c provides an average of glucose over time
HbA1c is used for acute glucose management

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: HbA1c testing provides an average of blood glucose levels over the past 2-3 months, helping to assess long-term glucose control.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Regarding using a portable glucose meter for diagnosis — which is correct?

options.text: A home meter value alone can establish diabetes
Portable meters guide monitoring; diagnosis requires accepted laboratory plasma glucose or standardized HbA1c testing
Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Point-of-care meter error is too variable for formal diagnosis and screening.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unexpectedly low laboratory glucose after delayed separation”?

options.text: Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Unexpectedly low laboratory glucose after delayed separation → Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypoglycemic symptoms despite a normal CGM reading during rapid change”?

options.text: Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Hypoglycemic symptoms despite a normal CGM reading during rapid change → Interstitial sensor lag.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Which should you review before “Glucose Specimens, SMBG & CGM”?
glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Understanding glucose transport is essential for glucose monitoring.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Which marker best reflects glycemic control over the preceding 2-3 weeks when HbA1c is unreliable because of hemolysis?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Fructosamine reflects glycated serum proteins, mainly albumin, over about 2-3 weeks and is independent of RBC survival.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which HbA1c is formed?

options.text: Oxidative stress on red blood cells

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: HbA1c forms when glucose nonenzymatically binds to hemoglobin, specifically the N-terminal valine of the beta chain.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: In a patient with hemolytic anemia, what would you expect regarding their HbA1c levels?

options.text: Normal HbA1c despite high glucose levels
High HbA1c due to increased glycation
Low HbA1c due to shortened RBC lifespan

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Shortened RBC survival in hemolytic anemia reduces the time available for glycation, leading to falsely low HbA1c levels.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What is the typical diagnostic threshold for diabetes based on HbA1c?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: A HbA1c of 6.5% or greater is used to diagnose diabetes.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Which condition can falsely elevate HbA1c levels?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia can alter the RBC population, leading to falsely elevated HbA1c levels.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Fructosamine is particularly useful in monitoring glycemic control in which scenario?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Fructosamine reflects glycemic exposure over 2-3 weeks, making it useful after rapid changes in therapy.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: How does fructosamine differ from HbA1c in terms of glycemic exposure time?

options.text: Fructosamine reflects 8-12 weeks, HbA1c reflects 2-3 weeks
Fructosamine reflects 2-3 weeks, HbA1c reflects 8-12 weeks

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Fructosamine measures glycated proteins over 2-3 weeks, while HbA1c integrates glycemic exposure over 8-12 weeks.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: In the context of diabetes diagnosis, which test is complementary to HbA1c?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Random plasma glucose can be used alongside HbA1c for diagnosing diabetes, especially in acute settings.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Regarding interpreting hba1c in hemolysis — which is correct?

options.text: A normal HbA1c always proves average glucose is normal
Hemolysis can falsely lower HbA1c because RBCs are removed before accumulating their expected glycation
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation
Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: HbA1c measures glycemia filtered through erythrocyte lifespan.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low HbA1c despite frequent high glucose in hemolytic anemia”?

options.text: Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c
Fructosamine has the shorter integration window
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Low HbA1c despite frequent high glucose in hemolytic anemia → Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What best explains the finding: “High HbA1c in iron-deficiency anemia”?

options.text: Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation
Fructosamine has the shorter integration window

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: High HbA1c in iron-deficiency anemia → Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Which should you review before “HbA1c & Fructosamine”?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Foundational knowledge on HbA1c and its role in diabetes.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Why can a urine nitroprusside ketone test underestimate DKA severity?

options.text: It is positive only when pH is normal
It detects albumin rather than ketones

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Nitroprusside detects mainly acetoacetate. BHB is the dominant ketone in DKA, so direct blood BHB is preferred.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What is the principal ketone body produced during prolonged fasting or diabetic ketoacidosis?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone body produced in ketosis, especially during diabetic ketoacidosis.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Which urine test is most reliable for detecting ketones in diabetic ketoacidosis?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Urine nitroprusside strips primarily detect acetoacetate and may underestimate the severity of DKA; a urine BHB test would be more accurate.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: A patient presents with Kussmaul breathing and abdominal pain. What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Kussmaul breathing is a compensatory mechanism for metabolic acidosis, commonly seen in diabetic ketoacidosis.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What is the significance of a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) of 250 mg/g?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: An ACR of 250 mg/g indicates moderately increased albuminuria, which suggests early diabetic kidney injury.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: In a patient with suspected diabetic ketoacidosis, which finding would best support the diagnosis?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: High blood beta-hydroxybutyrate levels are indicative of ketosis and support the diagnosis of DKA.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: How does the presence of urinary tract infection (UTI) affect the interpretation of albuminuria in diabetes?

options.text: It has no effect on albumin levels

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: A UTI can transiently raise albumin levels, necessitating repeat testing for confirmation of albuminuria.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: A patient with hyperglycemia and altered consciousness has minimal ketosis. Which condition is most likely?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: The presentation of extreme hyperglycemia with minimal ketosis suggests hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS).

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: How does the management of diabetic ketoacidosis differ from hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state?

options.text: HHS requires more aggressive electrolyte monitoring

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Both conditions require insulin therapy, but their management strategies differ significantly in fluid and electrolyte management.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Which test is essential for monitoring glycemic control in patients with diabetes and potential kidney complications?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) is crucial for assessing kidney injury in diabetic patients, alongside glycemic control tests.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Regarding using urine ketones to follow dka — which is correct?

options.text: A urine nitroprusside strip quantifies the major circulating ketone
It detects acetoacetate but not BHB; use blood BHB with acid-base data for diagnosis and monitoring

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: BHB predominates in DKA, so urine strips can understate the active ketone burden.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, fruity breath”?

options.text: Possible transient albuminuria requiring repeat confirmation

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, fruity breath → Ketotic high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What best explains the finding: “Profound dehydration and altered consciousness without marked ketones”?

options.text: Possible transient albuminuria requiring repeat confirmation

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Profound dehydration and altered consciousness without marked ketones → HHS with hyperosmolar neuronal dehydration.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Which should you review before “Ketones, Albuminuria & Metabolic Complications”?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Understanding glycemic markers is essential for interpreting ketone levels in emergencies.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: A patient with diabetes has glucose 180 mg/dL, BHB 4.5 mmol/L, pH 7.20, and bicarbonate 12 mmol/L. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: No diabetic emergency because glucose is below 200

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: The patient has diabetes, significant ketonemia, and metabolic acidosis. DKA can occur with glucose below 200 mg/dL.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Which of the following is a required criterion for diagnosing DKA?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: DKA requires ketosis, which is indicated by BHB >=3 mmol/L or urine ketones >=2+.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: What is the primary mechanism leading to metabolic acidosis in DKA?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: In DKA, absolute insulin deficiency leads to increased ketone production, resulting in metabolic acidosis.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: A patient presents with Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, and abdominal pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: These symptoms are classic for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of HHS?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: HHS is characterized by very high glucose levels (>=600 mg/dL) without significant ketogenesis.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: In DKA, why might serum potassium levels be normal or high despite total-body potassium depletion?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Acidosis and lack of insulin cause potassium to shift out of cells, leading to normal or high serum potassium levels.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: A patient with diabetes presents with a blood glucose of 180 mg/dL, BHB of 4 mmol/L, and a pH of 7.2. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Euglycemic DKA can occur with glucose levels below 200 mg/dL if ketosis and metabolic acidosis are present.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: How does the presence of hyperglycemia in DKA differ from that in HHS?

options.text: Glucose levels are irrelevant in both

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: HHS typically presents with much higher glucose levels compared to DKA.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Which laboratory finding would help differentiate DKA from nutritional ketosis?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Serum bicarbonate levels <18 mmol/L are indicative of metabolic acidosis in DKA, distinguishing it from nutritional ketosis.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Regarding recognizing euglycemic dka — which is correct?

options.text: Glucose below 200 mg/dL rules out DKA
Ketosis plus metabolic acidosis can be DKA even with glucose below 200 mg/dL
Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: The diagnosis depends on all three components, and euglycemic DKA is a recognized presentation.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kussmaul breathing with fruity breath and abdominal pain”?

options.text: Acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells while urine loses K
Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Kussmaul breathing with fruity breath and abdominal pain → Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Profound dehydration with delirium or focal neurologic signs”?

options.text: Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA
Acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells while urine loses K

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Profound dehydration with delirium or focal neurologic signs → Hyperosmolar neuronal dehydration in HHS.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Which should you review before “DKA & HHS: Recognition and Diagnosis”?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Understanding glycemic markers is essential for diagnosing DKA and HHS.

dka-hhs-management.stem: A patient with DKA has serum potassium 3.1 mmol/L. What is the next treatment priority?

options.text: Give routine bicarbonate regardless of pH

dka-hhs-management.explanation: With K <3.5 mmol/L, potassium must be replaced before insulin because insulin will shift K intracellularly and can provoke life-threatening hypokalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What is the primary initial treatment for a patient with DKA?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: The core therapy for DKA includes IV crystalloid fluids to restore circulation and improve renal function.

dka-hhs-management.stem: When should insulin therapy be initiated in a patient with DKA?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Insulin therapy should be started after initial assessment and resuscitation, particularly after ensuring potassium levels are safe.

dka-hhs-management.stem: A patient with DKA presents with a potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L. What is the appropriate management?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: In cases of hypokalemia (K < 3.5 mmol/L), potassium must be replaced before starting insulin to prevent complications.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What clinical finding indicates that insulin therapy is effective in DKA?

options.text: Decreased blood glucose with persistent acidosis

dka-hhs-management.explanation: In DKA, blood glucose may decrease while acidosis persists; insulin must continue until acidosis resolves.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What is the recommended insulin infusion rate for moderate DKA?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: The standard infusion rate for moderate DKA is 0.1 U/kg/h to effectively manage the condition.

dka-hhs-management.stem: How does fluid resuscitation help in the management of DKA?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Fluid resuscitation helps restore perfusion and reduces counterregulatory hormones, aiding in glucose management.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Which electrolyte management strategy is crucial when starting insulin in DKA?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Monitoring potassium levels is crucial as insulin can cause potassium to shift into cells, leading to hypokalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: How does the management of DKA relate to body fluid compartments?

options.text: Fluid shifts are not significant in DKA
Fluid resuscitation affects intracellular fluid volume

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Fluid resuscitation in DKA affects both extracellular and intracellular fluid volumes, impacting overall fluid balance.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Why is potassium management critical in DKA treatment concerning renal function?

options.text: Renal function has no impact on potassium levels
Insulin therapy is safe regardless of renal status
Potassium does not shift in DKA

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Renal function is crucial as it determines potassium excretion; impaired renal function can lead to hyperkalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Regarding starting insulin in dka with hypokalemia — which is correct?

options.text: Insulin is always the first infusion because it reverses DKA
If K is <3.5 mmol/L, replace potassium and delay insulin until K is safely above 3.5
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose
Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Insulin can abruptly shift potassium into cells and cause fatal arrhythmia or respiratory-muscle weakness.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Falling glucose but persistent BHB/acidosis”?

options.text: Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia
Fluid strategy must be reduced/monitored in cardiac compromise
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Falling glucose but persistent BHB/acidosis → Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weakness or arrhythmia after insulin starts”?

options.text: Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose
Fluid strategy must be reduced/monitored in cardiac compromise

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Weakness or arrhythmia after insulin starts → Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DKA & HHS: Fluids, Insulin & Potassium”?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Clinical application of DKA management principles.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Which should you review before “DKA & HHS: Fluids, Insulin & Potassium”?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Understanding fluid compartments is essential for managing DKA.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: A thyrotoxic patient has fever, agitation, HR 145/min, and pulmonary edema. What is the correct early antithyroid sequence?

options.text: Thioamide, then iodide at least 1 hour later
Iodide, then thioamide the next day

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: In thyroid storm, block new synthesis with a thioamide before giving iodide to acutely block hormone release.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What is the most common trigger of thyroid storm?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Infection is the most common precipitant of thyroid storm.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Which score is used to assess the likelihood of thyroid storm?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: The Burch-Wartofsky score is specifically designed to evaluate the likelihood of thyroid storm.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: In thyroid storm, which clinical finding is most indicative of multiorgan decompensation?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Heart failure is a key sign of multiorgan decompensation in thyroid storm.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What is the first-line treatment for thyroid storm?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Thioamide is the first-line treatment to block thyroid hormone synthesis in thyroid storm.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Which of the following is a trap in managing thyroid storm?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: All listed options are traps; iodide must follow thioamide, and treatment should be based on clinical presentation, not T4 levels.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: A patient presents with hyperglycemia and altered mental status. Which condition could precipitate both thyroid storm and DKA?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Infection can trigger both thyroid storm and DKA, linking the two conditions.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: In the context of thyroid storm, which treatment would also be beneficial in managing DKA?
thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Insulin is crucial in managing DKA and can also help in controlling hyperglycemia associated with thyroid storm.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Regarding diagnosing and sequencing therapy in thyroid storm — which is correct?

options.text: Wait for a very high free T4, then give iodide before the thioamide
Treat on clinical multiorgan decompensation; give thioamide first and iodide at least 1 hour later
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Hormone level does not grade severity, and iodide must follow synthesis blockade.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, HR >=130, agitation/delirium, heart failure, or GI/hepatic dysfunction”?

options.text: Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Fever, HR >=130, agitation/delirium, heart failure, or GI/hepatic dysfunction → Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe storm despite only modest FT4/FT3 elevation”?

options.text: Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Severe storm despite only modest FT4/FT3 elevation → Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Which should you review before “Thyroid Storm: Recognition & Management”?

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which insulin component primarily covers fasting and between-meal glucose production?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Basal insulin restrains background hepatic glucose output; prandial insulin covers carbohydrate absorbed from meals.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which insulin decreases blood glucose levels?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Insulin primarily decreases blood glucose by increasing GLUT4 translocation in muscle and adipose tissue, enhancing glucose uptake.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which of the following is a common clinical finding in a patient experiencing hypoglycemia?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Tachycardia is an adrenergic symptom that occurs during hypoglycemia due to the body's response to low glucose levels.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: In type 2 diabetes, when should basal insulin be considered?

options.text: When catabolism or severe hyperglycemia is present

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Basal insulin is indicated in T2DM when there is catabolism or severe hyperglycemia, particularly with HbA1c >10% or glucose >=300 mg/dL.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What is a potential complication of repeated insulin injections at the same site?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Repeated injections at the same site can lead to lipohypertrophy or lipoatrophy, causing lumps or dents in the skin.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which insulin regimen best describes the combination of basal and prandial insulin?

options.text: Only basal insulin for all needs
Only prandial insulin for all meals
Basal insulin for fasting and prandial for meals
Basal insulin for meals and prandial for fasting

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: A physiologic insulin regimen combines basal insulin for fasting/inter-meal needs with prandial insulin for meals.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: In the context of insulin therapy, how does ketogenesis relate to insulin deficiency?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Insulin suppresses ketogenesis; its deficiency leads to increased ketone production, especially in uncontrolled diabetes.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: How do insulin secretagogues work in relation to insulin therapy?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Insulin secretagogues stimulate the pancreas to secrete more insulin, complementing insulin therapy in diabetes management.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Regarding role of basal versus prandial insulin — which is correct?

options.text: Basal insulin should be increased to correct every post-meal spike
Basal insulin controls fasting/inter-meal glucose; prandial insulin targets meal excursions
Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Using basal insulin to chase meals causes overnight or fasting hypoglycemia.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, then confusion”?

options.text: Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation
Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, then confusion → Adrenergic followed by neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weight loss, ketosis, and glucose >=300 mg/dL in T2DM”?

options.text: Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation
Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Weight loss, ketosis, and glucose >=300 mg/dL in T2DM → Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Therapy & Regimens”?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Understanding ketogenesis is crucial for managing insulin therapy.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Sulfonylureas increase insulin secretion by which beta-cell action?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: KATP-channel closure depolarizes the beta cell, opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and triggers insulin exocytosis.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Sulfonylureas close ATP-sensitive K+ channels on pancreatic beta cells, leading to depolarization and increased insulin secretion.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of insulin secretagogues?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Hypoglycemia is a class-defining adverse effect of insulin secretagogues due to their mechanism of increasing insulin secretion.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: In which condition are insulin secretagogues contraindicated?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Insulin secretagogues are ineffective in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus due to the absence of functioning beta cells.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What is a potential consequence of using glyburide in a patient with renal impairment?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Glyburide can accumulate in renal impairment, leading to an increased risk of prolonged hypoglycemia.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Why are insulin secretagogues ineffective in treating Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus?

options.text: They stimulate insulin release from non-functional beta cells
They can only work in the presence of functioning beta cells

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Insulin secretagogues require functioning beta cells to release insulin, which are absent in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: How do insulin secretagogues relate to the pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus?

options.text: They enhance insulin secretion from remaining beta cells

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Insulin secretagogues enhance insulin secretion from the remaining functional beta cells in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the role of insulin secretagogues in diabetes management?

options.text: They are the first-line treatment for all diabetes types
They are used to stimulate insulin release in patients with functional beta cells
They are effective in all stages of diabetes
They replace the need for insulin therapy

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Insulin secretagogues are specifically used to stimulate insulin release in patients with functional beta cells, primarily in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Regarding why secretagogues do not treat t1dm — which is correct?

options.text: Any drug that increases insulin can replace injected insulin
Secretagogues can only release insulin from functioning beta cells; T1DM has absolute beta-cell failure
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide
Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: The mechanism depends on a cellular reserve that T1DM lacks.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What best explains the finding: “Prolonged hypoglycemia in renal impairment”?

options.text: Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide
There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Prolonged hypoglycemia in renal impairment → Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What best explains the finding: “No useful response in T1DM”?

options.text: There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide
Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: No useful response in T1DM → There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Secretagogues”?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Knowledge of insulin synthesis and secretion is critical for understanding how secretagogues work.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which diabetes drug class increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slows gastric emptying, and commonly causes weight loss?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists combine glucose-dependent islet effects with satiety and delayed gastric emptying, producing weight loss.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Nausea is a common adverse effect associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action for DPP-4 inhibitors?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: DPP-4 inhibitors work by preventing the degradation of endogenous GLP-1, thereby enhancing the incretin signal.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: A patient on a GLP-1 receptor agonist presents with severe abdominal pain. What is the most likely concern?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Severe abdominal pain in a patient on GLP-1 therapy raises suspicion for pancreatitis.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates GLP-1 receptor agonists from DPP-4 inhibitors?

options.text: Both classes cause significant weight loss
GLP-1 RAs produce meaningful weight loss

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists are known to produce meaningful weight loss, unlike DPP-4 inhibitors which are generally weight neutral.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which incretin-based therapy is most appropriate for a patient with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Liraglutide is prioritized for patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk due to its benefits.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: How does obesity contribute to insulin resistance, impacting incretin-based therapy efficacy?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Obesity decreases insulin receptor sensitivity, which can affect the efficacy of incretin-based therapies.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What role does C-peptide play in assessing the effectiveness of incretin-based therapies?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: C-peptide levels reflect endogenous insulin secretion, which is important in evaluating the response to incretin-based therapies.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Regarding glp-1 ra versus dpp-4 inhibitor — which is correct?

options.text: Both incretin classes produce the same weight loss
GLP-1 receptor agonists produce meaningful weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors are generally weight neutral

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Direct pharmacologic receptor agonism is stronger than preservation of endogenous GLP-1.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nausea with marked weight loss after a weekly injection”?

options.text: DPP-4 inhibitor rather than GLP-1 receptor agonist

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Nausea with marked weight loss after a weekly injection → GLP-1 receptor agonist effect.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe persistent abdominal pain”?

options.text: DPP-4 inhibitor rather than GLP-1 receptor agonist

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Severe persistent abdominal pain → Possible pancreatitis on incretin-based therapy.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Incretin-based Therapy”?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Understanding insulin secretion is crucial for grasping incretin effects.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: A patient with T2DM and symptomatic heart failure should generally avoid which insulin-sensitizing class?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: TZDs activate PPAR-gamma but cause sodium/fluid retention, edema, weight gain, and can worsen heart failure.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of metformin in treating type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Increases insulin secretion from the pancreas
Stimulates glucose uptake in the intestines
Increases glucose absorption in the kidneys

metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Metformin primarily inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, which lowers blood glucose levels.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of metformin?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Diarrhea is a common gastrointestinal side effect associated with metformin use.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: A patient on long-term metformin therapy presents with macrocytic anemia. What is the most likely cause?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Long-term use of metformin can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, resulting in macrocytic anemia.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Which of the following statements about thiazolidinediones (TZDs) is true?

options.text: They are safe in patients with heart failure
They activate PPAR-gamma to improve insulin sensitivity
They are primarily used for type 1 diabetes

metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: TZDs activate PPAR-gamma, which improves insulin sensitivity, but they should be avoided in heart failure due to fluid retention.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: In the context of gluconeogenesis, which process is directly inhibited by metformin?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Metformin inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, which is closely related to the Cori cycle.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What is a significant risk associated with the use of TZDs in patients with a history of heart failure?

options.text: Fluid retention leading to worsening heart failure
Hypoglycemia due to increased insulin sensitivity

metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: TZDs can cause fluid retention, which may worsen heart failure symptoms.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What is the recommended eGFR threshold for avoiding metformin use?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Metformin should be avoided in patients with an eGFR <30 mL/min due to the risk of lactic acidosis.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication for the use of TZDs?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: TZDs should be avoided in patients with heart failure due to the risk of fluid retention.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Regarding choosing a sensitizer in heart failure — which is correct?

options.text: Pioglitazone is safe because it does not directly depress contractility
Avoid TZDs in heart failure because fluid retention can precipitate or worsen congestion

metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: The relevant toxicity is volume retention, not negative inotropy.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neuropathy with macrocytic anemia on long-term metformin”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Neuropathy with macrocytic anemia on long-term metformin → Vitamin B12 deficiency.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Edema and heart-failure worsening after pioglitazone”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Edema and heart-failure worsening after pioglitazone → TZD-associated fluid retention.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Sensitizers: Metformin & TZDs”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Gluconeogenesis is directly affected by metformin's mechanism.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: A patient with T2DM and heart failure needs another glucose-lowering drug. Which class is specifically prioritized in the lecture algorithm?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors are prioritized for T2DM with heart failure. TZDs can worsen fluid retention and are a poor fit.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of SGLT2 inhibitors?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors primarily work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney, leading to increased glucosuria.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause genitourinary infections due to increased glucose in the urine, which promotes bacterial growth.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure is being considered for medication. Which class of drugs should be prioritized?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: In patients with heart failure, SGLT2 inhibitors are prioritized due to their proven cardiovascular benefits.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: What is the expected clinical finding after administering an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors delay carbohydrate absorption, leading to fermentation in the colon and causing flatulence and diarrhea.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: In a patient with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes, which medication class is most appropriate?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors are beneficial in CKD patients with diabetes due to their renal protective effects and cardiovascular benefits.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Which of the following medications is most effective for lowering postprandial glucose levels?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors specifically target postprandial glucose by delaying carbohydrate absorption in the intestine.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes is experiencing dizziness and polyuria after starting a new medication. Which class of drugs is most likely responsible?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Dizziness and polyuria are common side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors due to glucosuria and osmotic diuresis.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: In a patient with type 2 diabetes and a history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, which medication should be prioritized for treatment?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors are preferred in patients with ASCVD due to their cardiovascular outcome benefits.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Regarding selecting therapy when a major comorbidity is present — which is correct?

options.text: Always choose the drug with the largest HbA1c reduction
In heart failure, CKD, or ASCVD, prioritize agents with outcome benefit even when another class lowers HbA1c more
Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition
Alpha-glucosidase inhibition leaves carbohydrate for colonic fermentation

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Modern diabetes pharmacotherapy treats cardiorenal risk as well as glucose.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Genital infection with polyuria and dizziness after a -gliflozin”?

options.text: Alpha-glucosidase inhibition leaves carbohydrate for colonic fermentation
Comorbidity pattern favoring an SGLT2 inhibitor
Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Genital infection with polyuria and dizziness after a -gliflozin → Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “T2DM with heart failure”?

options.text: Comorbidity pattern favoring an SGLT2 inhibitor
Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition
Alpha-glucosidase inhibition leaves carbohydrate for colonic fermentation

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: T2DM with heart failure → Comorbidity pattern favoring an SGLT2 inhibitor.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Which is a clinical application of “SGLT2, Alpha-glucosidase & Drug Selection”?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Understanding systemic effects of diabetes medications can relate to skin conditions.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Which should you review before “SGLT2, Alpha-glucosidase & Drug Selection”?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Knowledge of islet hormones is crucial for understanding diabetes treatment mechanisms.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: A child falls onto an outstretched hand and presents supporting the affected arm; a bump is felt over the clavicle. Where does this bone most commonly fracture?

options.text: At the junction of the middle and lateral thirds

pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The clavicle most commonly fractures at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds; the medial fragment is elevated by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment is depressed by the weight of the limb.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: What is the most common site of clavicle fracture?

options.text: Junction of middle and lateral thirds

pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The clavicle typically fractures at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, which is its weakest point.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: Which structure is primarily responsible for holding the scapula to the thorax?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The scapula is held to the thorax primarily by muscles, as there is no bony articulation.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: During a fall on the shoulder, which physical exam finding is most indicative of a clavicle fracture?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: A bump at the middle-third clavicle is a classic sign of a clavicle fracture.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: What anatomical feature of the scapula contributes to its mobility but also to its instability?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The shallow glenoid cavity allows for greater mobility but also increases instability of the shoulder joint.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: A patient presents with a fractured clavicle. Which muscle is responsible for pulling the medial fragment upwards?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle pulls the medial fragment of the clavicle upwards after a fracture.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: How does the anatomy of the pectoral girdle relate to the function of the brachial plexus?

options.text: It provides structural support to the plexus
It protects the plexus from injury
It facilitates nerve branching from the plexus
It anchors the plexus to the thorax

pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The pectoral girdle's anatomy allows for the branching of the brachial plexus, facilitating innervation of the upper limb.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: Which muscle's balance is crucial for maintaining scapular position and function?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: The serratus anterior muscle is essential for stabilizing the scapula against the thoracic wall.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: What is the relationship between the pectoral girdle and the hip joint during upper limb and lower limb coordination?

options.text: Both girdles are stabilized by ligaments
Muscle imbalances affect both girdles similarly
Both girdles allow for similar ranges of motion
They are connected via the axial skeleton

pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: Muscle imbalances can affect the stability and function of both the pectoral girdle and the hip joint.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: Regarding clavicle fracture site — which is correct?

options.text: The clavicle usually breaks at its sternal (medial) end
It fractures at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds — the weakest point and transition of its two curves

pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: This is the classic exam site; the medial fragment elevates (SCM) while the lateral drops with the limb.

pectoral-girdle-bones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fall on shoulder → bump at the middle-third clavicle, arm supported by other hand”?
pectoral-girdle-bones.explanation: Fall on shoulder → bump at the middle-third clavicle, arm supported by other hand → Clavicle fracture (commonest site).

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: After an axillary lymph node dissection, a patient cannot fully abduct the arm and the medial border of the scapula protrudes when she pushes against a wall. Which nerve was injured?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) supplies serratus anterior; injury causes a winged scapula and inability to abduct the arm above horizontal (loss of upward scapular rotation). It is vulnerable during axillary surgery.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Which nerve is primarily responsible for innervating the serratus anterior muscle?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) innervates the serratus anterior, which is crucial for scapular protraction and upward rotation.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: A patient presents with a winged scapula when pushing against a wall. Which nerve is likely injured?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: Injury to the long thoracic nerve causes serratus anterior weakness, leading to winging of the scapula.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Which muscle is primarily responsible for the upward rotation of the scapula during arm abduction above 90°?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The serratus anterior is essential for upward rotation of the scapula, allowing for full arm abduction.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: A patient has difficulty elevating their arm and exhibits a drooping shoulder. Which muscle is most likely weakened?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: Weakness of the trapezius muscle, innervated by CN XI, leads to shoulder droop and difficulty in arm elevation.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: What is the primary action of the pectoralis major muscle?

options.text: Adducts and medially rotates the arm

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The pectoralis major primarily adducts and medially rotates the arm.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Which of the following statements about serratus anterior function is true?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The serratus anterior protracts the scapula and holds it against the thorax.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: How does the pectoralis minor contribute to scapular stability?

options.text: By stabilizing and depressing the scapula

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The pectoralis minor stabilizes and depresses the scapula, contributing to overall scapular stability.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: In a patient with a long thoracic nerve injury, which of the following findings would you expect?

options.text: Medial scapular border lifts off the thorax

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: A long thoracic nerve injury leads to serratus anterior weakness, causing the medial scapular border to lift off the thorax.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: How does the function of the serratus anterior relate to the brachial plexus?

options.text: It is innervated by the medial cord
It is innervated by the long thoracic nerve from C5-C7
It is involved in shoulder flexion
It stabilizes the humerus during adduction

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The serratus anterior is innervated by the long thoracic nerve, which is derived from the brachial plexus (C5-C7).

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Which muscle's action is crucial for the upward rotation of the scapula during arm elevation, linking it to the pectoral girdle anatomy?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: The serratus anterior's action is essential for upward rotation of the scapula, which is a key function of the pectoral girdle.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Regarding cause of a winged scapula — which is correct?

options.text: Winged scapula results from trapezius (CN XI) injury
Classic winging is from serratus anterior weakness (long thoracic nerve) — the medial border lifts off the chest wall; CN XI injury droops the shoulder instead

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: Serratus anterior anchors the scapula to the thorax and rotates it upward; losing it lets the medial border wing out.

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Medial scapular border lifts off the back when pushing a wall”?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: Medial scapular border lifts off the back when pushing a wall → Serratus anterior palsy (long thoracic nerve).

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Drooping shoulder + weak arm elevation above horizontal”?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: Drooping shoulder + weak arm elevation above horizontal → Trapezius weakness (CN XI).

superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Superficial Back & Pectoral Muscles”?
superficial-back-pectoral-muscles.explanation: While not directly related, understanding anatomical spaces can aid in overall anatomical knowledge.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: A newborn delivered with shoulder dystocia holds the affected arm adducted and medially rotated with the forearm pronated ("waiter's tip"). Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Erb-Duchenne palsy from upper-trunk (C5–C6) injury gives the "waiter's tip" posture (loss of abduction, lateral rotation, and elbow flexion). Lower-trunk (C8–T1) injury is Klumpke palsy with a clawed hand.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which structure divides the axillary artery into three parts?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: What is the clinical presentation of Erb-Duchenne palsy?

options.text: Adducted, medially rotated arm, pronated forearm
Loss of sensation in the hand

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Erb-Duchenne palsy results in an adducted, medially rotated arm and a pronated forearm, often described as a 'waiter's tip' posture.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which nerve is most likely affected in a patient with winged scapula after axillary lymph node dissection?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: The long thoracic nerve is responsible for innervating the serratus anterior, and its injury leads to winged scapula.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which of the following correctly describes Klumpke palsy?

options.text: Lower trunk injury causing claw hand
Medial cord injury causing loss of elbow flexion
Posterior cord injury causing wrist drop

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Klumpke palsy is a lower trunk injury (C8-T1) leading to intrinsic hand muscle loss, resulting in a claw hand.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: What is the primary function of the brachial plexus?

options.text: Supply blood to the upper limb
Provide sensory innervation to the hand
Transmit motor signals to shoulder muscles
Route nerves to the upper limb

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: The brachial plexus routes nerves to the upper limb, providing motor and sensory innervation.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: How does the anatomy of the pectoral girdle relate to the brachial plexus?

options.text: It provides structural support for the brachial plexus
It is the site of brachial plexus injury
It influences the vascular supply to the plexus
It affects the range of motion of the upper limb

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: The pectoral girdle's anatomy provides structural support and is crucial for the positioning of the brachial plexus.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which spinal nerves contribute to the formation of the brachial plexus?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: The brachial plexus is formed from the ventral rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: What is the relationship between dermatomes and the brachial plexus?

options.text: Dermatomes are unrelated to the brachial plexus
Dermatomes are mapped to the roots of the brachial plexus
Dermatomes only apply to the lower limb
Dermatomes are only relevant for sensory nerves

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Dermatomes correspond to the sensory innervation provided by the roots of the brachial plexus.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Regarding erb vs klumpke palsy — which is correct?

options.text: A "waiter's tip" posture comes from a lower trunk (C8–T1) lesion
Waiter's tip is UPPER trunk (C5–C6) = Erb palsy; the lower trunk (C8–T1) lesion (Klumpke) causes a clawed hand from intrinsic muscle loss

axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Upper-trunk loss affects shoulder abductors/lateral rotators and elbow flexors; lower-trunk loss hits the small hand muscles.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Adducted, medially rotated arm, pronated forearm ("waiter's tip")”?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Adducted, medially rotated arm, pronated forearm ("waiter's tip") → Erb palsy (upper trunk C5-6).

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clawed hand + intrinsic muscle loss ± Horner”?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Clawed hand + intrinsic muscle loss ± Horner → Klumpke palsy (lower trunk C8-T1).

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Axilla & Brachial Plexus”?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Clinical relevance of spinal cord injuries relates to brachial plexus injuries.

axilla-brachial-plexus.stem: Which should you review before “Axilla & Brachial Plexus”?
axilla-brachial-plexus.explanation: Understanding the pectoral girdle is essential for grasping axilla anatomy.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: After an anterior shoulder dislocation, a patient cannot abduct the arm and has numbness over the lateral aspect of the upper arm ("regimental badge"). Which nerve is injured?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The axillary nerve (posterior cord, C5–C6) runs through the quadrangular space and is injured by shoulder dislocation or surgical-neck fracture, paralyzing the deltoid and numbing the "regimental badge" area over the lower deltoid.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: Which muscle initiates the first 15 degrees of shoulder abduction?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The supraspinatus is responsible for initiating the first 0-15° of abduction before the deltoid takes over.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: What is the most common clinical finding in a supraspinatus tear?

options.text: Loss of sensation over the arm

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: A painful arc of 60-120° of abduction is characteristic of supraspinatus impingement or tear.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: What nerve is most commonly injured in a surgical neck fracture of the humerus?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The axillary nerve is commonly injured in surgical neck fractures, leading to deltoid paralysis and sensory loss.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: What is the primary function of the rotator cuff muscles?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The rotator cuff muscles dynamically stabilize the humeral head in the shallow glenoid cavity.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: A patient presents with a flattened shoulder contour and loss of sensation over the lower deltoid area after an anterior shoulder dislocation. Which nerve is likely injured?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The axillary nerve is injured in anterior shoulder dislocations, causing deltoid paralysis and sensory loss in the 'regimental badge' area.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: In a patient with a humeral shaft fracture, which muscle is most likely to be affected due to radial nerve injury?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The radial nerve innervates the deltoid indirectly through the axillary nerve, and its injury can lead to loss of shoulder abduction.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: Which anatomical structure is primarily responsible for the painful arc syndrome in shoulder abduction?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch can impinge on the supraspinatus tendon during the painful arc of abduction.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: How does the anatomy of the shoulder region relate to lymphatic drainage in breast cancer?

options.text: Lymphatics drain to the axillary nodes
Lymphatics drain to the cervical nodes
Lymphatics drain to the thoracic duct
Lymphatics drain to the subclavian vein

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: The lymphatic drainage from the breast primarily goes to the axillary lymph nodes, which are closely associated with the shoulder region.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: Regarding which muscle initiates abduction — which is correct?

options.text: The deltoid initiates arm abduction from 0°
Supraspinatus initiates the first ~15°; the deltoid then abducts 15–90° — so a supraspinatus tear weakens the START of abduction

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: Deltoid has a poor mechanical angle at 0°, so the cuff (supraspinatus) begins the movement.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful arc 60–120° of abduction”?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: Painful arc 60–120° of abduction → Supraspinatus impingement/tear.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flattened shoulder + numb "regimental badge" area after dislocation”?
shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: Flattened shoulder + numb "regimental badge" area after dislocation → Axillary nerve injury.

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Shoulder Region & Rotator Cuff”?

options.text: Breast Gross Anatomy, Blood Supply & Lymphatics

shoulder-region-rotator-cuff.explanation: Breast anatomy is adjacent to shoulder structures.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: A midshaft humeral fracture is complicated by inability to extend the wrist and fingers and numbness over the dorsal first web space. Which nerve is injured?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove against the humeral midshaft; injury there causes wrist drop (loss of wrist/finger extension) and sensory loss over the dorsal web space.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: Which nerve is most likely injured in a midshaft humeral fracture?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The radial nerve is located in the radial groove of the humerus and is at risk during midshaft fractures.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: What is the primary blood supply to the anterior compartment of the arm?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The brachial artery is the main blood supply to the anterior compartment, which includes muscles like biceps brachii.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: A patient presents with wrist drop after a humeral fracture. Which nerve is affected?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: Wrist drop indicates radial nerve injury, commonly associated with midshaft humeral fractures.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: Which muscle is primarily responsible for forearm flexion in all positions?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The brachialis is the main flexor of the forearm, functioning regardless of forearm position.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: What is the risk associated with a supracondylar humeral fracture?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: Supracondylar fractures can injure the brachial artery, leading to Volkmann ischemic contracture.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: Which structure is at risk during a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The axillary nerve is at risk during surgical neck fractures, leading to deltoid weakness.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: How does a midshaft humeral fracture affect the radial nerve?

options.text: Leads to numbness in the hand

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: A midshaft humeral fracture can injure the radial nerve, resulting in wrist drop due to loss of extensor function.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: A child presents with a humeral fracture. Which classification system is most relevant for understanding the injury?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The Salter-Harris classification is crucial for pediatric fractures as it describes growth plate involvement.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: In assessing a humeral fracture, which aspect of the cubital fossa is important for surgical intervention?
arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: Understanding the brachial artery's location in the cubital fossa is critical for managing humeral fractures.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: Regarding nerve injured by a midshaft humeral fracture — which is correct?

options.text: A midshaft humeral fracture injures the axillary nerve
Midshaft (radial groove) fractures injure the RADIAL nerve → wrist drop; the axillary nerve is injured at the SURGICAL NECK
Brachial artery injury → Volkmann contracture risk

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: The radial nerve lies in the spiral groove against the midshaft, so that is the fracture level that threatens it.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: What best explains the finding: “Wrist drop + numb dorsal web space after a midshaft humeral fracture”?

options.text: Brachial artery injury → Volkmann contracture risk

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: Wrist drop + numb dorsal web space after a midshaft humeral fracture → Radial nerve injury (radial groove).

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent radial pulse + pain after a supracondylar fracture”?

options.text: Brachial artery injury → Volkmann contracture risk

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.explanation: Absent radial pulse + pain after a supracondylar fracture → Brachial artery injury → Volkmann contracture risk.

arm-compartments-humerus-fractures.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Arm Compartments & Humerus Fractures”?

cubital-fossa.stem: Which structures lie in the cubital fossa, listed from lateral to medial?

options.text: Median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon
Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Brachial artery, biceps tendon, median nerve
Biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery

cubital-fossa.explanation: From lateral to medial the cubital fossa contains the biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, and median Nerve ("TAN"). The brachial artery bifurcates here into the radial and ulnar arteries.

cubital-fossa.stem: Which structure is NOT found in the cubital fossa?
cubital-fossa.explanation: The ulnar nerve is not a structure found in the cubital fossa; it runs posterior to the medial epicondyle.

cubital-fossa.stem: What is the correct order of structures in the cubital fossa from lateral to medial?

options.text: Median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon
Brachial artery, median nerve, biceps tendon
Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery

cubital-fossa.explanation: The mnemonic TAN helps remember the order: biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.

cubital-fossa.stem: Which clinical sign indicates the location of the brachial artery in the cubital fossa?

options.text: Brachial pulse medial to the biceps tendon

cubital-fossa.explanation: The brachial pulse is palpated medial to the biceps tendon, indicating the position of the brachial artery.

cubital-fossa.stem: What is the primary function of the bicipital aponeurosis in the cubital fossa?
cubital-fossa.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis serves as a protective layer for the underlying brachial artery and median nerve.

cubital-fossa.stem: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, which anatomical structure in the cubital fossa could be at risk during venipuncture?
cubital-fossa.explanation: The brachial artery lies deep to the median cubital vein and is at risk during venipuncture.

cubital-fossa.stem: A fracture of the humerus could potentially affect which structure in the cubital fossa?
cubital-fossa.explanation: A humeral fracture can lead to median nerve injury, which is located in the cubital fossa.

cubital-fossa.stem: Regarding order of cubital fossa contents — which is correct?

options.text: The median nerve lies lateral to the brachial artery in the fossa
From lateral to medial it is biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve — the median nerve is the most MEDIAL of the three
Brachial artery position in the fossa

cubital-fossa.explanation: The mnemonic TAN fixes the order; the artery lies between the tendon and the nerve.

cubital-fossa.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brachial pulse medial to the biceps tendon”?

options.text: Brachial artery under the bicipital aponeurosis
Brachial artery position in the fossa

cubital-fossa.explanation: Brachial pulse medial to the biceps tendon → Brachial artery position in the fossa.

cubital-fossa.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blood drawn from the median cubital vein”?

options.text: Brachial artery position in the fossa
Brachial artery under the bicipital aponeurosis

cubital-fossa.explanation: Blood drawn from the median cubital vein → Superficial vein in the roof.

cubital-fossa.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cubital Fossa”?

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: A young adult falls on an outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, but the initial wrist radiograph is normal. What is the best management?

options.text: Immobilize and re-image (or MRI) for a probable scaphoid fracture

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH indicates a scaphoid fracture even when early X-rays are negative; immobilize and re-image or obtain MRI, because a missed fracture risks avascular necrosis and non-union.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: What is the most common carpal bone to fracture due to a fall on an outstretched hand?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, particularly from a fall on an outstretched hand.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: Which fracture is characterized by dorsal displacement of the distal radius?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: A Colles fracture is defined by dorsal displacement of the distal radius, often resulting in a 'dinner-fork' deformity.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: What is the mechanism of injury for a Colles fracture?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: A Colles fracture typically occurs from falling on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: A patient presents with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. What should be the next step in management?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a scaphoid fracture, which may not be visible on initial X-rays; immobilization and re-imaging are crucial.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: What complication is associated with a scaphoid fracture if not properly managed?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Scaphoid fractures can lead to avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment due to its unique blood supply.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: A patient with a distal radius fracture presents with median nerve symptoms. What is the likely cause?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Lunate dislocation can compress the median nerve, leading to acute carpal tunnel syndrome after wrist trauma.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: How does a Galeazzi fracture differ from a Monteggia fracture?

options.text: Galeazzi involves the ulna; Monteggia involves the radius
Galeazzi involves the distal radius; Monteggia involves the proximal ulna
Galeazzi is a wrist fracture; Monteggia is a forearm fracture
Galeazzi is a stable fracture; Monteggia is unstable

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: A Galeazzi fracture involves a fracture of the distal radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint, whereas a Monteggia fracture involves a fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: Which of the following findings would suggest a scaphoid fracture in a patient with wrist trauma?
radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox is a classic sign of a scaphoid fracture following wrist trauma.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: Regarding snuffbox tenderness with a "normal" x-ray — which is correct?

options.text: A normal initial wrist X-ray rules out a scaphoid fracture
Scaphoid fractures are often radiographically occult early — with snuffbox tenderness, immobilize and re-image (or MRI) to avoid AVN/non-union

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Missing a scaphoid fracture risks avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment because its blood supply runs distal-to-proximal.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dinner-fork deformity after a fall on an outstretched hand”?

options.text: Lunate dislocation compressing the median nerve

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Dinner-fork deformity after a fall on an outstretched hand → Colles fracture (dorsally displaced distal radius).

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox”?

options.text: Lunate dislocation compressing the median nerve

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.explanation: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox → Scaphoid fracture.

radius-ulna-carpals-fractures.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Radius, Ulna, Carpal Bones & Fractures”?
