academic-authorship.stem: A senior professor is added as a co-author solely because they head the department, without any contribution to the study. This is:
academic-authorship.explanation: Crediting a non-contributor for prestige is gift/honorary authorship — unethical. Ghost authorship is the opposite: a real contributor left off the list.

academic-authorship.stem: Which contribution, on its own, satisfies the ICMJE criteria for authorship?

options.text: Only general supervision of the group
None alone — all four ICMJE criteria (contribution, drafting/revising, final approval, accountability) must be met

academic-authorship.explanation: ICMJE requires ALL four criteria together. Funding, supervision, or data collection alone are insufficient and warrant Acknowledgement rather than authorship.

academic-authorship.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for authorship according to ICMJE criteria?

options.text: Substantial contribution to conception or design
Final approval of the version to be published

academic-authorship.explanation: Providing funding alone does not meet the ICMJE criteria for authorship.

academic-authorship.stem: What is the primary role of the corresponding author in a research paper?

options.text: To conduct the majority of the research

academic-authorship.explanation: The corresponding author is responsible for handling submission and communication regarding the manuscript.

academic-authorship.stem: Which term describes the unethical practice of crediting someone who did not contribute to the research?
academic-authorship.explanation: Gift authorship refers to crediting individuals who did not contribute to the research work.

academic-authorship.stem: In the context of authorship, what does 'ghost authorship' refer to?

options.text: Including a non-contributor as an author
Excluding a contributor from the author list
Using someone else's ideas without credit

academic-authorship.explanation: Ghost authorship occurs when a real contributor is deliberately left off the author list.

academic-authorship.stem: Which of the following actions would be considered research misconduct under FFP?

options.text: Including all contributors in the acknowledgments
Altering data to fit a hypothesis
Submitting a manuscript to multiple journals
Providing proper citations for borrowed ideas

academic-authorship.explanation: Altering data to fit a hypothesis is considered falsification, a form of research misconduct.

academic-authorship.stem: How does the ICMJE define the role of a first author?

options.text: The one who contributed the least
The one who did the most work
The one who handled the manuscript submission
The one who approved the final version

academic-authorship.explanation: The first author is typically the individual who contributed the most work to the research and manuscript.

academic-authorship.stem: How can authorship disputes be prevented according to best practices?

options.text: Agree on authorship roles after submission
Discuss and agree on order and roles at the start
Include all contributors regardless of their input

academic-authorship.explanation: Preventing authorship disputes involves agreeing on authorship roles and order at the beginning of the project.

academic-authorship.stem: A researcher is diagnosed with diabetes. Which of the following criteria would be relevant for their management according to the linked module on diabetes diagnostic criteria (hen1-diabetes-diagnostic-criteria)?
academic-authorship.explanation: Fasting blood glucose levels are part of the diagnostic criteria for diabetes management.

academic-authorship.stem: In a study involving patients with pericardial effusion, which aspect of authorship would be critical to ensure ethical reporting of results according to the linked module on pericardial effusion (pericardial-effusion)?

options.text: Gift authorship of a senior physician
Ghost authorship by a medical writer

academic-authorship.explanation: Final approval of the manuscript is essential to ensure accountability and integrity in reporting results.

academic-authorship.stem: Regarding does funding earn authorship? — which is correct?

options.text: Providing the grant money or being the department head automatically makes you an author
Funding or supervision alone does NOT meet ICMJE criteria; without intellectual contribution + drafting + approval + accountability, that person belongs in Acknowledgements
ALL four required to be listed as an author
Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical

academic-authorship.explanation: Adding a non-contributor for status is gift/honorary authorship — explicitly unethical under ICMJE.

academic-authorship.stem: What best explains the finding: “ICMJE = contribution + drafting/revising + final approval + accountability”?

options.text: Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical
Real contributor deliberately left off the author list — unethical
ALL four required to be listed as an author

academic-authorship.explanation: ICMJE = contribution + drafting/revising + final approval + accountability → ALL four required to be listed as an author.

academic-authorship.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gift/honorary authorship”?

options.text: ALL four required to be listed as an author
Real contributor deliberately left off the author list — unethical
Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical

academic-authorship.explanation: Gift/honorary authorship → Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical.

academic-authorship.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Academic Authorship: ICMJE Criteria, Order & Misconduct”?

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which cell is the principal "bridge" that links the innate and adaptive immune responses by presenting antigen to naïve T cells?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Dendritic cells capture antigen, mature, migrate to lymph nodes, and present it on MHC to naïve T cells — bridging innate and adaptive immunity. They are the most potent antigen-presenting cells.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: The surface phenotype CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ identifies which cell?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Regulatory T cells are CD4⁺CD25⁺ and express the master transcription factor FoxP3; they suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which immune cell is the first responder to acute bacterial infections?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at the site of acute bacterial infections due to their rapid response.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What is the primary function of dendritic cells in the immune system?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which of the following statements about immune memory is true?

options.text: Innate immunity develops memory after repeated exposure
Only adaptive immunity has classical memory
Macrophages are responsible for immunological memory

immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Only adaptive immunity, involving B and T lymphocytes, has classical memory, allowing for faster and stronger responses upon re-exposure.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which cell type is characterized by the expression of CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ identifies regulatory T cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining self-tolerance.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What is the primary role of B cells in the immune response?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: B cells are responsible for producing antibodies, which are essential for humoral immunity against extracellular pathogens.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: How do innate immune cells recognize pathogens?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Innate immune cells recognize pathogens using pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) that detect broad microbial patterns.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: How does the skin contribute to the immune response?

options.text: By serving as a physical barrier and housing immune cells

immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: The skin acts as a physical barrier and contains immune cells that help to prevent pathogen entry, linking to the skin immune system module.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which immune cells are primarily involved in the response to intracellular pathogens?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD8⁺ T cells are primarily responsible for the cell-mediated immune response against intracellular pathogens.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What is the role of regulatory T cells in the immune system?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Regulatory T cells suppress immune reactions to maintain self-tolerance and prevent autoimmunity.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Regarding which arm has memory? — which is correct?

options.text: Innate immunity develops memory after repeated exposure
Only ADAPTIVE immunity (lymphocytes) has classical memory; innate responds identically each time

immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Memory = faster/stronger secondary response, a defining feature of B/T lymphocytes, not neutrophils/macrophages.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD3 on a lymphocyte”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD3 on a lymphocyte → Pan-T-cell marker.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ T cell”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ T cell → Regulatory T cell (self-tolerance).

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Skin immune cells are part of the innate immune response.

lymphoid-organs.stem: In a lymph node, the paracortex is populated predominantly by:
lymphoid-organs.explanation: The paracortex is the T-cell zone (with dendritic cells presenting antigen). B cells reside in cortical follicles; plasma cells accumulate in the medulla.

lymphoid-organs.stem: A splenectomised patient is at particularly high risk of overwhelming infection by:
lymphoid-organs.explanation: The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria and supports antibody responses to them, so asplenia predisposes to overwhelming pneumococcal/meningococcal/Haemophilus sepsis — hence vaccination.
B cells mature in the bone marrow, while T cells mature in the thymus.

lymphoid-organs.stem: What is the primary function of the spleen?

options.text: Filtration of blood and immune response

lymphoid-organs.explanation: The spleen filters blood and plays a critical role in the immune response, particularly against encapsulated bacteria.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which lymphoid organ is responsible for T cell maturation?
lymphoid-organs.explanation: The thymus is the organ where T cells mature through positive and negative selection.

lymphoid-organs.stem: What is indicated by the presence of germinal centers in lymphoid follicles?
lymphoid-organs.explanation: Germinal centers indicate an active B cell response involving affinity maturation and class switching.

lymphoid-organs.stem: A patient presents with overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis after splenectomy. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

lymphoid-organs.explanation: The spleen is critical for clearing encapsulated bacteria, and its absence predisposes to infections.

lymphoid-organs.stem: How do follicular helper T (Tfh) cells assist B cells in germinal centers?

options.text: By promoting class switching and affinity maturation

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Tfh cells help B cells undergo class switching and affinity maturation in germinal centers.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which lymphoid organ is primarily involved in filtering lymph and activating immune responses?
lymphoid-organs.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph and are sites where mature lymphocytes meet antigens and become activated.

lymphoid-organs.stem: How does the function of lymph nodes relate to the overall immune response?

options.text: They are sites for lymphocyte activation and proliferation

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Lymph nodes are critical for lymphocyte activation and proliferation upon encountering antigens.

lymphoid-organs.stem: What is the consequence of thymic hypoplasia in a patient?
lymphoid-organs.explanation: Thymic hypoplasia leads to decreased T cell maturation, resulting in T cell deficiency.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Regarding where do b cells mature? — which is correct?

options.text: B cells mature in the thymus like T cells
B cells mature in the BONE MARROW; the thymus is for T-cell maturation

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Both begin in marrow, but only T cells migrate to the thymus to mature. "B = Bone marrow, T = Thymus."

lymphoid-organs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Germinal centre in a lymphoid follicle”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Germinal centre in a lymphoid follicle → Active B-cell response (affinity maturation/class switch).

lymphoid-organs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis post-splenectomy”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis post-splenectomy → Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Lymphoid Organs: Primary & Secondary”?

options.text: Pudendal Neurovasculature, Erectile Tissues & External Genitalia

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Understanding lymphoid organs can provide context for immune responses in genitalia.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which should you review before “Lymphoid Organs: Primary & Secondary”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Understanding immune cells is essential for grasping lymphoid organ functions.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which Toll-like receptor recognises lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR4 (cell surface) recognises LPS; TLR3 = dsRNA, TLR7 = ssRNA, TLR9 = CpG DNA (all endosomal nucleic-acid sensors).

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Pattern-recognition receptors differ from antibodies and T-cell receptors in that they are:

options.text: Germline-encoded and recognise conserved microbial patterns
Specific for a single unique epitope

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: PRRs are germline-encoded, non-clonal, and recognise conserved PAMPs/DAMPs. Antigen-specific diversity via somatic recombination is unique to the adaptive BCR/TCR.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)?

options.text: It is located exclusively in the cytoplasm

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR4 is a surface PRR that specifically recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What is the primary signaling outcome of PRR engagement?

options.text: Activation of NF-κB and inflammatory cytokines

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: PRR engagement primarily leads to the activation of NF-κB, resulting in the production of inflammatory cytokines.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which of the following findings is indicative of acute inflammation?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Fever and elevated CRP levels are hallmark signs of the acute-phase response during acute inflammation.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What is the role of neutrophils in acute inflammation?

options.text: They are the first responders to infection

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Neutrophils are the first responders to sites of infection and play a crucial role in the innate immune response.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which statement correctly describes the specificity of pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs)?

options.text: PRRs are highly specific and clonally rearranged
PRRs recognize conserved patterns shared by many pathogens
PRRs are only found in adaptive immunity
PRRs can mutate to recognize new antigens

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: PRRs are germline-encoded and recognize conserved patterns (PAMPs), not unique antigens like antibodies.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: How does the innate immune response relate to renal defense mechanisms?

options.text: Both rely on adaptive immunity for pathogen recognition
Innate immune cells in the kidney respond to pathogens
Renal defense mechanisms are solely chemical barriers
Both systems utilize the same types of antibodies

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: The innate immune response includes immune cells in the kidneys that respond to pathogens, enhancing renal defense mechanisms.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What is the connection between PRRs and the skin immune system?

options.text: PRRs are only present in the skin
Skin PRRs detect pathogens and initiate inflammation
The skin immune system does not involve PRRs
PRRs are exclusively found in the bloodstream

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: PRRs in the skin detect pathogens and initiate inflammatory responses, playing a crucial role in skin immunity.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Regarding are prrs specific/clonal like antibodies? — which is correct?

options.text: Each PRR is clonally rearranged to recognise one unique antigen
PRRs are germline-encoded and recognise conserved shared PATTERNS (PAMPs) — not somatically rearranged like BCR/TCR

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Innate receptors are fixed and pattern-based; only adaptive receptors (Ig/TCR) are diverse and antigen-specific via V(D)J recombination.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What best explains the finding: “TLR4 recognising bacterial LPS”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR4 recognising bacterial LPS → Surface PRR for Gram-negative endotoxin.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What best explains the finding: “TLR9 recognising CpG DNA in an endosome”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR9 recognising CpG DNA in an endosome → Endosomal nucleic-acid sensing (viral/bacterial).

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Innate Immunity: Barriers, PRRs & Inflammation”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Renal defense mechanisms involve innate immune responses relevant to inflammation.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which should you review before “Innate Immunity: Barriers, PRRs & Inflammation”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Understanding innate immunity requires knowledge of the overall immune system.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: A virus down-regulates MHC class I on infected cells to evade cytotoxic T cells. Which innate cell is specifically triggered to kill these cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: Loss of MHC I removes the inhibitory signal to NK cells ("missing self"), triggering NK killing via perforin/granzyme — complementing CTLs, which require MHC I.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which cytokines are the principal ANTIVIRAL interferons that induce an antiviral state in neighbouring cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: Type I interferons (α/β) are produced by virus-infected cells and induce an antiviral state. IFN-γ (type II) mainly activates macrophages and is made by Th1/NK cells.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which NK cells recognize and kill virus-infected cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells identify and kill cells that have down-regulated MHC class I, a phenomenon known as 'missing self'.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which cytokine is primarily responsible for inducing an antiviral state in neighboring cells during a viral infection?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: Type I interferons (IFN-α/β) are key antiviral cytokines that induce an antiviral state in neighboring cells.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What is the role of CD16 on NK cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: CD16 (FcγRIII) on NK cells binds to the Fc region of IgG-coated target cells, facilitating antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which statement correctly describes the function of NK cells?

options.text: NK cells require prior sensitization to kill target cells
NK cells are inhibited by healthy cells displaying MHC class I
NK cells primarily kill cells with high levels of MHC class I
NK cells only kill tumor cells

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells are inhibited by the presence of MHC class I on healthy cells, allowing them to target cells that have lost MHC class I.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: In the context of skin immune responses, which innate immune cell type is primarily responsible for recognizing and responding to viral infections?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells play a crucial role in the innate immune response to viral infections by recognizing and killing infected cells.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: How do NK cells and CD8 cytotoxic T cells differ in their recognition of infected cells?

options.text: NK cells require MHC class I, while CD8 T cells do not
CD8 T cells kill without prior sensitization, while NK cells require it
NK cells kill cells that lose MHC class I, while CD8 T cells require MHC class I
Both kill cells through the same mechanism

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells kill cells that have down-regulated MHC class I, whereas CD8 T cells require the presence of MHC class I to recognize and kill infected cells.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Regarding nk cell target recognition — which is correct?

options.text: NK cells kill cells that display high levels of MHC class I
NK cells kill cells that LOSE/down-regulate MHC I ("missing self"); MHC I on healthy cells INHIBITS them

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: This is the mirror image of CTLs (which require MHC I) — NK cells cover the viral immune-evasion escape route.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What best explains the finding: “NK kills a cell that has lost MHC class I”?

options.text: Type II IFN (Th1/NK) — distinct from antiviral IFN-α/β

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK kills a cell that has lost MHC class I → "Missing self" removes inhibitory signal.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What best explains the finding: “NK kills an IgG-coated target via CD16”?

options.text: Type II IFN (Th1/NK) — distinct from antiviral IFN-α/β

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK kills an IgG-coated target via CD16 → ADCC (FcγRIII).

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which is a clinical application of “NK Cells, Interferons & Innate Effectors”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells can be involved in skin immune responses, linking basic science to clinical applications.

antibody-structure.stem: The antigen-binding specificity of an antibody is determined primarily by the:

options.text: Hypervariable (CDR) loops of the variable regions

antibody-structure.explanation: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs/hypervariable regions) of the heavy and light variable domains form the antigen-binding pocket. The Fc/constant region governs effector function.

antibody-structure.stem: Which region of the immunoglobulin molecule determines its isotype (class) and effector functions such as complement activation?

options.text: The variable region of the light chain

antibody-structure.explanation: The Fc — formed by the heavy-chain constant region — defines the isotype (γ/α/μ/ε/δ) and mediates effector functions (complement, Fc-receptor binding, placental transfer).

antibody-structure.stem: What is the basic structural unit of an antibody?

options.text: Two heavy chains and two light chains

antibody-structure.explanation: An antibody is composed of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, forming a Y-shaped structure.

antibody-structure.stem: Which part of the antibody is responsible for binding to antigens?
antibody-structure.explanation: The Fab region, which consists of the variable regions of the heavy and light chains, is responsible for antigen binding.

antibody-structure.stem: What determines the class of an antibody?
antibody-structure.explanation: The class of an antibody is determined by the heavy-chain constant region (isotype), while the light chain type does not define the class.

options.text: V(D)J recombination plus junctional diversity and somatic hypermutation

antibody-structure.explanation: Antibody diversity is generated by V(D)J recombination, junctional diversity, and somatic hypermutation.

antibody-structure.stem: In which part of the antibody is the antigen-binding site located?
antibody-structure.explanation: The antigen-binding site is located in the Fab region, formed by the variable regions of the heavy and light chains.

antibody-structure.stem: How does the Fc region of an antibody function?
antibody-structure.explanation: The Fc region mediates effector functions such as complement activation and determines the antibody's isotype.

antibody-structure.stem: How does B-cell tolerance relate to antibody specificity?

options.text: It ensures only high-affinity antibodies are produced
It prevents autoreactive B-cells from maturing

antibody-structure.explanation: B-cell tolerance prevents autoreactive B-cells from maturing, ensuring that only non-self-reactive antibodies are produced.

antibody-structure.stem: Which aspect of antibody structure is crucial for its function in immune response?
antibody-structure.explanation: The heavy-chain constant region determines the antibody's class and its effector functions, which are crucial for immune response.

antibody-structure.stem: Regarding what determines antibody class? — which is correct?

options.text: The light chain (kappa/lambda) determines the antibody class
The HEAVY-chain constant region (γ/α/μ/ε/δ) determines the isotype/class; light chains are only κ or λ
Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)
Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function

antibody-structure.explanation: Class = heavy-chain constant region. The variable region sets specificity; light-chain type does not define IgG vs IgA etc.

antibody-structure.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antigen-binding site location”?

options.text: Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function
Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)

antibody-structure.explanation: Antigen-binding site location → Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs).

antibody-structure.stem: What best explains the finding: “Complement/Fc-receptor binding”?

options.text: Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)
Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function

antibody-structure.explanation: Complement/Fc-receptor binding → Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function.

antibody-structure.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunoglobulin Structure & Diversity”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antibody-structure.explanation: Antibodies may play a role in neurodegenerative diseases.

antibody-structure.stem: Which should you review before “Immunoglobulin Structure & Diversity”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antibody-structure.explanation: Understanding B-cell development is crucial for grasping antibody structure.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Which immunoglobulin isotype is the only one that crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgG is the only isotype transported across the placenta (via FcRn), giving the newborn passive humoral immunity. IgA is provided postnatally via breast milk.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: A pentameric antibody that is the first produced in a primary response and the most efficient complement activator is:
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgM is a pentamer (with J chain), appears first in the primary response, and with 10 binding sites is the best classical-pathway complement activator (though of lower affinity than switched IgG).

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is the primary antibody produced during the initial stages of a primary immune response?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response due to its pentameric structure, allowing for effective complement activation.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What is the main function of IgG antibodies?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgG antibodies are excellent at complement activation, particularly in the classical pathway.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is primarily found in breast milk and provides passive immunity to newborns?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgA is the main antibody in breast milk, where it exists as a dimer and helps protect the infant's mucosal surfaces.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: A patient presents with anaphylaxis after exposure to peanuts. Which immunoglobulin is primarily responsible for this reaction?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgE antibodies bind to allergens and trigger degranulation of mast cells, leading to anaphylaxis.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: A laboratory test shows high levels of IgG with low levels of IgM. What does this indicate?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: High IgG with low IgM suggests a secondary immune response, indicating past infection and class switching.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is best known for its role in opsonization?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgG is the primary antibody involved in opsonization, marking pathogens for phagocytosis.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: How does class switching occur in B cells during the germinal center reaction?

options.text: By enhancing memory B cell formation

antibody-classes-functions.explanation: Class switching allows B cells to change the antibody isotype while maintaining specificity for the same antigen.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What is the role of T helper cells in the activation of B cells during the humoral response?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: T helper cells provide necessary signals (cytokines) for B cell activation and class switching.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Regarding first vs main antibody — which is correct?

options.text: IgG is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response
IgM is FIRST (primary response); IgG dominates later and in the secondary response

antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgM appears first (pentamer, good complement); class switching to IgG follows and gives the durable, high-affinity secondary response.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Only antibody crossing the placenta”?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: Only antibody crossing the placenta → IgG (neonatal passive immunity).

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “First antibody in a primary response; best complement activator”?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: First antibody in a primary response; best complement activator → IgM (pentamer, 10 binding sites).

complement-pathways.stem: The classical complement pathway is initiated by:

options.text: Antibody (IgM/IgG) bound to antigen activating C1
Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 on a microbial surface

complement-pathways.explanation: The classical pathway starts when C1 binds the Fc of antigen-bound IgM/IgG. MBL/mannose = lectin pathway; spontaneous C3 tickover + properdin = alternative pathway.

complement-pathways.stem: All three complement activation pathways converge on the formation of:

options.text: A C3 convertase that cleaves C3

complement-pathways.explanation: Each pathway generates a C3 convertase (classical/lectin C4b2a; alternative C3bBb) that cleaves C3 into C3a + C3b — the central convergence step leading to C5 convertase and the MAC.

complement-pathways.stem: Which complement activation pathway is initiated by antibody binding to an antigen?
complement-pathways.explanation: The classical pathway is triggered when antibodies (IgM or IgG) bind to antigens, leading to complement activation.

complement-pathways.stem: What is the primary role of C3 convertase in the complement system?

options.text: Cleaves C5 to initiate MAC formation

complement-pathways.explanation: C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b, which are crucial for opsonization and further complement activation.

complement-pathways.stem: Which of the following findings indicates activation of the lectin pathway?

options.text: Binding of mannose-binding lectin to a microbe

complement-pathways.explanation: The lectin pathway is activated when mannose-binding lectin (MBL) recognizes mannose on microbial surfaces.

complement-pathways.stem: What is a common misconception about the complement pathways?

options.text: C5 convertase is formed from C4b2a

complement-pathways.explanation: The alternative pathway is initiated independently of antibodies, which is a common misconception.

complement-pathways.stem: What is the mechanism of action for properdin in the alternative pathway?
complement-pathways.explanation: Properdin stabilizes the C3bBb complex in the alternative pathway, enhancing complement activation.

complement-pathways.stem: How does complement activation relate to hemolysis in patients with autoimmune disorders?
complement-pathways.explanation: In autoimmune disorders, antibody-antigen complexes can activate complement, leading to increased C3b and subsequent hemolysis of red blood cells.

complement-pathways.stem: Which complement component is critical for the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)?
complement-pathways.explanation: C5b is essential for initiating the assembly of the MAC, which ultimately leads to cell lysis.

complement-pathways.stem: What is the relationship between complement deficiencies and susceptibility to infections?

options.text: Deficiencies in C3 lead to increased susceptibility to pyogenic infections
C4 deficiency has no clinical significance

complement-pathways.explanation: C3 deficiency cripples all three complement pathways, leading to increased susceptibility to pyogenic infections.

complement-pathways.stem: Regarding convergence point of complement — which is correct?

options.text: The three complement pathways stay separate through to lysis
They CONVERGE at C3 (all form a C3 convertase); downstream (C5 → MAC) is shared

complement-pathways.explanation: Different triggers, same hub — that is why C3 deficiency cripples all three pathways and causes severe pyogenic infections.

complement-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antibody–antigen complex activating complement”?
complement-pathways.explanation: Antibody–antigen complex activating complement → Classical pathway (C1 binds Fc).

complement-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “MBL binding mannose on a microbe”?
complement-pathways.explanation: MBL binding mannose on a microbe → Lectin pathway (MASP → C4/C2).

complement-pathways.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complement: The Three Activation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-pathways.explanation: While not directly related, understanding complement can aid in grasping immune-related drug effects.

complement-pathways.stem: Which should you review before “Complement: The Three Activation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-pathways.explanation: Understanding hemolysis is crucial for grasping complement's role in immune responses.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: A young adult presents with a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. Which immune defect is most likely?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria infection is the hallmark of terminal complement (MAC, C5–C9) deficiency, because MAC-mediated lysis is the key defence against Neisseria.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Hereditary angioedema, presenting as recurrent non-pruritic swelling without urticaria, is caused by deficiency of:
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C1-inhibitor deficiency leads to unregulated activation of the classical/contact pathways with excess bradykinin, causing recurrent angioedema. DAF/CD59 loss causes PNH.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which complement component deficiency is most commonly associated with SLE-like presentations?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C2 deficiency is the most common early component deficiency leading to impaired clearance of immune complexes, resulting in SLE-like symptoms.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: What is the primary function of C3b in the complement system?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C3b coats microbes and enhances phagocytosis by binding to phagocyte receptors.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: A patient presents with recurrent Neisseria infections. Which complement deficiency is most likely responsible?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria infections indicate a deficiency in terminal complement components (C5–C9), which are crucial for MAC formation.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of hereditary angioedema?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Hereditary angioedema is due to C1-inhibitor deficiency, leading to recurrent non-pruritic swelling.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: C3 deficiency is associated with which of the following clinical presentations?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C3 deficiency results in severe, recurrent pyogenic infections and immune complex disease due to its central role in the complement system.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: How does C1 inhibitor deficiency lead to angioedema?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C1 inhibitor deficiency leads to unopposed bradykinin activity, causing recurrent non-pruritic angioedema.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: In the context of complement deficiencies, which module would provide insights into immune mechanisms of glomerular injury?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: The module on immune mechanisms of glomerular injury is relevant as it discusses how complement deficiencies can lead to kidney damage.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which module would help understand the role of complement in immunity to extracellular bacteria?

options.text: Immunity to Bacteria: Extracellular vs Intracellular

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: The module on immunity to bacteria covers the mechanisms by which the complement system aids in the defense against extracellular pathogens.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Regarding recurrent neisseria — which deficiency? — which is correct?

options.text: Recurrent Neisseria infection indicates an antibody (B-cell) deficiency
Recurrent Neisseria points to TERMINAL COMPLEMENT (C5–C9/MAC) deficiency — MAC lysis is essential against Neisseria

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Neisseria are uniquely susceptible to MAC-mediated lysis; recurrent neisserial disease is the classic clue to terminal complement deficiency.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections”?

options.text: PNH — loss of DAF/CD59 (GPI anchor defect)

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections → Terminal complement (C5–C9 / MAC) deficiency.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “SLE-like immune-complex disease + pyogenic infections”?

options.text: PNH — loss of DAF/CD59 (GPI anchor defect)

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: SLE-like immune-complex disease + pyogenic infections → Early classical component deficiency (C1/C2/C4).

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complement: Functions, Regulation & Deficiencies”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Links complement deficiencies to immune-mediated kidney diseases.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which should you review before “Complement: Functions, Regulation & Deficiencies”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Basic understanding of biochemical processes is helpful.

t-cell-activation.stem: Full activation of a naïve T cell requires TCR–peptide-MHC engagement plus a second signal delivered by:
t-cell-activation.explanation: Co-stimulation via CD28–B7 is signal 2. CTLA-4 binding B7 is inhibitory (a checkpoint), and CD8–MHC I is part of signal 1 for cytotoxic T cells.

t-cell-activation.stem: A T cell receives antigen recognition (signal 1) but no co-stimulation. The likely outcome is:

options.text: Differentiation into a cytotoxic T cell

t-cell-activation.explanation: Signal 1 without signal 2 induces anergy — a peripheral-tolerance mechanism that prevents responses to self-antigens presented without co-stimulation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What is the primary consequence of TCR engagement with antigen without co-stimulation?
t-cell-activation.explanation: TCR engagement without co-stimulation leads to anergy or tolerance, preventing inappropriate activation.

t-cell-activation.stem: Which molecule on T cells binds to B7 on antigen-presenting cells to provide co-stimulatory signal?
t-cell-activation.explanation: CD28 on T cells binds to B7 (CD80/CD86) on APCs to provide the necessary second signal for activation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What is the role of IL-2 in T-cell activation?
t-cell-activation.explanation: IL-2 is crucial for driving the clonal proliferation of activated T cells.

t-cell-activation.stem: Which of the following statements about CTLA-4 is true?

options.text: It competes with CD28 for B7 binding
It is expressed on naive T cells

t-cell-activation.explanation: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 binding, serving as an inhibitory checkpoint to dampen T-cell responses.

t-cell-activation.stem: In the context of immunotherapy, which mechanism is targeted by anti-PD-1 therapies?
t-cell-activation.explanation: Anti-PD-1 therapies block inhibitory checkpoints, enhancing T-cell activation against tumors.

t-cell-activation.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between T-cell activation and self-tolerance mechanisms?

options.text: T-cell activation requires only antigen recognition
Anergy prevents T-cell activation in the absence of co-stimulation
All T cells are activated in the presence of antigen

t-cell-activation.explanation: Anergy is a mechanism of self-tolerance that occurs when T cells recognize antigen without the necessary co-stimulation.

t-cell-activation.stem: Regarding consequence of signal 1 alone — which is correct?

options.text: A T cell that recognises antigen (signal 1) is always fully activated
Antigen recognition WITHOUT co-stimulation (signal 2) → anergy/tolerance, not activation

t-cell-activation.explanation: The two-signal requirement prevents activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of "danger"/co-stimulation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD28–B7 engagement”?
t-cell-activation.explanation: CD28–B7 engagement → Co-stimulation (signal 2) — required for full activation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “IL-2 autocrine loop”?
t-cell-activation.explanation: IL-2 autocrine loop → Drives T-cell clonal proliferation.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which CD4⁺ subset secretes IFN-γ to activate macrophages for defence against intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 cells (driven by IL-12, master TF T-bet) secrete IFN-γ to activate macrophages and support CD8 CTLs — the arm against intracellular microbes and the basis of granuloma formation.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: A mutation in FoxP3 causes severe multi-organ autoimmunity (IPEX) because it impairs which cell?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: FoxP3 is the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells; its loss abolishes Treg-mediated suppression → the fatal autoimmune syndrome IPEX.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which cytokine is primarily responsible for the differentiation of naïve CD4⁺ T cells into Th1 cells?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IL-12 is crucial for Th1 differentiation, promoting the production of IFN-γ.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What is the primary function of Th2 cells in the immune response?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th2 cells primarily support B-cell class switching and promote IgE production.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: A patient presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Which CD4⁺ T-cell subset is most likely defective?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th17 cells are crucial for recruiting neutrophils to combat extracellular fungi like Candida.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which transcription factor is associated with Th2 cells?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: GATA3 is the master transcription factor for Th2 cell differentiation.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What is the primary cytokine secreted by Th1 cells to activate macrophages?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IFN-γ is the key cytokine produced by Th1 cells to activate macrophages.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which of the following statements about Th1 and Th2 cells is correct?

options.text: Th1 cells are responsible for helminth defense.
Th2 cells activate macrophages against intracellular pathogens.
Th1 cells secrete IL-4 to promote IgE production.
Th1 cells are involved in defense against intracellular microbes.

cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 cells are specifically involved in the defense against intracellular microbes.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: How do Th1 cells enhance the activity of CD8⁺ T cells?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 cells produce IFN-γ, which enhances the cytotoxic activity of CD8⁺ T cells.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: In the context of T-cell activation, which cytokine is crucial for Th17 differentiation?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IL-6, along with TGF-β, is essential for the differentiation of Th17 cells.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Regarding th1 vs th2 target — which is correct?

options.text: Th2 cells are the main defence against intracellular bacteria like TB
Th1 (IFN-γ, macrophage activation) handles intracellular microbes; Th2 handles helminths/allergy (IgE, eosinophils)

cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 = intracellular + macrophages; Th2 = parasites/allergy. Swapping them is a classic error.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What best explains the finding: “IFN-γ activating macrophages”?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IFN-γ activating macrophages → Th1 (intracellular defence, granulomas).

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What best explains the finding: “IL-4/5/13 driving IgE + eosinophils”?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IL-4/5/13 driving IgE + eosinophils → Th2 (helminths, allergy).

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which is a clinical application of “CD4⁺ Helper T-Cell Subsets”?
