cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: A cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cell induces apoptosis in a virus-infected cell primarily by:

options.text: Releasing perforin and granzymes (and FasL–Fas signalling)

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: CTLs kill via perforin (pore formation) + granzymes (caspase-mediated apoptosis) and the FasL–Fas death-receptor pathway. They recognise viral peptide on MHC I.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Formation of a tuberculous granuloma depends on Th1 cells activating macrophages via:
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ and express CD40L to activate macrophages, enhancing killing of intracellular microbes and forming granulomas. This axis (IL-12/IFN-γ) is essential against mycobacteria.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Which MHC class do CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize for antigen presentation?
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: CD8 CTLs recognize antigens presented on MHC class I, which is found on all nucleated cells.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which CD8 CTLs induce apoptosis in target cells?
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: CD8 CTLs primarily induce apoptosis through the release of perforin and granzyme, which leads to cell death.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: A patient presents with disseminated mycobacterial infection. What is the most likely underlying defect?
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Disseminated mycobacterial infections are commonly associated with defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis, affecting macrophage activation.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Which finding is characteristic of CD8 CTL-mediated apoptosis?

options.text: Target-cell apoptosis via perforin and granzyme

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: CD8 CTLs induce apoptosis in target cells primarily through the perforin and granzyme mechanism.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of NK cells in the immune response?

options.text: Recognizing and killing MHC class II presenting cells
Killing cells with low MHC class I expression

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: NK cells are responsible for killing 'missing-self' targets, which are characterized by low expression of MHC class I.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: How do CD8 CTLs and NK cells complement each other in immune defense?

options.text: Both can kill cells with low MHC class I expression
Both induce apoptosis through perforin and granzyme

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Both CD8 CTLs and NK cells can induce apoptosis in target cells through the perforin and granzyme pathway.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What is the role of Th1 cells in enhancing CD8 CTL function?
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Th1 cells enhance CD8 CTL function by activating macrophages through the secretion of IFN-γ.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Regarding which mhc do ctls use? — which is correct?

options.text: Cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognise antigen presented on MHC class II
CD8 CTLs recognise antigen on MHC class I (on all nucleated cells); CD4 helpers use MHC II

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Rule of 8: CD8 × MHC I = 8. MHC I displays endogenous/viral peptides for CTL surveillance.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Target-cell apoptosis via pore + protease”?

options.text: Presented on MHC class I of the infected cell

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Target-cell apoptosis via pore + protease → Perforin + granzyme (CTL/NK).

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “FasL–Fas engagement killing a target”?

options.text: Presented on MHC class I of the infected cell

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: FasL–Fas engagement killing a target → Death-receptor apoptosis pathway.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Which should you review before “CD8 Cytotoxic T Cells & Effector Mechanisms”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: NK cells provide backup to CTLs in immune response.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: MHC class II molecules are expressed on:

options.text: Only professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)

mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC II is limited to professional APCs and presents exogenous antigen to CD4⁺ T cells. MHC I (with β2-microglobulin) is on all nucleated cells and presents to CD8⁺ T cells.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which HLA allele is most classically associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies. DQ2/DQ8 → coeliac; B*57:01 → abacavir hypersensitivity.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which of the following MHC molecules is expressed on all nucleated cells?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC class I is expressed on all nucleated cells, while MHC class II is restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: What is the primary structural component of MHC class I molecules?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC class I consists of a single α chain and β2-microglobulin, forming a closed peptide-binding groove.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which HLA allele is associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: In which cells is MHC class II primarily expressed?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC class II is expressed only on professional antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which of the following best describes the expression of HLA genes?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: HLA genes are highly polymorphic, codominantly expressed, and polygenic, allowing for a diverse range of MHC molecules.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: How does the diversity of MHC molecules impact transplant matching?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: The diversity of MHC molecules maximizes the range of peptides that can be presented, which is crucial for effective immune responses and transplant matching.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: How are T cells restricted in their recognition of antigens?

options.text: By recognizing peptides presented by any MHC
By recognizing peptides presented by self-MHC only
By recognizing only foreign MHC molecules

mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: T cells are MHC-restricted, meaning they can only recognize their specific peptide when presented by the individual's own MHC.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which process is essential for the presentation of peptides by MHC molecules?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: Antigen processing is critical for the generation of peptides that will be presented by MHC molecules to T cells.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Regarding where is mhc ii expressed? — which is correct?

options.text: MHC class II is expressed on all nucleated cells like MHC I
MHC II is restricted to professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); MHC I is on all nucleated cells

mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: Only APCs present exogenous antigen to CD4 helpers on MHC II; MHC I surveillance covers every nucleated cell.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “MHC I associates with β2-microglobulin”?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC I associates with β2-microglobulin → Structural requirement for surface expression.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “MHC II expressed only on APCs”?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC II expressed only on APCs → Dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: A viral protein synthesised in the cytosol of an infected cell is presented to T cells via:

options.text: MHC class II to CD4⁺ T cells
The proteasome/TAP pathway on MHC class I to CD8⁺ T cells
The invariant chain pathway to CD4⁺ T cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Endogenous cytosolic antigen is degraded by the proteasome, transported by TAP into the ER, loaded on MHC I, and presented to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Cross-presentation by dendritic cells refers to:

options.text: Presenting endogenous antigen on MHC II
Loading exogenous (engulfed) antigen onto MHC I to prime CD8⁺ T cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Cross-presentation lets dendritic cells place exogenous antigen onto MHC I to prime CD8⁺ CTLs against pathogens/tumours that do not directly infect the DC.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which MHC class presents endogenous antigens to CD8 T cells?
antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Endogenous antigens are presented on MHC class I, which is recognized by CD8 T cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What is the role of TAP in antigen processing?
antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing) transports peptides into the ER for loading onto MHC class I.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: A patient presents with absent MHC II expression and low CD4 T cell counts. What condition is likely?
antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Absent MHC II expression and low CD4 counts are indicative of bare lymphocyte syndrome type II.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which statement about cross-presentation is true?

options.text: It only occurs in B cells
It allows CD4 T cells to recognize endogenous antigens
It enables dendritic cells to present exogenous antigens on MHC I
It is exclusive to MHC class II

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Cross-presentation allows dendritic cells to present exogenous antigens on MHC class I, priming CD8 T cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What is the consequence of a viral inhibitor of TAP?

options.text: Evasion of CTLs and potential NK targeting
Decreased antigen presentation on MHC II

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: A TAP inhibitor blocks MHC I loading, allowing the virus to evade CTLs but become a target for NK cells due to 'missing self'.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: How does the MHC class I pathway differ from the MHC class II pathway?

options.text: MHC I presents exogenous antigens, MHC II presents endogenous
MHC I is recognized by CD4 T cells, MHC II by CD8 T cells
MHC I is loaded in the ER, MHC II in endosomes
MHC I is expressed on all nucleated cells, MHC II on professional APCs

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: MHC class I is expressed on all nucleated cells and presents endogenous antigens, while MHC class II is primarily on professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and presents exogenous antigens.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which T cell subset is primarily activated by MHC class II presentation?
antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: MHC class II molecules present antigens to CD4 T cells, which help coordinate the immune response.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Regarding which pathway presents cytosolic viral protein? — which is correct?

options.text: Viral proteins made inside the cell are presented on MHC class II to CD4 cells
Endogenous (cytosolic) antigen → proteasome/TAP → MHC class I → CD8 T cells
Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Internally synthesised (endogenous) antigen goes on MHC I. MHC II handles engulfed (exogenous) antigen. Cross-presentation is the special DC exception.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proteasome + TAP loading peptide onto MHC I”?

options.text: Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Proteasome + TAP loading peptide onto MHC I → Endogenous (cytosolic) pathway → CD8.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Invariant chain / CLIP on MHC II”?

options.text: Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Invariant chain / CLIP on MHC II → Prevents premature loading until the endosome.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antigen Processing & Presentation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Understanding immune response is relevant for diagnosing chronic infections.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which should you review before “Antigen Processing & Presentation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Understanding CD4 T cell function is essential for MHC II pathway.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: An immature B cell in the bone marrow that strongly binds a self-antigen can avoid deletion by further light-chain rearrangement. This process is called:
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Receptor editing rearranges a new light chain to change the BCR specificity away from self — a central-tolerance mechanism. Somatic hypermutation/class switching occur later in germinal centres.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: During B-cell development, which event occurs first?

options.text: Heavy-chain V(D)J rearrangement forming the pre-BCR

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: The heavy chain rearranges first and pairs with a surrogate light chain to form the pre-BCR checkpoint, before light-chain rearrangement completes the IgM receptor.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What is the first step in B-cell receptor gene rearrangement?

options.text: Clonal deletion of self-reactive B cells

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: The heavy chain rearranges first, followed by the light chain, which is essential for the formation of a functional B-cell receptor.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Which enzyme complex is crucial for V(D)J recombination in B cells?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: RAG1 and RAG2 are essential for the V(D)J recombination process that generates diverse B-cell receptors.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What mechanism allows immature B cells to change their receptor specificity?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Receptor editing allows immature B cells to rearrange their light chain genes to change their specificity and avoid self-reactivity.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What is the consequence of failed BTK signaling in B-cell development?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Failure of BTK signaling leads to an arrest at the pre-B cell stage, resulting in a lack of mature B cells.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Which of the following findings indicates successful heavy chain rearrangement in B-cell development?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: The formation of the pre-BCR indicates that the heavy chain has successfully rearranged and is functional.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: How do mature naïve B cells achieve diversity in antibody production?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Somatic hypermutation in germinal centers allows mature B cells to increase the affinity of their antibodies.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Which process is primarily responsible for the generation of memory B cells after antigen exposure?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Class switching allows B cells to produce different antibody isotypes, which is essential for memory B cell formation.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What is the role of Tfh cells in B-cell development?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Tfh cells provide help for B cells in germinal centers, facilitating somatic hypermutation and class switching.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Regarding order of chain rearrangement — which is correct?

options.text: The light chain rearranges before the heavy chain in B-cell development
The HEAVY chain rearranges first (forming the pre-BCR checkpoint); the light chain follows

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Heavy-chain success (pre-BCR) licenses progression before light-chain rearrangement completes the IgM BCR.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heavy chain rearranges before light chain”?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Heavy chain rearranges before light chain → Ordered V(D)J; pre-BCR checkpoint.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immature B cell edits its receptor to lose self-reactivity”?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Immature B cell edits its receptor to lose self-reactivity → Receptor editing (central tolerance).

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Which should you review before “B-Cell Development & Central Tolerance”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Understanding B-cell receptors requires knowledge of immunoglobulin structure.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Negative selection of thymocytes, occurring mainly in the thymic medulla, serves to:

options.text: Retain cells that can bind self-MHC
Delete thymocytes that bind self-antigen too strongly (central tolerance)
Convert CD8 cells to CD4 cells

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Negative selection deletes strongly self-reactive thymocytes (central tolerance), aided by AIRE-driven tissue-antigen expression. Positive selection (cortex) retains MHC-restricted cells.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Mutation of the AIRE gene causes multi-organ autoimmunity (APECED) because AIRE normally:

options.text: Drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in the thymus for negative selection

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: AIRE enables medullary thymic epithelial cells to express peripheral tissue antigens so that autoreactive T cells against them are deleted. Its loss lets self-reactive T cells escape → APECED/APS-1.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What is the primary outcome of positive selection in the thymus?

options.text: Survival of T cells that weakly bind self-MHC
Maturation of T cells into regulatory T cells
Exit of T cells to the peripheral circulation

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Positive selection ensures that thymocytes that can weakly bind self-MHC survive, allowing for an MHC-restricted T-cell repertoire.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which process is primarily responsible for the deletion of strongly self-reactive thymocytes?
t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Negative selection eliminates thymocytes that bind self-peptides too strongly, promoting central tolerance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: A mutation in the AIRE gene would most likely lead to which clinical finding?
t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: AIRE mutations impair negative selection, leading to the survival of autoreactive T cells and resulting in multi-organ autoimmunity.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which regulatory T cells prevent autoimmunity?
t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Regulatory T cells suppress autoreactive T cells through the release of inhibitory cytokines, contributing to peripheral tolerance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which statement correctly describes the two-step selection process in T-cell development?

options.text: Positive selection deletes self-reactive T cells
Negative selection keeps cells that recognize self-MHC
Positive selection keeps cells that recognize self-MHC

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Positive selection retains thymocytes that can weakly bind self-MHC, while negative selection removes those that react strongly to self-antigens.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: How does the failure of peripheral tolerance mechanisms contribute to autoimmunity?

options.text: By allowing autoreactive T cells to escape deletion
By increasing regulatory T cell numbers

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Failure of peripheral tolerance mechanisms allows autoreactive T cells that escaped thymic selection to become activated, leading to autoimmunity.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which aspect of T-cell development is directly linked to MHC structure and genetics?
t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Positive selection is dependent on the ability of TCRs to recognize self-MHC, which is determined by MHC structure and genetics.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: How does thymic selection relate to mechanisms of autoimmunity?

options.text: It prevents all forms of autoimmunity
It ensures only non-autoreactive T cells enter circulation
It enhances T-cell activation in the periphery
It increases the number of autoreactive T cells

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Thymic selection aims to eliminate autoreactive T cells, thus ensuring that only non-autoreactive T cells enter the peripheral circulation.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Regarding positive vs negative selection — which is correct?

options.text: Positive selection deletes self-reactive T cells
POSITIVE selection KEEPS cells that recognise self-MHC (cortex); NEGATIVE selection DELETES strongly self-reactive cells (medulla)

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Positive = survival of MHC-restricted cells; negative = removal of autoreactive ones. Reversing them is a top exam trap.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thymocyte survives by binding self-MHC (cortex)”?

options.text: Enables negative selection to tissue-specific self

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Thymocyte survives by binding self-MHC (cortex) → Positive selection → MHC restriction.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thymocyte deleted for strong self-antigen reactivity (medulla)”?

options.text: Enables negative selection to tissue-specific self

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Thymocyte deleted for strong self-antigen reactivity (medulla) → Negative selection → central tolerance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which is a clinical application of “T-Cell Development & Thymic Selection”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells
GnRH, FSH/LH Feedback & the Midcycle Surge

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Basic science of feedback mechanisms may have indirect relevance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which should you review before “T-Cell Development & Thymic Selection”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: T-cell activation is essential for understanding T-cell function post-selection.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A 9-month-old boy has recurrent pyogenic infections, undetectable B cells, and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes. The most likely diagnosis is:
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: A BTK defect blocks B-cell maturation → absent B cells and panhypogammaglobulinaemia in a male infant after maternal IgG wanes. DiGeorge is a T-cell defect; CGD is a phagocyte defect.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A boy has hypocalcaemic tetany, a conotruncal cardiac defect, and a T-cell deficiency. Which deletion is responsible?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) causes thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency + hypocalcaemia) with conotruncal heart defects — "CATCH-22".

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent pyogenic infections and laboratory tests reveal absent B cells and low immunoglobulin levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: The absence of B cells and low immunoglobulin levels in a male infant strongly suggests X-linked agammaglobulinaemia due to a BTK defect.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Which immunological defect is characterized by high levels of IgM and low levels of IgG, IgA, and IgE, along with susceptibility to opportunistic infections?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Hyper-IgM syndrome is due to a CD40L defect leading to impaired class switching, resulting in high IgM and low IgG/A/E levels.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A 3-year-old boy with eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia is suspected to have a primary immunodeficiency. Which condition is most likely?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is characterized by the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: In a patient with DiGeorge syndrome, which of the following findings would you expect?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is associated with thymic hypoplasia leading to T-cell deficiency and often presents with hypocalcaemia.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A patient with selective IgA deficiency experiences anaphylaxis after receiving blood transfusion. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: IgA deficiency always leads to severe infections

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency can lead to anaphylaxis due to the presence of anti-IgA antibodies in individuals receiving IgA-containing products.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A 2-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and oral thrush. Laboratory tests show absent T cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: The presentation of absent T cells and severe symptoms in infancy is characteristic of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: How does the defect in antigen presentation relate to primary immunodeficiency disorders?

options.text: It leads to increased B cell activation

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Defective antigen presentation can lead to T cell deficiencies, as seen in Bare Lymphocyte Syndromes, which are a type of primary immunodeficiency.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Which primary immunodeficiency disorder is most likely to affect the humoral immune response due to a defect in B cell activation?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) primarily affects B cell activation and leads to decreased antibody production.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Regarding selective iga deficiency reaction — which is correct?

options.text: IgA deficiency is always symptomatic with severe infections
Most selective IgA deficiency is asymptomatic; a classic clue is ANAPHYLAXIS to blood products/IVIG (anti-IgA antibodies)

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: It is the commonest and often silent PID; the exam hook is transfusion anaphylaxis, not overwhelming infection.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: What best explains the finding: “Boy with recurrent pyogenic infections, absent B cells, all Ig low”?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Boy with recurrent pyogenic infections, absent B cells, all Ig low → X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK).

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: What best explains the finding: “High IgM, low IgG/A/E, PCP”?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: High IgM, low IgG/A/E, PCP → Hyper-IgM (CD40L defect → no class switch).

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Which should you review before “Primary Immunodeficiency: Antibody, T-Cell & Combined”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Understanding antigen processing is crucial for grasping immunodeficiencies.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A child with recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus infections, granulomas, and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test most likely has:
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: CGD is a defect of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → infections with catalase-positive organisms and granulomas; the DHR/NBT test is abnormal.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A neonate has delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent bacterial infections without pus formation, and a markedly elevated neutrophil count. The defect involves:
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 results from defective β2-integrin (CD18) → neutrophils cannot adhere and transmigrate, causing pus-free infections, delayed cord separation, and blood neutrophilia.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What is the primary defect in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: CGD is caused by a defect in NADPH oxidase, leading to impaired respiratory burst and susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Which test is used to diagnose Chronic Granulomatous Disease?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: The DHR (dihydrorhodamine) flow test assesses the respiratory burst in phagocytes, confirming CGD.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A patient presents with recurrent infections and delayed umbilical cord separation. Which condition is most likely?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Delayed umbilical cord separation and recurrent infections without pus are characteristic of Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Why are patients with Chronic Granulomatous Disease particularly susceptible to catalase-positive organisms?

options.text: Catalase-positive organisms destroy their own H₂O₂
They cannot produce any reactive oxygen species

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Catalase-positive organisms can neutralize H₂O₂, which is essential for killing since CGD patients cannot generate it due to NADPH oxidase deficiency.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is marked by the presence of giant granules in leukocytes due to impaired lysosomal fusion.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A patient with recurrent Neisseria infections is suspected to have a complement deficiency. Which complement component is likely deficient?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Deficiency in terminal complement components (C5–C9) leads to increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: How does complement deficiency relate to antibody deficiencies in primary immunodeficiencies?

options.text: Both lead to recurrent viral infections
Both are caused by genetic mutations

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Complement deficiencies impair opsonization, similar to how antibody deficiencies reduce the ability to opsonize pathogens, leading to increased infections.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What is the relationship between phagocyte defects and extracellular bacterial infections?

options.text: Phagocyte defects primarily affect viral infections
Phagocyte defects increase susceptibility to all bacteria
Phagocyte defects lead to recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria
Phagocyte defects specifically predispose to infections with catalase-positive organisms

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Phagocyte defects, such as in CGD, specifically increase susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms due to impaired oxidative burst.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Regarding why catalase-positive organisms in cgd? — which is correct?

options.text: CGD patients get infected by all bacteria equally
CGD specifically → CATALASE-POSITIVE organisms, because catalase-negative bacteria supply their own H₂O₂ that the phagocyte can still use

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Without NADPH oxidase, phagocytes borrow H₂O₂ from catalase-negative microbes; catalase-positive organisms destroy their own H₂O₂, escaping killing.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent Staph/Aspergillus infections + granulomas”?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Recurrent Staph/Aspergillus infections + granulomas → CGD (NADPH oxidase defect, catalase⁺ organisms).

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What best explains the finding: “Abnormal DHR/NBT test”?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Abnormal DHR/NBT test → Confirms absent respiratory burst (CGD).

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Which should you review before “Primary Immunodeficiency: Phagocyte & Complement Defects”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Understanding complement defects is crucial for grasping primary immunodeficiencies.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: HIV causes progressive immunodeficiency principally by:

options.text: Depleting CD4⁺ helper T cells via gp120 binding

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: HIV gp120 binds CD4 (with CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors) and progressively depletes CD4⁺ T cells, collapsing cell-mediated immunity and leading to opportunistic infections (AIDS at CD4 <200).

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: A patient with a CD4 count of 120/µL develops a subacute pneumonia with diffuse infiltrates and marked hypoxia. The most likely opportunistic organism is:
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: At CD4 <200/µL, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is a classic AIDS-defining opportunistic infection reflecting loss of cell-mediated immunity; prophylaxis is co-trimoxazole.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which HIV causes immunodeficiency?

options.text: Direct destruction of CD8+ T cells

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: HIV primarily infects and depletes CD4+ T cells, leading to a collapse of cell-mediated immunity.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: Which of the following is an AIDS-defining illness?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a classic AIDS-defining illness associated with low CD4 counts.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: A patient with HIV presents with a CD4 count of 150/µL. Which opportunistic infection is he at highest risk for?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: With a CD4 count below 200/µL, the patient is at high risk for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: After chemotherapy, a patient develops neutropenic fever. What is the underlying cause of this condition?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Chemotherapy can lead to neutropenia, resulting in an increased risk of bacterial and fungal infections.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: Which of the following statements about secondary immunodeficiency is true?

options.text: It is primarily caused by genetic defects.
It is less common than primary immunodeficiency.
Malnutrition is a leading cause worldwide.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Secondary immunodeficiency is far more common than primary and can be caused by malnutrition, among other factors.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: A patient with a history of splenectomy presents with overwhelming sepsis. Which organism is he most susceptible to?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Patients without a spleen are particularly susceptible to encapsulated bacteria, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: How does the mechanism of immunodeficiency differ between HIV/AIDS and primary antibody deficiencies?

options.text: HIV causes direct B cell dysfunction, while primary deficiencies affect T cells.
HIV leads to CD4+ T cell depletion, while primary deficiencies involve specific antibody production defects.
HIV primarily affects phagocytes, while primary deficiencies affect T cells.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: HIV leads to depletion of CD4+ T cells, while primary antibody deficiencies specifically affect the ability to produce antibodies.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: In patients with primary immunodeficiency disorders, what is a common clinical finding that differs from those with secondary immunodeficiency due to HIV?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Patients with primary immunodeficiencies often present with recurrent bacterial infections, while those with HIV are more prone to opportunistic infections.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: Regarding primary vs secondary immunodeficiency frequency — which is correct?

options.text: Primary (genetic) immunodeficiencies are the most common cause of immunodeficiency
SECONDARY (acquired) immunodeficiency is far commoner — malnutrition worldwide, and HIV/drugs/malignancy clinically

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Primary defects are rare and usually present in childhood; most immunodeficiency encountered clinically is acquired.
CD4 <200/µL → AIDS threshold → high opportunistic-infection risk.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: What best explains the finding: “PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, CMV retinitis”?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, CMV retinitis → CD4/T-cell (cell-mediated) collapse in HIV.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: A vaccine made of pure bacterial capsular polysaccharide induces mainly low-affinity IgM with poor memory, especially in infants. This is because the antigen is:
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens: they cross-link BCRs but recruit no T-cell help, so the response is IgM-dominant with little class switching or memory. Conjugation to a protein makes it T-dependent.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: In a T-dependent antibody response, the critical "second signal" delivered from the follicular helper T cell to the B cell is:
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Tfh cells deliver help via CD40L–CD40 (plus cytokines), licensing the germinal-centre reaction. CD28–B7 co-stimulates the T cell itself; Fas–FasL is a cytotoxic pathway.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which T-dependent B-cell activation occurs?

options.text: Direct recognition of antigens by B cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: T-dependent B-cell activation requires CD40L–CD40 interaction for signal 2, alongside antigen recognition.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which type of antibody is primarily produced in response to T-independent antigens?
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: T-independent antigens typically elicit a response dominated by low-affinity IgM antibodies.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines have poor immunogenicity in infants?
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Polysaccharides are T-independent, leading to weak responses without T-cell help, especially in infants.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What is the role of follicular helper T (Tfh) cells in B-cell activation?

options.text: They provide cytokine support and CD40L interaction
They present antigens to B cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Tfh cells provide essential signals through cytokines and CD40L for T-dependent B-cell activation.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which of the following vaccines is an example of a conjugate vaccine?
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: The Hib vaccine is a conjugate vaccine that links a polysaccharide to a protein to enhance T-cell help.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: How does the germinal center reaction contribute to antibody affinity maturation?

options.text: By allowing somatic hypermutation and selection of high-affinity B cells
By increasing the number of B cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: The germinal center reaction involves somatic hypermutation and selection, leading to higher affinity antibodies.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: In the context of B-cell activation, how does the linked recognition principle apply to conjugate vaccines?

options.text: T cells and B cells recognize different epitopes of the same antigen
B cells do not require T-cell help
T cells provide help only for protein antigens

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Linked recognition allows B cells to receive T-cell help by recognizing different epitopes of the same antigen in conjugate vaccines.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is primarily involved in T-dependent responses and provides long-term immunity?
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: IgG is the main antibody produced in T-dependent responses, providing high affinity and memory.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Regarding why polysaccharide vaccines fail in infants — which is correct?

options.text: Infants fail to respond to polysaccharide vaccines because they cannot make any antibody
Polysaccharides are T-INDEPENDENT antigens → poor, memory-less responses in infants; conjugating to protein makes them T-dependent

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: The problem is lack of T-cell help/memory for polysaccharides, solved by protein conjugation — not a global inability to make antibody.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Protein antigen → high-affinity IgG + memory”?

options.text: Protein carrier recruits T-cell help (linked recognition)

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Protein antigen → high-affinity IgG + memory → T-dependent (Tfh help, germinal centre).

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polysaccharide antigen → mainly IgM, no memory”?

options.text: Protein carrier recruits T-cell help (linked recognition)

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Polysaccharide antigen → mainly IgM, no memory → T-independent (no T-cell help).

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Humoral Response: B-Cell Activation (T-dependent vs T-independent)”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Cushing's syndrome may affect immune responses but is not directly related.

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Understanding antibody classes is essential for grasping B-cell activation.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Compared with the primary response, the secondary antibody response to the same antigen is:
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Memory B cells produce a faster, larger, class-switched (IgG), higher-affinity secondary response — the basis of vaccination and boosters. The primary response is slow and IgM-dominant.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Affinity maturation of antibodies occurs in the germinal centre through:

options.text: V(D)J recombination in the bone marrow
Somatic hypermutation of the variable region followed by selection of high-affinity clones
Class switching of the heavy-chain constant region

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Affinity maturation results from somatic hypermutation (AID) of the V region plus selection of the highest-affinity B cells by Tfh/follicular dendritic cells in the germinal centre.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What is the primary function of somatic hypermutation in B cells?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Somatic hypermutation allows B cells to refine the affinity of their antibodies for specific antigens through mutation and selection.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Which cytokine is primarily responsible for promoting class switching to IgE?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: IL-4 is the key cytokine that drives class switching to IgE and IgG.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: A patient presents with high levels of IgM and low levels of IgG and IgA, along with absent germinal centers. What is the most likely underlying defect?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: This presentation is characteristic of a hyper-IgM syndrome, often caused by a defect in CD40L, preventing class switching.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Which statement about class switching is correct?

options.text: It changes the antigen specificity of antibodies
It alters the heavy-chain constant region only
It affects the variable region of antibodies
It occurs without T cell help

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Class switching only changes the heavy-chain constant region, maintaining the same antigen specificity.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: During a secondary immune response, which of the following is most likely to occur?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: The secondary immune response is characterized by a rapid and robust production of IgG due to memory B cells.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: How does the germinal center response contribute to vaccine efficacy?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: The germinal center response generates memory B cells that provide a faster and stronger response upon re-exposure to the antigen, enhancing vaccine efficacy.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What is the role of follicular dendritic cells in the germinal center?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Follicular dendritic cells present antigens to B cells, facilitating selection of high-affinity clones during affinity maturation.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: In the context of antibody classes, which function is primarily associated with IgA?
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: IgA is primarily involved in mucosal immunity, protecting mucosal surfaces from pathogens.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Regarding what changes in class switching? — which is correct?

options.text: Class switching changes the antigen specificity of the antibody
Class switching changes only the HEAVY-chain constant region (isotype/function); the variable region and specificity are unchanged
Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Switching alters effector class (IgM→IgG/A/E), not what the antibody binds. Affinity maturation refines binding via variable-region mutation.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rising affinity of antibody over weeks”?

options.text: Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Rising affinity of antibody over weeks → Somatic hypermutation + selection (affinity maturation).

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “IgM → IgG switch with same antigen specificity”?

options.text: Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: IgM → IgG switch with same antigen specificity → Class switching (constant region changes, not variable).

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Which should you review before “Germinal Centre, Affinity Maturation & the Memory Response”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Understanding antibody classes is essential for grasping class switching.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: The principal adaptive defence against an extracellular, toxin-producing bacterium is:
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Extracellular bacteria are countered by humoral immunity — antibody neutralises toxins, opsonises for phagocytosis, and activates complement. Cell-mediated immunity handles intracellular organisms.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Granuloma formation in tuberculosis primarily reflects which type of immune response?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Th1 cells (IFN-γ, CD40L) activate macrophages to contain intracellular bacteria in granulomas. This cell-mediated axis is why anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which type of immunity is primarily responsible for combating extracellular bacteria?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Humoral immunity, characterized by antibody production, is the main defense against extracellular bacteria.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What is the role of IFN-γ in the immune response to intracellular bacteria?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: IFN-γ is crucial for activating macrophages to enhance their ability to kill intracellular bacteria.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: A patient presents with recurrent infections from encapsulated bacteria. What underlying defect is most likely present?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Recurrent infections from encapsulated bacteria often indicate a defect in antibody or complement-mediated opsonization.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which of the following findings is indicative of a Th1-mediated immune response?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Granuloma formation with activated macrophages is characteristic of a Th1-mediated immune response to intracellular pathogens.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What is a common consequence of a cytokine storm during Gram-negative sepsis?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: A cytokine storm can lead to septic shock due to overwhelming inflammatory responses.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which statement about the defense against intracellular bacteria is true?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity, particularly through Th1 cells and macrophage activation, is essential for combating intracellular bacteria.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: How does the mechanism of antibody neutralization differ from complement activation in the context of extracellular bacteria?

options.text: Antibody neutralization is ineffective against encapsulated bacteria

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Complement activation enhances opsonization and can lead to the lysis of bacteria, while antibody neutralization primarily blocks toxins and adhesion.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What role does the complement system play in the defense against extracellular bacteria?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: The complement system opsonizes extracellular bacteria, facilitating their phagocytosis by immune cells.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Regarding defence against intracellular bacteria — which is correct?

options.text: Antibody is the main defence against intracellular bacteria like Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Intracellular bacteria need CELL-MEDIATED immunity (Th1/IFN-γ macrophage activation, CTL) — antibody cannot reach them
Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)
Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Antibody works on extracellular targets; intracellular pathogens require T-cell-driven macrophage activation and cytotoxicity.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antibody neutralising a bacterial exotoxin”?

options.text: Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria
Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Antibody neutralising a bacterial exotoxin → Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin).

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What best explains the finding: “Granuloma with activated macrophages (TB)”?

options.text: Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)
Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Granuloma with activated macrophages (TB) → Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunity to Bacteria: Extracellular vs Intracellular”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Histological understanding may aid in recognizing immune responses in tissues.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which should you review before “Immunity to Bacteria: Extracellular vs Intracellular”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Understanding complement is crucial for grasping humoral immunity.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: The immune response responsible for defence against helminth (worm) parasites is characterised by:

options.text: Th2 cytokines (IL-4/5/13) driving IgE and eosinophils

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Helminth defence is a Th2 response: IL-4/5/13 promote IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, and alternatively activated macrophages. Th1 handles intracellular bacteria.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), classically seen in severe secondary dengue infection, occurs when:

options.text: Non-neutralising antibody facilitates viral entry into Fc-receptor-bearing cells
T cells kill all infected cells

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: In ADE, cross-reactive non-neutralising antibody binds virus and promotes its uptake via Fc receptors into cells, enhancing infection — the basis of more severe secondary dengue.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate virus-infected cells?

options.text: Induction of apoptosis in B cells

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: CD8 CTLs recognize and kill virus-infected cells through MHC I presentation of viral peptides.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Which cytokines are primarily involved in the Th2 response to helminth infections?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 are key cytokines that drive the Th2 immune response against helminths.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What is the clinical significance of non-neutralising antibodies in dengue infections?

options.text: They always provide immunity against reinfection
They can enhance severity of secondary infections
They prevent viral entry into host cells
They are ineffective against all serotypes

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Non-neutralising antibodies can enhance the severity of secondary dengue infections through antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Which immune cells are primarily responsible for antifungal defense against Candida infections?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Neutrophils are crucial for the defense against invasive fungal infections like Candida.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: A patient presents with eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels. Which type of immune response is likely involved?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Eosinophilia and high IgE are characteristic of a Th2 immune response, typically seen in helminth infections.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: How does the influenza virus evade the immune response?

options.text: By inducing apoptosis in T cells

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Influenza evades immunity primarily through antigenic drift and shift, leading to changes in its surface antigens.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Which antiviral drug class is commonly used to treat respiratory viral infections?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors are commonly used to treat respiratory infections caused by influenza viruses.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: In a patient with a history of severe dengue, which immune mechanism is most likely responsible for their increased risk during a second infection?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) can lead to severe disease in patients with prior dengue infection due to non-neutralising antibodies.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Regarding antibody in dengue — which is correct?

options.text: Antibody from a prior dengue infection always protects against the next infection
Non-neutralising cross-reactive antibody can ENHANCE a second (different serotype) dengue infection via ADE → severe dengue

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Antibody-dependent enhancement is the exception where pre-existing antibody worsens disease — a key exam and vaccine-safety point.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Type I IFN + CTL clearing a virus”?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Type I IFN + CTL clearing a virus → Innate antiviral state + MHC-I-restricted killing.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe dengue on second infection”?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Severe dengue on second infection → Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunity to Viruses, Fungi & Parasites + Microbial Evasion”?

mucosal-immune-system.stem: The specialised epithelial cell that samples luminal antigen and delivers it to dendritic cells in a Peyer's patch is the:
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: M cells overlie Peyer's patches and transcytose luminal antigen to underlying immune cells; some pathogens (e.g. Salmonella) exploit them to invade.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Dimeric IgA is delivered into mucosal secretions by transcytosis across the epithelium via:

options.text: The polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR), leaving the secretory component

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: pIgR transports dimeric IgA across the epithelium; cleavage leaves the secretory component bound, protecting sIgA from gut proteases. FcRn transports IgG across the placenta.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What is the primary antibody produced at mucosal surfaces?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Secretory IgA is the most abundantly produced antibody at mucosal surfaces, providing crucial immune exclusion.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which cells are responsible for sampling luminal antigens in the gut?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: M (microfold) cells overlie Peyer's patches and are specialized for sampling luminal antigens.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What mechanism protects secretory IgA from degradation in the gut?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: The polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR) mediates transcytosis of IgA, leaving a secretory component that protects it from proteases.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: A patient presents with recurrent gastrointestinal infections. Which immunoglobulin deficiency is most likely responsible?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: IgA deficiency leads to a loss of secretory IgA barrier defense, resulting in recurrent mucosal infections.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which pathogen is known to exploit M cells to invade the gut epithelium?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Salmonella can invade the gut epithelium by exploiting M cells over Peyer's patches.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: How does secretory IgA contribute to mucosal immunity?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Secretory IgA works by immune exclusion, neutralizing and trapping microbes without triggering inflammation.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: How does exposure to antigens at one mucosal site affect distant mucosal sites?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Antigen exposure at one mucosal site can lead to the generation of IgA plasma cells at distant mucosal sites, a feature of the common mucosal immune system.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which cytokines promote IgA class switching in B cells?
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: TGF-β, APRIL, and BAFF are key cytokines that promote IgA class switching in B cells.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Regarding which antibody dominates mucosal defence? — which is correct?

options.text: IgG is the main antibody protecting mucosal surfaces
Secretory IgA (dimeric, with secretory component) is the dominant mucosal antibody — the most abundantly produced immunoglobulin
M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: sIgA provides non-inflammatory immune exclusion at mucosae; IgG dominates serum/systemic immunity.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Specialised epithelial cell sampling gut antigen”?

options.text: M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch
Loss of secretory IgA barrier defence

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Specialised epithelial cell sampling gut antigen → M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Secretory component attached to luminal IgA”?

options.text: M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch
Loss of secretory IgA barrier defence

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Secretory component attached to luminal IgA → pIgR-mediated transcytosis (protects from proteases).

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Mucosal Immune System & Secretory IgA”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: MALT lymphoma is directly related to mucosal immune dysfunction.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which should you review before “The Mucosal Immune System & Secretory IgA”?

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Understanding antibody production is crucial for grasping mucosal immunity.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Oral tolerance to ingested food antigens is mediated primarily by:

options.text: Regulatory T cells and tolerogenic cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10)

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Oral tolerance is an active, Treg-driven suppression of responses to ingested antigens (with TGF-β/IL-10 and tolerogenic dendritic cells); its failure contributes to food allergy and coeliac disease.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: A patient develops severe Clostridioides difficile colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotics. The key predisposing change is:

options.text: Dysbiosis with loss of colonisation resistance

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Antibiotics disrupt the protective commensal microbiota (dysbiosis), removing colonisation resistance and allowing C. difficile overgrowth — sometimes treated by restoring flora (faecal transplant).

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which oral tolerance is achieved?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Oral tolerance is primarily mediated by regulatory T cells that suppress immune responses to ingested antigens.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Which cytokine is most associated with promoting regulatory T cell development in the gut?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: TGF-β is crucial for the differentiation and expansion of regulatory T cells in the gut.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What clinical finding indicates successful oral tolerance to food antigens?

options.text: Immune non-response to ingested food antigen

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Immune non-response to ingested food antigens is a hallmark of successful oral tolerance.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Which of the following is a consequence of dysbiosis in the gut microbiota?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Dysbiosis can lead to a loss of tolerance and contribute to the development of food allergies.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What is the role of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by gut microbiota?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: SCFAs, such as butyrate, are known to expand regulatory T cells, promoting tolerance.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: How does the gut microbiota contribute to immune system development in germ-free animals?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: The gut microbiota plays a critical role in educating and maturing the immune system in germ-free animals.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Which mechanism connects oral tolerance to autoimmune conditions?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: A failure of Treg function can lead to a breakdown in oral tolerance, contributing to autoimmune conditions.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What finding would suggest a loss of colonisation resistance in a patient after antibiotic treatment?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: C. difficile infection is a common consequence of loss of colonisation resistance following antibiotic treatment.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Regarding default mucosal immune state — which is correct?

options.text: The healthy gut mounts an active inflammatory response to all bacteria it contains
The default mucosal state toward commensals/food is regulated TOLERANCE (Tregs), not inflammation

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Constant inflammation against the trillions of commensals would be harmful; tolerance is actively maintained and only overridden for true pathogens.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immune non-response to ingested food antigen”?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Immune non-response to ingested food antigen → Oral tolerance (Treg-mediated).

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What best explains the finding: “Commensals outcompeting a pathogen”?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Commensals outcompeting a pathogen → Colonisation resistance (healthy microbiota).

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Oral Tolerance & the Gut Microbiota”?

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Rheumatic heart disease following group A streptococcal pharyngitis is a classic example of:

options.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry), causing immune-mediated valvular damage after the organism is cleared.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which genetic defect causes fatal early-onset multi-organ autoimmunity (IPEX) by abolishing regulatory T-cell function?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: FoxP3 is the master transcription factor of Tregs; its loss abolishes peripheral suppression → IPEX. AIRE loss (central tolerance) causes APECED.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which autoimmunity occurs?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Autoimmunity arises from a loss of self-tolerance, leading to immune attacks on self-antigens.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which genetic defect is associated with APECED?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: APECED is caused by a mutation in the AIRE gene, leading to central tolerance failure.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What is the role of Tregs in autoimmunity?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Tregs play a crucial role in maintaining peripheral tolerance by suppressing self-reactive T cells.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: A patient presents with multi-organ autoimmunity. Genetic testing reveals a defect in AIRE. What condition is likely?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: AIRE mutation leads to APECED, characterized by multi-organ autoimmunity due to central tolerance failure.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What is the mechanism behind rheumatic fever following streptococcal infection?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Rheumatic fever is caused by molecular mimicry, where antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which HLA type is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis, indicating a genetic predisposition.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: How does molecular mimicry contribute to autoimmunity in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, molecular mimicry occurs when antibodies to *Campylobacter* cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which mechanism is primarily responsible for the development of type 1 diabetes?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is primarily mediated by type IV hypersensitivity, involving T cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Regarding molecular mimicry — which is correct?

options.text: Rheumatic fever damages the heart by direct streptococcal infection of the myocardium
It is molecular MIMICRY — antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens (immune-mediated, not direct infection)

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: The organism is cleared; the damage is autoimmune cross-reactivity, illustrating how infection triggers autoimmunity.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rheumatic fever after strep pharyngitis”?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Rheumatic fever after strep pharyngitis → Molecular mimicry (M protein ↔ cardiac antigen).

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multi-organ autoimmunity from AIRE mutation”?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Multi-organ autoimmunity from AIRE mutation → Central-tolerance failure (APECED).

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Self-Tolerance & Mechanisms of Autoimmunity”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Rheumatic fever exemplifies autoimmune disease with clinical implications.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which should you review before “Self-Tolerance & Mechanisms of Autoimmunity”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding T-cell activation is essential for grasping autoimmunity mechanisms.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism because the autoantibody:

options.text: Destroys thyroid follicular cells by complement
Forms immune complexes in the thyroid

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Graves disease features a stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody (type II, activating) that drives thyroid hormone overproduction — contrast with the blocking anti-AChR antibody of myasthenia gravis.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Which autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-dsDNA (and anti-Sm) are specific for SLE and anti-dsDNA correlates with disease activity/nephritis. ANA is sensitive but not specific.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Which autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and is associated with disease activity.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What is the mechanism of action of the stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibody in Graves disease?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: The stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibody activates the receptor, leading to increased thyroid hormone production.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: In myasthenia gravis, which clinical finding is most characteristic?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Fatigable weakness is the hallmark symptom of myasthenia gravis due to impaired neuromuscular transmission.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Which of the following statements about type II antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases is true?

options.text: All type II antibodies destroy target cells
Type II antibodies can block or stimulate receptors
Type II antibodies only cause inflammation
Type II antibodies are always pathogenic

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Type II antibodies can either block or stimulate receptor function, exemplified by Graves disease and myasthenia gravis.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What is the primary autoantibody involved in Goodpasture syndrome?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-GBM antibodies target type IV collagen in the basement membrane of the lungs and kidneys.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: How does the mechanism of type IV hypersensitivity relate to autoimmune diseases like multiple sclerosis?

options.text: It is mediated by T-cell activation
It leads to immediate hypersensitivity reactions

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by T-cell mediated destruction of myelin, which is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Which autoantibody is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and is used for diagnosis?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and are used as a diagnostic marker.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: In the context of autoimmune diseases, how does the concept of self-tolerance failure relate to type 1 diabetes?

options.text: It results in T-cell destruction of β cells
It induces antibody production against thyroid antigens

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: In type 1 diabetes, the failure of self-tolerance leads to T-cell mediated destruction of insulin-producing β cells in the pancreas.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Regarding type ii activating vs blocking — which is correct?

options.text: All type II antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases destroy the target cell
Type II can also modulate receptors: Graves = STIMULATING anti-TSH-R (hyperfunction); myasthenia = BLOCKING anti-AChR (hypofunction) — no cell destruction required

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Antibody against a receptor can activate or block it, not just trigger lysis — a favourite distinction (Graves vs MG).

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-dsDNA / anti-Sm”?

options.text: Myasthenia gravis (type II, blocking) → fatigable weakness

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-dsDNA / anti-Sm → Specific for SLE (systemic, type III).

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody”?

options.text: Myasthenia gravis (type II, blocking) → fatigable weakness

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody → Graves disease (type II, activating) → hyperthyroidism.

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Graves disease is a key example of an organ-specific autoimmune disease with clinical implications.
