autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Understanding organ-specific metabolism aids in grasping organ-specific autoimmune diseases.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Anaphylaxis occurring within minutes of a bee sting in a sensitised person is which type of hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Immediate reactions from allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells (histamine release) are type I hypersensitivity; systemic form = anaphylaxis, treated with adrenaline.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia indicates which hypersensitivity mechanism?

options.text: Type II (antibody against a fixed cell antigen)

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is type II: IgG/IgM coats red cells (detected by the direct Coombs test), causing complement lysis and splenic phagocytosis.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: What is the primary immunoglobulin involved in Type I hypersensitivity reactions?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: IgE is the primary immunoglobulin involved in Type I hypersensitivity, mediating allergic reactions.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which mechanism is primarily responsible for tissue damage in Type II hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody-mediated cytotoxicity against fixed antigens on cells.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: A patient presents with wheal-and-flare reaction after a skin prick test. What type of hypersensitivity is this indicative of?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: The wheal-and-flare reaction is characteristic of Type I hypersensitivity due to mast cell histamine release.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which of the following conditions is an example of Type II hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Graves' disease is a Type II hypersensitivity disorder characterized by antibody-mediated receptor activation.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: In which condition would you expect a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: A positive Coombs test indicates the presence of antibodies coating red blood cells, typical of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Type II).

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Type II hypersensitivity primarily targets which type of antigen?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity targets fixed antigens on specific cells or tissues, distinguishing it from Type III.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: How does Type II hypersensitivity differ from Type III in terms of antigen location?

options.text: Type II involves soluble antigens; Type III involves fixed antigens
Type II involves fixed antigens; Type III involves soluble antigens

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity involves fixed antigens on cells, while Type III involves soluble immune complexes that deposit in tissues.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: A patient with myasthenia gravis has antibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is a Type II hypersensitivity disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which hypersensitivity type is most likely to be involved in a transfusion reaction?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Transfusion reactions are primarily due to Type II hypersensitivity, where antibodies target transfused red blood cells.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: In which type of hypersensitivity would you expect eosinophil infiltration during the late phase response?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity features eosinophil infiltration during the late phase response, contributing to inflammation.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Regarding type ii vs type iii antibody target — which is correct?

options.text: Type II and type III hypersensitivity both involve soluble antigen–antibody complexes
Type II antibody targets a FIXED antigen on a specific cell/tissue; type III involves SOLUBLE circulating immune complexes that deposit

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Location of the antigen distinguishes them: fixed/cell-bound (II) vs soluble/deposited (III).

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: What best explains the finding: “Wheal-and-flare within minutes of allergen”?

options.text: Type II — antibody coating red cells
Type II — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses placenta

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Wheal-and-flare within minutes of allergen → Type I — mast-cell histamine (IgE).

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anaphylaxis: hypotension + bronchospasm + urticaria”?

options.text: Type II — antibody coating red cells
Type II — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses placenta

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Anaphylaxis: hypotension + bronchospasm + urticaria → Systemic type I → give adrenaline.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hypersensitivity Types I & II”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Clinical manifestations of hypersensitivity are explored in cutaneous immunology.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which should you review before “Hypersensitivity Types I & II”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Understanding autoimmune diseases is essential for grasping Type II hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: The tuberculin (Mantoux) skin test read at 48–72 hours is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: The delayed (48–72 h), antibody-independent, T-cell-mediated reaction to intradermal tuberculin is the prototypical type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and serum sickness are caused by:
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: These are type III reactions: soluble immune complexes deposit in tissues (glomeruli, vessels), activating complement and recruiting neutrophils to cause damage.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What is the primary mechanism of tissue damage in Type III hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity involves the deposition of immune complexes, leading to inflammation and tissue damage.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which of the following diseases is an example of Type III hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus involves immune complex formation, characteristic of Type III hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What is the expected timing for the peak response in a tuberculin skin test?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: The tuberculin skin test is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which peaks at 48-72 hours due to T-cell recruitment.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which finding is characteristic of serum sickness?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Serum sickness is characterized by immune complex deposition leading to inflammation and symptoms occurring days after exposure.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: In which hypersensitivity type do T cells play a central role?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by T cells without the involvement of antibodies.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: A patient presents with contact dermatitis after exposure to poison ivy. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a classic example of Type IV hypersensitivity, mediated by T cells.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: How does Type IV hypersensitivity differ from Type III in terms of immune response timing?

options.text: Type IV is immediate, Type III is delayed
Type III is immediate, Type IV is delayed

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity can occur quickly, but Type IV is specifically delayed, peaking at 48-72 hours.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which of the following mechanisms is involved in glomerular injury in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis involves immune complex deposition, characteristic of Type III hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What is the primary immune mechanism involved in graft rejection during transplantation?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Graft rejection primarily involves a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Regarding timing of type iv — which is correct?

options.text: All hypersensitivity reactions occur within minutes
Type IV is DELAYED — it peaks at 48–72 hours because it requires T-cell recruitment (no antibody involved)

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Only type I is immediate (minutes). Type IV is cell-mediated and delayed, which is why the tuberculin test is read at 2–3 days.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immune-complex deposition in glomeruli/vessels”?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Immune-complex deposition in glomeruli/vessels → Type III (soluble antigen + IgG + complement/neutrophils).

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test at 48–72 h”?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test at 48–72 h → Type IV delayed T-cell response.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hypersensitivity Types III & IV”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity is directly related to immune mechanisms in glomerular diseases.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which should you review before “Hypersensitivity Types III & IV”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Understanding types I and II is essential for distinguishing them from types III and IV.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: The total binding strength of a multivalent antibody (all its antigen-binding sites acting together) is termed:
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Avidity is the sum of all binding-site interactions; affinity is the strength of a single site–epitope bond. IgM has high avidity despite low per-site affinity.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Blood typing by mixing red cells with anti-A/anti-B sera relies on which antigen–antibody reaction?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Antibody cross-links particulate red cells into visible clumps (haemagglutination), the basis of ABO/Rh blood typing. Precipitation involves soluble antigens.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which antibodies facilitate the detection of antigens in serological tests?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Antibodies bind to antigens, cross-link them, and then facilitate detection through various methods.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Which statement correctly describes the difference between affinity and avidity?

options.text: Affinity is the total strength of all binding sites, while avidity is the strength of one binding site.
Affinity is the strength of one binding site, while avidity is the total strength of all binding sites.
Affinity and avidity are synonymous terms.
Avidity is only relevant for IgG antibodies.

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Affinity refers to the strength of a single antigen-binding site, while avidity is the cumulative strength of all binding sites on an antibody.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What can cause a false-negative result in a precipitation test?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Excess antibody can prevent the formation of the cross-linked lattice necessary for precipitation, leading to false-negative results.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: In a haemagglutination test for blood typing, what is the role of the antibody?

options.text: To cross-link red blood cells into visible clumps

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Antibodies cross-link particulate antigens, such as red blood cells, leading to visible agglutination.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: A patient shows a four-fold rise in antibody titre. What does this indicate?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: A four-fold rise in antibody titre is indicative of a recent or active infection.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: How does the avidity of IgM compare to that of IgG?

options.text: IgM has lower avidity due to fewer binding sites.
IgM has higher avidity due to more binding sites.
IgM and IgG have equal avidity.
IgG has higher avidity due to more binding sites.

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: IgM has higher avidity than IgG because it has 10 binding sites, allowing for stronger overall binding despite lower affinity per site.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Which immunoassay technique is most likely to be applied after understanding antigen-antibody principles?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Western blotting is an immunoassay technique that relies on antigen-antibody interactions, making it relevant after studying antigen-antibody principles.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: How might knowledge of antigen-antibody reactions apply to understanding the immune response in meningitis?

options.text: It helps in understanding the role of T cells.
It is crucial for interpreting serological tests for pathogens.
It has no relevance to meningitis.
It only applies to bacterial infections.

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Understanding antigen-antibody reactions is essential for interpreting serological tests that diagnose various types of meningitis.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Regarding affinity vs avidity — which is correct?

options.text: IgM binds poorly overall because each of its sites has low affinity
IgM has LOW per-site affinity but HIGH avidity (10 sites) → strong overall binding and good agglutination/complement activation
10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Avidity is the sum of all binding sites; multivalency compensates for low per-site affinity — the key affinity-vs-avidity point.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “IgM has high avidity but low per-site affinity”?

options.text: 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: IgM has high avidity but low per-site affinity → 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haemagglutination for ABO blood typing”?

options.text: 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Haemagglutination for ABO blood typing → Antibody cross-links (particulate) red cells.

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Antigen-antibody reactions are crucial in diagnosing meningitis.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Measuring a patient's CD4⁺ T-lymphocyte count in HIV infection is performed by:
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Flow cytometry stains cells with fluorochrome-labelled anti-CD antibodies and counts them individually — used for CD4 counts and immunophenotyping.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: In the standard HIV testing algorithm, a sensitive ELISA screen is followed by which specific confirmatory test?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: A positive sensitive ELISA screen is confirmed by a specific Western blot showing antibody bands to key viral proteins — screen sensitive, confirm specific.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What is the primary purpose of using ELISA in clinical diagnostics?

options.text: To quantify antigen or antibody levels

immunoassays-techniques.explanation: ELISA is primarily used for quantifying antigen or antibody levels in a sample.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Which assay is typically used as a confirmatory test after a positive HIV screening?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Western blot is used as a confirmatory test following a positive ELISA screening for HIV.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: In flow cytometry, what is the role of fluorochrome-labelled antibodies?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Fluorochrome-labelled antibodies are used in flow cytometry to quantify and analyze different cell types based on surface markers.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: A patient has a positive ANA test. Which technique would help identify specific autoantibodies?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Immunofluorescence is used to identify specific autoantibodies by visualizing their binding to antigens in tissue sections.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What is the correct sequence of tests in the standard HIV testing algorithm?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: The standard algorithm starts with a sensitive screening test (ELISA) followed by a specific confirmatory test (Western blot).

immunoassays-techniques.stem: How does flow cytometry assist in the diagnosis of leukemia?

options.text: By counting cells based on size

immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Flow cytometry assists in leukemia diagnosis by immunophenotyping cells using specific CD markers to identify cell types.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Which technique would be most appropriate for quantifying CD4 T-cells in an HIV patient?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Flow cytometry is the most appropriate technique for quantifying CD4 T-cells in HIV patients due to its ability to analyze individual cells.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Which assay would best help determine the presence of specific autoantibodies in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Immunofluorescence is best for determining specific autoantibodies in SLE by visualizing their binding patterns.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Regarding screen vs confirm — which is correct?

options.text: A confirmatory Western blot is used first because it is the most sensitive test
Screen with the SENSITIVE test (ELISA) first, then CONFIRM positives with the SPECIFIC test (Western blot)

immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Sensitive screening catches all true positives (few false negatives); specific confirmation removes false positives — the standard testing algorithm (e.g. HIV).

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What best explains the finding: “Colour change proportional to analyte in a microplate”?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Colour change proportional to analyte in a microplate → ELISA (enzyme-linked).

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive HIV screen confirmed by band pattern”?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Positive HIV screen confirmed by band pattern → ELISA screen → Western blot confirmation.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Which should you review before “Immunoassays: ELISA, Blotting, Flow Cytometry”?

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: A transplanted kidney turns dusky and thromboses within minutes of reperfusion. This hyperacute rejection is due to:

options.text: Pre-existing recipient antibodies against donor ABO/HLA antigens

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Hyperacute rejection results from pre-formed antibodies binding graft endothelium → complement activation and thrombosis in minutes; it is prevented by ABO matching and a pre-transplant crossmatch.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: A patient develops skin rash, diarrhoea, and cholestatic jaundice after an allogeneic bone-marrow transplant. This is:
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: In GVHD, immunocompetent donor T cells attack the immunosuppressed host — classically targeting skin, gut, and liver — a complication of bone-marrow/HSCT.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What type of graft is an organ transplanted from one individual to another of the same species?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: An allograft is a transplant between individuals of the same species but genetically different.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Which mechanism primarily drives hyperacute rejection?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-existing recipient antibodies leading to immediate graft loss.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: A patient experiences graft loss within minutes after transplantation. What is the most likely cause?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: The rapid onset of graft loss indicates hyperacute rejection due to pre-existing antibodies.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Which finding is characteristic of acute cellular rejection?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Acute cellular rejection can be reversed with steroids and typically occurs 1-2 weeks post-transplant.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What is the primary mechanism of chronic rejection?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Chronic rejection is characterized by progressive vascular intimal thickening and fibrosis over time.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: In graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), which organ is NOT typically affected?
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: GVHD primarily targets the skin, liver, and gut, but not the heart.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: How does the mechanism of acute rejection relate to hypersensitivity type IV?

options.text: Both are mediated by T cells

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Acute rejection involves T cells recognizing foreign MHC, similar to the T-cell mediated response in hypersensitivity type IV.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What is the relationship between transplant matching and the risk of rejection?

options.text: Matching has no effect on rejection

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Better transplant matching reduces the risk of rejection by minimizing differences in HLA.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Regarding cause of hyperacute rejection — which is correct?

options.text: Hyperacute rejection is caused by newly activated alloreactive T cells
Hyperacute rejection is caused by PRE-EXISTING recipient antibodies (ABO/anti-HLA) → immediate thrombosis; prevented by crossmatch

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: It happens in minutes — far too fast for a new T-cell response; it requires antibody that is already present.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Graft thrombosis within minutes of reperfusion”?

options.text: GVHD (donor T cells attack host skin/gut/liver)

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Graft thrombosis within minutes of reperfusion → Hyperacute rejection (pre-existing antibody).

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cellular rejection at 1–2 weeks, reversible with steroids”?

options.text: GVHD (donor T cells attack host skin/gut/liver)

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Cellular rejection at 1–2 weeks, reversible with steroids → Acute rejection (alloreactive T cells).

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Which should you review before “Transplantation: Allorecognition & Rejection”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Understanding hypersensitivity is crucial for grasping transplant rejection mechanisms.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and ciclosporin prevent rejection mainly by:

options.text: Blocking IL-2 production and T-cell activation

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors block the calcineurin–NFAT pathway, reducing IL-2 transcription and hence T-cell activation/proliferation — a cornerstone of maintenance immunosuppression.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Before a kidney transplant, a positive complement-dependent cytotoxicity crossmatch indicates:

options.text: Recipient antibodies against donor cells → high risk of hyperacute rejection
Donor T cells will attack the host

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: A positive crossmatch shows pre-formed recipient anti-donor antibodies that would cause hyperacute rejection — a contraindication to proceeding with that donor.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What is the primary purpose of HLA typing in organ transplantation?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: HLA typing improves graft survival by identifying the best tissue match between donor and recipient.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Which immunosuppressive drug class inhibits IL-2 production?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus and ciclosporin, block IL-2 production, crucial for T-cell activation.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What does a positive pre-transplant crossmatch indicate?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: A positive crossmatch indicates recipient antibodies react with donor cells, predicting a high risk of hyperacute rejection.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Which opportunistic infection is most commonly associated with immunosuppression post-transplant?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is a common opportunistic infection in immunosuppressed transplant recipients.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What is the inheritance pattern of HLA alleles?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: HLA alleles are inherited in a codominant manner, allowing for expression of both parental alleles.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: How does tacrolimus prevent T-cell activation?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin, leading to decreased IL-2 production and subsequent T-cell activation.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Which of the following is a consequence of immunosuppression in transplant patients?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Immunosuppression increases the risk of opportunistic infections due to a weakened immune system.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: In the context of T-cell activation, what is the significance of the two-signal rule?

options.text: It requires both antigen recognition and co-stimulation
It reduces the need for immunosuppressants

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: The two-signal rule states that T-cell activation requires both antigen recognition and a second signal from co-stimulatory molecules.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: How does understanding immunosuppressant drugs relate to transplant rejection mechanisms?

options.text: It clarifies the role of HLA typing
It informs strategies to prevent graft rejection
It determines the need for dialysis

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Knowledge of immunosuppressant drugs aids in developing strategies to prevent graft rejection by targeting T-cell activation.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Regarding meaning of a positive crossmatch — which is correct?

options.text: A positive crossmatch means the donor is a good HLA match and transplant should proceed
A POSITIVE crossmatch means recipient antibodies react with donor cells → high hyperacute-rejection risk → do NOT transplant

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: The crossmatch must be negative; a positive result reveals pre-formed donor-reactive antibody, contraindicating the transplant.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive pre-transplant crossmatch”?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Positive pre-transplant crossmatch → Contraindication — predicts hyperacute rejection.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tacrolimus/ciclosporin mechanism”?
Which is a clinical application of “Transplant Matching & Immunosuppression”?

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Transplantation is a key aspect of renal replacement therapy.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Understanding T-cell activation is crucial for grasping immunosuppression mechanisms.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: The three sequential phases of cancer immunoediting are:
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Immunoediting proceeds Elimination (surveillance kills tumour cells) → Equilibrium (immune pressure selects variants) → Escape (edited tumour evades immunity → clinical cancer).

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: A mutated protein expressed only by a patient's tumour cells and presented on MHC I is best classified as a:
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: A mutation-derived neoantigen unique to the tumour is a tumour-specific antigen (TSA). TAAs are normal self-proteins that are over-expressed or aberrantly expressed.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What type of antigen is specifically unique to tumor cells?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Tumor-specific antigens (TSA) are unique to tumor cells, including mutated neoantigens and viral antigens.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Which immune cells are primarily responsible for immunosurveillance against cancer?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) play a central role in the immunosurveillance and destruction of nascent transformed cells.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What mechanism allows NK cells to target tumor cells that down-regulate MHC I?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: NK cells recognize tumor cells that down-regulate MHC I through a mechanism known as missing-self recognition.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Which of the following findings supports the concept of immunosurveillance?

options.text: Increased cancer incidence in immunosuppressed patients
Increased tumor mutation burden in healthy individuals
Increased survival in patients with chronic infections

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: The increased cancer incidence in immunosuppressed patients provides strong evidence that the immune system normally controls tumors.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What is the first step in cancer immunoediting?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Elimination is the first step in cancer immunoediting, where the immune system destroys tumor cells.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: How does HPV contribute to cervical cancer development?

options.text: By inducing mutations in tumor suppressor genes
By presenting viral antigens as tumor-specific antigens
By promoting apoptosis of infected cells

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: HPV contributes to cervical cancer by presenting viral antigens as tumor-specific antigens, which can evade immune detection.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Which of the following best explains the increased cancer risk in immunosuppressed patients?

options.text: Increased mutation rates in normal cells

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: The increased cancer risk in immunosuppressed patients is primarily due to the loss of immunosurveillance, allowing tumors to develop.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: How do NK cells relate to tumor immune evasion mechanisms discussed in the Tumour Immune Evasion module?

options.text: They enhance MHC I expression on tumor cells
They can target tumors that down-regulate MHC I
They are ineffective against virus-associated tumors
They require prior sensitization to tumor antigens

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: NK cells can target tumors that down-regulate MHC I, which is a mechanism of tumor immune evasion.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Which of the following best connects the role of immunosuppression in cancer risk to the mechanisms of tumor spread discussed in the Cancer Spread module?

options.text: Immunosuppression allows for immune escape mechanisms

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Immunosuppression allows for immune escape mechanisms, which can facilitate tumor spread and metastasis.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Regarding evidence for immunosurveillance — which is correct?

options.text: Immunosuppression has no effect on cancer risk
Immunosuppressed patients (transplant, HIV) have markedly INCREASED cancer risk — strong evidence that the immune system normally controls tumours

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: The rise in (especially virus-related) cancers with immunosuppression demonstrates active immunosurveillance.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mutated neoantigen or viral protein on a tumour”?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Mutated neoantigen or viral protein on a tumour → Tumour-specific antigen (TSA).

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Over-expressed self-protein (e.g. CEA)”?
Which should you review before “Tumour Antigens & Cancer Immunosurveillance”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: NK cells play a crucial role in the immune response against tumors.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody, treats cancer by:

options.text: Blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitory checkpoint to reactivate anti-tumour T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Anti-PD-1 blocks the PD-1/PD-L1 brake that tumours use to switch off T cells, restoring T-cell-mediated tumour killing — a checkpoint-blockade immunotherapy.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: CAR-T cell therapy for B-cell malignancies most commonly targets which antigen?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: CAR-T cells for B-cell leukaemia/lymphoma are typically engineered to target CD19; a major toxicity is cytokine release syndrome from massive T-cell activation.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What mechanism allows tumors to evade T cell recognition by down-regulating MHC I?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Down-regulating MHC I reduces the presentation of tumor antigens, preventing recognition by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Which of the following therapies works by blocking PD-1 to enhance T cell activity against tumors?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 antibody that releases the inhibitory checkpoint on T cells, enhancing their anti-tumor activity.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What is a common adverse effect associated with CAR-T cell therapy?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Cytokine release syndrome occurs due to massive T-cell activation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which checkpoint inhibitors restore T cell function?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors block inhibitory signals (like PD-1/PD-L1), effectively 'releasing the brake' on T cells, allowing them to attack tumors.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of immune-related adverse events in checkpoint therapy?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Immune-related adverse events arise from loss of tolerance, leading to autoimmunity-like side effects due to reactivated T cells attacking normal tissues.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: How does CAR-T cell therapy specifically target B-cell malignancies?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: CAR-T cells are engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor that specifically targets the CD19 antigen found on B cells.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: In the context of T cell activation, how does checkpoint blockade relate to the two-signal rule?

options.text: It provides both signals for T cell activation
It enhances the first signal only
It removes the inhibitory signal allowing T cell response
It directly activates T cells without signals

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Checkpoint blockade removes the inhibitory signal, allowing T cells that have received the first signal to respond effectively to their target.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What role do tumor antigens play in the context of immune evasion and immunotherapy?

options.text: They are targeted by CAR-T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Tumor antigens are crucial for the recognition of cancer cells by immune cells, and therapies like CAR-T cells specifically target these antigens to elicit an immune response.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Regarding how checkpoint inhibitors work — which is correct?

options.text: Checkpoint inhibitors directly kill tumour cells like chemotherapy
They BLOCK inhibitory checkpoints (PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4) to "release the brake" on the patient's own T cells, which then attack the tumour
Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)
Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors work indirectly by reactivating T cells, not by direct cytotoxicity — hence their autoimmune-type side effects.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tumour expressing PD-L1”?

options.text: Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells
Engineered T cells target tumour antigen
Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Tumour expressing PD-L1 → Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion).

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Response to anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab)”?

options.text: Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)
Engineered T cells target tumour antigen
Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Response to anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab) → Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Tumour Immune Evasion & Cancer Immunotherapy”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Clinical implications of immune evasion may relate to broader cancer effects.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Administering preformed antitoxin (immunoglobulin) after a tetanus-prone wound is an example of:
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Giving preformed antibody provides immediate but short-lived protection with no memory — passive immunisation. Active immunisation (toxoid) would stimulate the host's own response.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which vaccine type is generally contraindicated in a significantly immunocompromised patient?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines can cause disease in immunocompromised hosts (and are avoided in pregnancy). Inactivated, toxoid, and subunit vaccines are non-replicating and safer.

vaccines-immunization.stem: What is the primary mechanism of live-attenuated vaccines?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines stimulate a strong immune response and generate memory through active immunity.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in pregnant women?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: The MMR vaccine is a live-attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of reversion and disease.

vaccines-immunization.stem: What is the primary benefit of conjugate vaccines in infants?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Conjugate vaccines provide a T-dependent response and generate memory, which is crucial for infants.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which type of vaccine requires boosters due to weaker immune response?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Inactivated vaccines typically require boosters because they elicit a weaker immune response compared to live-attenuated vaccines.

vaccines-immunization.stem: A patient presents with a deep laceration. What should be administered to provide immediate protection against tetanus?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Tetanus immunoglobulin provides immediate protection through passive immunization.

vaccines-immunization.stem: How does herd immunity protect vulnerable populations?

options.text: By providing immediate immunity to all
By reducing overall transmission in the community

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Herd immunity protects vulnerable populations by reducing overall transmission in the community, thereby indirectly protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which mechanism is primarily involved in the generation of memory B cells after vaccination?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Affinity maturation is a key process in the generation of memory B cells following vaccination, linking to the germinal center response.

vaccines-immunization.stem: What is the role of adjuvants in vaccines?

options.text: To enhance the innate immune response

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Adjuvants enhance the innate immune response, thereby strengthening and shaping the adaptive immune response to the vaccine.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which type of vaccine is most suitable for an immunocompromised patient?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Inactivated vaccines are safe for immunocompromised patients as they do not contain live pathogens that could cause disease.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Regarding live vaccines and immunosuppression — which is correct?

options.text: Live-attenuated vaccines are safe to give to immunocompromised patients because they are weakened
Live-attenuated vaccines are CONTRAINDICATED in significant immunocompromise/pregnancy — the attenuated organism can cause disease

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Without adequate immunity, even a weakened organism can replicate and cause infection; inactivated/subunit vaccines are used instead.

vaccines-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immediate protection but no memory”?

options.text: Risk of disease from the attenuated organism

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Immediate protection but no memory → Passive immunisation (preformed antibody).

vaccines-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Strong lifelong immunity from one/two doses”?

options.text: Risk of disease from the attenuated organism

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Strong lifelong immunity from one/two doses → Live-attenuated vaccine.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Vaccines & Immunisation”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which should you review before “Vaccines & Immunisation”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells
Germinal Centre, Affinity Maturation & the Memory Response

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Understanding memory response is crucial for vaccines.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Before starting an anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis, it is essential to screen for:
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: TNF maintains granuloma integrity, so anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB. Screening (and treating) latent TB before starting is standard practice.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: A therapeutic monoclonal antibody with the suffix "-umab" indicates it is:
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: The suffix ladder is -omab (murine) → -ximab (chimeric) → -zumab (humanised) → -umab (fully human); more human sequence means lower immunogenicity.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of anti-TNF biologics like adalimumab?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Anti-TNF biologics block the action of tumor necrosis factor-alpha, which is involved in inflammatory processes.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of checkpoint inhibitors like anti-PD-1?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors can lead to immune-related adverse events, including colitis due to loss of tolerance.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What is the rationale for screening for latent tuberculosis before starting anti-TNF therapy?

options.text: TNF is not involved in tuberculosis
TNF blockade can reactivate latent TB
Anti-TNF therapy is ineffective in TB
Screening is not necessary for any biologics

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: TNF is essential for granuloma integrity; blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Which immunosuppressant directly inhibits IL-2 production?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Ciclosporin inhibits calcineurin, leading to decreased IL-2 production and T-cell activation.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which rituximab exerts its therapeutic effect?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 on B cells, leading to their depletion.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: How does IVIG function in the context of antibody deficiency?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: IVIG provides passive immunoglobulin replacement, helping to bolster the immune response in antibody deficiency.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: In what way does the mechanism of action of anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab) relate to hypersensitivity reactions?

options.text: It removes free IgE from circulation

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Omalizumab binds to free IgE, preventing it from binding to mast cells and thus reducing allergic reactions.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: How does the use of checkpoint inhibitors relate to mechanisms of self-tolerance in autoimmunity?
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors can lead to a loss of self-tolerance, resulting in autoimmune-like side effects.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Regarding screening before anti-tnf therapy — which is correct?

options.text: Anti-TNF biologics can be started without any infection screening
Screen for latent TB (and hepatitis) BEFORE anti-TNF — TNF maintains granulomas, so blockade can reactivate TB
mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: TNF is essential for granuloma integrity (immunity bacteria extracellular intracellular); blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-CD20 (rituximab) depleting B cells”?

options.text: mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Anti-CD20 (rituximab) depleting B cells → mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis”?

options.text: mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis → Cytokine blockade (risk: TB reactivation).

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Which should you review before “Immunotherapy: Suppression, Stimulation & Biologics”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Understanding hypersensitivity is crucial for immunosuppressant mechanisms.

histology-methods-staining.stem: A cell with abundant rough ER (e.g. a plasma cell) shows strongly basophilic cytoplasm on H&E because:

options.text: The rRNA of ribosomes is acidic and binds haematoxylin

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Ribosomal RNA on the RER is negatively charged (acidic) and binds the basic dye haematoxylin → basophilic cytoplasm (Nissl bodies in neurons, "clock-face" plasma cells).

histology-methods-staining.stem: To highlight the glomerular basement membrane, the best stain is:
histology-methods-staining.explanation: PAS stains carbohydrate-rich structures magenta, including basement membranes, glycogen, and mucin. Osmium is for lipid; cresyl violet for Nissl.

histology-methods-staining.stem: What color does haematoxylin stain the nucleus?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Haematoxylin is a basic dye that binds to acidic components like DNA, resulting in a blue stain for the nucleus.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Which component is primarily responsible for the blue staining of Nissl bodies in neurons?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Nissl bodies contain abundant ribosomal RNA, which is basophilic and stains blue with haematoxylin.

histology-methods-staining.stem: What is the primary reason for eosinophilia in muscle cells?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Muscle cells are rich in proteins such as actin and myosin, which are positively charged and bind the acidic dye eosin, resulting in a pink stain.

histology-methods-staining.stem: A patient sample shows magenta staining of the basement membrane. Which stain was likely used?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain is used to identify carbohydrates, which appear magenta.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Which of the following statements about haematoxylin is correct?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Haematoxylin is a basic dye that specifically stains acidic components like nucleic acids blue.

histology-methods-staining.stem: How does light microscopy differ from electron microscopy in histology?

options.text: LM shows ultrastructure; TEM shows tissue architecture.
LM uses basic dyes; TEM uses acidic dyes.
LM provides a 3-D view; TEM provides a 2-D view.
LM shows tissue architecture; TEM shows internal ultrastructure.

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Light microscopy (LM) reveals tissue architecture, while transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveals internal ultrastructure.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Which histological method would be most appropriate for rapid intra-operative diagnosis?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Frozen sections are used for rapid intra-operative diagnosis due to their quick preparation time.

histology-methods-staining.stem: How does the staining of the nucleus relate to subcellular alterations in disease?

options.text: Nuclear staining indicates nucleic acid changes.

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Changes in nuclear staining can indicate alterations in nucleic acids, which may reflect disease processes.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Which staining method would be most relevant when studying chromatin alterations in the nucleus?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: H&E staining is fundamental for visualizing chromatin and nuclear structure in histological samples.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Regarding which dye stains the nucleus? — which is correct?

options.text: The nucleus is acidic so it must stain with the acidic dye (eosin)
DNA is acidic → it binds the BASIC dye haematoxylin → blue (basophilic)

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Acidic components bind basic dyes and vice versa. "Basophilic" describes the target loving the basic dye, not being basic itself.

histology-methods-staining.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blue cytoplasm in a plasma cell / neuron”?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Blue cytoplasm in a plasma cell / neuron → Abundant RER (rRNA) → basophilic (Nissl bodies).

histology-methods-staining.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pink cytoplasm in muscle / RBC”?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Pink cytoplasm in muscle / RBC → Protein-rich (actin/myosin, haemoglobin) → eosinophilic.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: On transmission electron microscopy the plasma membrane appears trilaminar because:

options.text: The two electron-dense phospholipid heads flank an electron-lucent lipid tail core
Integral proteins stain in three bands

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Osmium binds the polar heads, giving two dense outer lines with a lucent centre (the hydrophobic tails) — the "railroad track" trilaminar appearance.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which is an example of secondary active transport?

options.text: SGLT moving glucose using the Na⁺ gradient

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: SGLT couples "downhill" Na⁺ entry (gradient set by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to "uphill" glucose entry — secondary active transport. The ATPase itself is primary active; O₂ and K⁺-leak are passive.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What is the primary function of the glycocalyx on the cell surface?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: The glycocalyx primarily functions in cell recognition and adhesion, providing a protective layer on the cell surface.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which type of membrane protein can only be removed by disrupting the membrane?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Integral proteins span the membrane and are tightly bound, requiring membrane disruption for removal.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What transport mechanism is used for glucose uptake in the gut against its concentration gradient?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Glucose uptake in the gut occurs via SGLT, which is a secondary active transport mechanism that couples Na⁺ and glucose transport.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic finding of the plasma membrane on transmission electron microscopy (TEM)?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: The plasma membrane appears as a trilaminar structure on TEM, consisting of two dense lines of phosphate heads and a lucent lipid core.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates facilitated diffusion from active transport?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion moves against the gradient
Facilitated diffusion does not require ATP
Active transport uses channel proteins only

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Facilitated diffusion utilizes a protein carrier but does not require ATP, moving substances down their concentration gradient.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: How does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase contribute to cellular function?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the membrane potential by pumping 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, crucial for cell excitability.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: In the context of glucose monitoring, how does the SGLT mechanism relate to glucose absorption?

options.text: It facilitates glucose uptake in the intestines

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: SGLT facilitates glucose uptake against its gradient in the intestines, which is essential for glucose monitoring and management.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which junction type is crucial for maintaining the polarity of epithelial cells, allowing for differential transport?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Tight junctions are essential for maintaining epithelial cell polarity by preventing the free passage of substances between the apical and basolateral surfaces.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Regarding facilitated diffusion vs active transport — which is correct?

options.text: Any transport that needs a protein carrier uses ATP
Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier/channel but NO ATP (moves down-gradient); active transport uses ATP to move against the gradient
Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Carrier involvement ≠ energy use. Only active transport (or secondary active) works against the concentration gradient.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trilaminar "railroad track" on TEM”?

options.text: Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Trilaminar "railroad track" on TEM → Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What best explains the finding: “Integral protein cannot be washed off”?

options.text: Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Integral protein cannot be washed off → It spans the hydrophobic core (transmembrane).

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport”?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Transport mechanisms are critical for glucose monitoring in clinical settings.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: A cell specialised for steroid hormone synthesis would be expected to have abundant:
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: SER synthesises lipids and steroids (and detoxifies) — abundant in adrenal cortex, Leydig cells, and hepatocytes. RER dominates protein-secreting cells.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Which organelle contains catalase and oxidises very-long-chain fatty acids, and is NOT derived from the Golgi?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Peroxisomes use catalase to detoxify H₂O₂ and β-oxidise VLCFA; they arise by growth/division of existing peroxisomes, not from the Golgi (unlike lysosomes).

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What is the primary function of mitochondria in cells?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Mitochondria are known as the ATP factories of the cell, responsible for energy production through oxidative phosphorylation.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Which organelle is primarily involved in the synthesis of secretory proteins?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and is responsible for synthesizing membrane-bound and secretory proteins.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What type of cytoplasmic inclusions are PAS-positive in hepatocytes?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Glycogen inclusions in hepatocytes are detected by PAS staining, indicating their carbohydrate content.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Which organelle is responsible for breaking down hydrogen peroxide?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Peroxisomes contain enzymes like catalase that break down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: A patient presents with brown perinuclear granules in old cells. What do these granules represent?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Lipofuscin is a marker of aging and represents residual bodies in cells, often seen as brown granules.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding organelles and inclusions?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Inclusions are non-membranous stored materials, while organelles are metabolically active structures.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: How does the function of the Golgi apparatus relate to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum for their final destinations.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What staining method would best highlight ribosomes in a tissue sample?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Basophilic staining highlights ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum due to their high RNA content.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Regarding organelle vs inclusion — which is correct?

options.text: Glycogen and lipid droplets are organelles
They are INCLUSIONS — non-membranous stored material, not metabolically active organelles

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Organelles (mito, ER, Golgi, lysosome) carry out functions; inclusions (glycogen, lipid, pigment) are stored products or waste.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basophilic granular cytoplasm (Nissl bodies)”?

options.text: Mitochondria — inner-membrane folds house the ETC

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Basophilic granular cytoplasm (Nissl bodies) → Abundant RER (neurons, plasma cells).

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale/eosinophilic cytoplasm in steroid cells”?

options.text: Mitochondria — inner-membrane folds house the ETC

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Pale/eosinophilic cytoplasm in steroid cells → Abundant SER (adrenal cortex, Leydig, hepatocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: A hepatocyte shows a large, pale, vesicular nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. This indicates:

options.text: An actively transcribing, protein-synthesising cell (euchromatin + high rRNA output)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Open euchromatin (pale) plus a prominent nucleolus (rRNA/ribosome production) marks a metabolically active, synthesising cell. Dense hyperchromatic nuclei indicate quiescence.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: How many Barr bodies are present in a somatic cell with a 47,XXY karyotype?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Barr bodies = (number of X chromosomes − 1). With two X chromosomes, one is inactivated → 1 Barr body.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which of the following best describes euchromatin?

options.text: Loosely packed and pale, transcriptionally active
Visible as a Barr body in female cells

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Euchromatin is characterized by its loose packing and pale appearance, indicating active transcription.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What is the primary function of the nucleolus?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: The nucleolus is primarily involved in the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and the assembly of ribosomal subunits.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: A female patient presents with neutrophils exhibiting a drumstick appendage. What does this finding indicate?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: The drumstick appendage represents a Barr body, indicating the presence of an inactive X chromosome in female neutrophils.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which of the following findings would most likely indicate malignancy in a cell?

options.text: Enlarged pleomorphic nuclei with a high N:C ratio

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Enlarged pleomorphic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio are indicative of dysplasia or malignancy.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What is the mechanism behind the appearance of a small, dense, hyperchromatic nucleus in lymphocytes?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: The small, dense, hyperchromatic nucleus indicates a dominance of heterochromatin, reflecting transcriptional inactivity.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: How does the structure of chromatin relate to its function in gene expression?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Euchromatin is loosely packed and accessible, allowing for active transcription, while heterochromatin is condensed and inactive.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: In a histological examination of thyroid tissue, which feature indicates high protein synthesis activity?

options.text: Large, pale vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Small, compact nuclei with minimal cytoplasm

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Large, pale vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli indicate active protein synthesis, typical of cells like thyroid follicular cells.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which chromatin feature would you expect to see in a cell undergoing significant transcriptional activity?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Pale, dispersed euchromatin is indicative of active transcription, contrasting with the condensed structure of heterochromatin.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Regarding which chromatin is active? — which is correct?

options.text: The dark, dense heterochromatin must be the busy, active part
EUchromatin (pale, dispersed) is transcriptionally ACTIVE; heterochromatin (dark, condensed) is inactive
Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Condensed = packed away/silenced. Active genes need open, accessible euchromatin — which looks pale on H&E.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale vesicular nucleus + big nucleolus”?

options.text: Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Pale vesicular nucleus + big nucleolus → Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Small dense hyperchromatic nucleus”?

options.text: Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Small dense hyperchromatic nucleus → Heterochromatin dominant → inactive (lymphocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Nucleus: Envelope, Chromatin & Nucleolus”?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Nuclear features are relevant in thyroid histology.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which should you review before “The Nucleus: Envelope, Chromatin & Nucleolus”?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Understanding chromatin structure is essential for grasping nuclear function.

actin-microfilaments.stem: The core of an intestinal microvillus is composed of:
actin-microfilaments.explanation: Microvilli have a core of bundled actin filaments (with villin/fimbrin) anchored in the terminal web — non-motile absorptive projections. The 9+2 microtubule core belongs to motile cilia.

actin-microfilaments.stem: The contractile ring that divides a cell during cytokinesis is made of:
actin-microfilaments.explanation: The cleavage furrow is generated by an actin–myosin II contractile ring. Microtubules form the mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes, not the furrow.

actin-microfilaments.stem: What is the primary function of myosin in relation to actin?
actin-microfilaments.explanation: Myosin interacts with actin to generate force, primarily in muscle contraction.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Which of the following statements about actin microfilaments is true?

options.text: They are the thickest cytoskeletal filaments.
They are involved in cilia movement.
They polymerize from G-actin to F-actin.
They do not participate in cell motility.

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Actin microfilaments polymerize from globular G-actin to form filamentous F-actin.

actin-microfilaments.stem: What is the mechanism of action of cytochalasin?
actin-microfilaments.explanation: Cytochalasin blocks actin polymerization, disrupting actin filament dynamics.

actin-microfilaments.stem: During cytokinesis, which structure is formed by actin and myosin?
actin-microfilaments.explanation: The cleavage furrow is formed by the contractile ring of actin and myosin during cell division.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the composition of microvilli?
actin-microfilaments.explanation: Microvilli are supported by bundled actin filaments anchored in the terminal web.

actin-microfilaments.stem: How do *Listeria* and *Shigella* utilize actin for motility?

options.text: By hijacking host actin to form comet tails

actin-microfilaments.explanation: These pathogens polymerize host actin to create comet tails for intracellular movement.

actin-microfilaments.stem: How does actin contribute to cell junctions, particularly in epithelial cells?

options.text: By linking cadherins to the cytoskeleton

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Actin filaments link cadherins through catenins, forming the zonula adherens in epithelial cells.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Which of the following best explains the role of actin in muscle contraction?

options.text: Actin provides structural support to myofibrils
Actin serves as a track for myosin movement

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Actin serves as a track for myosin to pull on during muscle contraction, facilitating shortening of the sarcomere.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Regarding which filament cores microvilli? — which is correct?

options.text: Microvilli and cilia both have a microtubule core
Microvilli have an ACTIN core (non-motile); cilia have a MICROTUBULE 9+2 core (motile)
Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Do not conflate the two apical projections — actin = microvilli/stereocilia, microtubules = cilia/flagella.

actin-microfilaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thinnest filament (~6–8 nm)”?

options.text: Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brush border / microvillus core”?

options.text: Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Brush border / microvillus core → Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Which should you review before “Microfilaments: Actin, Myosin & Cell Motility”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Actin is crucial for the structure and function of cell junctions.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: A cross-section of a motile cilium shows a microtubule arrangement of:

options.text: A single central bundle of actin

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: The motile ciliary axoneme is 9+2 (nine outer doublets + a central pair), with dynein arms driving bending. The basal body/centriole is 9+0 triplets.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Fast anterograde axonal transport of vesicles from the neuronal soma to the synapse is powered by:
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Kinesin walks toward the microtubule plus end (anterograde: soma → terminal). Dynein handles retrograde transport back to the soma.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: What is the primary function of kinesin motor proteins?

options.text: Transporting cargo toward the cell body
Transporting cargo toward the axon terminal

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Kinesin is responsible for anterograde transport, moving cargo from the cell body toward the axon terminal.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Which structure is characterized by a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules?
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Motile cilia and flagella exhibit a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules, essential for their movement.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: What is the role of dynein in ciliary movement?

options.text: Sliding doublets to bend the cilium
Transporting cargo to the axon terminal

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Dynein arms slide the outer doublets of microtubules, facilitating the bending motion of cilia.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: A patient presents with situs inversus, bronchiectasis, and infertility. What is the likely underlying defect?
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: These symptoms are characteristic of primary ciliary dyskinesia due to a defect in dynein arms.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Which of the following statements about microtubules is FALSE?

options.text: They are the thickest filaments in the cytoskeleton.
They are nucleated at the centrosome.
They are composed of actin monomers.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Microtubules are composed of α/β-tubulin dimers, not actin monomers, which are the building blocks of microfilaments.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: How do microtubules differ from intermediate filaments?

options.text: Microtubules are thicker than intermediate filaments

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Microtubules are indeed thicker than intermediate filaments, which are more variable in diameter and not hollow.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: What is the primary role of the centrosome in relation to microtubules?
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: The centrosome serves as the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) and is responsible for nucleating new microtubules.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Which motor protein is responsible for retrograde transport in neurons?
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Dynein is the motor protein that facilitates retrograde transport, moving cargo toward the cell body.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: In the context of epithelial cells, how do microtubules contribute to cell function?
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Microtubules are crucial for the movement of cilia in epithelial cells, aiding in the clearance of mucus and pathogens.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Regarding kinesin vs dynein direction — which is correct?

options.text: Kinesin moves cargo toward the cell body (retrograde)
Kinesin = anterograde (toward the + end / axon terminal); dynein = retrograde (toward the − end / soma)

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Reversing them is a classic error. Anchor it: Kinesin "Kicks out," Dynein "Drags back."

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thickest filament (~25 nm), hollow”?
What best explains the finding: “9+2 axoneme on cross-section”?

intermediate-filaments.stem: A poorly differentiated malignant tumour stains positive for vimentin and negative for keratin. The most likely category is:
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Vimentin marks mesenchymal cells → sarcoma. Keratin would indicate carcinoma; GFAP a glioma. IF immunohistochemistry reveals the tumour's tissue of origin.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Which intermediate filament is characteristic of astrocytes?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is the astrocyte IF and marks astrocytic tumours (gliomas). Desmin = muscle, keratin = epithelium, neurofilament = neurons.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Which intermediate filament is primarily found in epithelial cells?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Keratin is the intermediate filament specific to epithelial cells, providing structural support.

intermediate-filaments.stem: What is the primary function of intermediate filaments in cells?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Intermediate filaments provide mechanical support and stability to cells, resisting stretch.

intermediate-filaments.stem: A patient presents with a tumor that is positive for vimentin. What is the likely origin of this tumor?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Vimentin positivity indicates a mesenchymal origin, suggesting a sarcoma.

intermediate-filaments.stem: In which condition would you expect to find Mallory bodies in hepatocytes?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Mallory bodies are associated with alcoholic liver disease, representing clumped keratin intermediate filaments.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Which statement about intermediate filaments is true?

options.text: They are dynamic and polar like microtubules.
They utilize motor proteins for movement.
They are involved in cell division.

intermediate-filaments.explanation: Intermediate filaments are stable, non-polar structures that do not use motor proteins.

intermediate-filaments.stem: A patient with a glioma shows positive staining for GFAP. What does this indicate?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: GFAP positivity indicates the tumor's astrocytic origin, characteristic of gliomas.

intermediate-filaments.stem: How are intermediate filaments related to cell junctions?

options.text: They are involved in gap junctions.

intermediate-filaments.explanation: Intermediate filaments anchor desmosomes, providing mechanical strength to cell junctions.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Which intermediate filament is associated with neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles contain neurofilaments and tau protein, characteristic of Alzheimer's pathology.

intermediate-filaments.stem: How do intermediate filaments differ from actin filaments?

options.text: Intermediate filaments are dynamic and polar.

intermediate-filaments.explanation: Unlike actin filaments, intermediate filaments are stable, non-polar, and do not have associated motor proteins.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Regarding are intermediate filaments dynamic like actin? — which is correct?

options.text: All cytoskeletal filaments use motor proteins and treadmill
IFs are stable, non-polar, and have NO motor proteins — they bear tension, unlike actin/microtubules

intermediate-filaments.explanation: IFs are the mechanical scaffold; only actin (myosin) and microtubules (kinesin/dynein) have motors and polarity.

intermediate-filaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Keratin-positive tumour”?
What best explains the finding: “Vimentin-positive tumour”?
Which should you review before “Intermediate Filaments: Tissue-Specific Cytoskeleton”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

intermediate-filaments.explanation: Basic understanding of cellular metabolism may support knowledge of tissue-specific functions.

epithelial-classification.stem: The epithelium lining the trachea, in which all cells contact the basement membrane but nuclei lie at different levels, is:
epithelial-classification.explanation: The respiratory tract is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — one layer that only appears stratified because of staggered nuclei.

epithelial-classification.stem: Simple squamous epithelium lining the pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial cavities is specifically called:
epithelial-classification.explanation: Mesothelium lines the serous body cavities; endothelium is the simple squamous lining of blood/lymphatic vessels. Urothelium is transitional epithelium of the urinary tract.

epithelial-classification.stem: What type of epithelium lines the alveoli of the lungs?
epithelial-classification.explanation: The alveoli are lined by simple squamous epithelium, which facilitates gas exchange.

epithelial-classification.stem: Which epithelium type is characterized by nuclei at different heights but all cells touching the basement membrane?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium appears layered due to varying nuclear heights, but is a single layer.

epithelial-classification.stem: Which epithelium type is found in the urinary bladder?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Transitional epithelium accommodates stretching and is found in the bladder.

epithelial-classification.stem: What is the primary function of simple cuboidal epithelium?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Simple cuboidal epithelium primarily functions in secretion and absorption.

epithelial-classification.stem: Which finding indicates stratified squamous keratinized epithelium?

options.text: Flat single layer lining a blood vessel

epithelial-classification.explanation: Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium has a dry, keratinized surface, characteristic of the epidermis.

epithelial-classification.stem: How does pseudostratified epithelium differ from stratified epithelium?

options.text: All cells touch the basement membrane
It is found only in the respiratory tract

epithelial-classification.explanation: Pseudostratified epithelium is a single layer where all cells contact the basement membrane, unlike stratified epithelium.

epithelial-classification.stem: Which type of epithelium is primarily involved in absorption and secretion in the gastrointestinal tract?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Simple columnar epithelium is specialized for absorption and secretion in the gut.

epithelial-classification.stem: What is the main role of the basement membrane in epithelial tissues?
epithelial-classification.explanation: The basement membrane provides structural support and anchorage for epithelial cells.

epithelial-classification.stem: Regarding pseudostratified vs stratified — which is correct?

options.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is a true multilayered (stratified) epithelium
