It is a SINGLE layer — every cell touches the basement membrane, but nuclei at different heights create a layered illusion

epithelial-classification.explanation: The defining feature is BM contact by all cells. Stratified epithelia have upper cells that do NOT touch the BM.

epithelial-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flat single layer lining a blood vessel”?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Flat single layer lining a blood vessel → Simple squamous = endothelium.

epithelial-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cuboidal cells around a colloid-filled follicle”?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Cuboidal cells around a colloid-filled follicle → Simple cuboidal = thyroid follicle.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: The brush (striated) border of the intestinal and proximal-tubule epithelium is composed of:
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The brush/striated border is a dense array of actin-cored microvilli that maximise absorptive surface. Cilia (microtubule, motile) belong to the airway/uterine tube.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: The lamina densa of the basal lamina is composed chiefly of:

options.text: Type III (reticular) collagen made by fibroblasts

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The lamina densa is a network of type IV collagen with perlecan (heparan sulfate), produced by the epithelium. Type III collagen forms the reticular lamina made by fibroblasts.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What type of cytoskeletal structure is found in microvilli?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Microvilli are composed of an actin filament core, which supports their structure and function in absorption.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of cilia?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Cilia are motile structures characterized by a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules, allowing them to move fluid across epithelial surfaces.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What is the primary function of the basement membrane?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The basement membrane serves as a selective filtration barrier, particularly in structures like the glomerulus.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which structure is responsible for anchoring the epithelium to the basement membrane?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Hemidesmosomes are specialized structures that anchor the epithelium to the basement membrane.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: On electron microscopy, which layer of the basement membrane is characterized by an electron-dense appearance?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The lamina densa is the electron-dense layer of the basement membrane, primarily composed of type IV collagen.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: A patient presents with infertility due to impaired sperm maturation. Which structure in the epididymis is likely affected?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Stereocilia in the epididymis are involved in sperm maturation and absorption; their dysfunction can lead to infertility.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which of the following correctly differentiates microvilli from cilia?

options.text: Both are motile and have a microtubule core
Microvilli are motile, cilia are non-motile
Microvilli have an actin core, cilia have a microtubule core
Microvilli are found in the respiratory tract, cilia are found in the intestine

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Microvilli have an actin core and are non-motile, while cilia have a microtubule core and are motile, which is a common exam distractor.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: How do cilia contribute to respiratory health?

options.text: By moving mucus out of the airway
By forming a barrier to pathogens

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Cilia in the respiratory tract move mucus out of the airway, helping to clear pathogens and debris.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What is the role of the basement membrane in the context of placental villi?

options.text: Acting as a barrier to maternal blood

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The basement membrane in placental villi acts as a barrier to maternal blood, allowing selective nutrient transfer while protecting the fetus.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Regarding microvilli vs cilia core — which is correct?

options.text: Both microvilli and cilia are motile and share a microtubule core
Microvilli = ACTIN core, non-motile (absorption); cilia = MICROTUBULE 9+2, motile (movement)

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Same "hair-like" look under LM, but opposite cytoskeleton and function — a very common exam distractor.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Striated/brush border in gut & PCT”?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Striated/brush border in gut & PCT → Dense actin-cored microvilli (absorption).

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Motile hairs moving mucus in the airway”?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Motile hairs moving mucus in the airway → Cilia (9+2 microtubule axoneme).

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Apical Specializations & the Basement Membrane”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Basement membrane's role in placental barrier relates to epithelial function.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which should you review before “Apical Specializations & the Basement Membrane”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Understanding cilia requires knowledge of microtubule structure and function.

cell-junctions.stem: Autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 (pemphigus vulgaris) disrupt which junction, causing keratinocytes to separate?
cell-junctions.explanation: Desmoglein is a desmosomal cadherin; anti-desmoglein antibodies break desmosomes → intraepidermal acantholytic blisters. Anti-hemidesmosome antibodies cause bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal).

cell-junctions.stem: Direct electrical coupling between cardiac muscle cells occurs through:
cell-junctions.explanation: Gap junctions of connexons allow ions to pass cell-to-cell, synchronising cardiac contraction (part of the intercalated disc, along with desmosomes for mechanical strength).

cell-junctions.stem: Which protein is primarily responsible for forming tight junctions?
cell-junctions.explanation: Occludin is a key component of tight junctions that helps seal the paracellular space.

cell-junctions.stem: What is the primary function of desmosomes in epithelial tissue?
cell-junctions.explanation: Desmosomes provide mechanical strength by anchoring intermediate filaments, allowing tissues to withstand stress.

cell-junctions.stem: Which junction type is crucial for electrical coupling in cardiac muscle?
cell-junctions.explanation: Gap junctions allow for direct electrical coupling between cardiac muscle cells, facilitating synchronized contraction.

cell-junctions.stem: In which junction are cadherins linked to actin filaments?
cell-junctions.explanation: Zonula adherens junctions utilize cadherins to link to actin filaments, providing lateral adhesion.

cell-junctions.stem: What is the primary anchoring filament in desmosomes?
cell-junctions.explanation: Desmosomes anchor to keratin intermediate filaments, while adherens junctions anchor to actin filaments.

cell-junctions.stem: A patient presents with blistering skin lesions. Which junction type is most likely affected?
cell-junctions.explanation: Hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane, and their failure can lead to blistering conditions like bullous pemphigoid.

cell-junctions.stem: How do gap junctions facilitate communication between cardiac muscle cells?

options.text: By anchoring to the basement membrane
By allowing ion flow through connexons

cell-junctions.explanation: Gap junctions consist of connexons that permit the passage of ions and small molecules, enabling electrical coupling.

cell-junctions.stem: Which type of junction is primarily involved in maintaining the integrity of the epithelial barrier?
cell-junctions.explanation: Tight junctions create a seal that prevents leakage between epithelial cells, maintaining barrier integrity.

cell-junctions.stem: How do intermediate filaments relate to desmosomes in epithelial cells?

options.text: They are not involved with desmosomes

cell-junctions.explanation: Intermediate filaments, specifically keratin, anchor desmosomes, providing mechanical stability to epithelial tissues.

cell-junctions.stem: What role do hemidesmosomes play in relation to the basement membrane?

options.text: They anchor cells to the basement membrane

cell-junctions.explanation: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane, crucial for tissue integrity.

cell-junctions.stem: Regarding which filament anchors the desmosome? — which is correct?

options.text: Both adherens junctions and desmosomes anchor to actin
Adherens junction → ACTIN; desmosome → KERATIN (intermediate filaments)

cell-junctions.explanation: Both use Ca²⁺-dependent cadherins, but the intracellular anchor differs — actin (belt) vs keratin IF (spot-weld).

cell-junctions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Occludin/claudin apical seal”?
cell-junctions.explanation: Occludin/claudin apical seal → Tight junction (blocks paracellular leak).

cell-junctions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cadherin linked to actin”?
cell-junctions.explanation: Cadherin linked to actin → Zonula adherens.

cell-junctions.stem: Which should you review before “Cell Junctions: The Junctional Complex”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

cell-junctions.explanation: Desmosomes anchor to keratin intermediate filaments.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: A gland in which the entire secretory cell disintegrates and becomes the secretory product uses which mode?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Holocrine secretion (sebaceous gland) sacrifices the whole cell. Merocrine = exocytosis with an intact cell; apocrine = apical cytoplasm pinched off.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Serous secretory cells (e.g. pancreatic acini) are recognised histologically by:

options.text: Pale, foamy cytoplasm with a flattened basal nucleus
Basophilic cytoplasm, a round nucleus, and apical zymogen granules

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Serous (protein-secreting) cells have basophilic RER-rich cytoplasm, a round central nucleus, and apical zymogen granules. Pale foamy cells with basal nuclei are mucous cells.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which type of secretion involves the entire cell disintegrating to release its product?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Holocrine secretion involves the entire cell breaking down to release its contents, as seen in sebaceous glands.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What is the primary mode of secretion for salivary glands?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Salivary glands secrete via merocrine mode, which involves exocytosis while preserving the cell.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which gland type is characterized by a duct and secretes its product onto a surface?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Exocrine glands have ducts and secrete their products onto epithelial surfaces.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Identify the secretion mode of mammary glands.
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Mammary glands utilize apocrine secretion, where part of the cell's cytoplasm is shed with the secretion.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What histological feature is indicative of serous secretory cells?

options.text: Basophilic acinar cells with zymogen granules

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Serous secretory cells are characterized by basophilic cytoplasm and zymogen granules, indicating protein secretion.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which gland type is incorrectly matched with its secretion mode? Sebaceous glands - Apocrine.
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Sebaceous glands secrete via holocrine mode, not apocrine; this is a common trap.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: How do exocrine glands differ from endocrine glands in terms of secretion?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Exocrine glands secrete onto epithelial surfaces, whereas endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which mode of secretion is primarily involved in the release of digestive enzymes from the pancreas?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: The pancreas primarily uses merocrine secretion to release digestive enzymes via exocytosis.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Regarding secretion mode of sebaceous glands — which is correct?

options.text: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum by apocrine (pinching off the apex)
Sebaceous glands are HOLOCRINE — the entire cell disintegrates to form the secretion
Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Apocrine sheds only apical cytoplasm (mammary/axillary sweat); holocrine sacrifices the whole cell (sebaceous).

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sebaceous gland secretion”?

options.text: Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Sebaceous gland secretion → Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Salivary/pancreatic secretion”?

options.text: Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Salivary/pancreatic secretion → Merocrine — exocytosis, cell preserved.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Glands: Exocrine vs Endocrine & Modes of Secretion”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Clinical relevance of skin glands relates to their exocrine functions.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which should you review before “Glands: Exocrine vs Endocrine & Modes of Secretion”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Understanding gland structure requires knowledge of connective tissue.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: A connective-tissue cell with an eccentric "clock-face" nucleus and deeply basophilic cytoplasm is a:
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: The clock-face (cartwheel) heterochromatin and RER-rich basophilic cytoplasm identify a plasma cell, which secretes antibodies (derived from B lymphocytes).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which connective-tissue cell releases histamine and heparin from metachromatic granules during allergic reactions?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Mast cells degranulate on IgE cross-linking, releasing histamine (vasodilation) and heparin — driving immediate hypersensitivity and inflammation.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which cell type is primarily responsible for synthesizing collagen in connective tissue?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Fibroblasts are the main cells that synthesize collagen and other extracellular matrix components.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What is the primary function of macrophages in connective tissue?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Macrophages are specialized for phagocytosis and play a key role in the immune response.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which of the following cells is characterized by a 'clock-face' nucleus?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Plasma cells are recognized by their eccentric, 'clock-face' nucleus and basophilic cytoplasm.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: How do mast cells contribute to allergic reactions?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Mast cells release histamine upon IgE cross-linking, leading to vasodilation and inflammation in allergic reactions.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What is the main difference between the origins of plasma cells and macrophages?

options.text: Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Plasma cells derive from B lymphocytes, while macrophages originate from monocytes.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which connective tissue cell type is primarily involved in wound healing?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Fibroblasts play a crucial role in wound healing by synthesizing collagen and other extracellular matrix components.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: In the context of liver pathology, which resident cell type is responsible for phagocytosis?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages in the liver that perform phagocytosis.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which connective tissue cell type is most likely to be involved in the inflammatory response in the skin?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Mast cells release histamine and other mediators that are key in the inflammatory response.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Regarding origin of the plasma cell vs macrophage — which is correct?

options.text: Plasma cells and macrophages both come from monocytes
Plasma cells derive from B LYMPHOCYTES (antibodies); macrophages derive from MONOCYTES (phagocytosis)

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Different lineages: B-cell → plasma cell (humoral), monocyte → macrophage (innate/APC).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Spindle cell making fibres”?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Spindle cell making fibres → Fibroblast (most common CT cell).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Metachromatic granular cell releasing histamine”?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Metachromatic granular cell releasing histamine → Mast cell (allergy/inflammation).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Connective Tissue Cells”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Connective tissue cells are directly involved in the pathology of cutaneous diseases.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which should you review before “Connective Tissue Cells”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Understanding connective tissue cells requires knowledge of the types of fibers they produce.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: The delicate branching fibres that form the supporting stroma of a lymph node and stain with silver but poorly with H&E are composed of:
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Reticular fibres are type III collagen — fine, argyrophilic (silver-staining), forming the stroma of lymphoid organs, liver, and bone marrow.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: A tendon, which must resist strong tension in one direction, is made of:
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue — parallel type I collagen bundles aligned for unidirectional tensile strength. The dermis is dense irregular.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What type of collagen is primarily found in dense regular connective tissue?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Dense regular connective tissue is characterized by parallel bundles of type I collagen, providing strength in one direction.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Which connective tissue fiber type is primarily responsible for the recoil of arteries?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Elastic fibers, composed of elastin and fibrillin, allow for the recoil of arteries after stretching.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: A biopsy reveals fine branching fibers that stain positively with silver stain in a lymph node. What type of fibers are these?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: The fine branching fibers in lymph nodes are reticular fibers, which are composed of type III collagen and are argyrophilic.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of loose connective tissue?

options.text: High cellularity and abundant ground substance

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Loose connective tissue is characterized by high cellularity and abundant ground substance, allowing for flexibility and support.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What is the primary function of ground substance in connective tissue?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Ground substance is a hydrated gel that fills space, resists compression, and serves as a medium for diffusion.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: In which type of connective tissue would you find a high concentration of type III collagen?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Reticular connective tissue is characterized by a fine mesh of type III collagen fibers, providing structural support in lymphoid organs.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: How does the composition of connective tissue fibers relate to cutaneous connective tissue diseases?

options.text: Altered collagen types lead to skin fragility
Increased elastic fibers cause skin laxity
Decreased ground substance results in thickened skin

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Alterations in collagen types can lead to conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which results in skin fragility.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Which type of connective tissue is primarily involved in the formation of the osteon in bone?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Bone is considered a specialized connective tissue that forms the osteon structure, providing strength and support.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Regarding reticular fibre composition — which is correct?

options.text: Reticular fibres are made of elastin
Reticular fibres are type III COLLAGEN (argyrophilic mesh); elastic fibres are elastin + fibrillin

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Reticular = collagen III (fine branching scaffold of lymphoid/marrow); do not confuse with elastic fibres.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thick eosinophilic parallel bundles in a tendon”?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Thick eosinophilic parallel bundles in a tendon → Dense regular type I collagen.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fine branching silver-stained mesh in a lymph node”?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Fine branching silver-stained mesh in a lymph node → Reticular fibres (type III collagen).

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Connective Tissue Fibres & Tissue Types”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Clinical relevance in understanding diseases affecting connective tissues.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which epidermal cell produces melanin and transfers it to surrounding keratinocytes?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Melanocytes (in the stratum basale) synthesise melanin in melanosomes and transfer it to keratinocytes for UV protection. Langerhans = immune APC; Merkel = touch receptor.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which membrane consists of connective tissue lined by cells but has NO epithelium?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The synovial membrane lining joint cavities is made of connective tissue with synoviocytes but lacks a true epithelium. Mucous, serous, and cutaneous membranes all have an epithelial layer.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which layer of the epidermis contains the mitotically active stem cells?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis where stem cells divide to replenish the skin.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What is the primary function of melanocytes in the epidermis?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Melanocytes are responsible for synthesizing melanin, which protects against UV radiation.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which epidermal layer is characterized by the presence of keratohyalin granules?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The stratum granulosum contains keratohyalin granules that contribute to keratinization.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What type of cell is primarily responsible for antigen presentation in the epidermis?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Langerhans cells are dendritic cells in the epidermis that present antigens to the immune system.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: In which type of skin is the stratum lucidum found?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin, such as the palms and soles.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which junctional complex is primarily responsible for mechanical strength in the epidermis?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Desmosomes provide mechanical strength by anchoring adjacent keratinocytes together.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: A patient presents with a skin biopsy showing anucleate keratin scales. Which layer of the epidermis does this finding represent?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Anucleate keratin scales are characteristic of the stratum corneum, the outermost layer of the epidermis.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: How does the structure of the epidermis relate to its function as a barrier?

options.text: Thick keratinized layers prevent water loss

membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The thick keratinized layers of the epidermis form a barrier that prevents water loss and protects against environmental damage.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What is the role of keratinocytes in the epidermis?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Keratinocytes are the primary cells in the epidermis that produce keratin, forming the skin barrier.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Regarding which layer divides? — which is correct?

options.text: The stratum corneum actively divides to renew the skin
The stratum BASALE contains the dividing stem cells; the corneum is dead, anucleate keratin

membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Renewal is bottom-up: mitosis at the base, cells mature and die as they ascend to form the surface barrier.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anucleate flattened keratin scales at the surface”?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Anucleate flattened keratin scales at the surface → Stratum corneum (keratinized barrier).

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clear cells in the basal layer”?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Clear cells in the basal layer → Melanocytes (melanin) or Merkel cells.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Body Membranes & the Epidermis”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which should you review before “Body Membranes & the Epidermis”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Understanding cell junctions is essential for grasping the structural integrity of the epidermis.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: A lamellated "onion-ring" mechanoreceptor in the deep dermis that senses vibration and deep pressure is a:
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The Pacinian corpuscle has concentric lamellae ("onion") and detects vibration/deep pressure. Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae detect light touch.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: The reticular layer of the dermis is composed predominantly of:
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The reticular dermis is dense irregular connective tissue (type I collagen + elastic fibres) providing strength. The papillary dermis is loose CT; the epidermis is epithelium.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which type of mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting light touch in the skin?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Meissner corpuscles are located in the dermal papillae and are specialized for light touch sensation.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: What is the primary function of sebaceous glands?

options.text: Secrete sebum to lubricate skin and hair
Provide structural support to hair follicles

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, which keeps the skin and hair supple.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which structure is responsible for the sensation of deep pressure and vibration?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles, located in the deep dermis, are specialized for detecting deep pressure and vibration.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: A patient presents with an inflamed sebaceous gland. What skin condition is most likely associated with this finding?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Inflamed sebaceous glands are commonly associated with acne due to blockage and inflammation.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which of the following structures is involved in the sensation of sustained touch?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Merkel discs are specialized for detecting sustained touch and pressure.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: How does the structure of the papillary dermis contribute to its function?

options.text: It provides strength through dense collagen
It contains mechanoreceptors for deep pressure
It interlocks with epidermal ridges to enhance nutrient supply

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The loose connective tissue of the papillary dermis interlocks with epidermal ridges, enhancing nutrient supply and forming fingerprints.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: In which layer of the skin would you find Pacinian corpuscles?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are located in the reticular dermis and hypodermis, where they detect deep pressure and vibration.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: How do eccrine sweat glands differ from apocrine sweat glands?

options.text: Eccrine glands open into hair follicles; apocrine glands open directly onto skin
Eccrine glands are activated at puberty; apocrine glands are not
Eccrine glands are involved in thermoregulation; apocrine glands are not
Eccrine glands secrete oily substances; apocrine glands secrete watery sweat

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Eccrine sweat glands are primarily involved in thermoregulation and open directly onto the skin surface.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: How are the functions of sensory receptors in the dermis related to the epidermis?

options.text: Epidermis provides structural support for dermal receptors
Epidermis and dermis work together to detect various stimuli

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The epidermis and dermis collaborate to provide a comprehensive sensory experience, detecting various stimuli through their respective receptors.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Regarding meissner vs pacinian — which is correct?

options.text: Pacinian corpuscles detect fine light touch in the fingertips
Pacinian = deep pressure/VIBRATION (deep dermis, lamellated); Meissner = light touch (dermal papillae)

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Location and modality differ: superficial Meissner for fine touch vs deep onion-ring Pacinian for vibration.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Onion-ring lamellated corpuscle in deep dermis”?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Onion-ring lamellated corpuscle in deep dermis → Pacinian corpuscle (pressure/vibration).

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Encapsulated receptor in a dermal papilla”?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Encapsulated receptor in a dermal papilla → Meissner corpuscle (light touch).

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Dermis, Sensory Receptors & Skin Appendages”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Skin conditions like melasma can involve dermal changes.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which should you review before “Dermis, Sensory Receptors & Skin Appendages”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Understanding the epidermis is essential for grasping dermal functions.

cartilage-types.stem: Which cartilage type lacks a perichondrium and is rich in type I collagen?
cartilage-types.explanation: Fibrocartilage (intervertebral disc, meniscus, pubic symphysis) has type I collagen and no perichondrium. Hyaline and elastic cartilage are type II with a perichondrium (articular hyaline is the exception with no perichondrium but still type II).

cartilage-types.stem: Growth of cartilage by division of chondrocytes within existing lacunae is termed:
cartilage-types.explanation: Interstitial growth expands cartilage from within (chondrocytes dividing in lacunae). Appositional growth adds new cartilage at the perichondrial surface.

cartilage-types.stem: What type of collagen is primarily found in hyaline cartilage?
cartilage-types.explanation: Hyaline cartilage is primarily composed of Type II collagen, which provides its glassy appearance and structural integrity.

cartilage-types.stem: Which cartilage type is characterized by a dark network of elastic fibers?
cartilage-types.explanation: Elastic cartilage contains elastic fibers in addition to Type II collagen, allowing it to maintain shape after deformation.

cartilage-types.stem: What is the primary distinguishing feature of fibrocartilage?

options.text: Rows of chondrocytes between collagen bundles

cartilage-types.explanation: Fibrocartilage is characterized by rows of chondrocytes situated between dense collagen bundles and lacks a perichondrium.

cartilage-types.stem: Which growth mode involves chondrocytes dividing within lacunae?
cartilage-types.explanation: Interstitial growth occurs when chondrocytes divide within their lacunae, leading to an increase in cartilage size from within.

cartilage-types.stem: Which statement about cartilage is FALSE?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type
Elastic cartilage retains shape after bending

cartilage-types.explanation: Fibrocartilage is primarily composed of Type I collagen, not Type II, making this statement false.

cartilage-types.stem: How does cartilage calcification relate to endochondral ossification?

options.text: Cartilage calcification occurs before intramembranous ossification
Calcified cartilage serves as a template for bone formation
Cartilage does not calcify during ossification

cartilage-types.explanation: During endochondral ossification, cartilage calcifies and serves as a template for the formation of bone.

cartilage-types.stem: What is the role of proteoglycans in cartilage?
cartilage-types.explanation: Proteoglycans help maintain hydration and resilience in cartilage, contributing to its mechanical properties.

cartilage-types.stem: Which type of cartilage is found in the intervertebral discs?
cartilage-types.explanation: Fibrocartilage is found in intervertebral discs, providing support and resistance to compressive forces.

cartilage-types.stem: What is the primary function of the perichondrium?
cartilage-types.explanation: The perichondrium supplies nutrients to cartilage through diffusion, as cartilage itself is avascular.

cartilage-types.stem: Regarding collagen type in cartilage — which is correct?

options.text: All cartilage is made of type I collagen
Hyaline and elastic cartilage = type II collagen; only FIBROcartilage = type I

cartilage-types.explanation: Type II is the default cartilage collagen; fibrocartilage is the tough type-I exception (and lacks a perichondrium).

cartilage-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glassy matrix, chondrocytes in isogenous groups, on a joint surface”?
cartilage-types.explanation: Glassy matrix, chondrocytes in isogenous groups, on a joint surface → Hyaline cartilage (type II).

cartilage-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cartilage with a dark network of elastic fibres in the ear”?
cartilage-types.explanation: Cartilage with a dark network of elastic fibres in the ear → Elastic cartilage.

cartilage-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cartilage: Hyaline, Elastic & Fibrocartilage”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

cartilage-types.explanation: Cartilage plays a crucial role in limb development and joint formation.

cartilage-types.stem: Which should you review before “Cartilage: Hyaline, Elastic & Fibrocartilage”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

cartilage-types.explanation: Understanding collagen types is essential for grasping cartilage structure.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: A large multinucleated bone cell derived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage that resorbs bone matrix is the:
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteoclasts are multinucleate, monocyte-derived cells that resorb bone via a ruffled border and acid hydrolases. Osteoblasts build matrix; osteocytes maintain it.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: In compact bone, the central canal of an osteon that carries blood vessels and nerves along the long axis is the:
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: The Haversian canal runs along the long axis at the centre of each osteon. Volkmann canals run transversely to connect osteons; canaliculi link osteocyte lacunae.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What is the primary function of osteoblasts in bone tissue?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteoblasts are responsible for the synthesis and mineralization of bone matrix, primarily by producing osteoid.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: Which cell type is responsible for bone resorption?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells that resorb bone by breaking down the mineralized matrix.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What histological feature characterizes an osteon?

options.text: Concentric lamellae around a central canal

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: An osteon, or Haversian system, is defined by its concentric lamellae surrounding a central vascular canal.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: Which of the following best describes the origin of osteoclasts?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteoclasts originate from the monocyte/macrophage lineage, unlike osteoblasts which come from mesenchymal stem cells.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What is the primary role of osteocytes in bone tissue?

options.text: Maintain bone matrix and sense mechanical load

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteocytes maintain the bone matrix and are involved in mechanosensing to respond to mechanical loads.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: Which type of bone is characterized by a disorganized structure and is typically found in fetal development?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Woven bone is a type of bone that is rapidly formed and has a disorganized structure, commonly seen in fetal development and fracture repair.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: How does the process of endochondral ossification relate to osteoclast function?

options.text: Osteoclasts resorb cartilage to allow bone formation
Osteoclasts are not involved in endochondral ossification
Osteoclasts form new bone during endochondral ossification

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: During endochondral ossification, osteoclasts resorb the cartilage model to facilitate the formation of bone.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What distinguishes spongy bone from compact bone in terms of structure?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Spongy bone is characterized by a lattice-like structure with red marrow in between, unlike the dense structure of compact bone.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: Regarding origin of the osteoclast — which is correct?

options.text: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts both come from the same osteoprogenitor stem cell
Osteoblasts/osteocytes come from mesenchymal osteoprogenitors; OSTEOCLASTS come from the monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Different lineages — that is why anti-RANKL/monocyte-targeting therapies specifically hit osteoclasts.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What best explains the finding: “Large multinucleated cell in a resorption (Howship) lacuna”?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Large multinucleated cell in a resorption (Howship) lacuna → Osteoclast (bone resorption).

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What best explains the finding: “Plump basophilic cells lining new bone surface”?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Plump basophilic cells lining new bone surface → Osteoblasts (matrix deposition).

ossification.stem: The flat bones of the cranial vault form by:
ossification.explanation: Cranial vault (and clavicle/mandible) bone forms directly from mesenchyme = intramembranous ossification. Long bones use endochondral ossification (cartilage model).

ossification.stem: Achondroplasia, the commonest form of short-limbed dwarfism, results from a gain-of-function mutation affecting:
ossification.explanation: Constitutively active FGFR3 suppresses proliferation-zone chondrocytes at the growth plate → reduced endochondral bone lengthening → short limbs with a relatively normal trunk.

ossification.stem: Which type of ossification is responsible for forming the flat bones of the skull?
ossification.explanation: Flat bones of the skull form through intramembranous ossification, which occurs directly from mesenchyme without a cartilage model.

ossification.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which long bones grow in length?
ossification.explanation: Long bones grow in length through endochondral ossification, which involves the replacement of a hyaline cartilage model.

ossification.stem: Which zone of the growth plate is characterized by hypertrophic chondrocytes?
ossification.explanation: The hypertrophy zone of the growth plate contains enlarged chondrocytes that contribute to bone lengthening.

ossification.stem: A child presents with short limbs but a normal-sized trunk and head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ossification.explanation: Achondroplasia is characterized by short-limbed dwarfism due to a defect in endochondral ossification.

ossification.stem: Which of the following statements about ossification is true?

options.text: All bones form by replacing a cartilage model
Intramembranous ossification occurs in long bones
Endochondral ossification is responsible for flat skull bones
Intramembranous ossification occurs directly from mesenchyme

ossification.explanation: Intramembranous ossification occurs directly from mesenchyme and is responsible for forming flat bones like those of the skull.

ossification.stem: How does the growth plate contribute to limb development?

options.text: By resorbing bone at the periosteum

ossification.explanation: The growth plate facilitates endochondral ossification, which is essential for the lengthening of long bones during limb development.

ossification.stem: What is the role of osteoblasts during appositional growth?

options.text: Lay down new bone on the periosteum
Form cartilage in the growth plate
Replace cartilage with bone in the diaphysis

ossification.explanation: Osteoblasts lay down new bone on the periosteum during appositional growth, contributing to bone width.

ossification.stem: Which type of cartilage is primarily involved in endochondral ossification?
ossification.explanation: Hyaline cartilage serves as the template for bone formation in endochondral ossification.

ossification.stem: What is the consequence of FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations in bone development?
ossification.explanation: FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations impair the proliferation of chondrocytes in the growth plate, leading to short-limbed dwarfism.

ossification.stem: Regarding which ossification makes flat skull bones? — which is correct?

options.text: All bones form by replacing a cartilage model (endochondral)
Flat skull bones (and the clavicle, mandible) form by INTRAMEMBRANOUS ossification — directly from mesenchyme, no cartilage template

ossification.explanation: Endochondral (cartilage-model) makes long bones and the skull base; intramembranous makes the flat cranial vault.

ossification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Skull/flat bone forming without a cartilage precursor”?
ossification.explanation: Skull/flat bone forming without a cartilage precursor → Intramembranous ossification.

ossification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Long bone lengthening at a cartilage plate”?
ossification.explanation: Long bone lengthening at a cartilage plate → Endochondral ossification (growth plate).

ossification.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Ossification: Intramembranous vs Endochondral”?

MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

ossification.explanation: Somite development is related to the formation of the axial skeleton and ossification.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, which of the following remains constant in length?
skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: The A band equals the thick (myosin) filament length, which does not change. The I band, H zone, and overall sarcomere all shorten as thin filaments slide inward.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: The skeletal muscle triad consists of:

options.text: One T-tubule and one cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum
One T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: The triad = one T-tubule + two terminal SR cisternae, positioned at the A–I junction, coupling depolarisation to Ca²⁺ release. Cardiac muscle has a dyad (T-tubule + one SR).

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What is the primary role of calcium ions in skeletal muscle contraction?

options.text: To bind to troponin and facilitate actin-myosin interaction
To energize myosin heads for cross-bridge cycling

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Calcium ions bind to troponin, causing a conformational change that moves tropomyosin and exposes binding sites on actin for myosin.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: Which of the following statements about the sarcomere is true?

options.text: The A band shortens during muscle contraction.
The I band remains constant during contraction.
The H zone disappears when the muscle contracts.
The Z line moves away from the M line during contraction.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: During contraction, the I band and H zone shorten while the A band remains constant; the Z lines move closer together.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What is the structural unit of skeletal muscle contraction?
skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: The sarcomere is the basic contractile unit of skeletal muscle, defined as the segment between two Z lines.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What clinical finding is associated with myasthenia gravis?

options.text: Ptosis and diplopia worsening with use

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is characterized by muscle weakness that worsens with activity, leading to symptoms like ptosis and diplopia.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: How does botulinum toxin affect skeletal muscle function?

options.text: Inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Botulinum toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine from motor neurons, leading to muscle paralysis.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: How does excitation-contraction coupling relate to muscle contraction?

options.text: It involves the sliding of actin over myosin.
It is the process of converting electrical signals into mechanical contraction.
It is the mechanism by which ATP is produced in muscle cells.
It describes the role of myoblasts in muscle fiber formation.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Excitation-contraction coupling refers to the process by which an action potential in the muscle fiber leads to muscle contraction through calcium release.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What energy system is primarily used during short bursts of high-intensity skeletal muscle contraction?
skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis provides quick energy for short, intense activities by breaking down glucose without oxygen.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: Regarding what shortens during contraction? — which is correct?

options.text: The A band shortens as the muscle contracts
The A band stays CONSTANT; the I band and H zone shorten as thin filaments slide inward

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Filaments do not shorten — they slide. The A band = thick filament length, which is unchanged.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral, multiple nuclei; cross-striations”?

options.text: Ca²⁺-release apparatus at the A–I junction

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Peripheral, multiple nuclei; cross-striations → Skeletal muscle fibre.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What best explains the finding: “A band constant on contraction; I band shortens”?

options.text: Ca²⁺-release apparatus at the A–I junction

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: A band constant on contraction; I band shortens → Sliding filament (thin slides over thick).

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Explains energy requirements for muscle contraction.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: The intercalated disc of cardiac muscle provides electrical coupling between cells through its:
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Gap junctions in the intercalated disc allow ions to pass cell-to-cell, letting the myocardium contract as a functional syncytium. Desmosomes/fascia adherens provide the mechanical coupling.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which feature is characteristic of smooth muscle?

options.text: Peripheral multiple nuclei and visible striations
A single central nucleus, no striations, and contraction via calmodulin/MLCK
A triad at the A–I junction

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle is spindle-shaped with one central nucleus, no striations, dense bodies instead of sarcomeres, and Ca²⁺–calmodulin–MLCK contraction. Intercalated discs and triads belong to cardiac/skeletal muscle.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What is the primary mechanism of contraction in smooth muscle?

options.text: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle contraction is mediated by calcium binding to calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK).

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which histological feature is characteristic of cardiac muscle?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Cardiac muscle is characterized by branched striated cells that contain 1-2 central nuclei.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What is the role of intercalated discs in cardiac muscle?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Intercalated discs provide both mechanical coupling (via desmosomes) and electrical coupling (via gap junctions) in cardiac muscle.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which of the following statements about smooth muscle is FALSE?

options.text: It has a single central nucleus.
It contracts via the troponin complex.
It is found in blood vessels.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle does not use troponin for contraction; instead, it uses calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: During excitation-contraction coupling in cardiac muscle, what triggers the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?

options.text: Calcium release from the extracellular space

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: In cardiac muscle, calcium influx through T-tubules triggers the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via a process known as calcium-induced calcium release.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which of the following structures is NOT found in smooth muscle?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle contains caveolae and dense bodies, but it does not have intercalated discs, which are specific to cardiac muscle.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: How does the contraction mechanism of smooth muscle differ from that of skeletal muscle?

options.text: Smooth muscle uses troponin, skeletal does not.
Skeletal muscle contraction is faster than smooth muscle.
Smooth muscle uses calmodulin, skeletal muscle uses troponin.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle contraction relies on calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase, while skeletal muscle contraction involves troponin.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which feature distinguishes cardiac muscle from smooth muscle?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated, while smooth muscle is non-striated, which is a key distinguishing feature.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Regarding regulatory protein of smooth muscle — which is correct?

options.text: Smooth muscle contraction is triggered by Ca²⁺ binding troponin, like skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle has NO troponin — Ca²⁺ binds CALMODULIN → activates MLCK → myosin phosphorylation

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Only striated (skeletal/cardiac) muscle uses troponin. Smooth muscle uses the calmodulin–MLCK pathway.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Branched striated cells joined by dark step-lines”?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Branched striated cells joined by dark step-lines → Cardiac muscle intercalated discs.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central single nucleus, no striations, spindle shape”?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Central single nucleus, no striations, spindle shape → Smooth muscle.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cardiac & Smooth Muscle”?

neuron-structure-types.stem: The sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglion are:
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are pseudounipolar — a single process leaves the soma and splits into peripheral and central branches. Bipolar = special senses; multipolar = most motor/CNS neurons.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Nissl bodies, seen as basophilic clumps in the neuronal soma, correspond ultrastructurally to:
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Nissl substance = rough ER plus free ribosomes (rRNA), hence its basophilia and role in protein synthesis. It is absent from the axon hillock and axon.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Which part of the neuron is responsible for receiving input?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Dendrites are specialized to receive synaptic input from other neurons.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What is the primary function of Nissl bodies in neurons?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Nissl bodies, composed of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes, are involved in protein synthesis.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What is the consequence of chromatolysis in a neuron?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Chromatolysis indicates a reaction to axonal injury, characterized by dispersed Nissl substance.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Where are Nissl bodies located in a neuron?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Nissl bodies are present in the soma and dendrites but absent from the axon and axon hillock.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Which type of neuron is characterized by a single process that splits into two branches?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Pseudounipolar neurons have a single process that bifurcates into central and peripheral branches.

neuron-structure-types.stem: How does kinesin function in axonal transport?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Kinesin is a motor protein that transports cargo from the soma to the axon terminal in an anterograde manner.

neuron-structure-types.stem: How does the structure of a pseudounipolar neuron relate to its function in sensory pathways?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: The pseudounipolar structure allows for efficient transmission of sensory signals to the central nervous system.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What role do microtubules play in neuron function?
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Microtubules are essential for axonal transport, facilitating the movement of organelles and proteins along the axon.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Regarding where are nissl bodies? — which is correct?

options.text: Nissl bodies extend throughout the neuron, including the axon
Nissl bodies are in the soma and dendrites but ABSENT from the axon hillock and axon

neuron-structure-types.explanation: The axon has no protein-synthesis machinery — it depends on transport from the soma; a classic identifying feature.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basophilic clumps in the soma (Nissl substance)”?

options.text: Single process splits into central + peripheral branch

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Basophilic clumps in the soma (Nissl substance) → RER + ribosomes → high protein synthesis.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pseudounipolar neuron in a dorsal root ganglion”?

options.text: Single process splits into central + peripheral branch

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Pseudounipolar neuron in a dorsal root ganglion → Single process splits into central + peripheral branch.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Neuron: Structure & Morphological Types”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Understanding neuron structure may aid in recognizing neurological signs in pneumonia.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Which should you review before “The Neuron: Structure & Morphological Types”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Axonal transport relies on microtubules and motor proteins.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which glial cell myelinates multiple axons in the central nervous system?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: One oligodendrocyte myelinates several CNS axons. In the PNS, each Schwann cell myelinates a single internode of one axon.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which neuroglial cell is derived from mesoderm (monocyte lineage) rather than neuroectoderm?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Microglia are the CNS resident macrophages, derived from the mesodermal/monocyte lineage. Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells are neuroectodermal.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which glial cell type is responsible for forming the blood-brain barrier?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Astrocytes have end-feet that contribute to the formation of the blood-brain barrier.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: What is the primary function of oligodendrocytes in the CNS?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons in the CNS, providing insulation.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: A patient presents with demyelination of multiple CNS axons. Which cell type is primarily affected?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are responsible for myelinating CNS axons, and their damage leads to demyelinating diseases like MS.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Schwann cells is true?

options.text: They can guide regeneration of PNS axons
They are the main immune cells in the PNS

neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Schwann cells myelinate one internode of one axon and play a role in guiding regeneration.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which glial cell type is the primary phagocyte in the CNS?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Microglia are the resident immune cells in the CNS responsible for phagocytosis.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: How do the myelination processes differ between the CNS and PNS?

options.text: CNS uses Schwann cells, PNS uses oligodendrocytes
CNS myelinates one axon, PNS myelinates many
CNS uses oligodendrocytes for multiple axons, PNS uses Schwann cells for one
Both use the same type of cell for myelination

neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons in the CNS, while Schwann cells myelinate one internode of one axon in the PNS.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which ethical principle from the Belmont Report is most relevant when conducting research involving human subjects in neuroglial studies?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Respect for persons emphasizes the need for informed consent and autonomy in research involving human subjects.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: In studying the organization of nerve fibers, which glial cell's role is crucial for the regeneration of peripheral nerves?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Schwann cells play a critical role in the regeneration of peripheral nerves by guiding axonal regrowth.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Regarding cns vs pns myelination — which is correct?

options.text: One Schwann cell myelinates many axons like an oligodendrocyte
Schwann cell = ONE internode of ONE axon (PNS); oligodendrocyte = MANY axons (CNS)

neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: One-to-one (Schwann) vs one-to-many (oligodendrocyte) — and it determines which disease affects which system.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFAP-positive star-shaped cell with vascular end-feet”?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: GFAP-positive star-shaped cell with vascular end-feet → Astrocyte (BBB, support).

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: What best explains the finding: “CNS cell myelinating several axons at once”?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: CNS cell myelinating several axons at once → Oligodendrocyte.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Neuroglia: CNS & PNS Support Cells”?

Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Rapid saltatory conduction along a myelinated axon depends on the presence of:

options.text: Nodes of Ranvier where the action potential regenerates

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier (gaps in myelin with clustered Na⁺ channels), speeding conduction. Continuous myelin without nodes would prevent regeneration of the impulse.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: The connective-tissue layer that surrounds an individual nerve fascicle and forms the blood–nerve barrier is the:
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The perineurium wraps each fascicle and forms the blood–nerve barrier. Epineurium wraps the whole nerve; endoneurium surrounds individual axons (epimysium is a muscle sheath).

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What is the primary function of myelin in nerve fibers?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Myelin serves to insulate axons, allowing for faster conduction of action potentials.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Which structure forms the blood-nerve barrier?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The perineurium wraps each fascicle and forms the blood-nerve barrier.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What occurs at the nodes of Ranvier during saltatory conduction?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are where action potentials propagate by jumping from node to node.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: A patient presents with slowed nerve conduction velocity. Which condition is most likely responsible?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Demyelination, as seen in conditions like multiple sclerosis, slows nerve conduction.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Which connective tissue layer surrounds individual axons?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The endoneurium is the innermost layer that surrounds each individual axon.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: How does myelination affect conduction velocity in nerve fibers?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Increased myelination enhances conduction velocity due to reduced capacitance and increased insulation.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: How does the structure of the neuromuscular junction relate to synaptic transmission?

options.text: It is a chemical synapse with ACh release
It does not involve calcium channels

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The neuromuscular junction is a chemical synapse where acetylcholine is released to transmit signals to muscles.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What role do voltage-gated Na⁺ channels play in action potential propagation?

options.text: They allow sodium influx during depolarization
They are only present in the CNS
They are found exclusively at synapses

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open during depolarization, allowing sodium influx that propagates the action potential.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Regarding nerve connective-tissue layers — which is correct?

options.text: The endoneurium wraps the entire nerve
Epineurium wraps the WHOLE nerve; perineurium wraps each FASCICLE; endoneurium surrounds each AXON

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Outer-to-inner order (Epi → Peri → Endo) is a favourite exam item — endoneurium is the innermost, around single axons.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gap in the myelin sheath with clustered Na⁺ channels”?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Gap in the myelin sheath with clustered Na⁺ channels → Node of Ranvier (saltatory conduction).

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Faster conduction in a thicker, more myelinated axon”?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Faster conduction in a thicker, more myelinated axon → Myelination + diameter increase velocity.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Nerve Fibres, Myelin, Synapses & Nerve Organization”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Histological understanding of neurons and glia is relevant for nerve organization.

Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport
