ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which collagen type forms the network of the basement membrane?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type IV collagen forms the non-fibrillar network of basement membranes. Type I = bone/tendon/skin, II = cartilage, III = reticular fibres.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: The property of cartilage ground substance to resist compression is due mainly to:
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Sulfated GAGs on aggrecan core proteins are strongly anionic and trap water, generating turgor that resists compression. Collagen provides tensile (not compressive) strength.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: What type of collagen is primarily found in bone and tendon?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen type in bone and tendon, providing tensile strength.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which component of the extracellular matrix is responsible for resisting compression?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Ground substance, composed of GAGs and proteoglycans, traps water and resists compressive forces.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: A patient presents with bleeding gums and poor wound healing. What vitamin deficiency is likely responsible?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Vitamin C is essential for the hydroxylation of proline in collagen synthesis; its deficiency leads to weakened collagen.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which type of collagen forms the reticular fibers in lymphoid organs?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type III collagen forms reticular fibers, providing a mesh-like structure in lymphoid organs.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: A patient with Marfan syndrome presents with tall stature and arachnodactyly. Which ECM component is defective?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Marfan syndrome is caused by a defect in fibrillin, which is crucial for the structure of elastic fibers.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which of the following statements about basement membrane collagen is true?

options.text: It is primarily type I collagen.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Basement membranes are made of type IV collagen, which forms a non-fibrillar network.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: How does collagen turnover relate to osteoporosis management?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: CTX-1 is a marker of collagen type I degradation, used to monitor bone resorption in osteoporosis.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which extracellular matrix component is crucial for thyroid follicle structure?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type IV collagen forms the basement membrane, which is essential for the structural integrity of thyroid follicles.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Regarding basement membrane collagen — which is correct?

options.text: Basement membranes are made of type I collagen
Basement membranes = type IV collagen (a network, non-fibrillar); type I is bone/tendon/skin

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type IV forms sheets, not fibres. "Floor/four" = basement membrane; type III = reticular mesh.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basement membrane collagen”?

options.text: Vitamin-C-dependent proline hydroxylation fails → weak collagen

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Basement membrane collagen → Type IV (network, non-fibrillar).

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reticular fibre mesh in a lymph node”?

options.text: Vitamin-C-dependent proline hydroxylation fails → weak collagen

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Reticular fibre mesh in a lymph node → Type III collagen.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Extracellular Matrix: Fibres & Ground Substance”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: ECM components are relevant in thyroid tissue structure.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: The transmembrane receptors that mechanically and chemically link the extracellular matrix to the intracellular cytoskeleton are:
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Integrins bridge ECM (laminin/fibronectin) to the actin/keratin cytoskeleton and transduce signals (survival, migration). Cadherins mediate cell–cell adhesion; connexins form gap junctions.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: A rising serum C-telopeptide (CTX-1) level in a postmenopausal woman most directly reflects:

options.text: Increased osteoclastic bone resorption (type I collagen breakdown)

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: CTX-1 is a type I collagen crosslink released when osteoclasts resorb bone; elevated levels indicate increased bone turnover/resorption, useful in monitoring osteoporosis.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which adhesive glycoprotein primarily anchors cells to the basal lamina?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Laminin is the key adhesive protein of the basal lamina, binding integrins and type IV collagen.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What is the primary function of integrins in cell adhesion?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Integrins serve as transmembrane bridges connecting the ECM to the cytoskeleton and facilitating signal transduction.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: A patient presents with elevated serum CTX-1. What does this indicate?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Elevated CTX-1 levels indicate increased osteoclastic activity and collagen breakdown, commonly seen in osteoporosis.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which of the following processes is primarily mediated by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: MMPs are enzymes responsible for degrading collagen and other ECM components during processes like wound healing and tumor invasion.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What is the consequence of a cell losing contact with the ECM?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Loss of ECM contact leads to anoikis, a form of programmed cell death due to the loss of integrin-mediated survival signals.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes fibronectin from laminin?

options.text: Fibronectin is found in the basal lamina, laminin in connective tissue
Laminin is the main adhesive protein in connective tissue
Fibronectin links cells to collagen, laminin to the basal lamina
Laminin is involved in cell signaling, fibronectin in apoptosis

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Fibronectin primarily links cells to collagen in connective tissue, while laminin is the adhesive protein of the basal lamina.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: How does the structure of the basement membrane relate to its function in epithelial tissues?

options.text: It provides a barrier to pathogens
It anchors epithelial cells and acts as a filtration barrier

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: The basement membrane anchors epithelial cells and acts as a filtration barrier, crucial for tissue integrity and function.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: How does integrin signaling influence keratinocyte behavior in the epidermis?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Integrin signaling enhances adhesion and survival of keratinocytes, which is essential for maintaining the epidermal barrier.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Regarding fibronectin vs laminin location — which is correct?

options.text: Laminin is the main adhesive protein of general connective tissue
Laminin = basal LAMINA adhesive; fibronectin = general connective-tissue adhesion (cell ↔ collagen)

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Match the name: Laminin → basal Lamina; fibronectin → the fibrous connective-tissue matrix.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Adhesive glycoprotein of the basal lamina”?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Adhesive glycoprotein of the basal lamina → Laminin (binds integrins + type IV collagen).

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Carcinoma breaching the basement membrane”?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Carcinoma breaching the basement membrane → MMP-mediated invasion → malignancy.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cell–Matrix Adhesion, Integrins & Collagen Turnover”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Cell-matrix adhesion is fundamental in skin biology and keratinocyte function.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Cell–Matrix Adhesion, Integrins & Collagen Turnover”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Understanding the basement membrane is crucial for grasping cell-matrix adhesion.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Chronic alcohol intake causes which adaptive subcellular change in hepatocytes?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Alcohol and drugs induce detoxifying enzymes, expanding the smooth ER — an adaptive, reversible hyperplasia. Megamitochondria may also appear in alcoholic liver disease.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Parakeratosis, seen in conditions such as psoriasis, refers to:

options.text: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum due to abnormal keratinocyte proliferation

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Parakeratosis = retained nuclei in the normally anucleate stratum corneum, reflecting accelerated/abnormal keratinocyte turnover — an example of the "proliferation" pattern of altered histology.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) hyperplasia in hepatocytes due to chronic alcohol consumption?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Smooth ER hyperplasia is an adaptive response that increases detoxification enzyme production, not a sign of cell death.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of megamitochondria in alcoholic liver disease?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Megamitochondria are abnormally large mitochondria that appear in conditions like alcoholic liver disease.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What histological change is indicated by the presence of neutrophils infiltrating colonic crypts?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Neutrophil infiltration in colonic crypts is a hallmark of cryptitis, indicating inflammation.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Which of the following best describes parakeratosis?

options.text: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Parakeratosis is characterized by the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, indicating abnormal keratinocyte proliferation.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum hyperplasia is often misinterpreted as irreversible damage. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: It is an adaptive, reversible response

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Smooth ER hyperplasia is an adaptive, reversible response to increased metabolic demand, not indicative of cell death.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: How does mitochondrial proliferation relate to oncocytomas?

options.text: It is a response to increased oxidative stress
It leads to decreased ATP production
It results in eosinophilic, mitochondria-packed cells

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Mitochondrial proliferation in oncocytomas results in eosinophilic, mitochondria-packed cells, characteristic of this tumor type.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: How can changes in nuclear morphology, such as hyperchromasia, be linked to subcellular alterations in disease?

options.text: They reflect chromatin aggregation and malignancy
They are unrelated to cellular injury

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Hyperchromasia is associated with chromatin aggregation, which is a common feature in malignant cells, reflecting subcellular alterations.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What is the relationship between mitochondrial alterations and the function of cytoplasmic organelles in disease?

options.text: Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to lysosomal degradation
Altered mitochondria affect the function of other organelles
Mitochondrial changes are independent of cytoplasmic organelles

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Mitochondrial alterations can significantly impact the function of other cytoplasmic organelles, affecting overall cellular health.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Regarding is ser hyperplasia irreversible damage? — which is correct?

options.text: Smooth ER proliferation in hepatocytes is a sign of irreversible cell death
It is an ADAPTIVE, reversible response to drug/alcohol metabolism (enzyme induction), not lethal injury

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Many subcellular changes are adaptive/homeostatic; distinguish reversible adaptation from lethal injury (blebbing with loss of viability, karyolysis).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hepatocyte SER hyperplasia in a chronic drinker”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Hepatocyte SER hyperplasia in a chronic drinker → Adaptive enzyme induction (detoxification).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Parakeratosis (nuclei retained in stratum corneum)”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Parakeratosis (nuclei retained in stratum corneum) → Abnormal keratinocyte proliferation (e.g. psoriasis).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Which should you review before “Clinical Cell Biology: Subcellular Alterations in Disease”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Understanding nuclear alterations is essential for grasping subcellular pathology.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Immunohistochemistry of an undifferentiated tumour is strongly positive for cytokeratin. This indicates the tumour is a:
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Cytokeratin marks epithelial cells, so keratin positivity identifies a carcinoma. Vimentin → sarcoma, GFAP → glioma; IF immunostaining reveals a tumour's tissue of origin.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: The Mallory body ("alcoholic hyalin") seen in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver disease is composed of aggregated:
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Mallory bodies are clumped keratin intermediate filaments within hepatocytes — a hallmark of alcoholic liver disease (also seen in NASH).

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Which intermediate filament type is primarily associated with epithelial tumors?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Keratin is the intermediate filament type that indicates epithelial origin, thus associated with carcinomas.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: What is the primary composition of Mallory bodies seen in alcoholic liver disease?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Mallory bodies are composed of aggregated keratin intermediate filaments within hepatocytes.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: In which condition would you expect to find GFAP-positive tumors?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: GFAP is a marker for astrocytic tumors, specifically gliomas.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Which finding is characteristic of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease are primarily composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: What is the mechanism behind situs inversus in Kartagener syndrome?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Kartagener syndrome is caused by a defect in ciliary dynein, leading to impaired ciliary movement and situs inversus.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: A patient presents with a tumor that is keratin-positive and vimentin-negative. What is the likely diagnosis?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: The keratin-positive, vimentin-negative profile indicates an epithelial origin, consistent with carcinoma.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Which cytoskeletal abnormality is linked to primary ciliary dyskinesia?
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is caused by defects in ciliary dynein arms, affecting ciliary function.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Regarding mallory body composition — which is correct?

options.text: Mallory bodies (alcoholic hyalin) are made of collagen or amyloid
Mallory bodies are aggregated KERATIN intermediate filaments in hepatocytes

intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: They are a cytoskeletal (keratin) inclusion, not an extracellular deposit — a classic alcoholic liver disease finding.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Keratin-positive, vimentin-negative tumour”?
What best explains the finding: “GFAP-positive brain tumour”?
Which is a clinical application of “Cytoskeletal Abnormalities & Diagnostic IF Markers”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: While not directly related, understanding cellular pathology can aid in broader clinical contexts.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Cytoskeletal Abnormalities & Diagnostic IF Markers”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Understanding junctional complexes is essential for grasping keratinocyte junction diseases.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: According to Fick's law, the rate of simple diffusion across a membrane is INCREASED by:
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Diffusion rate rises with a steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area, higher temperature, and lipid solubility; it falls with larger molecular size and greater membrane thickness/distance.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Osmosis is best defined as the movement of:

options.text: Solute from high to low concentration
Water across a semipermeable membrane toward higher solute concentration
Ions against their gradient using ATP

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from low solute (high water) toward high solute (low water) concentration.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: What is the primary driving force behind the movement of water during osmosis?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Osmosis is driven by the concentration gradient of solute, where water moves toward the area of higher solute concentration.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: According to Fick's law, which factor would NOT increase the rate of diffusion?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Increased membrane thickness decreases the rate of diffusion, as it is inversely proportional to distance.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: In a patient with pulmonary fibrosis, what is the expected effect on gas exchange?

options.text: Increased solubility of gases in blood

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis increases membrane thickness, which slows down the diffusion rate of gases like O₂ and CO₂.

options.text: Water moves toward lower solute concentration
Water moves toward higher solute concentration
Water moves equally in both directions
Water movement is independent of solute concentration

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water from an area of low solute concentration to an area of high solute concentration.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: How does temperature affect the rate of diffusion?

options.text: Increases rate by reducing molecular motion
Increases rate by increasing molecular motion
Has no effect on diffusion rate

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Higher temperatures increase molecular motion, which in turn increases the rate of diffusion.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: How does osmotic pressure relate to the number of solute particles in a solution?

options.text: Osmotic pressure decreases with more solute particles
Osmotic pressure is independent of solute particles
Osmotic pressure increases with more solute particles
Osmotic pressure is constant regardless of solute concentration

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Osmotic pressure increases with the number of solute particles, as it reflects the tendency of water to move toward higher solute concentrations.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: A patient presents with dehydration. Which physiological process is primarily responsible for water movement in their body?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: In dehydration, water moves through osmosis toward areas of higher solute concentration to maintain fluid balance.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: In a scenario where a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, what will happen to the cell volume?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, water moves out of the cell toward the higher solute concentration, causing the cell to shrink.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Regarding direction of osmosis — which is correct?

options.text: In osmosis, water moves toward the compartment with lower solute concentration
Water moves toward the compartment with HIGHER solute concentration (lower water concentration)

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Water follows solute: it diffuses down its own gradient, from high water (dilute) to low water (concentrated).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “O₂ and CO₂ crossing the alveolar membrane”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: O₂ and CO₂ crossing the alveolar membrane → Simple diffusion (lipid-soluble gases, down gradient).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Water moving toward the saltier compartment”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Water moving toward the saltier compartment → Osmosis (toward higher solute concentration).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Fluid balance can impact neurological function, linking basic science to clinical scenarios.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Red blood cells placed in an iso-osmotic solution of urea (which freely penetrates the membrane) will:

options.text: Swell and lyse (the solution is effectively hypotonic)

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Urea penetrates and equilibrates, contributing to osmolarity but NOT tonicity. The solution is iso-osmotic but hypotonic, so water enters and the cells swell/lyse.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: A cell placed in a hypertonic solution will:
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: A hypertonic solution has a higher effective solute concentration outside the cell, so water moves out and the cell shrinks (crenates).

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What is the primary determinant of tonicity?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Tonicity is determined by non-penetrating solutes, as they affect water movement across cell membranes.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Which solution would cause red blood cells to crenate?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: 3% saline is hypertonic, causing water to leave the cells and resulting in crenation.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What happens to cells placed in an iso-osmotic urea solution?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Urea is a penetrating solute; thus, while the solution is iso-osmotic, it is effectively hypotonic, causing cells to swell.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What is the plasma osmolality in a healthy adult?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Normal plasma osmolality is approximately 290 mOsm/kg, primarily due to Na⁺ salts, glucose, and urea.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Which of the following statements about osmolarity and tonicity is correct?

options.text: Hypertonic solutions do not affect cell volume

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Hypotonic solutions lead to cell swelling due to water influx; the other statements are incorrect.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: How does mannitol reduce cerebral edema?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Mannitol is a hypertonic solution that increases plasma osmolality, drawing water out of cells and reducing edema.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: How does the regulation of blood osmolarity relate to homeostasis?
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Regulating blood osmolarity is crucial for maintaining cell volume and overall homeostasis.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What role does diffusion play in osmolarity regulation?

options.text: It facilitates solute and water movement
It has no effect on osmolarity

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Diffusion facilitates the movement of solutes and water, which is essential for regulating osmolarity in body fluids.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Regarding iso-osmotic vs isotonic — which is correct?

options.text: A solution that is iso-osmotic to plasma is always isotonic (no volume change)
Not necessarily — if the solute PENETRATES the cell (e.g. urea), an iso-osmotic solution is actually HYPOTONIC and cells swell

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Only non-penetrating solutes contribute to tonicity; penetrating solutes equilibrate and don't hold water out.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “RBCs placed in distilled water swell and lyse”?

options.text: Hypertonic, non-penetrating → draws water out of cells

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: RBCs placed in distilled water swell and lyse → Hypotonic → water enters (haemolysis).

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cells shrink (crenate) in concentrated saline”?

options.text: Hypertonic, non-penetrating → draws water out of cells

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Cells shrink (crenate) in concentrated saline → Hypertonic → water leaves.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?

options.text: Oxytocin-driven intensification of uterine contractions during labour

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Oxytocin release intensifies contractions, which release more oxytocin — a self-amplifying positive-feedback loop that ends with delivery. The others are negative-feedback loops.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: In a homeostatic control system, the structure that compares the sensed value to the set point and coordinates the response is the:
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: The control centre (integrator) compares the sensor's input to the set point and directs the effector. The sensor detects the variable; the effector produces the response.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which insulin lowers blood glucose levels?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose through negative feedback, opposing the rise in glucose levels.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of oxytocin during labor?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Oxytocin amplifies uterine contractions through positive feedback until delivery occurs.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What physiological response occurs when body temperature drops?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Shivering is a negative feedback response that helps restore core temperature when it drops.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which statement about positive feedback is correct?

options.text: It maintains homeostasis by opposing change.
It amplifies a change to drive a process to completion.
It is the primary mechanism for temperature regulation.
It is used for gradual adjustments in physiological variables.

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies changes, unlike negative feedback which opposes changes to maintain homeostasis.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: During exercise, what anticipatory response occurs in the cardiovascular system?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Heart rate rises in anticipation of increased metabolic demand during exercise, demonstrating feedforward control.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: How does the body respond to increased plasma osmolality?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Increased plasma osmolality triggers the secretion of ADH, which helps retain water and dilute the plasma, a negative feedback mechanism.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What feedback mechanism is primarily involved in the regulation of GnRH and LH during the menstrual cycle?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: The regulation of GnRH and LH involves positive feedback, particularly during the midcycle surge leading to ovulation.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Regarding positive feedback and homeostasis — which is correct?

options.text: Positive feedback maintains homeostasis by opposing change
NEGATIVE feedback maintains homeostasis (opposes change); POSITIVE feedback amplifies a change to drive a process to completion (e.g. labour, clotting)

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Positive feedback is destabilising by design and is used for discrete "all-the-way" events, not for maintaining a steady state.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Insulin lowering high blood glucose”?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Insulin lowering high blood glucose → Negative feedback (opposes the rise).

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oxytocin intensifying labour contractions”?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Oxytocin intensifying labour contractions → Positive feedback (amplifies until birth).

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Homeostasis & Feedback Control”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Breathing control is a key physiological process regulated by homeostatic feedback.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which should you review before “Homeostasis & Feedback Control”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Understanding osmolarity is crucial for grasping homeostasis and fluid balance.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Using the "60-40-20" rule, the intracellular fluid represents approximately what fraction of total body water?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: ICF (~40% of body weight) is two-thirds of total body water (~60%); ECF (~20%) is one-third, subdivided into interstitial fluid (~15%) and plasma (~5%).

body-fluid-compartments.stem: The high intracellular potassium and high extracellular sodium concentrations are maintained primarily by:
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase actively pumps Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, establishing the characteristic ICF (high K⁺) vs ECF (high Na⁺) gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What percentage of total body water is found in the intracellular fluid (ICF)?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: According to the 60-40-20 rule, approximately 40% of body weight is in the ICF.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which mechanism primarily maintains the high intracellular potassium concentration?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase actively pumps K⁺ into cells and Na⁺ out, maintaining the high intracellular K⁺ concentration.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What is the primary reason for the movement of water from the extracellular fluid (ECF) into cells during hyponatraemia?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Hyponatraemia lowers ECF osmolality, causing water to move into cells, leading to swelling.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which of the following statements about body fluid compartments is FALSE?

options.text: ECF is one-third of total body water.
Interstitial fluid contains more proteins than plasma.

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Plasma is protein-rich compared to interstitial fluid, which is nearly protein-impermeable.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What is the primary role of albumin in the plasma?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Albumin generates oncotic pressure, which helps retain water within the vascular compartment.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: How does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase contribute to the resting membrane potential?

options.text: By generating a negative charge inside the cell

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps out 3 Na⁺ for every 2 K⁺ it brings in, creating a negative charge inside the cell.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: How does the regulation of body fluid compartments relate to homeostasis?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Regulation of body fluid compartments is essential for maintaining electrolyte balance, a key aspect of homeostasis.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What is the clinical significance of understanding fluid compartments in renal function?

options.text: It aids in understanding fluid overload.
It is irrelevant to renal physiology.

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Knowledge of fluid compartments is crucial in managing fluid overload conditions, particularly in renal patients.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Regarding icf vs ecf proportion — which is correct?

options.text: Most body water is in the extracellular fluid
Most body water is INTRACELLULAR (ICF ≈ two-thirds of total body water); ECF is only one-third

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The 60-40-20 rule: ICF 40% of body weight vs ECF 20% — the majority of water is inside cells.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “High intracellular K⁺, high extracellular Na⁺”?

options.text: Low ECF osmolality → water enters brain cells

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: High intracellular K⁺, high extracellular Na⁺ → Maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “ICF is two-thirds of total body water”?

options.text: Low ECF osmolality → water enters brain cells

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: ICF is two-thirds of total body water → 60-40-20 rule.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Body Fluid Compartments & Electrolyte Distribution”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Renal function is crucial for maintaining body fluid compartments and composition.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which should you review before “Body Fluid Compartments & Electrolyte Distribution”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Understanding body fluid compartments is essential for grasping homeostasis.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which feature distinguishes carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion?

options.text: It moves solute against the gradient
It shows saturation (a transport maximum) and competition

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Carrier-mediated transport saturates (limited carriers → Tm), is specific, and shows competition — unlike simple diffusion. Both are passive (down-gradient, no ATP).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Compared with carriers, membrane ion channels transport solutes:

options.text: Much faster, through a water-filled pore

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Channels form gated water-filled pores and conduct ions extremely rapidly (millions/sec), far faster than carriers, which must bind and change conformation. Both are passive.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What is the primary mechanism of facilitated diffusion?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is a passive process that allows solutes to move down their concentration gradient through a transport protein.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which of the following statements about channels is true?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Channels form water-filled pores that can be gated and allow for rapid transport of ions and water.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: In which scenario would you expect to see carrier saturation?

options.text: When the solute is actively transported

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Carrier saturation occurs when all available transporters are occupied, leading to a plateau in transport rate.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What is the primary defect in cystic fibrosis?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which encodes a chloride channel.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which of the following is a trap regarding facilitated diffusion?

options.text: It involves conformational change of proteins

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive and does not require ATP; this is a common misconception.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: How does facilitated diffusion differ from active transport?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion moves solutes against their gradient

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is a passive process that moves solutes down their concentration gradient, unlike active transport which requires energy to move solutes against their gradient.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: How does the transport of glucose via GLUT relate to the action potential in neurons?

options.text: Both are examples of facilitated diffusion
Both occur in the same cellular compartment

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: GLUT transporters facilitate glucose entry into cells via facilitated diffusion, similar to how ion channels facilitate ion movement during action potentials.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What common feature do glucose transport and one-carbon carrier transport share?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Both glucose transport via GLUT and one-carbon carrier transport can exhibit saturation when all transporters are occupied.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Regarding facilitated diffusion energy — which is correct?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion requires ATP because it uses a transport protein
Facilitated diffusion is PASSIVE (down-gradient, no ATP) — the protein just provides a path; only active transport uses energy

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Protein involvement ≠ energy use. Facilitated diffusion moves solute down its gradient without ATP; active transport moves against it with ATP.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transport rate plateaus at high substrate (Tm)”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Transport rate plateaus at high substrate (Tm) → Carrier saturation (all carriers occupied).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glucose entering cells via GLUT”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Glucose entering cells via GLUT → Facilitated diffusion (carrier, down gradient).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which should you review before “Passive Membrane Transport: Channels & Carriers”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Understanding oxygen transport is linked to passive transport mechanisms.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Glucose uptake by SGLT in the intestine and proximal tubule, moving glucose against its gradient using the inward Na⁺ gradient, is an example of:
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: SGLT couples downhill Na⁺ entry (gradient set by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to uphill glucose transport in the same direction — secondary active symport. GLUT (facilitated) moves glucose down-gradient.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is best classified as:
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses ATP directly to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in against their gradients — primary active transport (and electrogenic).

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Which of the following is an example of primary active transport?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase directly uses ATP to transport sodium and potassium ions against their gradients.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which glucose is reabsorbed in the renal tubules?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Glucose reabsorption in the renal tubules occurs via secondary active symport, coupling glucose transport with Na⁺.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Which of the following statements about secondary active transport is true?

options.text: It relies on ion gradients established by primary active transport.
It can occur without any energy input.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Secondary active transport relies on ion gradients created by primary active transport, such as the Na⁺ gradient.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What clinical finding would suggest inhibition of the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Inhibition of the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase reduces gastric acid secretion, a common effect of proton pump inhibitors.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: In the context of vesicular transport, which process is responsible for neurotransmitter release?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Neurotransmitter release at synapses occurs via exocytosis, where vesicles fuse with the membrane to release their contents.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: How does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase contribute to the resting membrane potential?

options.text: It generates a positive charge inside the cell.
It maintains a high intracellular Na⁺ concentration.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase creates an electrochemical gradient by pumping Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, which is crucial for the resting membrane potential.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Which type of transport mechanism is primarily involved in the movement of ions during the development of brain vesicles?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Primary active transport is crucial for establishing ion gradients necessary for the development and function of brain vesicles.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Regarding is secondary active transport atp-free? — which is correct?

options.text: Secondary active transport requires no energy because it uses no ATP
It uses no DIRECT ATP, but it depends on the Na⁺ gradient built by the ATP-consuming Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — so it is still energy-dependent

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The energy is "borrowed" from the Na⁺ gradient; block the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and secondary active transport fails too.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What best explains the finding: “Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 out / 2 in) using ATP”?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 out / 2 in) using ATP → Primary active transport (electrogenic pump).

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What best explains the finding: “SGLT moving glucose uphill with Na⁺”?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: SGLT moving glucose uphill with Na⁺ → Secondary active symport (Na⁺-coupled).

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Active & Vesicular Transport”?

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Vesicular transport is relevant in neural development and signaling.

action-potential-genesis.stem: The rapid depolarising (upstroke) phase of the neuronal action potential is caused by:

options.text: K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated K⁺ channels
Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Reaching threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; Na⁺ rushes in, reversing the potential toward +30 mV. Repolarisation is due to Na⁺ inactivation plus K⁺ efflux.

action-potential-genesis.stem: The "all-or-none" property of the action potential means that:

options.text: AP amplitude increases with stronger stimuli
A stimulus at or above threshold produces a full-amplitude AP, and stimulus strength is coded by frequency

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Once threshold is reached, the AP fires at full, fixed amplitude regardless of stimulus strength; a stronger stimulus increases AP frequency, not size. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no AP.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which an action potential is generated?
action-potential-genesis.explanation: An action potential is generated by the sequential opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels followed by K⁺ channels.

action-potential-genesis.stem: Which of the following findings indicates the repolarization phase of an action potential?
action-potential-genesis.explanation: Repolarization occurs when Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, allowing K⁺ to exit the cell.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What occurs during the hyperpolarization phase of an action potential?
action-potential-genesis.explanation: Hyperpolarization is due to the slow closure of K⁺ channels, which causes the membrane potential to briefly overshoot resting levels.

action-potential-genesis.stem: A stimulus that does not reach threshold will result in which of the following?

options.text: An action potential with reduced amplitude
An action potential with normal amplitude

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Only a stimulus that reaches or exceeds the threshold will generate an action potential; sub-threshold stimuli produce none.

action-potential-genesis.stem: How does a stronger stimulus affect action potential generation?
action-potential-genesis.explanation: The strength of a stimulus is encoded by the frequency of action potentials, not their amplitude.

action-potential-genesis.stem: How is the action potential in cardiac muscle similar to that in neurons?

options.text: Both rely solely on Na⁺ influx
Both are generated by ligand-gated channels
Both have a resting potential of +30 mV

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Both cardiac and neuronal action potentials exhibit a refractory period, which is critical for proper function.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What is a key difference between the action potential in neurons and cardiac cells?
action-potential-genesis.explanation: The duration of depolarization is significantly longer in cardiac action potentials compared to neuronal action potentials.

action-potential-genesis.stem: Regarding role of the na⁺/k⁺-atpase in the ap — which is correct?

options.text: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase directly produces the action potential
The AP is generated by ION FLOW through voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels; the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase only restores the gradients afterward
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: The pump maintains the gradients over time but is not the fast event; the up/down strokes are passive ion movements through gated channels.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rapid depolarisation to ~+30 mV”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Rapid depolarisation to ~+30 mV → Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Repolarisation back toward rest”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Repolarisation back toward rest → Na⁺ inactivation + voltage-gated K⁺ efflux.

action-potential-genesis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Genesis of the Neuron Action Potential”?

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Cardiac action potentials share fundamental mechanisms with neuronal action potentials.

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Basic genetics knowledge supports understanding of neuronal function.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot be generated because:
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: In the absolute refractory period the Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises, so no stimulus—however strong—can trigger another AP. This limits maximum firing frequency and enforces one-way conduction.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Saltatory conduction in myelinated axons is faster because the action potential:

options.text: Decreases in amplitude as it travels
Jumps between nodes of Ranvier where Na⁺ channels are concentrated

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Myelin insulates the internodes, so the AP regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier and effectively "jumps" between them (saltatory conduction), which is faster and more energy-efficient.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What is the primary mechanism that allows an action potential to propagate along an axon?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: An action potential propagates by depolarizing adjacent membrane regions to threshold, allowing regeneration of the AP.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Which of the following findings indicates that an action potential is non-decremental?

options.text: AP amplitude decreases along the axon
AP amplitude remains constant along the axon
AP can be evoked by a weak stimulus

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: The amplitude of the action potential remains constant along the axon due to regenerative propagation.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: During which period is it impossible to generate a second action potential, regardless of stimulus strength?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated, preventing any new action potential.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What physiological property allows myelinated axons to conduct action potentials faster than unmyelinated axons?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Myelinated axons utilize saltatory conduction, where action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier, increasing conduction speed.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Why does the action potential travel in one direction along an axon?

options.text: The axon is wider at one end
The membrane ahead is always depolarized
The region behind the impulse is refractory
The stimulus is always stronger in one direction

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: The action potential travels one way because the area just behind it is refractory, preventing backward propagation.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Which of the following conditions would most likely slow action potential conduction?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Demyelination, as seen in conditions like multiple sclerosis, disrupts saltatory conduction and slows action potential propagation.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: How does the mechanism of action potential propagation in neurons relate to cardiac action potentials?

options.text: Both are initiated by neurotransmitter release

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Both neuronal and cardiac action potentials involve sodium channel inactivation during the refractory periods, affecting excitability.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What is the relationship between action potentials in neurons and graded potentials?

options.text: Graded potentials can summate to trigger action potentials
Action potentials do not involve ion channels

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Graded potentials can summate and reach threshold to trigger an action potential, while action potentials are all-or-nothing events.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Regarding why does the ap travel one way? — which is correct?

options.text: The action potential can propagate in both directions along an axon
It travels ONE way because the membrane just behind it is refractory (Na⁺ channels inactivated), so it can only depolarise the forward, non-refractory region

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Refractoriness enforces unidirectional (orthodromic) propagation toward the synapse.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What best explains the finding: “AP amplitude constant along the axon”?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: AP amplitude constant along the axon → Regenerative (non-decremental) propagation.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What best explains the finding: “Impulse jumping node-to-node in a myelinated fibre”?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Impulse jumping node-to-node in a myelinated fibre → Saltatory conduction (fast, efficient).

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot be generated because the voltage-gated sodium channels are:

options.text: In the resting (closed but ready) state
Inactivated and unable to reopen until the membrane repolarises

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: After opening, the sodium channel's inactivation gate closes; these inactivated channels cannot reopen until repolarisation resets them, producing the absolute refractory period that ensures unidirectional propagation.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: The two defining properties that allow ion channels to generate precise electrical signals are:
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Ion channels are selective (a selectivity filter admits specific ions) and gated (they open/close in response to voltage, ligands or mechanical force); together these properties let membranes produce controlled ion movements.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What is the primary reason for the absolute refractory period in neurons?

options.text: The membrane potential is too high

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: The absolute refractory period occurs because voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: Which type of ion channel is primarily responsible for the rapid depolarisation phase of the action potential?
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open rapidly during depolarisation, allowing Na⁺ influx and generating the action potential.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What mechanism underlies the delayed repolarisation following the action potential?
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: The delayed repolarisation is due to the slower opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels, which allows K⁺ efflux.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: Which clinical finding indicates that a neuron cannot immediately re-fire after an action potential?
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: The absolute refractory period signifies that the neuron cannot generate another action potential due to inactivated Na⁺ channels.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: A patient presents with inherited long-QT syndrome. Which underlying mechanism is likely responsible?
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Inherited long-QT syndrome is often due to channelopathies affecting K⁺ channels, leading to prolonged repolarisation.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: How does the mechanism of local anesthetics relate to ion channels?
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Local anesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, preventing action potential propagation and nerve conduction.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: How does the action potential propagation relate to the resting membrane potential?

options.text: Resting potential affects Na⁺ channel inactivation
Resting potential determines K⁺ channel activation

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: The resting membrane potential establishes the baseline for depolarisation, which is essential for reaching the action potential threshold.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What is the relationship between action potential generation and graded potentials?

options.text: Graded potentials are always action potentials
Graded potentials can summate to trigger action potentials
Graded potentials are irrelevant to action potentials

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Graded potentials can summate and, if they reach the threshold, trigger an action potential.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: Regarding why a neuron is refractory — which is correct?

options.text: A neuron cannot re-fire immediately because the membrane potential is too high

The absolute refractory period exists because the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are INACTIVATED (their inactivation gate is shut) and cannot reopen until the membrane REPOLARISES — it is a channel-state phenomenon, not simply a voltage level
Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Refractoriness reflects the physical state of the sodium channels (inactivated, needing repolarisation to reset), which is what enforces one-way propagation and caps firing frequency.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absolute refractory period during the action potential”?

options.text: Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Absolute refractory period during the action potential → Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised).

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What best explains the finding: “One-way (unidirectional) impulse propagation”?

options.text: Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: One-way (unidirectional) impulse propagation → Refractoriness behind the impulse.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Ion Channels: Structure & Gating”?

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Antiarrhythmic drugs target ion channels, linking basic science to clinical application.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Which property distinguishes a graded potential from an action potential?

options.text: A graded potential varies in amplitude, can summate, and decays with distance
A graded potential travels without decrement
A graded potential has a refractory period

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials (receptor and synaptic potentials) vary in size with the stimulus, can summate, and spread passively with decay. Action potentials are all-or-none and regenerate to propagate without decrement.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: A longer membrane length (space) constant, allowing a signal to spread further before decaying, results from:

options.text: Low membrane resistance and high axial resistance
High membrane resistance and low axial (internal) resistance

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: The length constant increases when less current leaks across the membrane (high membrane resistance) and current flows more easily along the axon (low axial resistance, favoured by larger diameter and myelination), so the signal spreads further.
Graded potentials vary in amplitude and can summate, unlike action potentials which are all-or-none.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Which factor increases the length constant (λ) of a neuron?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: A larger axon diameter decreases axial resistance, allowing current to flow more easily and increasing the length constant.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What is the primary reason graded potentials cannot propagate long distances?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials decay with distance due to passive spread, preventing them from traveling long distances.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What is the main role of graded potentials in neuronal signaling?

options.text: To propagate signals over long distances

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials integrate synaptic inputs to determine whether the neuron will fire an action potential.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: How does myelination affect neuronal conduction?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Myelination increases membrane resistance, which enhances saltatory conduction by allowing the action potential to jump between nodes of Ranvier.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: How do graded potentials relate to GI smooth muscle activity?

options.text: They are unaffected by synaptic inputs

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials modulate the slow waves in GI smooth muscle, influencing contraction patterns.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What is the relationship between graded potentials and action potentials?

options.text: Graded potentials can travel long distances
Graded potentials can summate to trigger action potentials
Graded potentials are faster than action potentials

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials can summate to reach the threshold needed to trigger an action potential at the axon hillock.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Regarding graded potentials vs action potentials — which is correct?

options.text: Graded potentials propagate long distances the same way action potentials do

Graded potentials spread PASSIVELY and DECAY with distance (they cannot travel far); only the all-or-none ACTION potential regenerates itself to travel long distances without decrement — the graded potential's job is to reach threshold locally

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Treating graded potentials as long-distance signals ignores their decremental cable behaviour; they integrate inputs to decide firing, while the action potential does the faithful long-range transmission.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What best explains the finding: “A synaptic potential that varies in size and can summate”?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: A synaptic potential that varies in size and can summate → Graded potential (EPSP/IPSP).

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What best explains the finding: “Signal decaying with distance from its origin”?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Signal decaying with distance from its origin → Passive (electrotonic) spread — cable properties.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Graded Potentials & Cable Properties”?

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: The resting membrane potential of a neuron (≈ −70 mV) is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion, and why?

options.text: Na⁺, because Na⁺ channels dominate at rest
K⁺, because the resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺
Cl⁻, because Cl⁻ is actively pumped
Ca²⁺, because of Ca²⁺ leak channels

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: Open K⁺ leak channels make the resting membrane most permeable to K⁺, so the RMP sits near E_K (≈ −90 mV), pulled slightly positive by a small Na⁺ leak.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: The equilibrium (Nernst) potential of an ion is defined as the membrane voltage at which:

options.text: The ion is actively pumped fastest
The electrical and concentration forces on the ion are balanced, giving no net flux
All channels for the ion are closed
The ion is at its highest concentration

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: At the Nernst/equilibrium potential, the electrical gradient exactly opposes the concentration gradient, so there is no net movement of that ion.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What is the typical resting membrane potential (RMP) in neurons?
resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: The typical resting membrane potential in neurons is approximately -70 mV.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: Which ion's concentration gradient primarily determines the resting membrane potential?
resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: The resting membrane potential is primarily determined by the concentration gradient of K⁺ due to its high permeability at rest.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What happens to the resting membrane potential during hyperkalaemia?
resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: Hyperkalaemia increases extracellular K⁺, making E_K less negative and thus depolarizing the resting membrane potential.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: Which of the following best describes the Nernst equation?

options.text: Calculates the equilibrium potential for an ion

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a specific ion based on its concentration gradient.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: In a resting neuron, which ion has the greatest driving force for movement across the membrane?
resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: At rest, Na⁺ has a strong inward driving force because the membrane potential (-70 mV) is far from its equilibrium potential (+60 mV).

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: How does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase contribute to the resting membrane potential?

options.text: It generates a positive charge inside the cell
It allows Na⁺ to flow freely into the cell
It directly sets the RMP to +60 mV

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains ion concentration gradients, which are crucial for establishing the resting membrane potential.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: How does the resting membrane potential relate to the action potential generation?

options.text: RMP is irrelevant to action potential
RMP must be depolarized to threshold
RMP is always positive before action potential

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: The resting membrane potential must be depolarized to reach the threshold for action potential generation, linking it to the module on action potential genesis.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What effect does a decrease in extracellular K⁺ have on the resting membrane potential?
resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: Decreasing extracellular K⁺ makes E_K more negative, leading to hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: Regarding what the rmp is closest to — which is correct?

options.text: The resting membrane potential lies close to the sodium equilibrium potential
The RMP lies close to the POTASSIUM equilibrium potential (E_K ≈ −90 mV) because the resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺
Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: At rest, K⁺ leak channels dominate permeability, so the membrane potential is pulled toward E_K, not E_Na.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What best explains the finding: “RMP ≈ −70 mV, close to E_K”?

options.text: Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)
Vm (−70) far from E_Na (+60) → inward driving force
Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
↑extracellular K⁺ → E_K less negative → RMP less negative

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: RMP ≈ −70 mV, close to E_K → Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What best explains the finding: “E_K ≈ −90 mV”?

options.text: Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
Vm (−70) far from E_Na (+60) → inward driving force
↑extracellular K⁺ → E_K less negative → RMP less negative
Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: E_K ≈ −90 mV → Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient).

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: RMP concepts apply to hair cells in the inner ear for sensory transduction.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: According to the Goldman equation, the membrane potential at any moment is dominated by:

options.text: The ion with the highest intracellular concentration
The ion to which the membrane is currently most permeable
The ion pumped by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Whichever ion has the most negative equilibrium potential

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The Goldman equation weights each ion by its permeability, so the most permeable ion dominates Vm — K⁺ at rest, Na⁺ during the AP upstroke.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Hyperkalaemia (increased extracellular K⁺) affects the resting membrane potential by:

options.text: Depolarising the cell (E_K becomes less negative)

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Raising extracellular K⁺ makes E_K less negative; since the RMP tracks E_K, the cell depolarises — clinically dangerous for cardiac excitability.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What primarily determines the resting membrane potential (RMP) in a typical neuron?
goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The RMP is predominantly influenced by K⁺ permeability due to the high density of K⁺ leak channels.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Which ion's permeability increase leads to the upstroke of the action potential?
goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The upstroke of the action potential is caused by a rapid increase in Na⁺ permeability.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What is the effect of hyperkalaemia on cardiac cells?
goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Hyperkalaemia raises extracellular K⁺ concentration, leading to depolarization of cardiac cells.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What happens to the resting membrane potential if the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is inhibited?
goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase leads to gradual depolarization due to the loss of ion gradients.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Which statement correctly describes the mechanism of action potential generation?

options.text: Ion concentration changes drive rapid Vm changes
Permeability changes drive rapid Vm changes

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Action potential generation is primarily driven by changes in ion permeability, not concentration.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: How does the Goldman equation differ from the Nernst equation?

options.text: Goldman considers multiple ions; Nernst considers one
Goldman is for resting potential; Nernst is for action potential

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The Goldman equation calculates the resting potential based on the permeability of multiple ions, while the Nernst equation focuses on a single ion.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What is the relationship between resting membrane potential and action potential generation?
goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The resting membrane potential sets the baseline from which the threshold for action potential generation is determined.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Regarding what drives the moment-to-moment vm — which is correct?

options.text: Changes in ion CONCENTRATION cause the rapid changes in membrane potential during signalling
Rapid Vm changes are driven by changes in PERMEABILITY (channels opening/closing), not concentration — the Goldman principle
Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: One AP moves negligible ion amounts; it is the shift in relative permeability (to Na⁺, then K⁺) that swings Vm.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vm swings toward E_Na during the AP”?

options.text: Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Vm swings toward E_Na during the AP → Na⁺ permeability transiently dominates (Goldman).

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “RMP set mainly by K⁺ leak channels”?

options.text: Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: RMP set mainly by K⁺ leak channels → Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic terminal is triggered by the entry of which ion?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: The action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Acetylcholine's action at the synapse is terminated primarily by:
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: ACh is broken down in the cleft by acetylcholinesterase; monoamines like serotonin/dopamine are instead cleared mainly by reuptake.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What is the first step in the neurotransmitter life cycle at a chemical synapse?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: The life cycle begins with the synthesis of neurotransmitters before they are packaged into vesicles.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily cleared by enzymatic degradation in the synaptic cleft?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Acetylcholine is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What effect does acetylcholine have on skeletal muscle?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle through nicotinic receptors.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What mechanism do SSRIs use to increase synaptic serotonin levels?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: SSRIs block the serotonin reuptake transporter, increasing serotonin levels in the synaptic cleft.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Which neurotransmitter is considered the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: A patient presents with symptoms of depression. Which neurotransmitter system is most likely involved in the efficacy of SSRIs?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: SSRIs primarily target the serotonin system to alleviate symptoms of depression.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: In which way can the effect of a neurotransmitter be altered?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: The effect of a neurotransmitter depends on the receptor type it binds to, not the neurotransmitter itself.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which GABA exerts its inhibitory effect in the CNS?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: GABA primarily exerts its inhibitory effect by opening chloride channels, leading to hyperpolarization of the neuron.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: How do neuromodulators differ from classical neurotransmitters?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Neuromodulators act more slowly and modulate the strength of synaptic transmission rather than directly opening ion channels.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Regarding is a neurotransmitter inherently excitatory? — which is correct?

options.text: Acetylcholine is always excitatory because it activates muscle
The EFFECT depends on the RECEPTOR: ACh excites skeletal muscle (nicotinic) but inhibits/slows the heart (muscarinic)
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: A neurotransmitter's action is determined by the postsynaptic receptor and its ion channel, not the molecule alone.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ca²⁺ influx triggers NT release”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal
Main CNS excitatory vs inhibitory amino-acid NTs

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Ca²⁺ influx triggers NT release → Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What best explains the finding: “ACh cleared by acetylcholinesterase”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal
Main CNS excitatory vs inhibitory amino-acid NTs

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: ACh cleared by acetylcholinesterase → Enzymatic degradation in the cleft.
