cortical-areas-language.stem: Regarding broca vs wernicke aphasia — which is correct?

options.text: A patient who speaks fluently cannot have significant aphasia

WERNICKE (receptive) aphasia is FLUENT — speech flows effortlessly but is full of neologisms/"word salad" and comprehension is impaired, and the patient is often unaware; fluency does NOT equal normal language. BROCA (expressive) aphasia is the non-fluent one, with preserved comprehension

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Judging language by fluency alone misses Wernicke aphasia entirely; comprehension and repetition must be tested, because fluent speech can be meaningless while non-fluent speech can carry intact understanding.

cortical-areas-language.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension”?

options.text: Broca lesion adjacent to motor cortex (dominant MCA)

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension → Broca (expressive) aphasia — inferior frontal gyrus.

cortical-areas-language.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension”?

options.text: Broca lesion adjacent to motor cortex (dominant MCA)

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension → Wernicke (receptive) aphasia — superior temporal gyrus.

cortical-areas-language.stem: Which should you review before “Language Areas & Aphasia”?
cortical-areas-language.explanation: Wernicke's area is directly related to Wernicke's encephalopathy.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Fibres of the corpus callosum are an example of which type of cerebral white matter?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Commissural fibres connect the two hemispheres — the corpus callosum is the largest. Association fibres connect areas within one hemisphere (e.g. the arcuate fasciculus), and projection fibres connect the cortex with lower structures (e.g. the internal capsule).

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule characteristically produces:

options.text: A mild transient sensory tingle only
A dense contralateral hemiparesis out of proportion to the lesion size

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The internal capsule concentrates the corticospinal and thalamocortical fibres into a small area, so even a tiny (lacunar) lesion interrupts a large volume of traffic and causes a dense contralateral hemiparesis (pure motor stroke) — a deficit disproportionate to the lesion size.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Which lobe of the cerebrum is primarily responsible for executive functions and personality?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The frontal lobe is associated with executive functions, personality, and motor control.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: What type of white matter tract connects areas within the same hemisphere?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Association fibres connect different areas within the same hemisphere.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: A patient presents with dense contralateral hemiparesis after a small stroke. Which structure is most likely affected?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The internal capsule contains concentrated projection fibres, making small lesions disproportionately disabling.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Which finding is most indicative of a parietal lobe lesion?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Contralateral neglect is a classic sign of a non-dominant parietal lobe lesion.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: What is the primary function of the corpus callosum?

options.text: Connects areas within the same hemisphere

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The corpus callosum is the largest commissural fibre, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: A patient with a split-brain syndrome has had which structure affected?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Split-brain syndrome results from sectioning or agenesis of the corpus callosum.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: How does a lacunar stroke in the internal capsule lead to severe motor deficits?

options.text: It affects only the frontal lobe
It is located in the cortex

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The internal capsule contains concentrated motor and sensory pathways, so a small lesion can cause significant deficits.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Which area of the brain is primarily involved in language comprehension?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Wernicke's area, located in the temporal lobe, is responsible for language comprehension.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: What is the relationship between the internal capsule and the basal ganglia?

options.text: The internal capsule surrounds the basal ganglia
The internal capsule is part of the basal ganglia
The internal capsule connects the basal ganglia to the cortex
The internal capsule is unrelated to the basal ganglia

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The internal capsule runs between the basal ganglia and the cortex, carrying important motor and sensory pathways.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Regarding why an internal capsule lacune is so disabling — which is correct?

options.text: A very small deep stroke should cause only a minor deficit

The INTERNAL CAPSULE packs the entire corticospinal, corticobulbar and thalamocortical projection into a tiny cross-section, so a small (lacunar) lesion there can produce a DENSE contralateral hemiparesis and/or hemisensory loss — the deficit is out of all proportion to the lesion size

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Because projection fibres are concentrated in the capsule (unlike the spread-out cortex), a minute lesion interrupts a huge fraction of descending/ascending traffic — hence classic pure motor/sensory lacunar syndromes.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Personality change, disinhibition, executive dysfunction”?

options.text: Internal capsule (concentrated projection fibres) lacunar stroke

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Personality change, disinhibition, executive dysfunction → Frontal lobe lesion.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral neglect, apraxia, spatial disorientation”?

options.text: Internal capsule (concentrated projection fibres) lacunar stroke

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Contralateral neglect, apraxia, spatial disorientation → Parietal lobe lesion (esp. non-dominant).

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Which should you review before “Cerebral Lobes & White Matter”?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Understanding language areas is essential for grasping the functions of the temporal lobe.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Which sensory modality does NOT relay through the thalamus on its way to the cortex?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Olfaction is the exception — it projects directly to the olfactory/piriform cortex without a thalamic relay. Vision relays via the lateral geniculate, hearing via the medial geniculate, and body sensation via the VPL nucleus of the thalamus.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Regulation of body temperature, thirst, appetite and the circadian clock, together with control of the pituitary, is the role of the:
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The hypothalamus is the master homeostatic centre — regulating temperature, thirst/water balance, hunger, circadian rhythm (suprachiasmatic nucleus) and autonomic tone — and it commands the endocrine system through its control of the anterior and posterior pituitary.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Which thalamic nucleus is responsible for relaying visual information to the occipital cortex?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN) is specifically responsible for visual relay to the occipital cortex.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: A patient presents with contralateral loss of all sensory modalities and spontaneous pain. Which condition is most likely?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: This presentation is characteristic of Déjerine-Roussy syndrome, which results from a thalamic lesion.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: What is the primary function of the hypothalamus?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The hypothalamus is primarily responsible for regulating homeostasis, including temperature, thirst, and hunger.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Which of the following sensory modalities bypasses the thalamus?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Smell (olfaction) is the only sensory modality that bypasses the thalamus and directly reaches the olfactory cortex.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: A patient with diabetes insipidus likely has dysfunction in which part of the brain?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Diabetes insipidus is associated with hypothalamic dysfunction, particularly affecting ADH production.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: How does the hypothalamus influence the anterior pituitary?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The hypothalamus releases hormones into the portal circulation to control the anterior pituitary's function.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Which hypothalamic nucleus is primarily responsible for regulating circadian rhythms?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The Suprachiasmatic nucleus is the master clock that regulates circadian rhythms.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: How does the thalamus relate to the limbic system in terms of sensory processing?

options.text: Thalamus relays all sensory information to limbic structures
Limbic system bypasses thalamus for all sensory input
Thalamus integrates sensory and emotional information

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The thalamus integrates sensory information before it reaches the cortex, including emotional contexts processed by the limbic system.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: What role does the hypothalamus play in the feedback control of homeostasis?

options.text: It integrates sensory information for homeostatic responses
It solely controls the autonomic nervous system
It only responds to hormonal signals

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The hypothalamus integrates sensory information to maintain homeostasis through various physiological responses.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Regarding the sense that bypasses the thalamus — which is correct?

options.text: All sensory information is relayed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex

SMELL (olfaction) is the exception — olfactory input reaches the olfactory cortex DIRECTLY without a thalamic relay, whereas vision (LGN), hearing (MGN), body sensation (VPL) and taste/face (VPM) all relay through the thalamus

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: The olfactory system's direct cortical/limbic access (no thalamic gate) explains its strong, immediate links to memory and emotion and is a favourite exam distinction.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral loss of all sensory modalities + spontaneous pain”?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Contralateral loss of all sensory modalities + spontaneous pain → Thalamic (VPL) lesion — Déjerine-Roussy syndrome.

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Visual relay to the occipital cortex”?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Visual relay to the occipital cortex → Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).

diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.stem: Which should you review before “Diencephalon: Thalamus & Hypothalamus”?
diencephalon-thalamus-hypothalamus.explanation: Understanding homeostasis is crucial for grasping hypothalamic functions.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: A patient has right-sided face and arm weakness with expressive aphasia, but a relatively spared leg. The most likely occluded artery is the:
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The MCA supplies the lateral hemisphere — the face and arm region of the homunculus and (on the dominant, usually left, side) the language areas — so occlusion gives contralateral face/arm weakness with aphasia and relative leg sparing. The ACA supplies the medial leg area.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: The circle of Willis is functionally important chiefly because it:

options.text: Provides collateral anastomotic flow between the anterior and posterior circulations
Drains venous blood from the brain

cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The circle of Willis is an arterial anastomotic ring linking the internal carotid (anterior) and vertebrobasilar (posterior) systems via the anterior and posterior communicating arteries, allowing collateral flow if one vessel is occluded (though it is anatomically complete in only a minority).

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: Which artery primarily supplies the medial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere responsible for leg motor function?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial hemisphere, which includes the area responsible for leg movement.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: A patient presents with sudden onset of a 'thunderclap' headache. Which condition is most likely?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: A 'thunderclap' headache is characteristic of a ruptured berry aneurysm leading to subarachnoid hemorrhage.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: What is the primary function of the Circle of Willis?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The Circle of Willis provides collateral circulation between the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: A patient exhibits contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia. Which artery is most likely occluded?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral hemisphere, affecting the face and arm areas and potentially causing aphasia if in the dominant hemisphere.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: In a stroke affecting the anterior cerebral artery, which of the following deficits is expected?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial aspect of the hemisphere, leading to contralateral leg weakness.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: How does the Circle of Willis contribute to stroke management?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The Circle of Willis allows for collateral blood flow if one of the major arteries is occluded, which can help mitigate the effects of a stroke.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: Which clinical finding would suggest a stroke in the territory of the posterior cerebral artery?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe, leading to contralateral homonymous hemianopia when occluded.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: A patient has difficulty with language comprehension and production. Which area of the brain is most likely affected?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Wernicke's area, located in the dominant hemisphere, is responsible for language comprehension and production.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: In a patient with a lacunar stroke, which artery is most likely involved?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Lacunar strokes typically involve the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery, affecting deep structures.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: Regarding aca vs mca territory deficits — which is correct?

options.text: A hemisphere stroke weakens the whole opposite side equally

The homunculus is split between territories: the ANTERIOR cerebral artery supplies the MEDIAL cortex (the LEG area) → contralateral LEG-predominant deficit, whereas the MIDDLE cerebral artery supplies the LATERAL cortex (FACE and ARM area) → contralateral face/arm deficit (with aphasia if dominant) — the pattern localises the vessel

cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Because the motor/sensory homunculus drapes from the lateral (face/arm, MCA) over the top to the medial surface (leg, ACA), the distribution of weakness pinpoints which artery is occluded rather than being uniform.

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral leg weakness/sensory loss”?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Contralateral leg weakness/sensory loss → Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) territory (medial hemisphere).

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral face & arm weakness ± aphasia”?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Contralateral face & arm weakness ± aphasia → Middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory (dominant hemisphere).

cerebral-blood-supply.stem: Which should you review before “Cerebral Blood Supply & Circle of Willis”?
cerebral-blood-supply.explanation: Understanding language areas is crucial for interpreting MCA territory deficits.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid flows from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle through the:
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: CSF passes from the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro to the third ventricle, then through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and out the foramina of Luschka and Magendie into the subarachnoid space. Aqueduct stenosis is a classic cause of obstructive hydrocephalus.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: A biconvex (lens-shaped) haematoma with a lucid interval after temporal trauma is characteristic of a ruptured:
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: An extradural (epidural) haemorrhage is typically arterial — from the middle meningeal artery after a temporal skull fracture — producing a lens-shaped (biconvex) haematoma and a classic lucid interval before deterioration. Subdural bleeds (bridging veins) are crescent-shaped.
The choroid plexus is responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricles.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Which of the following correctly describes non-communicating hydrocephalus?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Non-communicating hydrocephalus is caused by a blockage within the ventricular system, preventing CSF from reaching the subarachnoid space.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: What is the most likely cause of a crescent-shaped hematoma in an elderly patient?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: A crescent-shaped hematoma is characteristic of subdural hemorrhage, often seen in elderly patients due to bridging vein rupture.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Which clinical finding is associated with communicating hydrocephalus?

options.text: Dilated ventricles with normal subarachnoid space

ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus is characterized by enlarged ventricles due to impaired absorption of CSF, often following meningitis.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: What is the primary function of arachnoid granulations?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Arachnoid granulations are responsible for the absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the venous blood.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: How does obstructive hydrocephalus differ from communicating hydrocephalus?

options.text: Communicating has a blockage within ventricles
Communicating has no block within ventricles

ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Obstructive hydrocephalus involves a blockage within the ventricular system, while communicating hydrocephalus involves impaired absorption but no blockage.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Which of the following conditions could lead to raised intracranial pressure due to impaired CSF absorption?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Meningitis can lead to impaired absorption of CSF at the arachnoid granulations, resulting in raised intracranial pressure.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: In which scenario would you expect ventricular dilation with normal subarachnoid space?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Ventricular dilation with a normal subarachnoid space is indicative of communicating hydrocephalus, where absorption is impaired but flow is intact.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Regarding communicating vs non-communicating hydrocephalus — which is correct?

options.text: "Communicating" hydrocephalus means the CSF is flowing normally, so it is the harmless type

"Communicating" refers only to the fact that the ventricles still COMMUNICATE with the subarachnoid space — the problem is failed ABSORPTION at the arachnoid granulations (e.g. after meningitis or SAH); "non-communicating" (obstructive) means a block WITHIN the ventricular system. Both raise pressure and can be dangerous

ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: The terms describe WHERE the CSF problem lies (obstruction within the ventricles vs impaired absorption downstream), not severity — both cause hydrocephalus, and the distinction guides where CSF flow fails.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ventricular dilatation with raised intracranial pressure”?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Ventricular dilatation with raised intracranial pressure → Hydrocephalus (excess CSF).

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dilated ventricles above an aqueduct block, normal subarachnoid space”?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Dilated ventricles above an aqueduct block, normal subarachnoid space → Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

ventricles-csf-circulation.stem: Which should you review before “Ventricles, CSF & Meninges”?
ventricles-csf-circulation.explanation: Understanding the meninges is crucial for grasping CSF circulation and related pathologies.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: A Pacinian corpuscle fires briskly when pressure is first applied and when it is removed, but falls silent during steady pressure. This behaviour is:
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Rapidly (phasically) adapting receptors such as Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles respond to CHANGE — the onset and offset of a stimulus — and stop firing during a sustained stimulus, making them detectors of vibration and movement.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: The intensity of a sensory stimulus is encoded principally by:

options.text: The amplitude (height) of the action potentials
The frequency of action potentials and the number of receptors recruited
The conduction velocity of the nerve

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none (constant amplitude), so intensity is coded by how FAST a receptor fires (frequency) and how MANY receptors are recruited — not by spike height. Modality is set by the labelled line, and duration by adaptation.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What type of receptor is primarily responsible for detecting fine touch and has a slow adaptation rate?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Merkel discs are slowly adapting receptors that respond to sustained pressure, making them essential for fine touch detection.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: Which mechanism describes how a stimulus is converted into a receptor potential?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Transduction is the process by which sensory receptors convert stimuli into electrical signals (receptor potentials).

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What is the primary characteristic of rapidly adapting receptors?

options.text: They fire continuously during a stimulus.
They detect changes in stimulus intensity.

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors, such as Pacinian corpuscles, respond primarily to changes in stimulus intensity rather than sustained stimuli.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What phenomenon enhances the ability to localize a stimulus by sharpening contrast?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Lateral inhibition enhances contrast and sharpens localization of sensory stimuli by inhibiting neighboring receptors.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: Which sensory receptor is primarily responsible for detecting temperature changes?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Thermoreceptors are specialized sensory receptors that detect changes in temperature.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: How does the size of a receptive field affect two-point discrimination?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Smaller receptive fields with higher receptor density allow for better two-point discrimination, as seen in areas like the fingertips.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: How does the mechanism of transduction relate to pain perception in nociceptors?

options.text: Transduction in nociceptors is independent of stimulus type.
Nociceptors transduce harmful stimuli into pain signals.
Pain perception does not involve transduction.

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Nociceptors transduce harmful or potentially damaging stimuli into pain signals, which is crucial for pain perception.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What role does the resting membrane potential play in sensory receptor function?

options.text: It determines the type of stimulus detected.
It influences the threshold for action potential generation.
It has no effect on sensory receptors.

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: The resting membrane potential influences the excitability of sensory receptors and their ability to generate action potentials in response to stimuli.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: Regarding rapidly vs slowly adapting receptors — which is correct?

options.text: A rapidly adapting receptor responds faster or is more sensitive than a slowly adapting one

"Rapidly adapting" means the receptor STOPS firing during a SUSTAINED stimulus (it signals CHANGE/onset-offset), whereas "slowly adapting" means it KEEPS firing throughout a sustained stimulus (signalling steady intensity) — adaptation refers to the decline of the response over time, not to speed or sensitivity

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Adaptation describes how the response changes during a maintained stimulus; rapidly adapting receptors (Pacinian, Meissner) are movement/vibration detectors, slowly adapting ones (Merkel, Ruffini) report ongoing pressure — confusing this misreads what each detects.

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What best explains the finding: “A receptor that fires only when a stimulus changes”?

options.text: Small receptive fields + high receptor density

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: A receptor that fires only when a stimulus changes → Rapidly (phasically) adapting receptor (e.g. Pacinian corpuscle).

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: What best explains the finding: “A receptor that fires throughout a sustained stimulus”?

options.text: Small receptive fields + high receptor density

sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: A receptor that fires throughout a sustained stimulus → Slowly (tonically) adapting receptor (e.g. Merkel disc).

sensory-receptors-transduction.stem: Which should you review before “Sensory Receptors & Transduction”?
sensory-receptors-transduction.explanation: Knowledge of skin appendages is essential for understanding sensory receptors.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Vibration sense and conscious proprioception are carried by the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway, which decussates (crosses) in the:

options.text: Spinal cord, at the level of entry

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The DCML first-order neuron ascends ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns and synapses in the dorsal column nuclei of the medulla; the second-order neuron then decussates in the medulla as the medial lemniscus. The spinothalamic tract, in contrast, crosses at the cord.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: A spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard) produces loss of pain and temperature on which side, relative to the lesion?

options.text: The opposite (contralateral) side, beginning a segment or two below the lesion

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The spinothalamic tract crosses within one or two segments of entry, so at a hemisection the ascending crossed fibres are damaged — causing CONTRALATERAL loss of pain and temperature (with ipsilateral loss of fine touch/proprioception and power), the dissociated Brown-Séquard pattern.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Which sensory modality is carried by the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway?
somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway is responsible for transmitting fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: At which level does the spinothalamic tract decussate?

options.text: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The spinothalamic tract decussates within one or two segments in the spinal cord at the dorsal horn.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: A patient presents with loss of vibration and proprioception. Which pathway is likely affected?
somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Loss of vibration and proprioception indicates a lesion in the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: In Brown-Séquard syndrome, which sensory loss occurs contralaterally?
somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: In Brown-Séquard syndrome, pain and temperature sensation is lost contralaterally due to the early crossing of the spinothalamic tract.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Which statement correctly describes the decussation of sensory pathways?

options.text: Both pathways cross at the same level
DCML crosses in the spinal cord, spinothalamic in the medulla
DCML crosses in the medulla, spinothalamic in the spinal cord
Both pathways cross in the thalamus

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway crosses in the medulla, while the spinothalamic tract crosses at the spinal cord.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: How does the sensory homunculus represent the body in the primary sensory cortex?

options.text: Equal representation for all body parts

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The sensory homunculus is organized based on the density of sensory innervation, with more sensitive areas represented larger.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Which sensory pathway is primarily involved in proprioception and how does it relate to spinal reflexes?

options.text: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus; it integrates with reflex arcs
Spinothalamic tract; it does not involve reflexes
Corticospinal tract; it mediates voluntary movement
Spinocerebellar tract; it carries unconscious proprioception

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway is involved in conscious proprioception and integrates with reflex arcs for motor responses.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: What is the role of the thalamus in sensory processing, and how does it relate to the sensory pathways discussed?

options.text: It is the primary sensory cortex
It relays sensory information to the cortex
It is involved in pain modulation

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: The thalamus serves as a relay station for sensory information from both the dorsal column-medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways to the primary sensory cortex.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Regarding level of decussation of the sensory tracts — which is correct?

options.text: Both major sensory pathways cross at the same level, so all sensory loss is contralateral to a cord lesion

The DCML (fine touch, vibration, proprioception) crosses HIGH in the MEDULLA, while the spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) crosses almost immediately at the CORD — so a cord hemisection causes IPSILATERAL touch/proprioception loss but CONTRALATERAL pain/temperature loss (Brown-Séquard)

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Because the two systems decussate at different levels, a single cord lesion produces dissociated, split-sided sensory loss — the classic Brown-Séquard pattern that pinpoints the lesion; assuming a common crossing level gives the wrong side.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loss of vibration and proprioception (positive Romberg)”?

options.text: Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) — tracts cross at different levels
Thalamic (VPL) or cortical lesion (both tracts already crossed)

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Loss of vibration and proprioception (positive Romberg) → Dorsal column–medial lemniscus lesion.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loss of pain and temperature”?

options.text: Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) — tracts cross at different levels
Thalamic (VPL) or cortical lesion (both tracts already crossed)

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Loss of pain and temperature → Spinothalamic (anterolateral) tract lesion.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Somatosensory Ascending Pathways”?
somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Proprioception is a key aspect of the DCML pathway.

somatosensory-ascending-pathways.stem: Which should you review before “Somatosensory Ascending Pathways”?
somatosensory-ascending-pathways.explanation: Understanding cortical organization is essential for grasping sensory pathways.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Sharp, well-localised "first" pain is conducted by which fibres, and dull, aching "second" pain by which?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Fast, myelinated Aδ fibres carry sharp, well-localised "first" pain; slow, unmyelinated C fibres carry dull, aching, poorly-localised "second" pain. Both synapse in the dorsal horn and ascend in the spinothalamic tract.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Rubbing a stubbed toe reduces the pain. The best explanation is:

options.text: Gate control — large-fibre (touch) input inhibits nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Gate control theory: non-painful large-fibre (Aβ, touch) input activates inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that "close the gate" on nociceptive (Aδ/C) transmission — the basis of rubbing an injury and of TENS. The PAG mediates descending, not touch-triggered, modulation.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Which type of nociceptive fiber is responsible for transmitting sharp, well-localized 'first' pain?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Aδ fibers are myelinated and transmit sharp, well-localized pain quickly.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: What mechanism explains the relief of pain when rubbing the affected area?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Gate control theory posits that non-painful input can inhibit pain transmission at the spinal cord level.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: A patient presents with pain in the left arm and jaw. What is the most likely explanation for this phenomenon?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: This is an example of referred pain due to convergence of visceral and somatic afferents in the dorsal horn.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily involved in the descending analgesic pathway from the periaqueductal gray?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Serotonin is one of the key neurotransmitters used in the descending pain modulation pathway.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: In the context of pain modulation, what is the role of the PAG-raphe system?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: The PAG-raphe system is involved in inhibiting nociceptive signals, thus modulating pain perception.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Which statement about referred pain is FALSE?

options.text: It results from convergence of visceral and somatic afferents.
It can be localized to a specific dermatome.
It indicates that pain has spread to another area.
It is often misattributed by the brain.

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Referred pain does not indicate that pain has physically spread; it arises from central convergence of signals.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: How does the mechanism of pain modulation relate to the sensory receptors involved in nociception?

options.text: Pain modulation does not involve sensory receptors.
Nociceptors detect tissue damage and signal pain.
Sensory receptors only transmit non-painful stimuli.

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Nociceptors are specialized sensory receptors that detect tissue damage and are crucial for signaling pain.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: What is the relationship between the descending analgesic system and the perception of pain in acute pyelonephritis?

options.text: It has no effect on pain perception.

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: The descending analgesic system can inhibit pain transmission, which is relevant in managing pain associated with conditions like acute pyelonephritis.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Regarding referred pain mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: Referred pain means the pain has physically spread to the distant site

Referred pain arises because visceral and somatic afferents CONVERGE on the same dorsal-horn (spinothalamic) neurons, so the brain misattributes visceral pain to the somatic dermatome — no pain has spread; the heart (T1–T4) refers to the arm/jaw, the diaphragm (C3–5) to the shoulder tip

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Understanding referred pain as central convergence, not physical spread, explains its fixed dermatomal patterns and why it localises the affected viscus by its segmental innervation — vital for recognising, e.g., cardiac pain.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sharp, well-localised "first" pain”?

options.text: Gate control — large-fibre input closes the dorsal-horn gate
Referred pain (visceral–somatic convergence in the dorsal horn)

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Sharp, well-localised "first" pain → Fast myelinated Aδ nociceptive fibres.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dull, aching, poorly localised "second" pain”?

options.text: Gate control — large-fibre input closes the dorsal-horn gate
Referred pain (visceral–somatic convergence in the dorsal horn)

pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Dull, aching, poorly localised "second" pain → Slow unmyelinated C nociceptive fibres.

pain-nociception-modulation.stem: Which should you review before “Pain: Nociception & Modulation”?
pain-nociception-modulation.explanation: Understanding nociceptors requires knowledge of sensory receptor function.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: A lesion of the left motor cortex causes weakness of the right side of the body because the corticospinal tract:

options.text: Decussates in the medullary pyramids (below the cortex)

motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Most corticospinal fibres cross at the medullary pyramids, so a lesion above this point (e.g. the motor cortex or internal capsule) produces weakness on the opposite (contralateral) side of the body.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Spasticity, hyper-reflexia and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response with no muscle wasting indicate:
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Increased tone (spasticity), hyper-reflexia, clonus and a Babinski sign, without wasting, are the signs of an upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesion. Lower motor neuron lesions cause flaccidity, areflexia, wasting and fasciculations.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Which structure is primarily responsible for executing voluntary movement?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: The motor cortex is the primary area responsible for executing voluntary movements.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: What is the main pathway for fine, skilled voluntary movement?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: The corticospinal tract is the main pathway for fine, skilled voluntary movement, especially of the distal limbs.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: A patient presents with spasticity and hyper-reflexia. What type of lesion is most likely present?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Spasticity and hyper-reflexia are indicative of an upper motor neuron lesion.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Which of the following findings would indicate a lower motor neuron lesion?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Muscle wasting is a characteristic finding of lower motor neuron lesions.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: A lesion in the corticospinal tract above the medullary pyramids would result in weakness on which side of the body?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Lesions above the decussation in the medulla cause contralateral weakness due to the crossing of fibers.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: In a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which combination of signs would you expect?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: ALS causes degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons, leading to spasticity (UMN signs) and fasciculations (LMN signs).

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: How do the basal ganglia influence voluntary movement?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: The basal ganglia are involved in selecting and scaling voluntary movements.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Which reflex type is primarily involved in the feedback mechanism for fine motor control?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: The stretch reflex is crucial for maintaining fine motor control and adjusting muscle tone during voluntary movements.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Regarding localising weakness by umn vs lmn signs — which is correct?

options.text: Weakness with brisk reflexes and weakness with absent reflexes indicate the same kind of lesion

UMN lesions give SPASTIC weakness with HYPER-reflexia, clonus and a Babinski sign (no wasting), whereas LMN lesions give FLACCID weakness with areflexia, WASTING and fasciculations — the reflex/tone pattern localises the lesion above vs below the anterior horn cell

motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Both cause weakness, but the accompanying tone, reflexes and wasting distinguish an upper- from a lower-motor-neuron lesion, which changes the localisation and differential entirely.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Spasticity, hyper-reflexia, clonus, up-going plantar”?

options.text: Corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla (below the lesion)

motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Spasticity, hyper-reflexia, clonus, up-going plantar → Upper motor neuron lesion.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flaccidity, areflexia, wasting, fasciculations”?

options.text: Corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla (below the lesion)

motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Flaccidity, areflexia, wasting, fasciculations → Lower motor neuron lesion.

motor-system-corticospinal-control.stem: Which should you review before “The Motor System & Corticospinal Tract”?
motor-system-corticospinal-control.explanation: Understanding reflexes is essential for differentiating UMN and LMN lesions.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: The knee-jerk (patellar) reflex is described as monosynaptic because:

options.text: The Ia afferent from the muscle spindle synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron with no interneuron
It is controlled by gamma motor neurons only

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: In the stretch (myotatic) reflex, the Ia afferent from the muscle spindle synapses directly onto the alpha motor neuron supplying the same muscle — a single synapse (monosynaptic), producing rapid contraction. The Golgi tendon organ reflex, by contrast, is disynaptic (via an inhibitory interneuron).

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: Generally brisk, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes with clonus indicate a lesion of the:

options.text: Upper motor neuron (loss of descending inhibition)

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Upper motor neuron lesions release the stretch reflex from descending inhibition, producing hyper-reflexia and clonus (with spasticity and a Babinski sign). Lower motor neuron or sensory afferent lesions break the reflex arc and cause absent or reduced reflexes.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: What type of reflex is the knee-jerk reflex?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The knee-jerk reflex is a monosynaptic reflex arc involving a single synapse between the sensory and motor neurons.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: What is the primary function of the Golgi tendon organ?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The Golgi tendon organ senses muscle tension and helps prevent muscle overload through autogenic inhibition.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: A patient exhibits hyper-reflexia. What does this indicate?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Hyper-reflexia indicates an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion due to loss of descending inhibition.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: Which statement correctly describes the muscle spindle's role in reflexes?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The muscle spindle senses muscle length and contributes to the monosynaptic stretch reflex that causes contraction.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: During a muscle contraction, which mechanism ensures the antagonist muscle relaxes?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is the mechanism that relaxes the antagonist muscle while the agonist contracts.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: How does the Golgi tendon organ prevent muscle overload?

options.text: By exciting the alpha motor neuron
By inhibiting the alpha motor neuron
By stimulating the gamma motor neuron

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The Golgi tendon organ inhibits the alpha motor neuron to prevent excessive muscle tension, a process known as autogenic inhibition.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: How are the muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ functionally different?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The muscle spindle drives contraction via a monosynaptic reflex, while the Golgi tendon organ inhibits contraction through a disynaptic reflex.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: How does the stretch reflex relate to the corticospinal tract?

options.text: It is mediated by the same neurons
It is independent of the corticospinal tract
It provides feedback to the corticospinal tract

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: The stretch reflex provides feedback to the corticospinal tract, helping to adjust motor output based on muscle length changes.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: What is the relationship between proprioceptors and sensory pathways?

options.text: Proprioceptors are part of the sensory pathways
Sensory pathways do not include proprioceptors

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Proprioceptors, such as muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs, are integral components of sensory pathways that provide information about body position and movement.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: Regarding muscle spindle vs golgi tendon organ — which is correct?

options.text: The muscle spindle and the Golgi tendon organ do the same job and drive the same reflex

They are OPPOSITES: the SPINDLE (parallel, senses LENGTH/stretch) drives the MONOSYNAPTIC stretch reflex that CONTRACTS the muscle, whereas the GOLGI TENDON ORGAN (in series, senses TENSION) drives a DISYNAPTIC reflex that INHIBITS the same muscle (autogenic inhibition) to protect against overload
Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle Ia → alpha motor neuron)
UMN lesion — loss of descending inhibition of the reflex arc

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Confusing the two inverts the reflex — one excites for length control, the other inhibits for tension protection; distinguishing them is essential to understanding reflex modulation and tone.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brisk knee-jerk after a tendon tap”?

options.text: UMN lesion — loss of descending inhibition of the reflex arc
LMN or sensory (afferent) lesion breaking the arc
Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle Ia → alpha motor neuron)

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Brisk knee-jerk after a tendon tap → Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle Ia → alpha motor neuron).

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyper-reflexia, clonus”?

options.text: Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle Ia → alpha motor neuron)
LMN or sensory (afferent) lesion breaking the arc
UMN lesion — loss of descending inhibition of the reflex arc

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Hyper-reflexia, clonus → UMN lesion — loss of descending inhibition of the reflex arc.

proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.stem: Which should you review before “Proprioceptors & Spinal Reflexes”?
proprioceptors-muscle-spindle-reflexes.explanation: Directly relates to the function and comparison of muscle spindles and GTOs.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: The principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters of the central nervous system are, respectively:
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Glutamate is the main excitatory CNS transmitter (AMPA/NMDA receptors) and GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain (glycine predominates in the spinal cord), opening chloride channels to hyperpolarise.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Fast excitatory synaptic transmission via a ligand-gated ion channel (e.g. an AMPA receptor) is an example of:
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that open directly when the transmitter binds, producing fast responses (e.g. AMPA for glutamate, GABA-A for GABA). Metabotropic receptors act more slowly via G proteins and second messengers.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: What is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Glutamate is recognized as the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for inhibitory signaling in the brain?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, opening Cl⁻ channels to hyperpolarize neurons.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: What mechanism do benzodiazepines use to enhance inhibition?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Benzodiazepines enhance the inhibitory effect by positively modulating GABA-A receptors.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which of the following statements about neurotransmitters is true?

options.text: The same neurotransmitter can have excitatory or inhibitory effects depending on the receptor.
All neurotransmitters act on ionotropic receptors.
Dopamine is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: The same neurotransmitter can indeed have different effects based on the type of receptor it binds to.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which neurotransmitter system is primarily involved in arousal and attention?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Noradrenaline, originating from the locus coeruleus, is key in modulating arousal and attention.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: How do ionotropic receptors differ from metabotropic receptors?

options.text: Ionotropic receptors are slower than metabotropic receptors.
Metabotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels.
Ionotropic receptors mediate fast synaptic responses.
Metabotropic receptors directly open ion channels.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Ionotropic receptors mediate fast synaptic responses by acting as ligand-gated ion channels.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily involved in the modulation of pain and nociception?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Glutamate plays a significant role in the modulation of pain and nociception in the CNS.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: What role does serotonin play in the CNS?

options.text: It is involved in mood and sleep regulation.
It is the main neurotransmitter for motor control.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Serotonin is crucial for mood regulation and sleep, acting as a modulator in various CNS functions.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Regarding what determines excitation vs inhibition — which is correct?

options.text: A neurotransmitter is intrinsically excitatory or inhibitory

The SAME transmitter can excite or inhibit depending on the RECEPTOR and the ion it controls — e.g. acetylcholine excites at nicotinic receptors but can inhibit via some muscarinic receptors; the postsynaptic receptor, not the transmitter alone, sets the effect
GABA (brain) and glycine (spinal cord) — open Cl⁻ channels

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Attributing a fixed sign to the transmitter ignores receptor diversity; the ionic consequence (depolarising cation entry vs hyperpolarising Cl⁻ entry), set by the receptor, is what makes a synapse excitatory or inhibitory.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “Main excitatory CNS transmitter”?

options.text: GABA (brain) and glycine (spinal cord) — open Cl⁻ channels

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Main excitatory CNS transmitter → Glutamate (AMPA/NMDA receptors).

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “Main inhibitory transmitters (brain vs cord)”?

options.text: GABA (brain) and glycine (spinal cord) — open Cl⁻ channels

cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Main inhibitory transmitters (brain vs cord) → GABA (brain) and glycine (spinal cord) — open Cl⁻ channels.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which is a clinical application of “CNS Neurotransmission Systems”?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Involves neurotransmitter systems in autonomic functions.

cns-neurotransmission-systems.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Neurotransmission Systems”?
cns-neurotransmission-systems.explanation: Provides foundational knowledge on neurotransmitter systems.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: The NMDA receptor is described as a "coincidence detector" for long-term potentiation because it opens only when:

options.text: Glutamate binds, regardless of membrane potential
Glutamate binds AND the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised (relieving the Mg²⁺ block)

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: At rest the NMDA channel is blocked by Mg²⁺. It opens only when glutamate is bound AND the postsynaptic cell is depolarised enough to expel the Mg²⁺, admitting Ca²⁺. Requiring simultaneous presynaptic (glutamate) and postsynaptic (depolarisation) activity makes it a coincidence detector — the basis of Hebbian LTP.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Long-term potentiation (LTP), the leading cellular model of memory, is expressed largely through:

options.text: Removal of AMPA receptors from the synapse
A Ca²⁺-triggered increase in AMPA receptors and synaptic strength
Permanent loss of the presynaptic terminal
Conversion of glutamate synapses to GABA synapses

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: LTP is triggered by Ca²⁺ entering through NMDA receptors, which activates kinases (e.g. CaMKII) that insert additional AMPA receptors and strengthen the synapse. Low-level Ca²⁺ instead activates phosphatases that remove AMPA receptors, producing long-term depression (LTD).

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: What is the primary mechanism underlying long-term potentiation (LTP)?

options.text: Increased release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic neuron
Insertion of AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane
Decreased calcium influx through voltage-gated channels

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: LTP is characterized by the insertion of AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane, which strengthens synaptic transmission.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Which receptor acts as a coincidence detector in synaptic plasticity?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: The NMDA receptor requires both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to open, making it a coincidence detector.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: What is the consequence of excessive calcium entry through NMDA receptors?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: Excessive calcium entry through NMDA receptors can lead to excitotoxicity and neuronal death.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of Ca²⁺ in long-term potentiation?

options.text: Large Ca²⁺ influx activates kinases leading to AMPA receptor insertion
Ca²⁺ causes hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic neuron

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: A large influx of Ca²⁺ activates kinases, which leads to the insertion of AMPA receptors and strengthens the synapse.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Which statement correctly describes long-term depression (LTD)?

options.text: It is induced by high-frequency stimulation
It involves the removal of AMPA receptors
It is solely dependent on presynaptic activity

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: LTD is characterized by the removal of AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic membrane, resulting in decreased synaptic strength.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: How does neuroplasticity relate to recovery after brain injury?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: Neuroplasticity allows the brain to reorganize its circuits after injury, facilitating recovery and rehabilitation.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Which process is most directly linked to the concept of Hebbian learning?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: Hebbian learning is based on the principle that simultaneous activation of pre- and postsynaptic neurons strengthens the synapse, which is mediated by NMDA receptor coincidence detection.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: What is the relationship between synaptic plasticity and memory formation?

options.text: Memory is solely dependent on neurotransmitter release
Synaptic plasticity underlies the mechanisms of learning and memory
Memory formation does not involve synaptic changes
Only long-term depression is involved in memory

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: Synaptic plasticity, through processes like LTP and LTD, is fundamental to the mechanisms of learning and memory.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Regarding why the nmda receptor is a coincidence detector — which is correct?

options.text: The NMDA receptor opens as soon as glutamate binds, like an ordinary ligand-gated channel

The NMDA receptor needs TWO things at once: glutamate binding AND postsynaptic DEPOLARISATION to expel the Mg²⁺ ion that blocks its pore at rest — only then does it open and admit Ca²⁺; this dual requirement makes it a "coincidence detector" that reports simultaneous pre- and post-synaptic activity (the molecular basis of Hebbian LTP)

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: The voltage-dependent Mg²⁺ block is precisely what lets the NMDA receptor detect coincident activity and drive associative strengthening — miss it and LTP's associativity and input-specificity make no sense.

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lasting increase in synaptic strength after high-frequency stimulation”?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: Lasting increase in synaptic strength after high-frequency stimulation → Long-term potentiation (LTP).

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: What best explains the finding: “A receptor requiring both glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to open”?
synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: A receptor requiring both glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to open → NMDA receptor (Mg²⁺-block coincidence detector).

synaptic-plasticity-learning.stem: Which should you review before “Synaptic Plasticity & Learning”?

options.text: Long-Term Depression & the Basis of Memory

synaptic-plasticity-learning.explanation: LTD is a counterpart to LTP and crucial for memory concepts.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts predominantly influence:

options.text: Posture, balance and antigravity (extensor) muscle tone

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The brainstem (extrapyramidal) tracts — vestibulospinal and reticulospinal — control posture, balance and antigravity extensor tone in axial/proximal muscles, providing the background for the fine voluntary movement of the corticospinal tract.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Decerebrate (extensor) posturing, compared with decorticate (flexor) posturing, indicates a lesion that is:

options.text: Above the red nucleus and less severe
Below the red nucleus and generally more severe

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Decorticate posturing (arm flexion) reflects a lesion above the red nucleus; decerebrate posturing (arm extension) reflects a more caudal lesion below the red nucleus with unopposed extensor drive, and is generally the more severe finding.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Which brainstem tract is primarily responsible for maintaining antigravity extensor tone?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The vestibulospinal tract is responsible for maintaining antigravity extensor tone, crucial for balance.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: What type of posturing is characterized by arm flexion and indicates a lesion above the red nucleus?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Decorticate posturing (arm flexion) indicates a lesion above the red nucleus, where the rubrospinal tract is still functional.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Which tract is involved in reflex head and eye turning toward visual stimuli?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The tectospinal tract mediates reflex head and eye movements in response to visual stimuli.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: A patient exhibits decerebrate posturing. What does this indicate about the location of their brain lesion?

options.text: At the level of the red nucleus

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Decerebrate posturing indicates a lesion below the red nucleus, where extensor drive is unopposed.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: What is the primary function of the reticulospinal tract?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The reticulospinal tract is involved in regulating posture and locomotion.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: A patient presents with decorticate posturing following a traumatic brain injury. What is the likely prognosis compared to decerebrate posturing?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Decorticate posturing indicates a higher lesion and is generally associated with a better prognosis than decerebrate posturing.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: How does the vestibulospinal tract interact with the reticulospinal tract in maintaining posture?

options.text: They act independently of each other
Both work together to maintain extensor tone

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Both the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts work together to maintain extensor tone and posture.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Which brainstem tract is primarily responsible for coordinating activity between spinal segments during locomotion?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The propriospinal system coordinates activity between spinal segments, essential for locomotion.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Regarding decorticate vs decerebrate posturing — which is correct?

options.text: Decerebrate (extensor) posturing indicates a less severe, higher lesion than decorticate posturing

DECEREBRATE (arm EXTENSION) posturing reflects a MORE CAUDAL lesion (below the red nucleus) and is generally WORSE than DECORTICATE (arm FLEXION) posturing (lesion above the red nucleus); a change from decorticate to decerebrate signals deterioration

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: The level of the lesion determines which brainstem drives are unopposed; the more caudal decerebrate pattern (extensor) indicates deeper brainstem involvement and a poorer prognosis than decorticate.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antigravity/extensor postural tone”?

options.text: Lesion above the red nucleus (rubrospinal flexor preserved)
Lesion below the red nucleus (unopposed extensor drive)

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Antigravity/extensor postural tone → Vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: What best explains the finding: “Decorticate posturing (arm flexion)”?

options.text: Lesion below the red nucleus (unopposed extensor drive)
Lesion above the red nucleus (rubrospinal flexor preserved)

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Decorticate posturing (arm flexion) → Lesion above the red nucleus (rubrospinal flexor preserved).

brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.stem: Which should you review before “Brainstem Motor Centres & Descending Tracts”?
brainstem-descending-motor-tracts.explanation: Understanding brainstem anatomy is essential for grasping motor tracts.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: The hypokinetic features of Parkinson disease (bradykinesia, rigidity) result from:

options.text: Loss of substantia nigra dopamine, underactivating the direct pathway and overactivating the indirect pathway

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine reduces direct-pathway (go) activity and increases indirect-pathway (stop) activity, strengthening the thalamic brake and reducing movement — the hypokinetic Parkinsonian picture. Dopamine normally promotes movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus classically causes:

options.text: Hemiballismus (wild flinging movements of the contralateral limbs)

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Damage to the subthalamic nucleus removes its excitatory drive to the GPi (part of the indirect/stop pathway), releasing movement and producing hemiballismus — violent flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: Which structure in the basal ganglia is primarily responsible for tonically inhibiting the motor thalamus?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: The globus pallidus internus (GPi) is the output nucleus that tonically inhibits the motor thalamus, acting as a brake on movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: In Parkinson's disease, which pathway is primarily underactive due to dopamine loss?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Dopamine loss in Parkinson's disease leads to underactivity of the direct pathway, resulting in reduced movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: A patient presents with bradykinesia and rigidity. Which finding would you expect on examination?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Bradykinesia and rigidity are classic signs of Parkinson's disease, which may also include a resting tremor.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: What is the primary effect of dopamine on the direct pathway of the basal ganglia?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway, promoting movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: Which statement regarding the basal ganglia is true?

options.text: They modulate a tonic inhibitory brake on the thalamus.
They are solely responsible for initiating movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: The basal ganglia modulate movement by selecting and scaling it through a tonic inhibitory brake on the thalamus, rather than directly commanding muscle contraction.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: A patient with hemiballismus would most likely have a lesion in which structure?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Hemiballismus is caused by a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, leading to wild flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: How does the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia affect motor control?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: The indirect pathway inhibits movement by increasing the inhibition of the thalamus, thus tightening the brake on movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: Which condition is characterized by a loss of striatal neurons leading to chorea?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Huntington's disease is characterized by the degeneration of striatal neurons, resulting in chorea.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: In the context of basal ganglia function, how does dopamine relate to the corticospinal tract?

options.text: Dopamine directly stimulates the corticospinal tract.
Dopamine modulates basal ganglia output, which influences the corticospinal tract.
Dopamine has no effect on the corticospinal tract.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Dopamine modulates the output of the basal ganglia, which in turn influences the activity of the corticospinal tract, affecting voluntary movement.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: How does the modulation of movement by the basal ganglia relate to the function of the cerebellum?

options.text: The basal ganglia select and scale movement, while the cerebellum coordinates it.
The cerebellum has no role in movement control.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: The basal ganglia are involved in selecting and scaling movements, while the cerebellum coordinates and fine-tunes those movements for precision.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: Regarding what the basal ganglia do in movement — which is correct?

options.text: The basal ganglia directly command muscles to contract

The basal ganglia SELECT and SCALE movement (facilitate wanted, suppress unwanted) by modulating a tonic inhibitory "brake" (GPi) on the thalamus — they do NOT directly drive muscles; the corticospinal tract does that

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Basal-ganglia disorders cause too much or too little movement (dyskinesias/bradykinesia), not paralysis, precisely because they modulate movement rather than execute it — distinguishing them from corticospinal (weakness) lesions.

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability”?

options.text: D1 excites direct, D2 inhibits indirect pathway

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability → Parkinson disease (SNc dopamine loss — hypokinetic).

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chorea (irregular, dance-like movements)”?

options.text: D1 excites direct, D2 inhibits indirect pathway

basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Chorea (irregular, dance-like movements) → Huntington disease (striatal degeneration — hyperkinetic).

basal-ganglia-circuitry.stem: Which should you review before “Basal Ganglia Circuitry”?
basal-ganglia-circuitry.explanation: Understanding basal ganglia requires knowledge of cerebral structures.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: A patient has an intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing) and dysdiadochokinesia of the right arm. The lesion is in the:
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion, so right-arm incoordination (intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia) localises to the right cerebellar hemisphere (cerebrocerebellum).

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: The primary role of the cerebellum in movement is to:

options.text: Coordinate and time movement, correcting errors (making it smooth and accurate)

cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: The cerebellum compares intended with actual movement and corrects errors, coordinating timing, balance and skilled movement; it does not initiate movement (cortex/basal ganglia) or directly drive muscles (corticospinal tract → LMN).

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: Which of the following is a classic sign of a cerebrocerebellar lesion?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Intention tremor is specifically associated with lesions in the cerebrocerebellum, affecting skilled limb movements.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: What is the primary function of the vestibulocerebellum?

options.text: Regulation of balance and eye movements

cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: The vestibulocerebellum is primarily responsible for balance and eye movement regulation.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: A patient presents with truncal ataxia and nystagmus. Which part of the cerebellum is likely affected?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Truncal ataxia and nystagmus indicate a lesion in the vestibulocerebellum.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: Which mechanism explains why cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral signs?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Cerebellar output crosses to the contralateral cortex and then the corticospinal tract crosses again, resulting in ipsilateral signs.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: A patient exhibits dysdiadochokinesia and scanning speech. Which type of cerebellar lesion is most likely?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Dysdiadochokinesia and scanning speech are indicative of cerebrocerebellar lesions.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: How does the cerebellum contribute to motor learning?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates and times movements, which is essential for motor learning.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: A patient with a history of alcohol use presents with gait ataxia. Which cerebellar region is likely affected?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Alcohol primarily affects the spinocerebellum, leading to gait ataxia.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: How do cerebellar lesions differ from cortical lesions in terms of symptom laterality?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral symptoms due to the double crossing of outputs.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the cerebellum and the basal ganglia?

options.text: They coordinate different aspects of movement

cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: The cerebellum and basal ganglia coordinate different aspects of movement, with the cerebellum focusing on timing and coordination.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: Regarding laterality of cerebellar signs — which is correct?

options.text: A cerebellar lesion causes signs on the opposite side of the body, like a cortical lesion

Cerebellar signs are IPSILATERAL (same side as the lesion) because the cerebellar output crosses to the contralateral cortex and the corticospinal tract crosses again — the double crossing nets out to the same side

cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: The "double cross" is what makes cerebellar localisation different from most cortical/corticospinal lesions; expecting contralateral signs mislocalises the lesion to the wrong hemisphere.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intention tremor (worsening toward a target) + dysmetria”?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Intention tremor (worsening toward a target) + dysmetria → Cerebrocerebellar (lateral hemisphere) lesion.

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Broad-based gait ataxia”?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Broad-based gait ataxia → Spinocerebellar (vermis) lesion (e.g. alcohol).

cerebellum-anatomy-function.stem: Which should you review before “The Cerebellum”?
cerebellum-anatomy-function.explanation: Corticospinal control is crucial for understanding movement initiation versus coordination.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: A unilateral lesion of the central auditory pathway (e.g. auditory cortex) does NOT cause deafness in one ear because:

options.text: The central auditory pathway is bilateral, so each ear projects to both hemispheres
Hearing does not require the cortex

auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: Above the cochlear nuclei the auditory pathway is bilateral (crossing at the superior olive and beyond), so each ear is represented in both hemispheres; a unilateral central lesion therefore spares one-ear hearing, and true unilateral deafness localises to the ear or CN VIII.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: High-frequency sounds are detected at which part of the cochlea?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The cochlea is tonotopically organised: the stiff basilar membrane at the base responds to high frequencies, and the apex to low frequencies, so pitch is coded by place — an organisation preserved throughout the auditory pathway.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: What structure in the ear amplifies sound before it reaches the cochlea?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify sound and match impedance before transmitting vibrations to the cochlea.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: Which part of the cochlea responds to high-frequency sounds?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The base of the cochlea is tonotopically organized to respond to high frequencies due to its stiff basilar membrane.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: A patient presents with unilateral hearing loss. Which of the following findings would suggest a peripheral cause?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: Unilateral deafness localizes to the ear or CN VIII, indicating a peripheral issue rather than a central lesion.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: What is the primary role of the superior olivary nuclei in the auditory pathway?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The superior olivary nuclei compute sound localization by comparing interaural time and intensity differences.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: Which of the following statements about unilateral central auditory lesions is true?

options.text: They cause deafness in the opposite ear.
They spare hearing in both ears.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: Unilateral central lesions do not cause deafness in one ear due to the bilateral nature of the central auditory pathway.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: How does the medial geniculate nucleus function in the auditory pathway?

options.text: It relays auditory information to the cortex.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The medial geniculate nucleus serves as the thalamic relay for auditory information before it reaches the primary auditory cortex.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: How does the auditory pathway connect to the brainstem anatomy?

options.text: Cochlear nuclei are located in the thalamus.
The inferior colliculus integrates auditory reflexes.
The medial geniculate nucleus is part of the cortex.
The superior olivary nuclei are not involved in sound localization.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The inferior colliculus, located in the midbrain, integrates auditory reflexes and is a key relay in the auditory pathway.

auditory-pathway-anatomy.stem: Which structure in the auditory pathway is responsible for processing sound frequency before reaching the cortex?
auditory-pathway-anatomy.explanation: The medial geniculate nucleus processes and relays frequency-specific auditory information to the primary auditory cortex.
