Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting and psoriatic arthritis support the diagnosis.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: The "6 P's" (purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar papules/plaques) with lacy white Wickham striae describe:
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Lichen planus presents as purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar (flat-topped) papules and plaques with lacy white Wickham striae, favouring the flexor wrists, ankles and oral mucosa; it is associated with hepatitis C. It is treated with topical corticosteroids.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in psoriasis?

options.text: Herald patch followed by oval plaques

papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Psoriasis is characterized by silvery-scaled plaques primarily located on extensor surfaces.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: What is the mechanism behind the Auspitz sign in psoriasis?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: The Auspitz sign occurs due to increased keratinocyte turnover leading to pinpoint bleeding when scales are removed.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: A patient presents with violaceous flat-topped papules with lacy white lines on the wrists. What is the most likely diagnosis?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: The described features are characteristic of lichen planus, which presents with the '6 P's' and Wickham striae.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: A 30-year-old male develops new psoriatic lesions at the site of a recent scratch. What phenomenon does this illustrate?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: The development of new lesions at sites of trauma is known as the Koebner phenomenon.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes psoriasis from eczema?

options.text: Psoriasis presents with sharply demarcated plaques
Eczema is associated with nail pitting

papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Psoriasis is characterized by sharply demarcated plaques, while eczema typically affects flexural surfaces and presents with weepy lesions.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: A patient has a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree pattern rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: The herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree pattern is classic for pityriasis rosea.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: How does psoriasis relate to cutaneous immunology and hypersensitivity?

options.text: It is primarily a fungal infection
It is caused by viral agents

papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition involving a Th17 response, linking it to cutaneous immunology.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: What is the first-line treatment for extensive psoriasis?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: For extensive psoriasis, phototherapy is often the first-line treatment after topical agents.

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: Regarding psoriasis vs eczema distribution — which is correct?

options.text: Scaly itchy plaques in the elbow and knee region are most likely eczema

Distribution helps distinguish them: PSORIASIS classically affects the EXTENSOR surfaces (elbows, KNEES), scalp and lumbosacral area with sharply demarcated SILVERY plaques (Auspitz/Koebner, nail pitting), whereas atopic ECZEMA favours the FLEXURES (antecubital/popliteal fossae) with ill-defined, weepy/lichenified dermatitis — extensor-silvery vs flexural-eczematous

papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: The extensor vs flexural pattern (plus scale character and nail/joint clues) separates psoriasis from eczema, which have different treatments and associations (psoriatic arthritis vs atopy).

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Silvery-scaled plaques on elbows/knees with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal”?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Silvery-scaled plaques on elbows/knees with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal → Psoriasis (Auspitz sign).

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Violaceous flat-topped papules with lacy white lines, on flexor wrists/oral mucosa”?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Violaceous flat-topped papules with lacy white lines, on flexor wrists/oral mucosa → Lichen planus (Wickham striae).

papulosquamous-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Papulosquamous Diseases”?
papulosquamous-diseases.explanation: Understanding immune mechanisms is crucial for grasping papulosquamous diseases.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Flaccid blisters with painful oral erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign, and intercellular "chicken-wire" IgG on immunofluorescence indicate:
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG against desmoglein 3 (±1), producing intra-epidermal acantholysis with flaccid blisters, oral erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and an intercellular ("chicken-wire") IgG pattern on direct immunofluorescence. It is potentially fatal and requires immunosuppression.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces, granular IgA) is the cutaneous manifestation of:
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with coeliac disease; granular IgA is deposited at the dermal papillae. A gluten-free diet treats both the gut and skin disease, and dapsone gives rapid relief of the intense itch. The name reflects the herpetiform grouping, not a viral cause.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: What is the primary target of antibodies in pemphigus vulgaris?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3, leading to loss of keratinocyte adhesion.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Which finding is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid?

options.text: Tense blisters on an urticarial base

vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense, intact blisters on an urticarial base and typically spares the oral mucosa.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: What histological finding is associated with pemphigus vulgaris on direct immunofluorescence?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris shows intercellular 'chicken-wire' IgG on direct immunofluorescence.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Which statement about the Nikolsky sign is true?

options.text: It is positive in bullous pemphigoid
It is negative in pemphigus vulgaris
It is a sign of less severe disease

vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: A positive Nikolsky sign indicates flaccid blister formation, characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris, which is more severe.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: What is the first-line treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: The primary treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis is a gluten-free diet, which addresses the underlying cause related to coeliac disease.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: How does the mechanism of action differ between pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris causes intra-epidermal splits due to loss of keratinocyte adhesion, while bullous pemphigoid affects the dermal-epidermal junction.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Which condition is associated with granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: How does the management of pemphigus vulgaris differ from that of bullous pemphigoid?

options.text: Bullous pemphigoid is treated with immunosuppressants
Pemphigus is treated with systemic steroids
Bullous pemphigoid requires a gluten-free diet

vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is treated with systemic steroids due to its severity, while bullous pemphigoid may be managed with topical or systemic steroids.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Which histological feature is critical for differentiating between pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: The location of the split (intra-epidermal in pemphigus vs. sub-epidermal in bullous pemphigoid) is critical for differentiation.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Regarding nikolsky sign and blister fragility — which is correct?

options.text: Tense, intact blisters are the more dangerous, aggressive autoimmune blistering disease

It is the opposite: PEMPHIGUS (intra-epidermal, anti-desmoglein) produces FLACCID, fragile blisters that rupture easily with a POSITIVE Nikolsky sign and is the more DANGEROUS disease, whereas bullous PEMPHIGOID (subepidermal) produces TENSE, intact blisters with a NEGATIVE Nikolsky and is generally less severe — fragility (flaccid/Nikolsky+) signals the higher-level, more serious split

vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: The more superficial (intra-epidermal) split of pemphigus makes blisters fragile and the disease life-threatening, so the flaccid/Nikolsky-positive picture — not the dramatic tense blisters of pemphigoid — is the red flag.

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flaccid blisters and painful oral erosions, skin shears with pressure”?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Flaccid blisters and painful oral erosions, skin shears with pressure → Pemphigus vulgaris (Nikolsky positive, intra-epidermal).

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tense intact blisters on an urticarial base in an elderly patient, mouth spared”?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Tense intact blisters on an urticarial base in an elderly patient, mouth spared → Bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal).

vesiculobullous-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Vesiculobullous Diseases”?
vesiculobullous-diseases.explanation: Understanding skin anatomy is crucial for grasping the mechanisms of vesiculobullous diseases.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Crops of tender, red, non-ulcerating nodules on the anterior shins that resolve like a bruise are characteristic of:
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Erythema nodosum is a reactive septal panniculitis presenting as tender red nodules on the shins that do not ulcerate and heal with bruise-like colour change. It signals a systemic trigger (streptococcus, sarcoidosis, TB, drugs, IBD, pregnancy), which should be sought.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Palpable purpura on the lower legs most specifically indicates:
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Palpable (raised) purpura reflects inflammation of vessel walls — leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis (Type III immune-complex) — and warrants evaluation for triggers and systemic/renal involvement. Flat, non-palpable purpura instead suggests a platelet or coagulation disorder.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: What is the most common cause of erythema nodosum?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Erythema nodosum is most commonly associated with Streptococcus infection, among other causes.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Which clinical finding is characteristic of cutaneous vasculitis?

options.text: Tender red nodules on the shins

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Non-blanching raised purpuric papules are indicative of cutaneous vasculitis, distinguishing it from other skin conditions.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: What mechanism underlies the formation of palpable purpura in cutaneous vasculitis?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Palpable purpura in cutaneous vasculitis is due to Type III hypersensitivity, involving immune complex deposition.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: A child presents with purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: The combination of symptoms in this child is characteristic of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura).

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes between palpable and non-palpable purpura?

options.text: All purpura indicates a low platelet count
Palpable purpura suggests a coagulation disorder

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Palpable purpura indicates vasculitis, while non-palpable purpura suggests a platelet or coagulation disorder.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: In a patient with erythema nodosum, which investigation is most appropriate to identify the underlying cause?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: A chest X-ray is appropriate to check for sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, common triggers of erythema nodosum.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: How does the mechanism of cutaneous vasculitis relate to hypersensitivity reactions?

options.text: It is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction
It involves immune complex deposition (Type III)
It is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV)
It is an autoimmune response (Type II)

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Cutaneous vasculitis is characterized by immune complex deposition, which is a hallmark of Type III hypersensitivity reactions.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: What anatomical structure is primarily affected in panniculitis?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Panniculitis specifically involves inflammation of the subcutaneous fat layer.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Regarding palpable vs non-palpable purpura — which is correct?

options.text: All purpura reflects a low platelet count or clotting problem

PALPABLE purpura (raised, you can feel it) implies VASCULITIS — inflammation of the vessel wall (leukocytoclastic, Type III) — and mandates a search for systemic/renal involvement, whereas FLAT (macular, non-palpable) purpura suggests a PLATELET or COAGULATION disorder; whether the purpura is palpable is the key bedside branch point

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: The "palpable" quality distinguishes an inflammatory vessel disease (needing vasculitis work-up including kidneys) from a haemostatic problem (needing platelet/coagulation work-up) — different diagnoses and investigations entirely.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Crops of tender red nodules on the shins that heal like bruises”?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Crops of tender red nodules on the shins that heal like bruises → Erythema nodosum (septal panniculitis).

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-blanching, raised purpuric papules on the lower legs”?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Non-blanching, raised purpuric papules on the lower legs → Leukocytoclastic (small-vessel) vasculitis — palpable purpura.

panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.stem: Which should you review before “Panniculitis & Cutaneous Vasculitis”?
panniculitis-vasculitis-skin.explanation: Understanding hypersensitivity mechanisms is crucial for grasping the pathophysiology of panniculitis and vasculitis.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Violaceous discolouration of the eyelids (heliotrope) with violaceous papules over the knuckles (Gottron papules) and proximal muscle weakness indicates:

options.text: Dermatomyositis (with a need to screen for malignancy)

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules with proximal muscle weakness and raised CK are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. In adults it is associated with underlying malignancy, so age-appropriate cancer screening is required at diagnosis.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: A patient with tight sclerotic skin limited to the hands/face, Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis and telangiectasia most likely has which antibody?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia), associated with anti-centromere antibodies. Diffuse systemic sclerosis (widespread skin + early internal organ disease) is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase).

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What skin finding is characteristic of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: The malar rash is a classic presentation of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, distinguishing it from other forms.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Which autoantibody is commonly associated with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Anti-Scl-70 is a marker for diffuse scleroderma, while anti-centromere is associated with limited scleroderma.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: In dermatomyositis, which skin manifestation is considered pathognomonic?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Gottron papules are specific to dermatomyositis and indicate the presence of the disease.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind the photosensitivity seen in lupus erythematosus?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Photosensitivity in lupus is due to UV-induced apoptosis of keratinocytes, triggering an immune response.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What is the first clinical sign often seen in systemic sclerosis?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Raynaud phenomenon is frequently the first sign of systemic sclerosis, indicating vascular involvement.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Why is cancer screening crucial in adult dermatomyositis?

options.text: It is primarily a skin disease
It has a low association with malignancy
It can be a paraneoplastic syndrome

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Adult dermatomyositis can indicate an underlying malignancy, necessitating thorough cancer screening.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Which skin finding is indicative of morphea?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Morphea presents as localized sclerotic plaques without systemic involvement, differentiating it from other conditions.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: How does dermatomyositis relate to connective tissue diseases?

options.text: It is a purely dermatological condition
It is unrelated to autoimmune processes

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Dermatomyositis is associated with underlying malignancies, highlighting its systemic implications within connective tissue diseases.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What is a common treatment approach for photosensitive lupus?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Photoprotection is essential in managing photosensitive lupus to prevent exacerbation of skin lesions.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Regarding adult dermatomyositis and malignancy — which is correct?

options.text: Dermatomyositis is only a skin and muscle disease needing symptomatic treatment

Adult-onset DERMATOMYOSITIS carries a significantly INCREASED risk of an underlying MALIGNANCY, so a new diagnosis mandates AGE-APPROPRIATE CANCER SCREENING (it can be a paraneoplastic marker) — treating only the skin/muscle without looking for cancer misses a potentially lethal association

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Because dermatomyositis can be paraneoplastic, the skin signs (heliotrope, Gottron) are a prompt to search for occult malignancy — a high-yield association that changes work-up beyond the skin and muscle.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds”?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds → Acute cutaneous lupus (systemic LE).

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging”?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging → Discoid lupus erythematosus.

cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Connective Tissue Diseases”?
cutaneous-connective-tissue-diseases.explanation: Knowledge of connective tissue cells is foundational for understanding connective tissue diseases.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests a severe (life-threatening) cutaneous drug reaction rather than a benign eruption?

options.text: A symmetric pink maculopapular rash in a well patient
Mucosal erosions with skin pain and epidermal detachment
A rash appearing exactly 7 days after the drug

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Mucosal involvement, skin pain and epidermal detachment (positive Nikolsky) indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN — a severe cutaneous adverse reaction requiring immediate drug cessation and urgent supportive care. A well patient with an isolated maculopapular rash usually has a benign morbilliform eruption.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: A widespread rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and hepatitis appearing 4 weeks after starting an anticonvulsant is:

options.text: DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: DRESS is a delayed (2–8 week) severe reaction with rash, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement (commonly hepatitis), classically to anticonvulsants, allopurinol or sulfonamides. It requires prompt drug withdrawal and monitoring for organ damage.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What is the most common type of cutaneous drug reaction?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: The morbilliform eruption is the most common type of cutaneous drug reaction, typically appearing 4-14 days after drug initiation.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: A positive Nikolsky sign indicates epidermal detachment, which is a hallmark of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What mechanism underlies the morbilliform drug eruption?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Morbilliform eruptions are mediated by Type IV hypersensitivity reactions.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: A patient presents with a dusky patch that recurs at the same site after taking a medication. What is the likely diagnosis?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: A fixed drug eruption is characterized by a round dusky patch that recurs at the same site with each exposure to the drug.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which of the following findings would indicate a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR)?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Fever and lymphadenopathy are red flags indicating a potential SCAR, necessitating immediate drug cessation.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: A patient develops a widespread rash, fever, and eosinophilia 4 weeks after starting a new anticonvulsant. What condition is most likely?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: DRESS syndrome typically presents 2-8 weeks after drug exposure with a combination of rash, fever, eosinophilia, and systemic involvement.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: How does the mechanism of DRESS syndrome differ from that of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

options.text: DRESS is Type I, SJS is Type IV
DRESS has delayed onset, SJS is immediate
DRESS involves mucosal surfaces, SJS does not
DRESS is always fatal, SJS is not

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: DRESS syndrome has a delayed onset (2-8 weeks) compared to the more immediate onset of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which of the following drug reactions is most likely to require HLA screening to prevent severe outcomes?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is associated with specific HLA alleles, and screening can help prevent severe reactions.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Regarding benign rash vs early scar — which is correct?

options.text: Any drug rash can be watched while continuing the drug, since most are harmless

While most drug rashes are benign morbilliform eruptions, you MUST screen for RED FLAGS of a SCAR — mucosal erosions, skin PAIN/blistering/detachment (Nikolsky+), facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or deranged LFTs — because SJS/TEN and DRESS are life-threatening and require IMMEDIATE drug cessation; missing these early is fatal

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Early SJS/TEN or DRESS can start looking like an ordinary rash, so the presence of any red flag (not the rash alone) determines urgency — continuing the drug in an evolving SCAR can be lethal.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric pink maculopapular rash ~1 week after a new drug, patient well”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, urgent care

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Symmetric pink maculopapular rash ~1 week after a new drug, patient well → Morbilliform (benign) drug eruption.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “A dusky round patch recurring at the same site with each drug exposure”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, urgent care

cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: A dusky round patch recurring at the same site with each drug exposure → Fixed drug eruption.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cutaneous Drug Reactions”?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Understanding vesiculobullous diseases aids in differentiating types of skin reactions.

cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Drug Reactions”?
cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Understanding drug allergies is essential for recognizing cutaneous drug reactions.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: A vascular birthmark that appears in the weeks after birth, enlarges over months, then spontaneously regresses over several years is a(n):
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Infantile haemangiomas are vascular tumours that typically appear after birth, proliferate, then involute over years; problematic lesions (threatening vision, airway or ulcerating) are treated with propranolol. Port-wine stains are capillary malformations that persist and may signal Sturge-Weber when in the V1 distribution.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Atopic dermatitis in older children characteristically involves the:
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: In older children and adults, atopic dermatitis favours the flexures (antecubital and popliteal fossae) with itchy, ill-defined, often lichenified dermatitis; in infants it involves the face and extensor surfaces. It reflects a skin-barrier (filaggrin) defect and the atopic march.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: What is the most common childhood inflammatory skin disease characterized by itchy dermatitis in flexural areas?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Atopic dermatitis is the most prevalent inflammatory skin condition in children, often presenting in flexural areas.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Which viral exanthem presents with high fever followed by a rash as the fever resolves?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Roseola, caused by HHV-6, is characterized by high fever followed by a rash once the fever subsides.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: A child presents with bright red, 'slapped cheek' erythema. Which condition is most likely?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Bright red, 'slapped cheek' erythema is characteristic of erythema infectiosum caused by parvovirus B19.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: What is the key distinguishing feature of an infantile hemangioma compared to a port-wine stain?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Infantile hemangiomas typically appear after birth and involute over time, unlike port-wine stains which are present at birth and persist.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: A 2-year-old child has a persistent flat port-wine stain on the face. What should be considered?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: A port-wine stain in the V1 trigeminal area warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Which condition requires oral antifungal treatment in children?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Tinea capitis, or scalp ringworm, necessitates oral antifungal therapy for effective treatment.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: How does atopic dermatitis relate to the atopic march?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Atopic dermatitis is often the first manifestation in the atopic march, which may progress to asthma and allergic rhinitis.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: What is the mechanism of action of propranolol in treating problematic infantile hemangiomas?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Propranolol reduces vascular proliferation, which helps in treating problematic infantile hemangiomas.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Which condition is characterized by a honey crusted appearance on the skin?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Impetigo is characterized by honey-crusted lesions, typically due to bacterial infection.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Regarding haemangioma vs port-wine stain — which is correct?

options.text: All vascular birthmarks are permanent and should be treated the same way

They behave oppositely: an INFANTILE HAEMANGIOMA (a vascular TUMOUR) usually appears AFTER birth, proliferates, then spontaneously INVOLUTES over years (treat only if vision/airway/ulceration threatened — propranolol), whereas a PORT-WINE STAIN (a capillary MALFORMATION) is present at birth, PERSISTS and grows with the child, and if in the V1 trigeminal distribution warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome

pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Tumour (haemangioma, involutes) vs malformation (port-wine, persists) determines prognosis and management — reassurance/observation vs laser and syndrome work-up — so distinguishing them avoids both over- and under-treatment.

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy dermatitis of the antecubital/popliteal flexures in a child with asthma”?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Itchy dermatitis of the antecubital/popliteal flexures in a child with asthma → Atopic dermatitis (atopic march).

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “High fever for days, then a rash as the fever resolves”?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: High fever for days, then a rash as the fever resolves → Roseola (HHV-6).

pediatric-skin-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Common Pediatric Skin Diseases”?
pediatric-skin-diseases.explanation: Understanding infections is crucial for diagnosing skin diseases.

hair-diseases.stem: A smooth, round patch of complete hair loss with short "exclamation-mark" hairs at the margin, in an otherwise healthy scalp, is characteristic of:
hair-diseases.explanation: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune, non-scarring alopecia causing smooth round patches of hair loss with pathognomonic exclamation-mark hairs; the follicles are preserved, so regrowth is possible. It may be associated with other autoimmune conditions.

hair-diseases.stem: The key feature distinguishing a scarring (cicatricial) alopecia from a non-scarring one on examination is:

options.text: Loss of follicular openings (indicating permanent follicle destruction)

hair-diseases.explanation: Scarring alopecias destroy the hair follicle, so the scalp shows loss of follicular openings and permanent hair loss; non-scarring alopecias preserve the follicular openings and can regrow. Recognising loss of openings prompts biopsy and prompt treatment to save remaining follicles.

hair-diseases.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind androgenetic alopecia?
hair-diseases.explanation: Androgenetic alopecia is primarily caused by DHT-mediated follicular miniaturization, leading to hair thinning.

hair-diseases.stem: Which finding is characteristic of alopecia areata?

options.text: Smooth round bald patches with exclamation-mark hairs
Scaly scalp patches with broken hairs

hair-diseases.explanation: Alopecia areata is characterized by smooth round bald patches and the presence of exclamation-mark hairs.

hair-diseases.stem: Which type of alopecia is associated with permanent hair loss due to follicular destruction?
hair-diseases.explanation: Cicatricial alopecia leads to permanent hair loss due to the destruction of hair follicles.

hair-diseases.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair shedding 2 months after childbirth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
hair-diseases.explanation: Telogen effluvium is characterized by diffuse hair shedding following a stressor such as childbirth.

hair-diseases.stem: What is the primary treatment for tinea capitis?
hair-diseases.explanation: Tinea capitis requires oral antifungal treatment due to its fungal nature and the need for systemic therapy.

hair-diseases.stem: Which condition is characterized by loss of follicular openings and requires early biopsy for treatment?
hair-diseases.explanation: Cicatricial alopecia is characterized by loss of follicular openings and necessitates early biopsy to preserve remaining follicles.

hair-diseases.stem: How does cicatricial alopecia differ from non-scarring alopecia in terms of follicle preservation?

options.text: Follicles are preserved in cicatricial alopecia
Cicatricial alopecia leads to irreversible follicle loss

hair-diseases.explanation: Cicatricial alopecia results in irreversible follicle loss, while non-scarring alopecia preserves follicles and can potentially regrow hair.

hair-diseases.stem: A patient with discoid lupus erythematosus presents with hair loss. Which linked condition should be considered in diagnosis?
hair-diseases.explanation: Discoid lupus erythematosus is a type of cicatricial alopecia, which can cause permanent hair loss due to follicular destruction.

hair-diseases.stem: Which module's content is essential for understanding the histological basis of hair diseases?
hair-diseases.explanation: The Skin Anatomy & Histology module provides essential knowledge about the structure of hair follicles and their diseases.

hair-diseases.stem: Regarding scarring vs non-scarring alopecia — which is correct?

options.text: All hair loss can eventually regrow with the right treatment

SCARRING (cicatricial) alopecias DESTROY the follicle — shown by LOSS of follicular openings — so hair CANNOT regrow there; the goal is early biopsy and anti-inflammatory treatment to save the REMAINING follicles. Only NON-scarring alopecias (androgenetic, alopecia areata, telogen effluvium) preserve the follicle and can regrow

hair-diseases.explanation: Because scarring alopecia causes irreversible follicle loss, recognising it early (loss of follicular openings) is time-critical to preserve unaffected hair — treating it like reversible hair loss wastes the window.

hair-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bitemporal recession and vertex thinning in a man”?
hair-diseases.explanation: Bitemporal recession and vertex thinning in a man → Androgenetic alopecia (DHT miniaturisation).

hair-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Smooth round bald patch with exclamation-mark hairs”?
hair-diseases.explanation: Smooth round bald patch with exclamation-mark hairs → Alopecia areata (autoimmune).

hair-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Diseases of Hair”?
hair-diseases.explanation: Discoid lupus is a scarring alopecia related to connective tissue diseases.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Sharply demarcated, symmetric, completely depigmented (milky-white) macules due to autoimmune destruction of melanocytes describe:
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Vitiligo is acquired autoimmune destruction of melanocytes producing well-demarcated depigmented patches (accentuated under Wood's lamp), often associated with other autoimmune disease such as thyroid disease. Albinism, by contrast, is a congenital defect of melanin synthesis with melanocytes present.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Symmetric brown patches on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, worsened by sun exposure, are characteristic of:
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Melasma is a hyperpigmentation driven by ultraviolet light and hormones (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), producing symmetric brown facial patches, more common in women and darker skin types. Management centres on strict photoprotection plus topical lightening agents (e.g. hydroquinone, retinoids).

pigmentary-disorders.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind vitiligo?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Vitiligo is characterized by the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, leading to depigmented patches on the skin.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Which clinical finding is most characteristic of albinism?

options.text: Symmetric brown patches on the face
Brown discoloration at sites of resolved acne

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Albinism presents with generalized hypopigmentation and is associated with ocular abnormalities and increased risk of skin cancer.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: What is the main treatment strategy for melasma?

options.text: Sun protection and topical lightening agents

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Melasma management focuses on sun protection and the use of topical lightening agents to reduce pigmentation.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Which statement correctly differentiates vitiligo from albinism?

options.text: Both conditions are due to a lack of melanin
Vitiligo involves a loss of melanocytes, while albinism involves a synthesis defect
Albinism is acquired, while vitiligo is congenital
Vitiligo presents with generalized hypopigmentation, while albinism is patchy

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Vitiligo is characterized by the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, while albinism is due to a genetic defect in melanin synthesis.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: What is the most common cause of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation typically occurs following inflammation, such as from acne or eczema, especially in individuals with darker skin.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in pityriasis versicolor?

options.text: Milky-white patches accentuated by Wood's lamp
Finely scaly hypo/hyperpigmented macules, KOH positive
Symmetric brown patches on the cheeks

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Pityriasis versicolor presents with finely scaly macules that can be hypo or hyperpigmented and are KOH positive.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: How does melasma relate to skin aging?

options.text: It is a result of genetic aging
It is primarily caused by UV exposure and hormonal changes
It does not relate to skin aging
It is a sign of skin cancer risk

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Melasma is influenced by UV exposure and hormonal changes, which are also factors in skin aging.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Which condition's management overlaps with the principles of skin neoplasms?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Management of albinism includes sun protection to reduce skin cancer risk, similar to strategies used in skin neoplasms.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Regarding vitiligo vs albinism — which is correct?

options.text: Vitiligo and albinism are both just an absence of skin colour, so they are essentially the same

They differ mechanistically: VITILIGO is ACQUIRED autoimmune DESTRUCTION of melanocytes (melanocytes are ABSENT in patches, often with autoimmune associations), whereas ALBINISM is an INHERITED defect in melanin SYNTHESIS (melanocytes are PRESENT but cannot make pigment, e.g. tyrosinase deficiency, with ocular involvement) — one loses the cells, the other keeps them but cannot produce pigment

pigmentary-disorders.explanation: The mechanism changes everything: vitiligo is patchy, acquired and autoimmune (screen for thyroid disease, may repigment with immunotherapy), while albinism is generalised, congenital and needs lifelong sun/eye protection and cancer surveillance.

pigmentary-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sharply demarcated, symmetric, milky-white depigmented patches”?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Sharply demarcated, symmetric, milky-white depigmented patches → Vitiligo (autoimmune melanocyte loss).

pigmentary-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Generalised hypopigmentation with ocular signs and high sunburn/cancer risk”?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Generalised hypopigmentation with ocular signs and high sunburn/cancer risk → Albinism (melanin synthesis defect).

pigmentary-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Pigmentary Disorders”?
pigmentary-disorders.explanation: Understanding melanocyte biology is essential for pigmentary disorders.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: The foundation (first-line, everyday) treatment of atopic dermatitis is:

options.text: Liberal emollients/moisturisers for barrier repair (plus trigger avoidance)

eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Because atopic dermatitis is driven by a skin-barrier defect, liberal daily emollients (with trigger/irritant avoidance) are the foundation of care. Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors are added for flares, with phototherapy and systemic/biologic agents reserved for severe disease.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: Greasy yellow scaling on the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds, associated with Malassezia yeast, describes:
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Seborrhoeic dermatitis produces greasy yellow scale in sebaceous-rich areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds), associated with Malassezia; it appears as cradle cap in infants and is prominent in Parkinson's disease and HIV. Treatment includes antifungal shampoos and mild topical steroids.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: What is the primary defect in atopic dermatitis?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Atopic dermatitis is characterized by a barrier defect primarily due to filaggrin mutations, leading to increased transepidermal water loss and susceptibility to allergens.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: Which clinical finding is most indicative of eczema herpeticum?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Eczema herpeticum presents with rapidly worsening eczema characterized by painful, punched-out erosions and systemic symptoms such as fever.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: What is the mechanism of action of topical calcineurin inhibitors in eczema treatment?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Topical calcineurin inhibitors work by blocking T cell activation, thereby reducing inflammation in conditions like eczema.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: A cleaner develops hand dermatitis after exposure to detergents without prior sensitization. What type of dermatitis is this?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: This scenario describes irritant contact dermatitis, which occurs due to direct damage from irritants rather than an immune response.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: In a patient with atopic dermatitis, which area is most likely to show lichenification due to chronic scratching?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Chronic scratching in atopic dermatitis typically leads to lichenification in flexural areas such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: How does eczema relate to the physiology of skin barrier function?

options.text: Eczema is caused by excessive sebaceous gland activity
Eczema is linked to a defect in skin barrier integrity
Eczema is due to increased keratinocyte turnover

eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Eczema is associated with a defect in skin barrier integrity, leading to increased transepidermal water loss and susceptibility to irritants and allergens.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in allergic contact dermatitis?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is mediated by a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction, involving T cell activation upon re-exposure to the allergen.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: Regarding eczema herpeticum recognition — which is correct?

options.text: Worsening, painful eczema is just a bad flare that needs stronger topical steroids

Rapidly worsening eczema with PAINFUL, monomorphic PUNCHED-OUT erosions/vesicles, fever and malaise suggests ECZEMA HERPETICUM (disseminated herpes simplex) — a dermatological EMERGENCY needing systemic ACICLOVIR, not more topical steroid (steroids alone can worsen it)

eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Missing eczema herpeticum and escalating steroids can lead to widespread HSV dissemination and serious complications; the painful punched-out lesions and systemic upset are the clues to switch to antivirals urgently.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy, lichenified flexural dermatitis in a child with asthma/hay fever”?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Itchy, lichenified flexural dermatitis in a child with asthma/hay fever → Atopic dermatitis (atopic march, barrier defect).

eczema-dermatitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden painful punched-out erosions/vesicles over eczema with fever”?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Sudden painful punched-out erosions/vesicles over eczema with fever → Eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) — emergency.

eczema-dermatitis.stem: Which should you review before “Eczema & Dermatitis”?
eczema-dermatitis.explanation: Understanding contact dermatitis requires knowledge of hypersensitivity mechanisms.

acne-vulgaris.stem: Which drug is reserved for severe, scarring nodulocystic acne and requires a pregnancy-prevention programme due to teratogenicity?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Oral isotretinoin is highly effective for severe nodulocystic/scarring acne but is a potent teratogen, so it is used only within a strict pregnancy-prevention programme with monitoring of lipids and liver function. Milder acne is managed with topical retinoids/benzoyl peroxide and oral antibiotics or hormonal therapy.

acne-vulgaris.stem: To limit antibiotic resistance, topical antibiotics for acne should be used:
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Topical (and oral) antibiotics in acne should be combined with benzoyl peroxide, which reduces the development of C. acnes resistance; antibiotic monotherapy is avoided. First-line therapy centres on topical retinoids plus benzoyl peroxide, escalating by severity.

acne-vulgaris.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which isotretinoin treats severe acne?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Isotretinoin primarily normalizes keratinization, which helps to prevent the formation of comedones.

acne-vulgaris.stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of isotretinoin?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Dry skin and lips are well-known side effects of isotretinoin due to its effects on sebaceous glands.

acne-vulgaris.stem: A 15-year-old male presents with multiple open and closed comedones on his face. What is the most likely underlying cause?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Increased androgen levels lead to increased sebum production, which contributes to the formation of comedones.

acne-vulgaris.stem: What is the most significant risk associated with the use of isotretinoin in women of childbearing age?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen and can cause severe fetal malformations, necessitating strict pregnancy prevention measures.

acne-vulgaris.stem: Which type of acne lesion is characterized by deep painful nodules that may scar?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Nodulocystic lesions are severe forms of acne that can lead to scarring.

acne-vulgaris.stem: A patient with acne presents with brown marks on their skin after lesions have resolved. What is this condition called?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common after acne resolution, especially in individuals with darker skin.

acne-vulgaris.stem: How does the treatment ladder for acne vulgaris relate to the management of skin conditions in dermatologic therapy?

options.text: Both require patient education on hygiene
Both emphasize the importance of systemic antibiotics

acne-vulgaris.explanation: The treatment ladder for acne vulgaris begins with topical treatments, which is a common approach in dermatologic therapy.

acne-vulgaris.stem: What is the relationship between acne vulgaris and skin anatomy as taught in skin anatomy & histology?

options.text: Acne is unrelated to skin structure
Acne primarily affects the epidermis only

acne-vulgaris.explanation: Acne vulgaris is a disease of the pilosebaceous unit, which is a key concept in skin anatomy and histology.

acne-vulgaris.stem: Regarding isotretinoin and pregnancy — which is correct?

options.text: Isotretinoin is just a strong acne treatment that can be started like any other

Oral ISOTRETINOIN is a potent TERATOGEN causing severe fetal malformations, so it can only be prescribed within a strict PREGNANCY-PREVENTION programme (reliable contraception before, during and for a period after treatment, with pregnancy testing) — alongside monitoring of LFTs/lipids and awareness of mood effects; it is never started casually in a person who could become pregnant

acne-vulgaris.explanation: The teratogenicity is the single most important safety issue with isotretinoin, so mandatory contraception/pregnancy prevention (not just efficacy) governs its use — a high-yield prescribing safeguard.

acne-vulgaris.stem: What best explains the finding: “Open (blackhead) and closed (whitehead) comedones on the face”?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Open (blackhead) and closed (whitehead) comedones on the face → Non-inflammatory acne (follicular plugging).

acne-vulgaris.stem: What best explains the finding: “Deep painful nodules and cysts that scar”?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Deep painful nodules and cysts that scar → Severe nodulocystic acne (isotretinoin candidate).

acne-vulgaris.stem: Which should you review before “Acne Vulgaris”?
acne-vulgaris.explanation: Understanding the pilosebaceous unit is essential for acne pathology.

skin-neoplasms.stem: A slow-growing pearly papule with a rolled border, surface telangiectasia and central ulceration on the face is most likely:
skin-neoplasms.explanation: A pearly, translucent papule with rolled edges, telangiectasia and central ulceration ("rodent ulcer") on sun-exposed skin is a basal cell carcinoma — the commonest skin cancer, locally invasive but almost never metastasising, treated by excision.

skin-neoplasms.stem: The single most important prognostic factor for a primary cutaneous melanoma is:
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Breslow thickness — the depth of tumour invasion measured histologically — is the strongest prognostic factor in primary melanoma and guides staging and management. The ABCDE features (especially Evolution/change) help identify suspicious lesions for early excision, which is curative when thin.

skin-neoplasms.stem: What is the most common type of skin cancer?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer, characterized by slow growth and a low risk of metastasis.

skin-neoplasms.stem: Which feature is most indicative of melanoma according to the ABCDE rule?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Diameter >6 mm is one of the key features of melanoma in the ABCDE rule for assessing pigmented lesions.

skin-neoplasms.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which UV radiation contributes to skin cancer?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: UV radiation causes direct DNA damage, leading to mutations that can result in skin cancer.

skin-neoplasms.stem: A patient presents with a firm, scaly nodule on their lip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: A firm, scaly nodule on the lip is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, which can metastasize.

skin-neoplasms.stem: Which statement about basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is true?

options.text: It is the most common skin cancer
It presents as a flat scaly lesion

skin-neoplasms.explanation: BCC is indeed the most common skin cancer and is known for its low metastatic potential.

skin-neoplasms.stem: How does Breslow thickness relate to melanoma prognosis?

options.text: It indicates the presence of metastasis
It correlates with the depth of invasion
It determines the need for chemotherapy

skin-neoplasms.explanation: Breslow thickness measures the depth of invasion and is the single strongest prognostic factor in melanoma.

skin-neoplasms.stem: A patient with a history of actinic keratosis presents with a new ulcerated lesion on sun-exposed skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: The ulcerated lesion on sun-exposed skin in a patient with actinic keratosis suggests squamous cell carcinoma, which can arise from such lesions.

skin-neoplasms.stem: How does the risk of metastasis differ between basal cell carcinoma and melanoma?

options.text: BCC rarely metastasizes, melanoma frequently does
BCC frequently metastasizes, melanoma rarely does

skin-neoplasms.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive but almost never metastasizes, while melanoma has a high risk of metastasis.

skin-neoplasms.stem: Which skin cancer is most likely to be associated with immunosuppression?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is more likely to metastasize and is associated with immunosuppression, particularly in high-risk areas.

skin-neoplasms.stem: What is the primary preventive measure against skin cancer related to UV exposure?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Photoprotection is the primary preventive measure against skin cancer caused by UV exposure.

skin-neoplasms.stem: Regarding metastatic potential of bcc vs scc vs melanoma — which is correct?

options.text: All skin cancers carry a similar risk of spreading and death

Their behaviour differs greatly: BASAL cell carcinoma is locally invasive but almost NEVER metastasises (excellent prognosis); SQUAMOUS cell carcinoma CAN metastasise (especially on lip/ear, in scars or immunosuppression); and MELANOMA is the one that readily metastasises and kills, with prognosis set by Breslow depth — so a changing pigmented lesion is the true red flag

skin-neoplasms.explanation: Triaging by metastatic potential (BCC low, SCC moderate, melanoma high) focuses urgency on melanoma and higher-risk SCC, rather than treating all skin lesions as equally dangerous or equally benign.

skin-neoplasms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pearly papule with rolled edge, telangiectasia and central ulcer on the face”?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Pearly papule with rolled edge, telangiectasia and central ulcer on the face → Basal cell carcinoma (rarely metastasises).

skin-neoplasms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Firm scaly/ulcerated nodule on the lip or sun-damaged skin”?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Firm scaly/ulcerated nodule on the lip or sun-damaged skin → Squamous cell carcinoma (can metastasise).

skin-neoplasms.stem: Which should you review before “Skin Neoplasms”?
skin-neoplasms.explanation: Understanding treatment principles is crucial for managing skin neoplasms.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which topical corticosteroid potency is most appropriate for treating an inflammatory rash on the face?

options.text: It does not matter which potency

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Facial skin is thin and highly absorptive, so only mild topical corticosteroids should be used there to avoid atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis and systemic absorption. Potent steroids are reserved for thick skin (e.g. palms/soles) or resistant plaques, for the shortest effective duration.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: For a dry, thickened (lichenified) chronic plaque, the most suitable and potent topical vehicle is generally a(n):
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Following the "if it's dry, wet it" principle, greasy occlusive ointments are the most hydrating and potent vehicle for dry, lichenified lesions, increasing drug penetration. Lotions, gels and solutions suit weepy or hairy areas ("if it's wet, dry it").

dermatologic-therapy.stem: What is the primary reason for using a greasy ointment for a dry, lichenified plaque?

options.text: It enhances absorption of the active ingredient
It is less likely to cause irritation
It is more potent and occlusive

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Greasy ointments are more occlusive, enhancing the potency and hydration for dry lesions.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which topical corticosteroid would be most appropriate for a child with eczema on the face?
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Hydrocortisone is a mild steroid suitable for sensitive areas like the face and for use in children.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: What is a common side effect of prolonged use of potent topical corticosteroids on thin skin?
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Prolonged use of potent corticosteroids can lead to skin atrophy, especially on thin skin areas.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which statement about topical corticosteroid potency is true?

options.text: Potent steroids can be used anywhere without concern
Mild steroids are safe for all body areas
Potency should match the site of application
All steroids have the same absorption rate regardless of site

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Topical corticosteroid potency must be matched to the site due to varying absorption rates and risk of side effects.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: What is the mechanism of action for narrowband UVB therapy in psoriasis?
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Narrowband UVB therapy reduces inflammatory cytokines, helping to manage psoriasis.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which systemic agent is commonly used for severe psoriasis that does not respond to topical therapies?
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Methotrexate is a systemic agent used for severe psoriasis when topical treatments fail.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: How does the treatment of eczema relate to the management of psoriasis?

options.text: Both can be treated with topical corticosteroids
Both are exclusively managed with phototherapy

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Eczema and psoriasis can both be treated with topical corticosteroids, highlighting the overlap in dermatologic therapies.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: In the context of systemic dermatologic therapy, how does the management of acne vulgaris differ from that of psoriasis?

options.text: Acne is treated only with topical agents
Psoriasis requires systemic agents more often
Both conditions are treated with the same systemic agents
Acne does not respond to phototherapy

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Psoriasis often requires systemic agents due to its severity, while acne is typically managed with topical treatments initially.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Regarding matching topical steroid potency to body site — which is correct?

options.text: A potent topical steroid is fine to use anywhere, including the face, as long as it clears the rash

Steroid potency must be MATCHED to the SITE: skin is THIN and highly absorptive on the FACE, flexures and genitals, so only MILD steroids should be used there (potent ones cause atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis and even systemic absorption), whereas thick skin (palms/soles) tolerates and needs POTENT steroids

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Because absorption and atrophy risk depend on skin thickness, using a potent steroid on the face or flexures causes disfiguring local side-effects and possible HPA suppression — site-appropriate potency is essential to safe topical steroid use.

dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Skin thinning, striae and telangiectasia after prolonged potent steroid use”?

options.text: Thin facial skin → high absorption → lower potency

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Skin thinning, striae and telangiectasia after prolonged potent steroid use → Topical corticosteroid atrophy (side-effect).

dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Choice of a greasy ointment for a dry, lichenified plaque”?

options.text: Thin facial skin → high absorption → lower potency

dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Choice of a greasy ointment for a dry, lichenified plaque → Vehicle selection ("dry → wet"; occlusion ↑ potency).

dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Dermatologic Therapy”?
dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Topical therapies for acne are essential for understanding dermatologic therapy.

skin-examination-approach.stem: On examining a rash, applying pressure with a glass slide (diascopy) causes the redness to blanch. This indicates:
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Erythema is due to dilated dermal vessels and blanches on pressure (diascopy) as blood is pushed out; purpura is extravasated blood and does NOT blanch. Palpable non-blanching purpura specifically suggests vasculitis.

skin-examination-approach.stem: An itchy dermatitis distributed in the antecubital and popliteal flexures is most consistent with:
skin-examination-approach.explanation: A flexural distribution (antecubital/popliteal fossae) is characteristic of atopic eczema, whereas psoriasis favours extensor surfaces. Recognising distribution patterns is a key part of the systematic dermatological examination.

skin-examination-approach.stem: What is the primary purpose of examining special sites such as the scalp and nails during a dermatological examination?

options.text: To find diagnostic clues that may not be visible on the main lesion
To evaluate the effectiveness of previous treatments

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Special sites often harbor diagnostic clues like nail pitting in psoriasis or oral erosions in pemphigus, which may be missed if only the main lesion is examined.

skin-examination-approach.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristic of atopic eczema?

options.text: Flexural distribution of an itchy dermatitis

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Atopic eczema typically presents with an itchy dermatitis that has a flexural distribution, particularly in the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

skin-examination-approach.stem: A patient presents with a purpuric rash that does not blanch on diascopy. What does this finding indicate?
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Purpura that does not blanch indicates extravasated blood, commonly seen in vasculitis, rather than erythema which blanches.

skin-examination-approach.stem: Which of the following is a common trap in dermatological examinations?

options.text: Focusing only on the lesion the patient is concerned about

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Limiting the examination to the presenting complaint can miss important diagnostic clues found on the rest of the skin or special sites.

skin-examination-approach.stem: A patient presents with a rash that is distributed symmetrically across the body. Which condition is most likely?
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Lupus erythematosus often presents with a symmetrical distribution of rashes, particularly on sun-exposed areas.

skin-examination-approach.stem: Which of the following findings would most likely indicate a diagnosis of pemphigus?
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Oral mucosal erosions are a classic sign of pemphigus, indicating the presence of autoimmune blistering.

skin-examination-approach.stem: How does a dermatological examination relate to identifying hand nerve lesions?

options.text: Skin lesions can indicate nerve damage.
Dermatological signs can mask underlying nerve issues.
Skin type affects nerve conduction studies.
Nerve lesions can cause skin changes.

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Nerve lesions, such as those affecting the median or ulnar nerves, can lead to skin changes like atrophy or altered sensation in the affected areas.

skin-examination-approach.stem: What is the significance of using diascopy in dermatological examinations?

options.text: To differentiate between erythema and purpura

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Diascopy helps distinguish between erythema, which blanches, and purpura, which does not, aiding in diagnosis.

skin-examination-approach.stem: Regarding examining beyond the presenting lesion — which is correct?

options.text: It is enough to examine only the lesion the patient is worried about

A proper dermatological examination inspects the WHOLE skin surface and the SPECIAL SITES (scalp, nails, mucosae, palms/soles) — diagnostic clues (nail pitting, oral erosions, subtle distribution) are frequently found AWAY from the presenting lesion, and hidden lesions (e.g. a melanoma on the back) can be missed if only the complaint is examined

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Limiting the exam to the presenting complaint misses distribution patterns and special-site signs that make the diagnosis, and risks overlooking dangerous incidental lesions.

skin-examination-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nail pitting/onycholysis found on examining the nails”?
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Nail pitting/onycholysis found on examining the nails → Psoriasis clue (special-site examination).

skin-examination-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Purpura that does not blanch on diascopy”?
skin-examination-approach.explanation: Purpura that does not blanch on diascopy → Extravasated blood (purpura) vs blanching erythema.

skin-examination-approach.stem: Which should you review before “Approach to the Dermatological Examination”?

options.text: Hand Nerve Lesions: Median, Ulnar & Radial

skin-examination-approach.explanation: Understanding nerve lesions can aid in recognizing skin manifestations related to nerve damage.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: A KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation of skin scrapings is used to detect:
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: KOH dissolves keratin, revealing fungal hyphae (dermatophytes) or the "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance of pityriasis versicolor under the microscope. It is a rapid bedside test for suspected superficial fungal infection.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: The preferred biopsy technique for a lesion suspected of being melanoma is:
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Excisional biopsy removes the whole lesion at full thickness, allowing accurate measurement of Breslow depth — the most important prognostic factor in melanoma. A shave biopsy risks transecting the lesion and preventing accurate staging.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What does KOH microscopy reveal in a dermatophyte infection?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: KOH microscopy dissolves keratin, allowing visualization of fungal hyphae characteristic of dermatophyte infections.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: Which biopsy type is preferred for suspected melanoma?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: An excisional biopsy is necessary to obtain full thickness for accurate Breslow depth measurement in melanoma.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What is the mechanism of coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Coral-red fluorescence indicates erythrasma, a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What does a positive patch test at 72–96 hours indicate?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: A positive patch test indicates allergic contact dermatitis, which is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What finding is characteristic of herpes simplex virus on a Tzanck smear?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: The Tzanck smear shows multinucleate giant cells, which are indicative of herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus infections.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: How does the approach to dermatological examination relate to KOH microscopy?

options.text: KOH microscopy is used to confirm systemic diseases
KOH microscopy is a bedside test following examination
KOH microscopy is irrelevant to dermatological examination
KOH microscopy is used for immediate allergy testing

dermatologic-investigations.explanation: KOH microscopy is a bedside test that follows the initial dermatological examination to confirm fungal infections.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What is the significance of Breslow depth in melanoma management?

options.text: Determines the need for immediate surgery

dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Breslow depth is a key prognostic factor in melanoma that guides treatment decisions and management strategies.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: Regarding biopsy choice for suspected melanoma — which is correct?

options.text: A quick shave biopsy is fine to sample any suspicious pigmented lesion

A suspected MELANOMA should undergo EXCISIONAL biopsy (removing the whole lesion with a narrow margin) so the pathologist can measure the full BRESLOW THICKNESS (depth) — the key prognostic factor; a SHAVE biopsy may transect the lesion and prevent accurate depth measurement, compromising staging

dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Because Breslow depth determines melanoma prognosis and management, a partial/shave biopsy that cuts across the lesion can under-stage it — excisional biopsy preserves the information needed.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyphae on KOH microscopy of a scaly plaque”?

options.text: Preserve full thickness for Breslow depth (melanoma)

dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Hyphae on KOH microscopy of a scaly plaque → Dermatophyte infection.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multinucleate giant cells on a Tzanck smear”?

options.text: Preserve full thickness for Breslow depth (melanoma)

dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Multinucleate giant cells on a Tzanck smear → Herpes simplex/varicella-zoster.

dermatologic-investigations.stem: Which should you review before “Dermatological Investigations”?
dermatologic-investigations.explanation: Understanding the examination approach is essential before performing dermatological investigations.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: Generalised pruritus in the absence of any primary skin rash should prompt evaluation for:

options.text: Systemic causes such as lymphoma, cholestasis, uraemia, thyroid disease or iron deficiency

skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Itch without a primary rash can be a marker of systemic disease — lymphoma (especially Hodgkin), cholestasis, chronic kidney disease/uraemia, thyroid disease and iron deficiency — so it warrants a systemic work-up rather than only topical treatment.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: The abrupt onset of extensive acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese older adult should raise suspicion of:
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: While acanthosis nigricans usually reflects insulin resistance, its abrupt, extensive (± mucosal) appearance in a non-obese or older patient can be paraneoplastic — classically associated with gastric adenocarcinoma — warranting malignancy evaluation.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: What is the most likely underlying condition associated with sudden onset extensive acanthosis nigricans in an older patient?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Sudden onset extensive acanthosis nigricans can indicate a paraneoplastic syndrome, particularly gastric adenocarcinoma.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: Which skin sign is most indicative of dermatomyositis?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Heliotrope rash is a classic skin manifestation of dermatomyositis, often associated with underlying malignancy.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: A patient presents with tender nodules on the shins. Which systemic condition should be investigated?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Tender shin nodules are characteristic of erythema nodosum, which can be triggered by sarcoidosis among other conditions.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: What mechanism underlies the skin manifestation of pellagra?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Pellagra is caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, leading to the classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: A patient presents with generalized pruritus without a rash. Which condition is least likely to be the cause?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Generalized pruritus without a rash is commonly associated with lymphoma, cholestasis, and uraemia, but psoriasis typically presents with a rash.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: Which skin finding is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: The malar rash is a characteristic skin finding in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: How does the presence of erythema nodosum relate to systemic diseases?

options.text: It indicates a benign skin condition
It suggests a need for cancer screening
It is solely due to infections
It is a sign of nutritional deficiency

skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Erythema nodosum can be associated with systemic diseases like sarcoidosis and IBD, warranting further investigation for underlying conditions, including cancer.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: Which skin sign could indicate a need for evaluation of connective tissue diseases?
skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Heliotrope rash is associated with dermatomyositis, a connective tissue disease, indicating the need for further evaluation.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: Regarding acanthosis nigricans significance — which is correct?

options.text: Acanthosis nigricans is always just a benign sign of obesity

Acanthosis nigricans usually reflects INSULIN RESISTANCE (obesity, type 2 diabetes, PCOS), but when it appears ABRUPTLY, is EXTENSIVE/severe or involves mucosae in a non-obese/older patient, it can be a PARANEOPLASTIC sign (classically of gastric adenocarcinoma) — so the tempo and extent determine whether malignancy work-up is needed
Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance; if abrupt → paraneoplastic)

skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Missing the paraneoplastic pattern (sudden, extensive acanthosis) could overlook an underlying cancer; the clinical context (gradual/obese vs abrupt/extensive) changes the work-up entirely.

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Velvety hyperpigmented flexural plaques”?

options.text: Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance; if abrupt → paraneoplastic)

skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Velvety hyperpigmented flexural plaques → Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance; if abrupt → paraneoplastic).

skin-signs-systemic-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Generalised itch with no primary rash”?

options.text: Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance; if abrupt → paraneoplastic)

skin-signs-systemic-disease.explanation: Generalised itch with no primary rash → Systemic pruritus (lymphoma/cholestasis/uraemia/thyroid/iron).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: The epidermal layer responsible for ongoing renewal, containing dividing stem cells on the basement membrane, is the:
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: The stratum basale (basal layer) sits on the basement membrane and contains the dividing keratinocyte stem cells and melanocytes; daughter cells migrate upward, differentiating through the spinosum and granulosum into the dead corneocytes of the stratum corneum over roughly 28 days.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Melanocytes protect the skin from ultraviolet damage by:

options.text: Transferring melanin to keratinocytes, where it caps and shields the nucleus

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Melanocytes make melanin in melanosomes and transfer it to neighbouring keratinocytes, where it forms a supranuclear cap that absorbs UV and protects keratinocyte DNA. One melanocyte supplies about 36 keratinocytes (the epidermal melanin unit).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What is the primary function of keratinocytes in the epidermis?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Keratinocytes form a barrier against pathogens by undergoing keratinization and creating a protective outer layer.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Which layer of the epidermis contains the most mature keratinocytes?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: The stratum corneum contains the most mature keratinocytes, which are dead, flattened cells that provide a barrier.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: In psoriasis, what histological finding is typically observed in the stratum corneum?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Psoriasis is characterized by parakeratosis, which is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum due to accelerated keratinocyte turnover.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What is the role of desmosomes in the epidermis?

options.text: Anchor keratinocytes to the basement membrane

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Desmosomes link keratinocytes to each other, providing structural integrity to the epidermis.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Which condition is characterized by intra-epidermal blistering due to loss of keratinocyte adhesion?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by intra-epidermal blistering due to the loss of adhesion between keratinocytes.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: How does melanin protect keratinocyte DNA from UV damage?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Melanin absorbs UV light, thereby protecting keratinocyte DNA from damage that can lead to skin cancer.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between keratinocytes and melanocytes?

options.text: Melanocytes are more numerous than keratinocytes

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Melanocytes synthesize melanin and transfer it to keratinocytes, where it forms a protective cap over the nucleus.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What is the primary defect in ichthyosis related to keratinocyte biology?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Ichthyosis is characterized by disordered keratinization, leading to scaling and thickened skin.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: How do hemidesmosomes differ from desmosomes in the epidermis?

options.text: Hemidesmosomes link keratinocytes to each other
Desmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane
Hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane
Desmosomes are involved in melanin transfer

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane, while desmosomes link keratinocytes to each other.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Regarding where melanin ends up — which is correct?

options.text: Skin colour comes from melanin stored inside melanocytes

Melanocytes SYNTHESISE melanin (in melanosomes) but TRANSFER it to surrounding KERATINOCYTES, where it forms a supranuclear "cap" shielding keratinocyte DNA from UV — so most epidermal pigment resides in keratinocytes, not melanocytes; skin-colour differences reflect melanin amount/type and distribution, not melanocyte number

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Understanding melanin transfer explains why pigment protects keratinocyte DNA (and why melanocyte number is similar across skin colours), underpinning pigmentary disorders and photoprotection.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis)”?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis) → Accelerated keratinocyte turnover (psoriasis).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “The proliferating basal layer on the basement membrane”?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: The proliferating basal layer on the basement membrane → Stratum basale (epidermal stem cells).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Which should you review before “Epidermis & Keratinocyte Biology”?
