epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Understanding body membranes is essential for grasping epidermal structure.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Sebaceous glands of the pilosebaceous unit secrete sebum by which mechanism?

options.text: Holocrine (disintegration of the whole secretory cell)

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Sebaceous glands are holocrine — the entire secretory cell disintegrates to release sebum. They are androgen-driven and central to acne. Eccrine sweat glands are merocrine, and apocrine glands release by decapitation/apocrine secretion.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Thermoregulatory sweating is provided by which gland, under which unusual autonomic control?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Eccrine glands provide thermoregulatory sweating and are the classic "sympathetic cholinergic" exception — sympathetically innervated but using acetylcholine (muscarinic), which is why antimuscarinic drugs reduce sweating.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What type of secretion do sebaceous glands utilize?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Sebaceous glands use holocrine secretion, where the entire cell disintegrates to release sebum.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Which layer of the dermis contains loose connective tissue and dermal papillae?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: The papillary layer of the dermis is characterized by loose connective tissue and interdigitating dermal papillae.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: A patient presents with excessive sweating that is not relieved by anticholinergic medications. Which type of gland is primarily responsible for this symptom?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Eccrine glands are responsible for thermoregulatory sweating and are under sympathetic-cholinergic control.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Which of the following findings is most indicative of psoriasis affecting the nail matrix?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Nail pitting is a classic diagnostic clue associated with psoriasis.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which apocrine glands contribute to body odor?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Apocrine glands secrete into hair follicles, and their secretion is broken down by bacteria, leading to body odor.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: A patient with hidradenitis suppurativa has occluded apocrine glands. Which area is most likely affected?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa primarily affects areas with apocrine glands, such as the axilla and groin.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: How do eccrine and apocrine glands differ in their secretion mechanisms?

options.text: Eccrine are holocrine; apocrine are merocrine
Eccrine are merocrine; apocrine are holocrine
Eccrine are merocrine; apocrine are apocrine

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Eccrine glands secrete via merocrine mechanisms, while apocrine glands have a different mode of secretion.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Which of the following conditions is most directly related to the dysfunction of the pilosebaceous unit?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Acne vulgaris is directly related to the dysfunction of the pilosebaceous unit, particularly the sebaceous glands.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What is the primary role of eccrine glands in thermoregulation?

options.text: Release of sweat directly onto the skin

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Eccrine glands release sweat directly onto the skin surface, playing a crucial role in thermoregulation.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Regarding eccrine vs apocrine glands — which is correct?

options.text: All sweat glands are the same and produce body odour

ECCRINE glands are distributed over the whole body, open directly onto the skin and produce watery THERMOREGULATORY sweat (sympathetic-cholinergic), whereas APOCRINE glands are limited to the axilla/groin/areola, open into HAIR FOLLICLES and produce a secretion that bacteria break down into ODOUR (and can occlude → hidradenitis suppurativa) — different distribution, function and clinical disease

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Distinguishing thermoregulatory eccrine from odour-producing apocrine glands explains hyperhidrosis vs body odour vs hidradenitis, which have different treatments.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sebaceous gland secreting by disintegration of its whole cells”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Sebaceous gland secreting by disintegration of its whole cells → Holocrine secretion (pilosebaceous unit).

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thermoregulatory sweating blocked by antimuscarinics”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Thermoregulatory sweating blocked by antimuscarinics → Eccrine glands are sympathetic-cholinergic.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Which should you review before “Dermis, Appendages & Skin Glands”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Understanding skin appendages is crucial for grasping dermal functions.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: The sun protection factor (SPF) of a sunscreen primarily quantifies protection against:
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: SPF measures protection against UVB (the sunburn/DNA-damaging band). Because UVA drives dermal ageing and contributes to carcinogenesis, a "broad-spectrum" sunscreen covering both UVA and UVB is needed, applied generously with reapplication.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Which patient has the highest risk of sunburn and skin cancer and needs the most emphatic photoprotection advice?

options.text: A Fitzpatrick type VI patient who never burns
A Fitzpatrick type I–II patient who always burns and rarely tans
Anyone regardless of skin type equally
A patient who already uses sunscreen

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Fitzpatrick types I–II (fair skin that always burns, rarely tans) have the least melanin protection and the highest risk of sunburn and skin cancer, so they warrant the strongest photoprotection counselling — though all skin types benefit from protection.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which UVA contributes to skin aging?

options.text: Leads to collagen and elastin damage

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: UVA penetrates the dermis and causes damage to collagen and elastin, leading to skin aging.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Which type of UV radiation is primarily responsible for causing sunburn?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: UVB radiation is responsible for causing sunburn and is the main carcinogen affecting the epidermis.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: A patient with Fitzpatrick skin type I is at increased risk for which of the following?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Fitzpatrick type I patients always burn and have the highest risk for sunburn and skin cancer.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Which treatment is most effective for reducing fine wrinkles and dyspigmentation due to photodamage?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Topical retinoids like tretinoin stimulate collagen production and improve fine wrinkles and dyspigmentation.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What is a common misconception regarding SPF ratings of sunscreens?

options.text: Higher SPF provides complete protection against all UV damage
SPF should be reapplied every hour
SPF is irrelevant for skin types I and II

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: A high SPF only measures UVB protection; it does not guarantee complete protection against UVA damage.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: A patient presents with scaly lesions on sun-exposed areas. Which treatment is most appropriate to prevent progression to SCC?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Cryotherapy is an effective treatment for actinic keratoses, which can progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: How does photoprotection relate to the risk of keratinocyte carcinomas?

options.text: Only UVA contributes to keratinocyte carcinomas
Photoprotection is irrelevant for skin aging
Broad-spectrum sunscreen reduces the risk of both photoaging and keratinocyte carcinomas
Skin type does not influence cancer risk

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Broad-spectrum sunscreen protects against both UVA and UVB, reducing the risk of photoaging and keratinocyte carcinomas.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What is the relationship between Fitzpatrick skin types and skin aging?

options.text: Lower types have lower UV risk
Lower types are more prone to photoaging
Skin type does not affect aging

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Lower Fitzpatrick types (I–II) are more prone to sunburn and photoaging due to their inability to tan effectively.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Regarding what spf covers — which is correct?

options.text: A high SPF alone gives complete protection against all UV-related damage

SPF measures protection against UVB (sunburn) only — a high SPF that is NOT broad-spectrum leaves UVA (dermal ageing, some carcinogenesis) largely uncovered; effective photoprotection needs a BROAD-SPECTRUM product (UVA+UVB), applied generously and reapplied, PLUS clothing/shade/avoidance

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Relying on SPF number alone (UVB) misses UVA damage; broad-spectrum coverage and behaviour are essential for genuine protection against ageing and cancer.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Deep dermal collagen/elastin damage from long-wavelength UV”?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Deep dermal collagen/elastin damage from long-wavelength UV → UVA (aging).

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sunburn and epidermal DNA damage from shorter-wavelength UV”?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Sunburn and epidermal DNA damage from shorter-wavelength UV → UVB (burning/carcinogenesis).

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: The principal antigen-presenting (dendritic) cell of the epidermis, central to sensitisation in allergic contact dermatitis, is the:
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Langerhans cells are the epidermal dendritic antigen-presenting cells; they capture antigen and migrate to lymph nodes to prime T cells, a key step in allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV) and immune surveillance.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Psoriasis is predominantly driven by which T-helper pathway, targeted by modern biologics?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Psoriasis is driven largely by the Th17 (IL-17/IL-23) axis (with Th1), which is why anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 biologics are effective. Atopic dermatitis is Th2-driven (IL-4/IL-13), targeted by dupilumab.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What is the primary function of Langerhans cells in the skin?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Langerhans cells are specialized dendritic cells that capture and present antigens to T cells, playing a crucial role in immune surveillance.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Which cytokine is primarily involved in the Th2 response associated with atopic dermatitis?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: IL-4 is a key cytokine in the Th2 immune response, contributing to the pathophysiology of atopic dermatitis.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What is the role of antimicrobial peptides in skin immunity?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Antimicrobial peptides, such as defensins and cathelicidin, play a critical role in the innate immune defense by limiting skin infections.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: In psoriasis, which immune pathway is primarily targeted by biologics?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Psoriasis is driven by Th17-mediated inflammation, making the Th17 pathway a primary target for biologic therapies.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Keratinocytes are involved in skin immunity by releasing which of the following?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Keratinocytes actively participate in skin immunity by releasing both cytokines and antimicrobial peptides in response to pathogens.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: How do Toll-like receptors (TLRs) contribute to skin immunity?

options.text: By recognizing pathogens and triggering cytokine release
By presenting antigens to T cells

skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Toll-like receptors on keratinocytes recognize pathogens and trigger the release of cytokines, initiating an immune response.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What is the relationship between skin barrier dysfunction and eczema?

options.text: Barrier dysfunction leads to increased infection risk
Barrier dysfunction is unrelated to eczema
Barrier dysfunction promotes T cell activation

skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Skin barrier dysfunction can lead to increased susceptibility to infections and contribute to the development of eczema.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Which immune cells are primarily involved in the hypersensitivity reactions seen in contact dermatitis?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: T cells, particularly CD4+ T helper cells, play a central role in mediating the delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions seen in contact dermatitis.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Regarding keratinocytes as immune cells — which is correct?

options.text: Keratinocytes are just passive structural/barrier cells with no immune role

Keratinocytes are ACTIVE participants in cutaneous immunity — they express pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors), sense danger, and secrete CYTOKINES (IL-1, TNF, chemokines) and antimicrobial peptides that recruit and instruct immune cells, initiating and amplifying inflammatory responses (as in psoriasis)

skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Recognising keratinocytes as immune effectors (not just bricks) explains how skin initiates inflammation and why cytokine-targeted biologics are effective.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “The epidermal antigen-presenting dendritic cell”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: The epidermal antigen-presenting dendritic cell → Langerhans cell.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Keratinocytes releasing cytokines in response to a pathogen”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Keratinocytes releasing cytokines in response to a pathogen → Innate immune sensing (TLRs).

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Which should you review before “The Skin Immune System”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Knowledge of innate barriers and pattern recognition is crucial for understanding skin immunity.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A patient develops itchy dermatitis 2–3 days after their skin contacts a nickel belt buckle, with a positive patch test. This is which hypersensitivity type?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity, appearing 48–72 h after re-exposure in a sensitised person and diagnosed by patch testing. Type I (IgE) reactions such as urticaria are immediate.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Transient itchy wheals that each resolve within 24 hours (urticaria) are typically mediated by:

options.text: IgE and mast-cell histamine release (Type I)

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Urticaria is usually a Type I, IgE/mast-cell-mediated reaction releasing histamine, with transient individual wheals (<24 h). It is treated with antihistamines, reserving adrenaline for anaphylaxis/airway angioedema.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: What is the primary immunological mechanism involved in Type I hypersensitivity reactions?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are primarily mediated by IgE antibodies that trigger mast cell degranulation.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A patient presents with itchy wheals that resolve within 24 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: The transient itchy wheals that resolve within 24 hours are characteristic of Type I urticaria.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is characterized by delayed onset and requires prior sensitization?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions are delayed and require prior sensitization, as seen in allergic contact dermatitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A patient develops a rash 48 hours after contact with poison ivy. What is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: A patch test is used to confirm allergic contact dermatitis, which is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Which of the following findings is most indicative of Type III hypersensitivity?

options.text: Itchy dermatitis at a patch test site

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Palpable purpura is a classic finding associated with Type III hypersensitivity reactions, such as leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A cleaner develops hand dermatitis without prior sensitization. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Irritant contact dermatitis occurs without prior sensitization and is common in occupational settings.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: In a patient with a drug allergy, which hypersensitivity type is most likely involved if they develop a rash within minutes of exposure?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions occur within minutes and are mediated by IgE and mast cells, often seen in drug allergies.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A patient presents with a blistering rash and a history of autoimmune disease. Which type of hypersensitivity is most likely responsible?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity involves cytotoxic antibodies, which can lead to autoimmune blistering diseases.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Regarding urticaria vs contact dermatitis timing — which is correct?

options.text: All allergic skin reactions appear immediately after exposure

Timing separates the mechanisms: TYPE I urticaria is IMMEDIATE (minutes, IgE/mast-cell, transient wheals), whereas TYPE IV allergic contact dermatitis is DELAYED (48–72 hours, T-cell) — so a rash appearing days after contact points to a delayed T-cell reaction (patch-test positive), not an immediate IgE allergy

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: The immediate-vs-delayed distinction changes the mechanism, diagnostic test (prick vs patch) and treatment; assuming all reactions are immediate misclassifies delayed contact dermatitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transient itchy wheals resolving within 24 h”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Transient itchy wheals resolving within 24 h → Type I urticaria (IgE/mast-cell).

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy dermatitis at a nickel-contact site, patch-test positive”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Itchy dermatitis at a nickel-contact site, patch-test positive → Type IV allergic contact dermatitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Hypersensitivity Reactions”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Understanding drug allergies is essential for managing cutaneous hypersensitivity.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Loss-of-function mutations in which protein impair the skin barrier and predispose to ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Filaggrin aggregates keratin and yields natural moisturising factor; loss-of-function mutations produce a dry, defective barrier causing ichthyosis vulgaris and strongly predisposing to atopic dermatitis (and the atopic march). Emollient barrier repair is foundational.

skin-barrier-function.stem: The permeability barrier of the skin is provided mainly by:

options.text: The stratum corneum (corneocytes in intercellular lipid lamellae)

skin-barrier-function.explanation: The stratum corneum forms the permeability barrier as a "brick and mortar" structure — corneocytes (bricks) embedded in ceramide-rich intercellular lipid lamellae (mortar) — limiting transepidermal water loss and excluding microbes/allergens.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What is the primary structural component of the stratum corneum that contributes to the skin's permeability barrier?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Corneocytes, which are rich in keratin and filaggrin, serve as the 'bricks' in the skin's permeability barrier.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Which condition is most directly associated with loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin lead to ichthyosis vulgaris and predispose individuals to atopic dermatitis.

skin-barrier-function.stem: A patient presents with dry skin and increased transepidermal water loss. What underlying mechanism is likely responsible?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Increased transepidermal water loss is indicative of barrier dysfunction, particularly in the stratum corneum.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Which of the following best explains the role of emollients in managing atopic dermatitis?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Emollients primarily function to repair the skin barrier, reducing transepidermal water loss and preventing flare-ups.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What is a common misconception regarding the treatment of eczema?

options.text: Only steroids are needed during flares
Barrier defects are secondary to inflammation
Dry skin is not related to eczema

skin-barrier-function.explanation: A barrier defect, such as filaggrin loss, is a primary driver of eczema, and treating it is essential for long-term management.

skin-barrier-function.stem: How does the skin microbiome contribute to the skin barrier function?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: The skin microbiome helps maintain barrier function by competing with pathogens and supporting immune responses.

skin-barrier-function.stem: In patients with atopic dermatitis, what is the primary effect of using emollients regularly?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Regular use of emollients primarily increases skin hydration by repairing the barrier, which is foundational in managing atopic dermatitis.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Regarding barrier defect as cause vs consequence in eczema — which is correct?

options.text: Dry, cracked skin in eczema is only a result of the inflammation, so treating inflammation alone is enough

A BARRIER DEFECT (e.g. filaggrin loss) is a PRIMARY driver of atopic dermatitis — the leaky barrier lets in allergens/microbes that trigger inflammation and itch — so EMOLLIENT-based barrier repair is FOUNDATIONAL, used continuously alongside anti-inflammatory therapy (not just steroids for flares); ignoring the barrier leads to relapse

skin-barrier-function.explanation: Because the barrier defect both causes and perpetuates eczema, continuous emollient use (not just treating inflammation during flares) is essential to control disease and reduce steroid need.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dry skin with increased transepidermal water loss”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Dry skin with increased transepidermal water loss → Barrier (stratum corneum) dysfunction.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis in the same patient”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis in the same patient → Filaggrin loss-of-function mutation.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Which should you review before “The Skin Barrier”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Understanding skin immune cells is essential for grasping the immunological aspect of the skin barrier.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Before applying compression bandaging to a leg ulcer thought to be venous, it is essential to:

options.text: Exclude significant arterial disease (check the ankle-brachial pressure index)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Compression treats venous ulcers but worsens arterial (ischaemic) ulcers, so the ankle-brachial pressure index must confirm adequate arterial supply before compression is applied. Arterial ulcers (painful, punched-out, low ABPI) need revascularisation, not compression.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: A painless ulcer under a callus at a metatarsal head in a person with long-standing diabetes is best explained by:

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy with pressure/repetitive trauma (diabetic foot ulcer)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Diabetic (neuropathic) foot ulcers are painless because of peripheral neuropathy and occur at pressure points (e.g. metatarsal heads) with callus, often complicated by ischaemia and infection. Management includes offloading, glycaemic control, debridement and infection treatment.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What is the most common cause of chronic leg ulcers?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Venous hypertension is the most common cause of chronic leg ulcers, leading to venous ulcers in the gaiter area.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Which characteristic finding is associated with arterial ulcers?

options.text: Painful punched-out ulcer on the toes

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Arterial ulcers are typically painful and present as punched-out lesions, often located on the toes.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What is the primary treatment for venous ulcers?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Compression therapy is the primary treatment for venous ulcers to reduce venous hypertension.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Why is compression therapy contraindicated in arterial ulcers?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Compression can worsen ischemia in arterial ulcers, leading to potential tissue loss.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: A patient presents with a non-healing ulcer with a rolled edge. What is the most appropriate next step?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: A non-healing ulcer with atypical features, such as a rolled edge, should be biopsied to rule out malignancy.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: How does chronic inflammation contribute to the pathophysiology of chronic wounds?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Chronic inflammation inhibits healing processes, keeping the wound in a prolonged inflammatory state.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Which of the following is a common feature of diabetic foot ulcers?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Diabetic foot ulcers are often painless and typically occur under pressure points, such as metatarsal heads.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: How does venous ulcer management relate to wound healing mechanisms?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Managing venous ulcers primarily involves improving venous return through compression, which aids in healing.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What systemic factor can exacerbate chronic wounds and is also linked to vascular health?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Hyperglycemia is a systemic factor that can exacerbate chronic wounds and is closely linked to diabetic conditions affecting vascular health.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Regarding compression in leg ulcers — which is correct?

options.text: All leg ulcers benefit from compression bandaging

Compression is the treatment for VENOUS ulcers but is DANGEROUS in ARTERIAL disease — so you must EXCLUDE significant arterial insufficiency (check the ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX) BEFORE applying compression; compressing an ischaemic (arterial) leg can worsen ischaemia and cause tissue loss
Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Applying compression to an arterial ulcer worsens ischaemia and can lead to amputation, so ABPI must confirm adequate arterial supply before compression — a critical safety step.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Shallow ulcer over the medial malleolus with oedema and haemosiderin staining”?

options.text: Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Shallow ulcer over the medial malleolus with oedema and haemosiderin staining → Venous ulcer (compression, normal ABPI).

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful punched-out ulcer on the toes with a cold, pulseless foot”?

options.text: Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Painful punched-out ulcer on the toes with a cold, pulseless foot → Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress).

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Which should you review before “Chronic Wounds & Leg Ulcers”?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Understanding venous pressure can aid in assessing venous ulcers.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Erysipelas differs from cellulitis in that erysipelas:

options.text: Is superficial (upper dermis) with sharply demarcated, raised borders (usually streptococcal)

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and lymphatics, producing a sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red plaque (usually streptococcal, often facial or on the shins), whereas cellulitis extends deeper with ill-defined borders (staph or strep).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis rather than simple cellulitis?

options.text: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings with systemic toxicity
A slowly enlarging patch over weeks

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis classically causes severe pain out of proportion to the (initially modest) skin findings, with rapid progression and systemic toxicity (± crepitus/necrosis). It is a surgical emergency needing urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What is the most common causative organism of impetigo?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Impetigo is primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, with S. aureus being the most common.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which clinical finding is characteristic of erysipelas?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Erysipelas presents with a sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red plaque, often accompanied by fever.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What distinguishes necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis?

options.text: Pain out of proportion to skin findings

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis is characterized by pain out of proportion to the modest skin findings, indicating a surgical emergency.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What is the first-line treatment for a fluctuant abscess?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Fluctuant abscesses require incision and drainage for effective treatment, often in conjunction with antibiotics.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which of the following is a surgical emergency requiring urgent intervention?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency that requires urgent debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: How does Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) primarily affect children?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: SSSS causes widespread skin peeling due to the action of exfoliative toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: How does the treatment of cellulitis differ from that of necrotising fasciitis?

options.text: Cellulitis can be treated with oral antibiotics
Necrotising fasciitis is treated with topical agents

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Cellulitis can often be treated with oral antibiotics, while necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical intervention.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which bacterial skin infection is most likely to present with systemic toxicity and crepitus?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis is characterized by systemic toxicity and crepitus due to gas formation in tissues.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Regarding necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis — which is correct?

options.text: Severe leg pain with only mild redness is just cellulitis that antibiotics will fix

PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION to modest skin findings, with rapid progression, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis, signals NECROTISING FASCIITIS — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY requiring urgent DEBRIDEMENT plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, NOT antibiotics alone; early skin signs can look deceptively mild

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis is rapidly fatal and its surface appearance underplays the deep destruction, so recognising disproportionate pain/toxicity and acting surgically (not just medically) is life-saving.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Honey-coloured crusts on a child's face”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Honey-coloured crusts on a child's face → Impetigo (S. aureus/S. pyogenes).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red facial plaque with fever”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red facial plaque with fever → Erysipelas (streptococcal, superficial).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which should you review before “Bacterial Skin Infections”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Understanding antibiotics is crucial for treating bacterial skin infections.

viral-skin-infections.stem: A child with atopic eczema develops widespread painful, punched-out vesicles/erosions and fever. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) — needs systemic aciclovir

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Disseminated HSV over eczematous skin (eczema herpeticum) produces painful, monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever/malaise — a dermatological emergency requiring systemic aciclovir. It should not be mistaken for a simple eczema flare or impetigo.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Extensive or persistent molluscum contagiosum in an adult should prompt consideration of:
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum (a poxvirus) causes umbilicated papules, usually self-limiting in children; extensive or persistent disease in an adult suggests immunosuppression such as HIV, warranting evaluation.

viral-skin-infections.stem: What is the primary treatment for a patient diagnosed with eczema herpeticum?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Eczema herpeticum is a dermatological emergency requiring systemic aciclovir for effective treatment.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic clinical finding of herpes zoster?

options.text: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Painful dermatomal vesicles not crossing the midline

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Herpes zoster presents with painful dermatomal vesicles that do not cross the midline.

viral-skin-infections.stem: What is the mechanism of action of aciclovir?

options.text: Inhibition of viral entry into cells

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Aciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase, preventing viral replication.

viral-skin-infections.stem: A patient presents with painful punched-out erosions over eczematous skin and fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: The presentation is consistent with eczema herpeticum, a serious complication of eczema.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Which of the following statements about HPV is true?

options.text: All types of HPV cause warts
High-risk types are associated with cancer

viral-skin-infections.explanation: High-risk types of HPV, such as 16 and 18, are associated with cervical cancer and other malignancies.

viral-skin-infections.stem: How does the presentation of molluscum contagiosum differ in immunocompromised patients compared to healthy individuals?

options.text: It can be extensive and persistent

viral-skin-infections.explanation: In immunocompromised patients, molluscum contagiosum can present as extensive and persistent lesions.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Which of the following viral infections is most likely to present with 'dew-drop' vesicles?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox, characterized by 'dew-drop' vesicles.

viral-skin-infections.stem: How does the management of herpes simplex virus infections relate to the treatment of varicella-zoster virus infections?

options.text: Both are treated with systemic aciclovir

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Both herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus infections are treated with systemic aciclovir.

viral-skin-infections.stem: What is a common complication of untreated varicella-zoster virus infection in adults?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Post-herpetic neuralgia is a common complication following herpes zoster in adults.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Regarding eczema herpeticum recognition — which is correct?

options.text: Rapidly worsening, painful eczema just needs stronger topical steroids

Painful, monomorphic PUNCHED-OUT erosions/vesicles with fever over eczematous skin suggest ECZEMA HERPETICUM (disseminated herpes simplex) — a dermatological EMERGENCY needing systemic ACICLOVIR; escalating topical steroids alone can worsen it and allow HSV to disseminate

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Missing eczema herpeticum and treating it as a steroid-responsive flare risks widespread HSV dissemination and serious complications; the painful punched-out lesions and systemic upset are the clues to give antivirals urgently.

viral-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent grouped vesicles on the lip”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Recurrent grouped vesicles on the lip → HSV reactivation (cold sore).

viral-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful punched-out erosions + fever over eczema”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Painful punched-out erosions + fever over eczema → Eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) — emergency.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Which should you review before “Viral Skin Infections”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Understanding antiviral treatments is crucial for managing viral skin infections.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: When treating a patient for scabies, it is essential to also:

options.text: Treat only the patient and observe others
Treat all close/household contacts simultaneously and launder bedding/clothing

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: All close/household contacts (even asymptomatic) must be treated simultaneously and bedding/clothing laundered, because the itch lags infestation and untreated contacts cause re-infestation ("ping-pong"). Post-scabetic itch afterward is managed with emollients/steroids, not more scabicide.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Thick hyperkeratotic crusts containing thousands of mites, highly contagious, in an elderly immunosuppressed patient describe:
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a hyperinfestation with thousands of mites forming thick crusts (often less itchy) in the immunosuppressed/elderly; it is extremely contagious (care-home outbreaks) and requires combined topical plus repeated oral ivermectin and strict infection control.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What is the primary causative agent of scabies?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Scabies is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Which of the following is a pathognomonic sign of scabies?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Burrows in the skin, particularly in web spaces, are characteristic of scabies.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What is the mechanism behind the persistent itch after successful scabies treatment?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: The persistent itch is due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, not treatment failure.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Which treatment is recommended for crusted scabies?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Crusted scabies requires a combination of topical and repeated oral ivermectin due to the high mite load.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: A child presents with intense itching and nits in their hair. What is the most likely diagnosis?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Nits cemented to hair shafts are indicative of head lice (pediculosis capitis).

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: In the context of scabies, what is the importance of treating all close contacts simultaneously?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Treating all close contacts prevents reinfestation, commonly referred to as 'ping-pong' transmission.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: How do the treatment strategies for scabies and helminthic infections differ?

options.text: Scabies requires treating contacts, helminths do not

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Scabies treatment includes treating contacts to prevent reinfestation, which is not a standard practice for helminthic infections.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Which of the following findings would suggest a diagnosis of crusted scabies rather than typical scabies?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Thick hyperkeratotic crusts are characteristic of crusted scabies, especially in immunosuppressed individuals.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Regarding persistent itch after scabies treatment — which is correct?

options.text: If itching continues after scabies treatment, the treatment failed and needs immediate repeating

Scabies itch is a DELAYED HYPERSENSITIVITY reaction, so it commonly PERSISTS for 2–4 WEEKS AFTER successful eradication — this is POST-SCABETIC itch, treated with emollients/topical steroids/antihistamines, NOT automatically more scabicide (over-treatment causes irritant dermatitis); re-treat only if there is evidence of ongoing/reinfestation

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Because the itch lags the infestation and outlasts cure, assuming persistent itch means failure leads to unnecessary repeated scabicide and irritant dermatitis — the hypersensitivity nature must be recognised.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nocturnal itch with grey burrows in finger web spaces”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Nocturnal itch with grey burrows in finger web spaces → Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei).

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itch persisting weeks after correct scabies treatment”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Itch persisting weeks after correct scabies treatment → Post-scabetic hypersensitivity (not treatment failure).

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Scabies & Pediculosis (Clinical)”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Understanding scabicides like permethrin and ivermectin.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: A young patient develops crops of small, drop-like scaly papules over the trunk about two weeks after a sore throat. This is:
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Guttate psoriasis presents as small "drop-like" papules, classically after a streptococcal throat infection in a young person. It may resolve or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis, and treatment includes topical therapy/phototherapy.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which systemic complication should be actively screened for in patients with psoriasis?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Up to about 30% of psoriasis patients develop psoriatic arthritis, which can be destructive if untreated, so joint symptoms should be screened for. Psoriasis is also associated with metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease, warranting cardiometabolic risk assessment.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What is the most common clinical presentation of chronic plaque psoriasis?

options.text: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Chronic plaque psoriasis typically presents as well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, especially on extensor surfaces.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which mechanism is primarily responsible for the pathophysiology of psoriasis?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Psoriasis is characterized by Th17 cell-mediated inflammation leading to accelerated keratinocyte turnover.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: A patient presents with small drop-like papules after a recent sore throat. What type of psoriasis is this indicative of?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Guttate psoriasis often follows streptococcal infections and presents as small drop-like papules.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What is the significance of the Auspitz sign in psoriasis?

options.text: Demonstrates pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: The Auspitz sign refers to pinpoint bleeding that occurs when scales are removed from psoriatic plaques.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which of the following statements about psoriasis is FALSE?

options.text: Psoriasis is a purely skin problem.
It can lead to psoriatic arthritis.
It is associated with increased cardiovascular risk.
It can be triggered by certain medications.

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Psoriasis is not just a skin problem; it is a systemic inflammatory disease that can lead to joint issues and other comorbidities.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What is the first-line treatment for mild localized psoriasis?

options.text: Topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Mild localized psoriasis is typically treated with topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: How does the treatment of psoriasis relate to the principles of systemic dermatologic therapy?

options.text: Psoriasis is treated only with topical agents.
Systemic therapy is reserved for mild cases.
Moderate to severe psoriasis requires systemic or biologic therapy.

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Moderate to severe psoriasis necessitates systemic or biologic therapy, aligning with principles of systemic dermatologic therapy.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which aspect of psoriasis management is crucial due to its systemic nature?

options.text: Screen for psoriatic arthritis and comorbidities

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Given that psoriasis is a systemic disease, screening for psoriatic arthritis and other comorbidities is essential in management.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Regarding psoriasis as systemic disease — which is correct?

options.text: Psoriasis is purely a skin problem treatable with creams

Psoriasis is a SYSTEMIC inflammatory disease: up to ~30% develop PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS (potentially destructive — screen for joint symptoms), and it carries increased cardiometabolic and psychological morbidity — so management includes comorbidity screening and, for moderate-severe disease, systemic/biologic therapy, not just topical creams

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Treating psoriasis as skin-only misses joint destruction and cardiovascular risk; recognising it as systemic changes screening and escalates therapy appropriately.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal → Plaque psoriasis (Auspitz sign).

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Small drop-like papules after a sore throat in a young person”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Small drop-like papules after a sore throat in a young person → Guttate psoriasis (post-streptococcal).

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which should you review before “Psoriasis: Clinical Types & Management”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Understanding cell adhesion is relevant to psoriasis pathology.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: A child presents with palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, joint pain, abdominal pain and haematuria. The diagnosis is:
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), the commonest childhood vasculitis, presents with palpable purpura (buttocks/legs), arthralgia, abdominal pain and nephritis, with IgA immune-complex deposition. Renal involvement should be monitored with urinalysis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Palpable (raised, non-blanching) purpura is the hallmark of:
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Palpable purpura (you can feel the raised lesion) indicates inflammation of vessel walls — small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis (immune-complex/Type III). Flat, non-palpable purpura instead suggests a platelet or coagulation disorder.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What is the hallmark clinical finding of small-vessel vasculitis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Palpable purpura on dependent areas, especially the lower legs, is the hallmark of small-vessel vasculitis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Which of the following is a common cause of cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Infection is one of the common causes of cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: A child presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: These symptoms are characteristic of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura).

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What histological finding is characteristic of leukocytoclastic vasculitis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: The presence of neutrophil fragments, also known as 'nuclear dust', is characteristic of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Why is urinalysis important in a patient with cutaneous vasculitis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Urinalysis is crucial to assess for renal involvement, which can change the prognosis and management of the patient.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: In a patient with cutaneous vasculitis, which finding would indicate systemic involvement?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Nephritis with hematuria indicates systemic involvement and necessitates further evaluation.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: How does cutaneous vasculitis relate to blood vessel histology?

options.text: It is characterized by inflammation of vessel walls
It is unrelated to blood vessel structure

cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Cutaneous vasculitis involves inflammation of the walls of small blood vessels, which is a key aspect of its pathology.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Which mechanism underlies the pathology of IgA vasculitis?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: IgA vasculitis is primarily an immune-complex (Type III) hypersensitivity reaction.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Regarding assessing systemic involvement in cutaneous vasculitis — which is correct?

options.text: Skin vasculitis (palpable purpura) is just a skin problem that will settle on its own

Cutaneous vasculitis can be the visible sign of SYSTEMIC vasculitis, so palpable purpura mandates evaluation for a TRIGGER and for ORGAN involvement — especially RENAL disease (URINALYSIS for blood/protein) — because renal or other systemic involvement changes prognosis and requires immunosuppression, not just observation

cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Missing renal or systemic involvement behind skin vasculitis risks progressive organ damage; urinalysis and a systemic assessment are essential even when the skin looks isolated.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raised, non-blanching purpuric papules on the lower legs”?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Raised, non-blanching purpuric papules on the lower legs → Small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Purpura + arthralgia + abdominal pain + haematuria in a child”?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Purpura + arthralgia + abdominal pain + haematuria in a child → IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein).

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Vasculitis”?

options.text: Blood Vessel Histology: Wall Layers & Vessel Types

cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Knowledge of blood vessel histology is essential for understanding the pathology of vasculitis.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules with proximal muscle weakness are pathognomonic of:

options.text: Dermatomyositis (with a need to screen for malignancy in adults)

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: The heliotrope (violaceous eyelid) rash and Gottron papules (over the knuckles) with proximal weakness and raised CK are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis; in adults it is associated with underlying malignancy, so cancer screening is required.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: The malar (butterfly) rash of acute cutaneous lupus characteristically:
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: The lupus malar rash is a photosensitive erythema over the cheeks and nose that spares the nasolabial folds — a helpful feature distinguishing it from rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis, which typically involve those folds.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus?

options.text: Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is characterized by a photosensitive malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind the skin manifestations of dermatomyositis?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Dermatomyositis skin manifestations are primarily due to autoantibody-mediated damage.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: A patient presents with a violaceous rash on the eyelids and knuckles, along with proximal muscle weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: The combination of heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and proximal muscle weakness is characteristic of dermatomyositis.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Which of the following findings would most likely prompt cancer screening in an adult patient?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Adult dermatomyositis is associated with an increased risk of malignancy, prompting cancer screening.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What is the risk associated with subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus?

options.text: Neonatal lupus and congenital heart block

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is associated with anti-Ro antibodies and carries a risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: How does the photosensitivity in cutaneous lupus differ from that in dermatomyositis?

options.text: Both conditions have similar photosensitivity mechanisms

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Both cutaneous lupus and dermatomyositis exhibit photosensitivity, but the specific manifestations differ.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Which skin manifestation is most likely to lead to scarring in patients with lupus?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Discoid lupus erythematosus is characterized by scarring, atrophic plaques.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Regarding malar rash location — which is correct?

options.text: The lupus malar rash covers the whole face including the folds beside the nose

The lupus "butterfly" malar rash characteristically SPARES the NASOLABIAL FOLDS (the creases from nose to mouth) — a feature that helps distinguish it from rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis, which typically INVOLVE the nasolabial folds; the sparing reflects the photosensitive, sun-exposed distribution

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Nasolabial-fold sparing is a specific clue separating acute cutaneous lupus from common facial rashes (rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis) that involve those folds, refining the differential.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds → Acute cutaneous lupus (SLE).

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging → Discoid lupus erythematosus.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Lupus & Dermatomyositis”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Understanding photoprotection is crucial for managing cutaneous lupus and dermatomyositis.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Fever, painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign after starting allopurinol indicates:
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Painful skin with mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment (Nikolsky positive) is SJS/TEN — a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (allopurinol is a classic culprit, HLA-B*58:01-linked). Management is immediate drug cessation and burns-unit supportive care, with urgent ophthalmology for eye involvement.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: DRESS syndrome is distinguished from a simple drug rash by:

options.text: Appearing within minutes of the drug
A delayed (2–8 week) onset with fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: DRESS is a delayed (2–8 week) severe reaction with rash, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement (commonly hepatitis), classically to anticonvulsants, allopurinol or sulfonamides — requiring prompt drug withdrawal and organ monitoring.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What is the primary mechanism underlying Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: SJS is primarily a delayed T-cell-mediated drug reaction leading to keratinocyte apoptosis.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which drug is most commonly associated with DRESS syndrome?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Allopurinol is a well-known culprit of DRESS syndrome, characterized by eosinophilia and systemic symptoms.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: A patient presents with a painful rash, mucosal erosions, and epidermal detachment after starting carbamazepine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: The symptoms are characteristic of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially with the history of carbamazepine use.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which finding is a red flag indicating a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR)?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Skin pain and blistering are red flags that suggest a potential SCAR, necessitating immediate drug cessation.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What is the appropriate management step for a patient suspected of having SJS/TEN?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Immediate cessation of the offending drug is crucial in managing SJS/TEN to prevent further complications.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: A patient develops a widespread rash with fever and facial edema 3 weeks after starting an anticonvulsant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: The timing and symptoms are consistent with DRESS syndrome, which includes fever and facial edema.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: How does the mechanism of AGEP differ from that of SJS/TEN?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: AGEP is characterized by the rapid onset of numerous sterile pustules, differentiating it from SJS/TEN.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: How can knowledge of HLA testing from drug hypersensitivity modules aid in managing SCARs?

options.text: It helps in diagnosing all drug allergies
It can predict risk for specific drug reactions
It eliminates the need for drug cessation
It provides a cure for SCARs

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: HLA testing can identify individuals at risk for specific drug reactions, guiding safer prescribing practices.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: In what way does understanding SCARs enhance the management of cutaneous drug reactions?

options.text: It allows for the continuation of all drug therapies
It identifies benign rashes that require no intervention
It emphasizes the importance of recognizing red flags for urgent action
It reduces the need for patient education on drug side effects

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Recognizing red flags for SCARs is critical for timely intervention and preventing severe outcomes.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Regarding benign drug rash vs early scar — which is correct?

options.text: A drug rash can be watched while the drug is continued, since most are harmless

Although most drug rashes are benign morbilliform eruptions, you MUST screen for RED FLAGS of a SCAR — mucosal erosions, skin PAIN/blistering/detachment (Nikolsky+), facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or deranged LFTs — because SJS/TEN and DRESS are life-threatening and require IMMEDIATE drug cessation; continuing the drug in an evolving SCAR can be fatal
SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Early SJS/TEN or DRESS can resemble an ordinary rash, so the presence of any red flag (not the rash alone) determines urgency; continuing the culprit in a developing SCAR risks death.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment → SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mucocutaneous blistering weeks after allopurinol/carbamazepine”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Mucocutaneous blistering weeks after allopurinol/carbamazepine → SJS/TEN (HLA-linked culprits).

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (SCARs)”?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Foundational knowledge for recognizing drug allergies.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A well 3-day-old newborn has blotchy erythema with scattered pustules on a red base; a smear shows eosinophils. The most likely diagnosis is:
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a common benign self-limiting rash of the first days of life in a well baby — blotchy erythema with pustules containing eosinophils — needing only reassurance. Vesicles/erosions in an unwell neonate would instead raise concern for HSV.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A nappy rash that involves the skin folds and shows satellite pustules is most likely due to:
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Irritant nappy dermatitis typically spares the folds, whereas candidal nappy rash involves the folds with satellite pustules and requires a topical antifungal. Recognising the pattern directs correct treatment.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What is the characteristic finding in erythema toxicum neonatorum?

options.text: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Greasy yellow scales on the scalp

neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Erythema toxicum neonatorum presents as blotchy erythema with pustules in a well newborn during the first days of life.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Which skin condition in infants is associated with greasy yellow scales on the scalp?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Cradle cap, or seborrhoeic dermatitis, is characterized by greasy yellow scales on the scalp and sometimes the face or flexures.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A neonate presents with a nappy rash that spares the skin folds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Irritant nappy dermatitis typically spares the skin folds and is caused by urine and feces occlusion.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What distinguishes candidal nappy dermatitis from irritant nappy dermatitis?

options.text: Involvement of skin folds with satellite pustules

neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Candidal nappy dermatitis involves the skin folds and presents with satellite pustules, unlike irritant dermatitis which spares the folds.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A newborn presents with grouped vesicles and erosions on the skin. What is the most critical next step?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Grouped vesicles and erosions in a neonate suggest herpes simplex virus infection, which is an emergency requiring investigation.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: How does atopic dermatitis typically present in infants?

options.text: On the face and extensor surfaces

neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Atopic dermatitis in infants commonly affects the face and extensor surfaces before becoming flexural later in childhood.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: In a case of congenital cataracts due to galactokinase deficiency, which skin condition might be observed in the infant?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Milia, which are tiny keratin cysts, can be observed in infants with various conditions, including metabolic disorders like galactokinase deficiency.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Which skin condition might be confused with irritant nappy dermatitis but requires a different treatment approach due to its distinct presentation?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Candida nappy dermatitis involves the folds with satellite pustules and requires topical antifungal treatment, unlike irritant dermatitis.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Regarding irritant vs candidal nappy rash — which is correct?

options.text: All nappy rashes are the same and treated with barrier cream alone

The pattern distinguishes them: IRRITANT nappy dermatitis SPARES the skin FOLDS (the convex surfaces in contact with the nappy are affected) and responds to barrier care, whereas CANDIDAL nappy rash INVOLVES the FOLDS with SATELLITE pustules and needs a TOPICAL ANTIFUNGAL — treating candida as simple irritant dermatitis fails

neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Fold involvement with satellites signals candida, which requires antifungal therapy; the sparing-vs-involvement pattern directs correct treatment.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blotchy erythema with pustules in a well newborn, first days”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Blotchy erythema with pustules in a well newborn, first days → Erythema toxicum neonatorum (benign).

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nappy rash sparing the skin folds”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Nappy rash sparing the skin folds → Irritant nappy dermatitis.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Which should you review before “Neonatal & Infantile Skin Conditions”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Understanding metabolic conditions can aid in recognizing skin manifestations.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Six or more large café-au-lait macules, especially with axillary freckling, suggest which genodermatosis?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Multiple (≥6) large café-au-lait macules with axillary/inguinal freckling are diagnostic features of neurofibromatosis type 1 (also neurofibromas, Lisch nodules). Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches and angiofibromas.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: A persistent flat vascular birthmark present at birth in the ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution should prompt evaluation for:
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A port-wine stain (capillary malformation) in the V1 distribution can be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome (leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma), so it warrants neuroimaging and ophthalmological evaluation. Unlike haemangiomas, port-wine stains persist.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What is the typical clinical course of an infantile haemangioma?

options.text: It is present at birth and persists indefinitely.
It appears after birth, proliferates, and then involutes.
It appears at birth and gradually fades without treatment.
It is always symptomatic and requires immediate intervention.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Infantile haemangiomas typically appear after birth, proliferate for several months, and then involute over the years.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Which of the following birthmarks is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A port-wine stain, particularly in the V1 distribution, is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: A 5-year-old presents with six café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. What condition should be suspected?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: The presence of six or more café-au-lait macules along with axillary freckling is indicative of Neurofibromatosis type 1.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What is the primary treatment for a problematic infantile haemangioma?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Propranolol is the primary treatment for problematic infantile haemangiomas that threaten vision, airway, or feeding.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Which of the following statements about vascular birthmarks is true?

options.text: All vascular birthmarks require immediate treatment.
Infantile haemangiomas and port-wine stains behave similarly.
Infantile haemangiomas involute, while port-wine stains persist.
Port-wine stains can be treated with propranolol.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Infantile haemangiomas are vascular tumors that involute, while port-wine stains are malformations that persist.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: A patient presents with blistering of the skin from minor trauma since birth. What condition is most likely?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Epidermolysis bullosa is characterized by blistering of the skin from minor trauma, often present from birth.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: How does the management of a port-wine stain differ from that of an infantile haemangioma?

options.text: Port-wine stains are treated with propranolol, while haemangiomas are not.
Port-wine stains persist and may require laser treatment, while haemangiomas involute.
Both conditions are managed with observation only.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Port-wine stains persist and may require laser treatment, whereas infantile haemangiomas typically involute and are treated only if problematic.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Which of the following findings is associated with tuberous sclerosis?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Ash-leaf macules are a characteristic finding in tuberous sclerosis.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: How does Neurofibromatosis type 1 relate to congenital anomalies?

options.text: It is classified as a vascular malformation.
It is a genetic disorder with skin manifestations that indicate systemic evaluation.
It is primarily a benign skin condition.
It does not require any further investigation.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a genetic disorder with skin manifestations that warrant systemic evaluation for associated anomalies.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What is a key difference between the management of infantile haemangiomas and congenital melanocytic naevi?

options.text: Infantile haemangiomas may require propranolol, while congenital naevi are typically observed.
Congenital naevi always require laser treatment.
Both conditions are treated with topical steroids.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Infantile haemangiomas may require propranolol if problematic, while congenital melanocytic naevi are typically observed unless they pose a risk for melanoma.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Regarding haemangioma vs port-wine stain behaviour — which is correct?

options.text: All vascular birthmarks are permanent and require the same treatment

They behave oppositely: an INFANTILE HAEMANGIOMA (vascular TUMOUR) appears AFTER birth, proliferates then spontaneously INVOLUTES (treat only if function-threatening/ulcerating — propranolol), whereas a PORT-WINE STAIN (capillary MALFORMATION) is present at birth, PERSISTS and grows with the child (laser), and if in the V1 distribution warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Tumour (involutes) vs malformation (persists) determines whether to observe/treat and whether to screen for an associated syndrome — distinguishing them avoids both over- and under-treatment.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What best explains the finding: “A red vascular lesion appearing after birth that later involutes”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A red vascular lesion appearing after birth that later involutes → Infantile haemangioma (propranolol if problematic).

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What best explains the finding: “A persistent flat port-wine stain in the V1 trigeminal area”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A persistent flat port-wine stain in the V1 trigeminal area → Consider Sturge-Weber syndrome.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Which should you review before “Birthmarks & Genodermatoses”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Understanding congenital anomalies is essential for recognizing birthmarks and their implications.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: The single most important initial distinction when assessing hair loss is whether it is:
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Scarring alopecia destroys follicles permanently (loss of follicular openings) and needs prompt biopsy/treatment to save remaining hair, whereas non-scarring alopecia is potentially reversible. This distinction drives urgency and management, before considering pattern.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Diffuse hair shedding beginning about 2–3 months after childbirth, with a positive hair-pull test and full recovery expected, is:
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Telogen effluvium is a reversible, diffuse shedding occurring 2–3 months after a stressor (e.g. childbirth, illness, weight loss), as hairs pushed into telogen are shed. The hair-pull test is positive, and regrowth follows once the trigger resolves.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What is the primary distinguishing feature of scarring alopecia?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Scarring alopecia is characterized by smooth scarred patches with loss of follicular openings, indicating permanent hair loss.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Which condition is characterized by round bald patches with exclamation-mark hairs?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition that presents with smooth, round bald patches and exclamation-mark hairs.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What is the mechanism behind telogen effluvium?

options.text: Permanent hair loss due to scarring

alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Telogen effluvium is characterized by delayed diffuse shedding that occurs 2-3 months after a triggering stressor.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair shedding 3 months after childbirth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: The timing of hair shedding following childbirth is consistent with telogen effluvium, which is reversible.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: In a patient with suspected tinea capitis, which examination finding would be most indicative?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Tinea capitis typically presents as a scaly patch with broken hairs, especially in children.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Which of the following statements about telogen effluvium is true?

options.text: It typically occurs 2-3 months after a stressor.

alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Telogen effluvium is characterized by a 2-3 month delay in hair shedding following a stressor, making it reversible.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: How does discoid lupus erythematosus relate to scarring alopecia?

options.text: It is a type of non-scarring alopecia.
It leads to permanent hair loss and requires biopsy.
It is characterized by exclamation-mark hairs.

alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Discoid lupus is a form of scarring alopecia that leads to permanent hair loss and necessitates early biopsy and treatment.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Which hair loss condition is most likely to present with a positive hair-pull test?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: A positive hair-pull test is indicative of telogen effluvium, where hair shedding is active.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Regarding telogen effluvium timing — which is correct?

options.text: Diffuse hair shedding must be from something happening right now

TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM is a DELAYED diffuse shedding that typically occurs 2–3 MONTHS AFTER a triggering stressor (severe illness, childbirth, surgery, rapid weight loss, certain drugs) — because the trigger pushed hairs into telogen (rest) which then shed months later — so the cause must be sought in the RECENT PAST, not only the present; it is reversible

alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: The 2–3 month lag means the causative stressor is historical; looking only at current events misses the trigger, and understanding the delay reassures patients that regrowth follows.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Smooth scarred patch with loss of follicular openings”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Smooth scarred patch with loss of follicular openings → Cicatricial (scarring) alopecia — permanent, biopsy.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diffuse shedding 2–3 months after childbirth/illness, positive hair-pull”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Diffuse shedding 2–3 months after childbirth/illness, positive hair-pull → Telogen effluvium (reversible).

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Which should you review before “Clinical Approach to Alopecia”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Understanding scarring alopecia requires knowledge of discoid lupus.

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: Symmetric brown patches on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, worsened by sun exposure, are characteristic of:
